en: *Continued Lamp: Surviving Drafts*, Scroll One.
Compiled by the Chan Master Dongwu Tongwen, a successor to the Patriarchs;
collated by the Layman of Lizhe, Shih Pei of Huating. Ming Dynasty.
Dharma Heir of Chan Master Tiantong Hua of the Eighteenth Generation under Dajian of the Linji School.
Chan Master Mitan Xianjie of Tiantong in Qingyuan Prefecture was the son of the Zheng family of Fuzhou. His mother dreamed that an old monk from Mount Lu entered her quarters before he was born.
From childhood, he was exceptionally intelligent and keen-witted; having left home to become a monk, he did not shrink from traveling extensively to visit various masters of the Dharma.
Later, he went to Mingguo in Quzhou to call upon Ying’an. Because the Master was solitary and rigid, it was difficult for him to gain entry, and he repeatedly encountered scoldings. One—
One day, as he entered the room, Guo'an asked, "What is the True Dharma Eye? The Master immediately replied, "A broken sand pot. Guo'an nodded his head in approval.

After several months, Guo'an took his leave to return home to visit his parents. As Guo'an departed, the Master sent him off with this verse: "The words that trigger great penetration Open wide the crown of the head in the presence of reality.

We have followed one another for four years now; Your interrogations have left no trace within me. Though I have not yet entrusted you with the bowl and robe, The spirit of your bearing already swallows all."
"Qian and Kun! Yet you take the True Dharma Eye and call it a broken sand-pot. On this journey to pay your respects, you must by all means avoid evasive maneuvers.
I have a final word; when you return, I require that you follow it. Later, he appeared in the world at Wugu in Quzhou, then moved to Jingshan Huazang in Xiangfu.
Before long, he was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Jing Mountain. He subsequently moved to Lingyin, where he spent his final years at Tai Mountain.
[The monk] said, "Venerable Sir, what is it like when empty space is extinguished? The Master said, "The punishment shall not be doubled for a crime.
He ascended the hall and said, "Niutou [Falan] spoke horizontally and vertically, yet he did not know there was a 'gate-bolt' above.

There are some types of lacquer buckets who cannot distinguish east from west or south from north. They immediately ask, 'What is the gate-bolt above? How is this different from urinating with one's eyes open?"
The Bed. Huizang had a turning word that lies neither in the upward nor the downward direction; even the Great Compassionate One with a thousand hands cannot find it by groping about.

When the rain is cold, there is nowhere to spread out [the bedding]. Today, we shall all labor together to offer this to the great assembly. After a long silence, he said: "Master Bodhidharma had no front teeth.
He ascended the hall and said: "The World-Honored One spoke what was not spoken; he twisted the crooked to make it straight. Kāśyapa..."
Hearing and hearing again, I look toward the void and offer this address: Mazu’s “Mind is Buddha” is like hanging up a sheep’s head while selling dog meat;

Zhaozhou’s interrogation of the hermitage master is like buying high and selling low—it is not worth a single coin. As for Mañjuśrī, the teacher of the seven Buddhas, why was he unable to emerge from the woman’s samādhi?
The river sky and lunar halo, the fish divide their portions; when the wind stirs through the oak leaves, the deer...
Nurturing the Sprouts. Ascending the hall, he strikes the meditation staff. "When deluded, one is deluded only by this very thing.

He strikes once more. "When awakened, one awakens only to this very thing. Even if you were to forget both delusion and awakening, it would still be like adding a further layer of rags upon a heap of refuse.

Is there anyone who can utter a single phrase from the state where the total function is uniquely liberated—where the east surges up and the west sinks down? If you cannot speak such a word, [the flower]...
He departed for his own country. Throwing down his staff, thirty years later he ascended the hall and, citing the Elder Master Jinfeng’s address to the assembly, said:
"Thirty years ago, this old monk had the heart of a grandmother; thirty years later, I have no grandmotherly heart."

At that time, a monk asked, "What is the 'motherly heart' [of compassion] from twenty years ago? Feng said, "If you ask about the ordinary, I answer as the ordinary; if you ask about the sagely, I answer as the sagely.
The monk asked, "What is the absence of the 'motherly heart' after twenty years? Feng said, "If you ask about the ordinary, I do not answer as the ordinary;
if you ask about the sagely, I do not answer as the sagely. The Master said, "Had Wugu seen this at the time, he would have simply given a cold laugh."
"Two sounds. If this old fellow were suddenly to have a flash of realization, he would naturally not fall into the conceptual traps of ordinary or sagehood.
Upon ascending the hall, the Master raised the koan of the old woman burning the hermitage and said: "Few in the monastic community have ever brought up or examined this case.
Today, I, Zen Master Jie, shall strip my face bare; I cannot avoid suffering a defeat, for I wish to have it scrutinized by those everywhere."
He then summoned the great assembly. The old woman’s inner chamber was deep, secure, and as impenetrable as a sealed door;
yet she cast flowers upon withered wood and kindled flames from cold ashes. This monk stood alone and towering, accustomed to plunging into surging tides;
he casually cut off the heaven-showering waves, leaving not a single drop upon his person in the end. If one examines this closely, it is like striking a cangue or breaking a chain.
If it were locked, it would not be non-existent. If these two people were like that, they would not have even dreamed of the Buddha-dharma.
Where does Wugujie’s such holding up of the matter ultimately lead? After a long silence: "A handful of willow threads cannot be gathered; they are draped with mist upon the jade balustrade.

Ascending the hall, he said: "When the string is moved, the melody is distinct; when the leaves fall, one knows autumn. To raise one and clarify three is to weigh every detail with the precision of a scale."
It is like a king wielding a sword; whether he kills or gives life depends on the moment. This is still but the windless, surging waves.
On the single path beyond, the thousand sages hold hands and walk together, yet they must enter the hells of the *niraya*. At such a time as this, what should one do?
"In Jiangnan and Liangzhe, spring is cold and autumn is hot. [He] ascended the hall and said: "The entire universe and great earth—call it a single phrase."
Child, bearing a cangue and wearing shackles, do not call this "one phrase. When the karmic consciousness is vast and boundless, one must penetrate through both ends;
then one is pure and naked, bare and clear, with nothing to grasp. Thus, the school of Bodhidharma would be swept away like dust. Therefore, the Great Master Yunmen said:
"The entire universe and great earth being without even a hair’s breadth of fault—this is still a turning phrase. Do you not see?
To present a single dharma is merely to offer half of the teaching; one must further know the occasion for the full presentation.
Great Master Yunmen’s sword has long since departed, yet you are now marking the boat where it sank. Later, he passed away and was interred in a stupa on the central peak of the monastery.
Chan Master Baizhu Shan Deng of Kuangxiao Monastery in Quzhou was the son of the Min family from Wujiang in Huazhou. A monk asked:
"When the World-Honored One was born, he pointed with one hand toward heaven and with the other toward earth, saying, 'Above heaven and below heaven, I alone am honored.'"
"What is the meaning? The Master said, "One person transmits what is false; ten thousand people transmit what is real. The monk said, "When there is spirit, one adds to that spirit;
where there is no elegance, there is elegance nonetheless. The Master said, "Praise indeed! Praise is insufficient.
The monk said, "It is just as the Great Master Yunmen said: 'If I had seen him at that time, I would have struck him with a single blow and given him to a dog.'"
"Eat! If you wish for peace throughout the world, after all, what kind of eyes do you possess? The Master said, "Realize it behind your head.
Ascending the hall, he said: "By day there is bustling clamor; by night there is profound stillness. One walks with a rolling gait along the long corridors, step by step lacking nothing.
Yet failing to recognize the master of the house, one enters the wild weeds in full body. There, one bumps into Fu Dashi, who asks after his well-being."
Mālāṭa lies ill in the city of Vaiśālī; how many know when the dawn breaks? If one is a person of extraordinary capacity, they do not seek it elsewhere.
Why is this so? He lets out a shout. When going downhill, one does not run; such a swift opportunity is difficult to encounter.
Nanshujishi was a native of Fuzhou. Having long relied upon Ying’an, he attained a sudden and profound realization through the koan of Zhaozhou’s “The dog has no Buddha-nature.
He composed a verse which says: “The dog has no Buddha-nature; Rāhu enters its destiny.
It is not that it kills people; Rather, it is surely killed by others. Ying’an praised him for his unencumbered liberation. At the end of the Shaoxing era, he passed away at Guizong.
The Layman Li Hao, Minister of the Court of Ceremonials, styled De-yuan and known by the sobriquet Zheng-xin (Right Faith), read the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* in his youth;
it was as if he were visiting an old homeland, which he remembered with such clarity that he never forgot it. Later, he went to Mingguo Temple to seek instruction from the master.

When entering the room, Ying’an struck him in the chest and asked, "After you die, Minister, where will you go? The layman was startled, and sweat poured down his body. Ying’an shouted at him to leave. The layman withdrew and continued his private study. He did not...
Within ten days, he had directly ascended to the innermost sanctum. He sent a verse to his fellow practitioner Yan Kangchao, saying:
"The gate has a shop of Sun Bin; the home harbors the wife of Gan Zhi. Sleeping at night and rising early— Who awakens, and who is deluded?
There was also a seller of rouge who had long studied under Ying’an and was quite conceited. A gentleman presented him with this verse: "Without applying red powder, she is naturally elegant."
Often Zen practitioners stop short upon reaching this point; only after passing through the enclosures of past and present do they come here to receive a blow from my fist.
The Professor Yan Kangchao was a layman from Changxing in Huzhou.

He once sought the Way from Xuetang at Jianfu Monastery and later attained the essential instruction upon meeting Ying’an at Ba’en Monastery. He once composed a verse which says: “Zhaozhou’s dog has no Buddha-nature.”
I say that the dog has Buddha-nature; suddenly, upon these words, one knows for oneself where one belongs.

From now on, do not trust Zhaozhou’s mouth. Exert your spirit and shake yourself free. To follow behind others—there is no skill there. Riding a cow while searching for the cow is enough to make people laugh to death.
Only now do I realize my former errors.
Chan Master Zhong’an Huikong of Fashi Monastery in Quanzhou, a successor in the lineage of Chan Master Jiaozhongguang, was a native of the Cai clan from Ganzhou.

On the first day of spring, he ascended the hall, took up his staff, and struck once, saying, "First, I strike the head of the Spring Ox. He struck again, saying, "Afterward, I strike the tail of the Spring Ox. Startled!
Rising from the void to enter within a lotus fiber, Śākyamuni has no way to hide his tracks; Maitreya hurries off for a thousand li, yet Mañjuśrī knows exactly where he lands.
Clapping his hands, he laughs with joy. But tell me, what is it that causes this joy?

Last night, the spring breeze entered the gate, and immediately a thousand flowers were seen blooming upon the pestle. [He ascends the hall: "A thousand households of pavilions, in a single instant..."

Autumn wind: one only perceives the coolness arising in one’s robes and sleeves; one does not realize that the leaves are falling from the gardens. If you can realize this at such a moment, then truth is complete in every encounter.
If it is not yet so, then let us meet with formal greetings of cold and warmth. [Ascending the hall, he raised the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: "The Buddha said to Subhūti:
'In all those lands, whatever various kinds of thoughts there are among sentient beings, the Tathāgata knows them all.'"
Why is this? The Tathāgata has said that all minds are non-minds; it is precisely for this reason they are called "mind.
Do you understand? "The spring breeze fills one with joy; the horse's hooves race swiftly. In a single day, one beholds the flowers of the entire Chang'an.

A monk asked, "The Buddhas of the past established the model of the *kaṭhina* ceremony and the summer retreat (*an-gu*). What is the fundamental principle behind these? The Master said, "Mount Sumeru is cast into a lapis lazuli bowl. The monk then...
"Ho! The Master then struck him.
Chan Master Tanmi Huyen of Jingci Monastery in Lin’an was the son of the Lu family of Tiantai. He left home to become a monk under Daorong of Zifu Monastery.
At sixteen, he received full ordination and studied the Tiantai teachings. Later, he abandoned them to go and attend upon Dahui at Mount Jing, and subsequently visited [other masters].

Xuechao Yici An entered Min, where he stayed at both Dong and Xi Chan monasteries, yet found no resonance with either. He then visited Jiaozhong in Southern Quan, where he was made to serve as the *yuezong* (manager of the assembly).
Upon resigning from that post, he returned to his former quarters. One day, Jiaozhong raised the kōan concerning Xiangyan striking the bamboo;

Yici attained sudden enlightenment and presented a verse to Jiaozhong. When Jiaozhong questioned him on the story of Xuansha’s "not yet reaching the ultimate," Yici responded without hesitation. Thereupon, Jiaozhong...
The Master entrusted him, saying, "My son, you may now go see Miaoxi. Obeying this command, the teacher went to Mei Yang and served there diligently for four years.
After taking up residence, he ascended the hall and said: "When the Buddhas appear in the world, they commit robbery and murder; when the Patriarchs come from the West, they blow wind and set fires."
The spiritual friends of the past and present have the mouth of a Buddha but the heart of a snake; the monks of the world throw themselves into their cages and traps of their own accord.
Is there no man of natural integrity and exceptional character who will extend a hand for the sake of the lineage and uphold the Buddha-dharma?
After a long silence, he said: "Even if there were such a thing, it must be cut into three pieces. He ascended the hall and said: "Deshan’s informal sermon was 'no answering questions.
For a thousand ages, the monastic communities have made this a subject of idle gossip. Those who ask questions receive thirty blows; they are accustomed to talking nonsense and making a fuss.
At that time, a monk stepped forward, intending to break through [Deshan's barrier], and Deshan struck him immediately. Elegant and refined, Deshan had not even heard the monk's words.
Question: "With a cangue upon your head and shackles upon your feet, where are you from? A single meeting wounds the spirit; the man from Silla smiles with hands clasped.

Before even stepping onto the ship's railing, he deserves thirty blows. He continues to deceive as before. Today, Huyen makes such a critical judgment and reprimands him out of compassion; he too deserves thirty blows. Now tell me: *Note:
This passage is a dialogue from the *Wumenguan* (The Gateless Barrier), Case 24, concerning the encounter between Master Huairang and Mazu Daoyi. The text provided here is a commentary on that case.*
"This is reward; this is punishment. Let those who possess the eye of study examine and discern this.

Entering the hall, [the Master] raised the precedent of Yunmen’s question to a monk regarding the karmic cause and condition of "Luminous stillness and illumination pervade the sands of the Ganges. The Master said: "Fishing for shrimp on level ground; shooting a soaring osprey across the vast heavens."
The lame old Yunmen committed a thousand errors and ten thousand mistakes. Later, upon his passing, he was interred at his home mountain.
Chan Master Weiyin of Xingan in Qizhou, whose courtesy name was Wuyin, was the son of the Li family of Changle.
At the age of eleven, he left Min to become a novice under Master Guang of Ganjiang, with whom he studied for five years before finally receiving the full precepts.
Fú served [Yunmen] for one day. Guǎng bestowed upon him the "Verses on the Fifty-three Spiritual Friends" from the *Buddhagotravibhāga* and assigned him to the various *vina* (chant-leaders).

The Master attended by his side and heard the lines: "Sometimes one must see the Buddhas of the ten directions; at times of no-activity, idly observe the single mind. Thereupon, he grasped the essential point.
Guǎng marveled at the sharpness of his faculties and sent him back to Fújiān to pay his respects to Fóxīn of Gǔshān.
When he reached the time of the elder masters Dongchan Yue’an Guo and Xichan Lan’an Xu, Huian was residing at Guishan;
the Master went there to seek instruction. One night at midnight, while searching for his hand towel, he suddenly attained great enlightenment.

At dawn, he hurried to the abbot’s quarters to communicate what he had realized, presenting this verse: "Karmic consciousness is vast and boundless, having no basis whatsoever. Last night at the third watch..."
Looking back with a single glance, a segment of numinous light is primordially and uniquely revealed. Master An unconsciously smiled and nodded in agreement.
Later, he traveled over the ridge to meet Yan Wan’an at Jianfu Monastery in Fanyang. During his entry into the inner quarters, his responses were swift and agile.
Yan raised his voice sternly, saying, "This man from Fuzhou has been corrupted by others. The entire assembly was struck with astonishment. Not long after, he departed once more.
Meiyang met Dahui. Dahui asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master replied, "Meeting face-to-face; there is no other dharma. Dahui asked, "How does one maintain this?
The Master replied, "When hungry, eat; when tired, sleep. Subsequently, he followed Dahui back to the north.
One day Dahui asked, "Many people enter the room [for private instruction]; how many can truly express it? How many..."
[Zhaozhou] said, "The human path is not attached. Yunmen said, "Yi-dhen, you must simply watch. Suddenly, Hui [Zhaozhou] extended his hand and asked, "How does my hand compare to the Buddha’s hand?
Yunmen said, "The weather is cold; please, Master, let me put on my sleeves. Hui immediately struck him with a bamboo staff and asked, "Tell me, was that a reward for you or a punishment?
Yunmen then presented ten or so verses to elucidate the karmic encounters between the Buddhas and patriarchs.
Hui remarked: "The World-Honored One’s first words upon birth were: 'To emerge with one's head already is an early mistake; how much more so to open one's mouth and claim supremacy?
Had he been able to keep his tongue deeply hidden at that time, he would have spared his descendants the burden of idle sorrows. Hui struck the rhythm of this verse with great appreciation.
Later, he propagated the Dharma at Tiantai Zhenru, Baen, Shanglan in Yuzhang, and Qingyuan in Jizhou. Wherever he went, the landscape was transformed.
A monk asked, "Regarding Sanxing’s saying, 'When I meet a person, I come forth; when I come forth, I do not act for others'—what is the meaning of this?
The Master said, "The flower is moved, and the butterfly arrives with it. [The monk] asked, "Xinghua said, 'When I meet a person, I do not come forth.'"
"If one emerges [from the state of non-action], one immediately becomes a person. Furthermore, how is this so? The Master said, "One buys a stone and finds it surpasses the clouds.
Ascending the hall, he raised the case: A monk asked Yunmen, "What is it like when the trees are stripped of their leaves? Yunmen said, "The golden wind reveals its body.

The Master said, "Yunmen strikes the collar from his sleeve and digs into the lapel from beneath his armpit; he is indeed a skilled hand. Yet, if you examine it closely, he cannot avoid being pulled by the threads."
[He held up] a cord. Someone asked, "When the leaves fall from the tree of repaying kindness, what then? He simply said to him, "Next year there will be new branches again;
the spring wind’s vexation shall never cease. Ascending the hall, he took up his staff and said:
"Within the lands of the ten directions, there is only the One Vehicle Dharma. This here is the staff of Hengquan; which one is the One Vehicle Dharma?"
*Zhuo!*—With one strike, the momentum of a thousand peaks collapses at the edge of the mountain range; the sound of ten thousand streams returns to vanish upon the sea.
On the nineteenth day of the fifth month in the third year of the Shaohui era (Renzi), he manifested illness. He wrote a verse, saying: "The final phrase is entrusted face-to-face;
to deliberate or reflect upon it is merely the circulation of worldly conventions. Thereupon, he sat in the full lotus posture and passed away. Recorded by Luo Hu Ying Zhongwen.
Regarding his conduct:
Chan Master Duan’an Zu Zhu of Gong’an, Jingzhou, a successor in the lineage of Chan Master Yan of Donglin, was a native of Nanping. He ascended the hall and said: "It is not mind, it is not..."
This Buddha is not a thing. He has drained the wild fox’s saliva to the dregs and kicked over the mountain demon’s den.
Within the level fields and shallow grasses, he reveals the tawny-tailed tiger; amidst the vast emptiness of space, he releases the magnificent falcon soaring through the high heavens. A-he-he!
Revealing the wind-bone. Carelessly brought forth before the assembly—what exactly is it? *Du! Du!* [He] ascended the hall: "Jade dew hangs from the green grass;
golden wind stirs the white water-lilies. A single cry from a cold wild goose awakens those who have not yet awakened."
Chan Master Fayuan of Ba’en in Tingzhou was a native of Guozhou. One day he ascended the hall and, citing the karmic occasion of Juzhi pointing his finger, said:
"The beautiful lady has risen from sleep and is too lazy to comb her hair; she takes up her golden hairpin and, having inserted it, leaves it at that.
For the most part, it is her natural bone and flesh that are so fine—she is elegant even without the application of rouge and powder."
Chan Master Kengtang Yanchong of Jingci Monastery in Lin’an was the son of the Sheng family of Yuqian.
In his youth, he relied upon Master Yikan of Mingkong Monastery as his teacher. He first studied under various masters, including Dayu Hongzhi, Zhengtang, and Daryuan.
Later, he heard Donglin say to the assembly: "In this place of mine, there is nothing else mysterious or subtle; there is only wood-shavings soup and iron-nail rice, served at will."
"You chew on it," [Linji] said. The Master was secretly pleased by this. He went to pay his respects and set forth what he had perceived.

Linji said, "According to your way of seeing, you are sitting right within the mirror-like awareness. At this, the Master became indignant and cast away everything he had previously attained all at once.
One day, hearing a monk cite Nanquan’s saying, "People of this time see this single flower as being like a dream," he silently gained something.
Qicheng said, "Striking the grass is only intended to startle the snake. The next day, when entering the room, Linji asked, "Where was it that Yantou secretly conveyed his meaning?
The Master said, "Today I have caught that old thief. Linji said, "The life of the Great Master Bodhidharma rests in your hands.
As the Master was about to open his mouth, he was suddenly struck across the chest with a fist and attained great enlightenment.
He was so moved that sweat poured down his back. Nodding his head, he said to himself, "Was Linji’s remark that Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma was not much more than this mere empty talk?
He then composed a verse, saying: "To act for others, one must act thoroughly; To kill a man, one must see the blood. Deshan and Yantou— Ten thousand miles, a single line of iron.
After Linran had taken up residence, he ascended the hall and said: "The World-Honored One did not speak..."
[The Master] spoke. "Kāśyapa hears what he has not heard. He struck the meditation platform with his staff and said: "Where do the flowing waters and yellow leaves come from?
An ox, trailing cold crows, passes through a distant village. He ascended the hall and raised the case of Xuefeng, who had addressed the assembly, saying:
"The entire earth is this gate of liberation; one cannot enter it even if someone pulls you by the hand. The Master said: "Great Xuefeng split the talk into two pieces. The entire earth is this..."
“Why use the gates of liberation? To drag [them] along for what purpose? He ascended the hall and said: “If you go on in this way all the time, the grass before the Dharma Hall will be ten feet deep.
If you come back in this way all the time, the mud beneath your heels will be three feet deep.

Tell me, how is it then? Every three years there is an intercalary month; the rooster cries at the fifth watch. He ascended the hall and raised the example of his late master, Wan’an, who said: “Sitting upon the Buddha’s seat, he hews...”
The Buddha’s feet—yet he did not pay respect to Confucius of the Eastern House, but instead went abroad to study ritual and music.

The Master said: "To enter the water and enter the mud is indeed not impossible; but what could our former teacher do? The cicada clings to the withered tree; its weeping is exhausted, yet it does not turn back.
He struck his staff and said: "Truly, there is one who does not turn back. I, Jingci, prostrate three times before you within this incense burner. *Upasampadā* (ordination).
The Hall. The Buddhas of the three periods speak of existence within non-existence—like picking up flowers and needles from a tangled thicket.
The six generations of patriarchs seek non-existence within existence—like a monkey reaching for the moon reflected in water. Setting aside these two paths, how can one discuss and realize the truth?
I care not for matters of rise and fall; all day long I dwell amidst the clouds upon Lake Dongting. Yuan’an, having accepted the invitation of Zhìzhě, led the assembly at Nánshān. There it was:
This old Demon King has a pair of piercing eyes that flash like lightning. His mouth is like a blood-basin as he scolds the Buddhas and Patriarchs;

his teeth are like sword-trees as he reviles all quarters. Though the winds of karma have blown upon him many times, they could not move him; only when the wind blows at the side of Mount Yunhuang can he be moved.
Together with Sengtou Tuo and Fu Dashi, this band of ruffians remains the same as the old fellow Meng Bala, deceiving countless others.
"Stupid man and woman! With eyes wide open, you enter the boiling cauldron with such solemnity.
Suddenly, a monk comes forth and says, "Since you are a good spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), why do you lead people into the boiling cauldron? To him, he simply replies, "This is not your realm.
Later, when he passed away, his stupa was erected at the southern hermitage of the monastery.
Chan Master Zhizhe Yu’nan Zhenci of Wuzhou was a native of Tongchuan. His secular surname was Li. In his youth, he relied upon Chengdu Zhengfa Monastery to leave the household life.
After receiving full ordination, he traveled among lecture halls, where he listened to a discourse on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (specifically the *Awakening of Faith*).

Upon reaching the passage: "The four elements are each separate; where, then, does this illusory body now abide? Ultimately it has no substance and is truly identical to a phantom," he attained a profound realization. He then composed [the following]:
The verse says: "A single bright pearl is within me; touch it or move it, and it emits light that shakes the earth.
He presented this to various lecturers, but none were able to understand it. Returning home, he presented it to his own teacher, who then tested him with the koan of the dog having no Buddha-nature.
The teacher said, "Though there be hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, millions, or billions of koans, they do not go beyond this verse. His teacher then—

He was rebuked and driven out. The Master then traveled south to Mount Lu, where he took up residence at Yuan Tong. At that time, Wan’an was serving as the West Hall Preceptor. When he entered the room for the assembly, he raised the following koan: "A monk asked Yunmen, 'When one brushes away the dust to see the Buddha, what then? Yunmen said, 'The Buddha is also dust. As soon as Wan’an uttered these words, the Master let out a shout and pointed to his chest, saying, "The Buddha is also dust. He then offered this verse: Brushing away the dust— The Buddha is also dust. The Buddha is also dust. The Buddha is also dust. The Buddha is also dust. The Buddha is also dust. Kaishan went to live in a thatched hut to the left of him and subsequently went to serve him. On the eighth day of the third month in the Gengshen year of the Xiangshi era, he attained sudden enlightenment.

The layman Ruru Yan Bing, a successor of Chan Master Xuefeng Ruan, was once asked by a monk about the story of Zhaozhou seeing a novice attendant with a master at South Spring.

Chan Master Xichan Daguan of Tiantong in Mingzhou was a dharma heir of Chan Master Yichan of Jingci. He was the son of the Zhao family of Yiwu. Initially, he studied under Ying’an;
next, he visited Wunan at Daochang; and later, within the quarters of Shui’an at Jingci, he attained clear realization of the teachings bequeathed by these two elders.

While at Shouchu, he struck the mark with a single word and returned to Longxiang. At Baitang, he was appointed as the first seat. Later, after serving at four monasteries, he was summoned by imperial decree to ascend to Lingyin. There, he ascended the hall and cited the kōan of the Second Patriarch asking Bodhidharma for peace of mind, offering this verse: The Second Patriarch asked, "Please grant me peace of mind. Bodhidharma replied, "Bring forth your mind, and I shall set it at peace. The Second Patriarch said, "I have sought my mind for many years, yet I cannot find it. Bodhidharma said, "Since you have no mind, what need is there to set it at peace? At these words, the Second Patriarch attained great enlightenment. Chan Master I-an Youquan of Huazang in Changzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Quanshen of Daochang. He was born into the Qi family of Qihua in Lin’an.
At the age of fourteen, he received full ordination; at eighteen, he went to Lingyin Temple to pay his respects to Master Fozhi. At that time, Wuan was serving as the First Seat.

In the meditation hall, the Master was questioned about how all dharmas are established from the root of non-abiding. After a long time, he attained realization and replied: "Sewing a needle in the dark; drawing breath through the ears.

The Abbot approved and secretly transmitted the seal of mind to him. Once, while sitting in meditation through the night until dawn, the Master forgot to spread his alms bowl as the gruel server arrived.

A neighboring monk touched him with his hand, whereupon the Master was awakened to the truth and spoke this verse: Sitting alone in the empty room, The moonlight shines upon my body. The morning bell sounds outside the window; I do not know whether it is day or night.
A dark-lacquered Kunlun man grips his fishing pole; the ancient sail is hoisted high as he descends the turbulent rapids.

Amidst the shadows of reeds, he plays with the bright moon, drawing the blind tortoise onto the fishing boat. Once, Fozhi asked, "When the mind encompasses the vast void and its measure expands to fill the dharma-realm, what then?
The Master replied, "The great ocean does not harbor a dead corpse. Fozhi struck the seat and said, "This boy will one day..."
"You should occupy this seat to scold the Buddhas and revile the Patriarchs. The Master further concealed his brilliance;
he subsequently visited Ying'an at Guizong and studied under Dahui at Jingshan. Later, when Wuan resided at Daochang, he appointed the Master to share the teaching seat.
After taking up residence, he ascended the hall and said: "Today, the mouth of the sack is tied shut; monks with clear eyes, do not wander about in confusion. Where mental activity ceases..."
A turn of the body; even a sneeze becomes the lion’s roar. In a sandalwood grove, one may gallop at will. Raising the eyebrows, they grow upon the crown of the head;
carving flesh to form a sore, one reveals the family’s shame. Ascending the hall, he said: "Zen, Zen—without faction, without partiality.
When lost, there is a thousand miles of separation; when awakened, it is right on the lips. Therefore, when a monk asked Shishuang, 'What is Zen? Shishuang replied:"
A tile from a deer-pen. Furthermore, a monk asked Muzhou, "What is Chan? Muzhou said, "A fierce fire frying oil. Another monk asked Shoushan, "What is Chan?
Shoushan said, "A monkey climbing a tree, its tail trailing to the treetop. Great assembly, the Way has no crossroads;
wherever one stands is solitary and precarious. These three great elders traveled the living path before sound and employed the numinous mechanism outside of time.
If one examines this with the true eye of a Zen monk (*sōng*), there is indeed a distinction between superior and inferior. One person is like Zhang Liang entering the fray;
another is like Xiang Yu employing his troops; and another is like Kongming gauging the enemy. If anyone can discern these clearly, [they will understand].
One may stand shoulder to shoulder with the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Suddenly, a monk comes forth and says, "Venerable sir, you have split your words into two pieces.
Just now you said that the Way has no crossroads, no factions, and no partiality; why do you now distinguish so much between superior and inferior?
How will you respond? Do you understand? "Holding hands while climbing the mountain, we exert our strength together"—this is drawing breath from the throat.
He knew his time had come. In the autumn of the *gengzi* year of the Chunxi era, he manifested a slight illness; having written a verse, he sat in the lotus posture and passed away.
Upon cremation, his teeth and tongue remained unburnt, and countless five-colored *śarīra* were obtained. His remains were interred at Yugeitapa Wanian Temple on the left side of Hengshan.
Chan Master Chidun Zhiying of Tiantong in Mingzhou, a successor of Chan Master Jiaoshan Ti, cites the karmic conditions of Bodhidharma meeting Emperor Wu, and offers this verse:
“Lifting up the first hammer of Mount Sumeru, The jade pass and golden lock are difficult to break open. To apply a heavy back-stomp again is but empty toil.”
[It requires] strength. One should regret having come from ten thousand miles away.
Zen Master Tuigan Daoci of Jingshan, a successor of Zen Master Yinzhi of Jing Mountain, was asked by a monk: "Xuefeng said at Wangzhou Pavilion, 'I give you..."

The Master replied, “The nostrils point their large ends downward. [The Master] asked, “As for Guo-hu...”
Suddenly entering the abbot’s quarters; Baofu entering the monks’ hall—what is the meaning of this?
The Master said: "The water flows cold from beside the bamboo; the wind comes fragrant from within the flowers.
He ascended the hall and said: "This great matter is all-pervasive; even before I left Dongxia, I had already met you all. But tell me—"
"What is it like when we meet face-to-face? How many with horns and heads have gone on to become dragons? Shrimp and crabs still strain their eyes as before.
Entering the hall, he said: "The Ultimate Way is rooted in the one mind; the dharma of the mind is rooted in non-abiding. The essence of the non-abiding mind is numinous awareness, never obscured;
its nature and characteristics are quiescent. Therefore it is said: 'When I beat the drum, those in the four great continents participate together. He held up his staff.
The staff is horizontal; it spans the heavens and earth and the great land. The bowl is spread out; it covers the sands of the Ganges.
Reaching this point, where the Elephant King walks, foxes and hares leave no tracks. When the moon in the water appears, wind and clouds naturally differ.

Chan Master Ziju of Deshan in Changde Prefecture was a native of Tongchuan. He ascended the hall and said: "When seeing the very act of seeing, that which is seen is not true seeing;
even seeing is already detached from seeing, and seeing cannot reach it. He gave a shout: "The whale swallows the ocean until it is empty, revealing the coral branches!
Suddenly, if a monk among the assembly were to come forward and say, "Venerable Sir, stop this drowsy talk," then—
"I grant him one eye. He ascended the hall, held his staff horizontally across his chest, and said: "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven;
seven, six, five, four, three, two, one. Count them forward and backward in rotation until you reach the inexhaustible days of the future."
Because of the seven, one is seen; when one is seen, the seven vanish. Treading upon the vast void, even the iron ox breaks into a sweat.
Breath is cut off; there is no trace. He throws down his staff. You must further let go of this very thing; only then will the work of study be completed.
Ascending the hall, he held up the staff and said: "Sometimes one takes away the person but does not take away the environment; the staff moves freely in all directions. Sometimes..."
"To take away the object but not the person; the mountain monk is sevenfold topsy-turvy.
Sometimes both person and object are taken away; the staff and I erase our traces and swallow our voices. Sometimes neither person nor object is taken away.
[He plants his staff. "It accompanies me for a thousand miles; it carries you across ten thousand mountains. But what if one suddenly bumps into Great Master Linji? How then?"
A shout! Without clarifying the seal of the mind-ground, it is difficult to pass through the patriarchs’ barrier.

On the occasion of the Dharma assembly of Master Xian of Linan Chan Monastery in Wenzhou, a successor of Chan Master Wan-nian Fen, he ascended the hall and raised up the case of Chongshou, who addressed the assembly, saying: "If you recognize the bench..."
The disciples were more than enough to fill the circle. Yunmen said, "If you recognize the bench, heaven and earth are vastly different.
The Master said, "Old man Chongshou sits people to death; Great Master Yunmen runs people to death. Longming, however, is not like this:
"If you recognize the bench, its four legs rest firmly on the ground; when you wish to sit, you sit; when you wish to rise, you rise. He ascended the hall and raised this case.
The Story of Zhaozhou’s Examination of the Old Woman. The verse says: A lady of ice and snow, her countenance most extraordinary; She constantly takes up her jade flute to blow for others.
Within the melodies, boundless hearts are moved; To the Lord of Spring alone, she grants the first branch.
Chan Master Da Miao Yi-an Jian of Tanzhou was a native of Guiji. He ascended the hall and said: "The trees have fallen, the sky is bare;
the heavens are cold, the waters are frozen. The Old Śākyamuni has nowhere to hide his body.

Demolishing the eastern fence to patch the western wall, he runs into the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin, who requests instruction on the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation. How truly extraordinary! Yet he replies, 'A golden light.'"
Mingyun: After the formal session, go for tea. Entering the hall: The Old Barbarian opened a single path that is most direct;
he simply said, "Rest, and you attain Bodhi. This supreme, pure, and luminous mind is not obtained from others.
Yet later people failed to find its gate, running hither and thither, north and south, east and west, throughout the years and seasons without a single place of rest. Do you all [understand]?
"Can you rest? Enough, enough. He ascended the hall and said: "I cite a case where Master Huìtáng one day asked a monk, 'Where have you come from? The monk replied, 'From Nánxióng Prefecture.

The Master said, 'What do you intend to do upon coming here? The monk said, 'To visit venerable elders. The Master said, 'It would be better for you to return home. The monk asked, 'I do not understand;
what is the meaning of the Master’s instruction for me to return home? The Master replied, 'Three [generations] of the local village...'"
He bought a slice of fish, about the size of a palm. The Master said, "I would rather have my body shattered into fine dust than ever again blind the eyes of a monk.
Huìtáng was slightly better; some people say this is because it is difficult to forget what is familiar.

There was no common ground for conversation. He ascended the hall and presented the *kōan* of the King of Kaśmīra questioning the Venerable Siṃha regarding the emptiness of the aggregates (*skandha-śūnyatā*).
The Master offered this verse: "When did the Venerable One ever attain the emptiness of the aggregates? The King of Kaśmīra needlessly cut down the spring breeze himself.
After the rain, the peach blossoms have already fallen; They have dyed the flowing waters of the stream crimson."
Chan Master Xue’an Congjin of Tiantong in Mingzhou was a native of Nanxi in Yongjia. His secular surname was Zheng.

He received the tonsure at the Yanzi Monastery under Puan. He visited Xinwen at Ruiyan, where one day, while entering the master’s room, Xinwen posed the question, "A flake of snow on a red-hot stove.
As the Master was about to answer, he suddenly attained realization. He remained in attendance for three years, after which he traveled to Min to see Fozhi at Xilin.
Chan. [The Master] was asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From Siming. Zhi asked, "Have you ever seen the Mad Bagu?

The Master gave a shout. Zhi struck him. The Master caught his fist and said, "Master, you must not be so hasty. Zhi said, "Blind fellow! Stand over here. At that time, Xinwen was the abbot of Jiangxin.
When the Master returned to visit him, he appointed Yun as the Rector (Weina). One day, he questioned the Master about "One."
"A single shout distinguishes guest and host; illumination and function act simultaneously. [The student] asked, "What is this 'one shout that distinguishes guest and host'? The Master then shouted.

[The student] asked, "Of this one shout, which is the guest and which is the host? The Master said, "As a guest, it is always the guest; as a host, it is always the host. [The student] laughed and said, "You have become confused again.

The Master then presented a verse: "A single shout distinguishes guest and host; It follows the conditions of the occasion. If you can discern its meaning, You will not fall into the trap of the two paths."
However, his eyes were clouded; he performed a backflip and went off, trampling a frog to death. Initially, he resided at Lingyan in Yizhen, then moved to Tiantong.
A monk asked, "What is the realm of Lingyan? The Master said, "The Cold Spring of Deer-Run soaks the bright moon."
In Longdougang, white clouds are deeply hidden. A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, "At midnight, Mount Sumeru has its nostrils placed upon it. The monk asked, "What is Chan? The Master said, "Looking up, one does not see the sky. The monk asked, "What is the Way?
The Master said, "The whole body enters the wild grasses. He ascended the hall and said: "When the golden mallet is moved, the Buddhas of the three periods [of time]..."
One dares not face it head-on. When the laws and teachings are put into practice, external paths and celestial demons all fold their hands in submission.

Steep and towering, there is originally nothing to grasp or look up to; pure and naked, there is no need for contrivance. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, there is no need for doubt.
Let good and evil, right and wrong, be laid down all at once. Only then may one mix mud and water, pull the plow and drag the harrow, moving freely and spontaneously in every direction.
In total, there is no obstruction. At this very moment, tell me: how does one sing the Song of Great Peace? After a long silence:
"The iron boat lies across the ancient ford; the old family style is restored anew. Ascending the hall: To turn one’s body within the diamond circle is to strike the nostrils of Śakra;
to let go of the hand atop the precipice is to bring forth the eyes of Bodhidharma. Thus it was three times back and forth.
The momentum has not yet ceased; once the wheel of the Dharma has turned, its force cannot be halted. Holding the sting of a scorpion upside down, he commands the Śrāvakas as servants;
stroking the whiskers of a tiger in the proper direction, he calls the Bodhisattvas his slaves. Śākyamuni has already passed away and Maitreya has not yet been born;
the ancestral commands of the Buddha-Dharma are entirely in the hands of this new Tian Tong. For now, how will he manage the holding back and letting go? After a long silence: "A holeless [needle]."
An iron hammer was hurled directly at his face; a pure wind arose, pervading heaven and earth.

On the twenty-third day of the seventh month in the sixth year of the Qingyuan era, he requested a bath, changed his robes, wrote this verse, cast down his brush, and passed away. He was eighty-four years of age and seventy years since his ordination.
His entire body was interred to the right of the Xinwen Pagoda.

Chan Master Wansong Huana Dalian, the dharma successor of Chan Master Yunju Hui, spoke this verse in praise of the "Emerging from the Mountains" image: "Virtue fulfilled and practice perfected, he is through and through impoverished;
Unable to bear his emaciation, his hair hangs in disarray. His transgressions against heaven are now beyond counting— Within the state of *vaiśeṣika*, there is but one."

Chan Master Pò'ān Zuǎn of Wòlóng in Kuīzhōu,
the nineteenth-generation successor of National Teacher Tiāntóng Jié under Dàjiàn, was a native of the Wáng family of Guǎng'ān; he followed Master Jiān of Dēishān.
He shaved his head and soon received full ordination. He traveled extensively, visiting various masters throughout the land, until he arrived at Wanshou Monastery in Suzhou.

There, during a snowy night while sitting in meditation, he thought to himself that after several years of wandering as a pilgrim, he had still not attained stability. As he was immersed in this persistent state of frustration, he suddenly heard the bell strike.
He hurried to the rear hall and, raising his head, saw the two characters "Zhao Tang" (Hall of Illumination). His doubts were instantly resolved. Subsequently, he went to see Shuian Yi at Shuanglin.
Shui said, "Setting aside for a moment the matter of Venerable Siṃha being beheaded by the king of Kaśmīra, tell me, why does the bearded man of the Western Heaven have no beard?
The Master said, "This story is not brought up except at the Twin Trees. Shui said, "A skilled Chan guest!"
The Master said, "Your mind does not betray others, and your face shows no color of shame. Shui then pushed the door open with his hand. The Master said, "I have seen through you.
When Shui retired from his post at the monastery, he went to visit Mian at Wugu and was appointed as the guest prefect. One day, in the meditation hall, Mian raised the koan:
"It is not the wind moving; it is not the banner moving. At these words, the Master attained a sudden and great enlightenment. The next day, Mian encountered him...
Before the quarters, the Master said to him, "You must not employ any artifice; try to reveal some sign of your realization.
The Master responded at once, "There is a guest in the Abbot’s quarters. The Master laughed heartily.

Later, when the Master moved to Jiangshan, the other attended him, serving him closely for five years until he had mastered all his essential teachings. As he took his leave to return to Sichuan, the Master sent him off with this verse: "Ten thousand..."
Coming south from the village, the mountain stream flows turbulently; rushing like a blade, it crosses over and strikes the profound gate. At the crown of the head, the vajra-eye is struck blind.

His coming and going were like a pearl rolling across a platter. When the Master arrived at Kuizhou, the Minister Yang Gongfu invited him to leave the seclusion of his retreat and assume the abbacy of Wolong Monastery.
Not long after, he departed again and traveled to the region of Wu, where he served as the head of the community at Jingshan and Lingyin.
Subsequently, he resided at Jianfu in Changzhou, Lingyan in Zhenzhou, Xiufeng and Qionglong in Suzhou, and Zifu in Huzhou. Finally...
Zhang Qi of Yuezhai invited the Master to open the mountain monastery at Huiyun. He presided over six monasteries in total.

When the Master was leading the assembly at Lingyin, a practitioner requested further instruction, saying: "I am like a monkey that cannot be caught; I pray you will grant me some guidance. The Master said: "What is the use of trying to catch it?
It is like wind blowing across water; ripples form naturally. At that time, Wuzhun was standing by his side. Great...
Wu. Ascending the hall, he said: "When Yangqi first settled here, the walls of the house were sparse; the entire bed was strewn with snow-white pearls. Shrink your necks and sigh in silent lament;
I am reminded of the ancients who dwelt beneath the trees. The Master added: "Yangqi competes for victory, not for inferiority."
At Xiu Peak, we compete in inferiority, not in victory. Having newly settled at Xiu Peak, there is neither intimacy nor estrangement. Every single one harbors a pearl from the deep blue sea;

though the lakes and mountains fill the eyes, they can never be seen enough. Śākyamuni and Maitreya are his servants. Ascending the hall, he raised the example of his late teacher, Master Mimian, who said:
"If someone asks about the affairs of winter, [the answer is] 'The capital produces great yellow [myrobalan]. For the sake of a single grain of rice, one loses..."
"Half a year's worth of grain. Xiu Feng, however, was not like this. When asked about matters concerning winter, he said: "In the capital, they produce great yellow [myrobalan];

seeking only a single grain of rice, one instead obtains a hundred years' worth of provisions. Or, if an administrator says, "Venerable sir, venerable sir, do not speak of a hundred years' worth of provisions;
even half a year's worth is no small amount," he simply tells him: "Just prepare a heart of resolve, and it will certainly not fail."
[The Master] said, "It is deceptive. He ascended the hall and raised the following case: Dongshan Wushan said, "What is Chan? The Jambū tree is on the southern shore of the sea.
Near, it is not apart from the mind; far, it is a hundred thousand eight thousand [miles]. Ultimately, what is Chan?
The Chan Master said, "Qionglung also has a way of explaining it. What is Chan? The Jambū tree is on the southern shore of the sea. [He] propped [it up].
Heaven supports the earth; the earth props up heaven. It cannot be explained through clever words; it requires only mind-to-mind transmission.
Ultimately, how is it? "Zen, Zen. Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "It is not mind, not Buddha, not a thing. This mountain monk cannot restrain his impatience;
for your sakes, I shall provide a way to cast it all aside. He took up his staff and struck once. "The flowing water silently erodes the rocks by the stream. I urge you..."
Setting aside these difficulties of right and wrong, he ascended the hall and said: "Before the fifteenth day, it is as clear as a mirror;

after the fifteenth day, it is as black as lacquer. But what of this very fifteenth day? The oriole migrates to the lofty trees and chirps repeatedly; the butterflies dote on the fragrant clusters and fly about in pairs.
He then presented a verse for the presiding seat-master, saying: "To see while remaining detached from seeing is not true seeing. Return.
When the eight returns have been exhausted, there is nothing left to return. Leaves fall from the autumn sky, and the mountain’s bones are laid bare. Who knows who can recognize old Gautama?
Before passing into *parinirvāṇa*, the Master wrote a letter to bid farewell to his friends and disciples. He then composed a verse, saying: "The final word has already become a source of distress;
having written it out before others, there are thousands of errors and ten thousand mistakes. Having finished writing, he sat upright and passed away. This was in the fourth year of the Jiading era.
It was the ninth day of the sixth month of that year. At that time, he was residing at Mount Jing; according to his final instructions, his bones were to be scattered among the trees.
The abbot, Shiqiao, erected a stupa on a separate peak and interred them to the right of it. He was seventy-six years of age and forty-nine years since his ordination.
Chan Master Songyuan Chongye of Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou was the son of the Wu family of Longquan in Chuzhou. From childhood, he was outstanding and extraordinary.
In his youth, he aspired to the Dharma that transcends the world. At the age of twenty-three, he left home and first visited Mishiji at Lingshi.
He then went to see Dahui Zonggao at Mount Jing, where Dahui, ascending the hall, praised Ying’an of Jiangshan for his direct and swift way of guiding others.

Upon hearing this, the Master set out before dawn. Having arrived, he entered the inner quarters and sought instruction morning and evening. One day, Duanzhou asked, "The World-Honored One had a secret word;
Kāśyapa did not conceal it. What do you say to this? The Master replied, "I leave the Master in a state of bewilderment."

Dongshan An let out a single shout in a piercing voice. The Master attained realization. Dongshan was greatly pleased and regarded him as a vessel of the Dharma; he spoke a verse to encourage him to shave his head.
At the beginning of the Longxing era, he received full ordination at the Bailian Vihara in Lin’an. From then on, he traveled extensively to study under various great masters.
Rarely did anyone meet his intent. He then entered Min to see Mukan Genkaku. Upon seeing him, the Master took his leave.
Genkaku cited the saying, "The phrase with no phrase is like a vine leaning against a tree. The Master said, "Torn asunder. Genkaku asked, "Layao said, 'A fine pile of rotten firewood,' did you hear?
The Master said, "Adding a point to an arrow. Genkaku said, "My brother’s response is such that even an old monk like I cannot surpass it; what can be done about it?"
"Not yet. In another day, when the fly-whisk handle is in your hand, you will be able neither to act for others nor to test others.
The Master said, "To act for others—making an ordinary person of common ground leap directly into the realm of the sages—is indeed difficult. But as for testing people:

if one strikes them as they pass right in front of you, one already knows their very marrow before they have even opened their mouths. What difficulty is there in that? Yong raised his hand and said, "I understand."
"I have already told you that opening one's mouth does not depend on the tongue; you shall know this for yourself later.
Over a year passed before he met Mian at Xishan in Quzhou. Whenever [the Master] questioned him, Mian would simply smile. The Master was earnest in his pursuit of ultimate realization.
He reached the point of forgetting both sleep and food. When Mian moved from Jiangshan to Huazang and then to Jingshan, the Master followed him in all instances.
One day, while Mian was hanging up the plaque for the communal *入室* (entering the room) session, he asked a monk, "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing.

As the Master stood by his side, he attained a sudden and great awakening, exclaiming: "Today I have finally understood what Master Muguan meant when he said, 'Opening one's mouth is already..."* (The sentence trails off).
On his tongue, his spontaneous eloquence was unrestrained and versatile. When Mian Xian moved to Lingyin, the Master was subsequently appointed to share the seat.
He then went forth into the world at Chengzhao in Pingjiang, and later transferred to Guangxiao in Jiangyin, Yuzhu in Wuxing, Jianfu in Raozhou, Xiangshan in Mingzhou, and Huqiu in Pingjiang.
In the third year of the Qingyuan era, the seat of Lingyin became vacant, and he was summoned to fill it.

The Abbot, acting as the Acting Seat-Holder (Zhībùchù), ascended the hall and said: "In general, to uphold the School of the Patriarchs, one must possess the correct eye atop the head and the efficacious talisman suspended behind the elbow.
For instance, when Bǎoshòu opened the hall, Sānshèng pushed forward a monk; Bǎoshòu struck him immediately.
Sānshèng said, 'To act for others in such a way will blind the eyes of the entire city of Zhènzhōu. Bǎoshòu then cast down his staff."
The staff-bearer returned to the abbot’s quarters. These two venerable elders, through their casual yet pressing exchanges, revealed the very marrow of Linji’s mind.
Yet they failed to realize that life and death were entirely in the hands of this monk. Is there anyone who can discern this?
In years past, seeking fire, he obtained it with the smoke; today, carrying water, he returns with the moon. (New Year’s Day Address) — Yuan.
At dawn, when all things are manifest, there are times to let go and times to cut off. Without sparing even two eyebrows, he shifts the sitting mat and the tray.
Buddhist Dharma and worldly dharma are, in their entirety, a single piece. Since they are both Buddhist Dharma and worldly dharma, how can they become one?
Simply prepare a heart of resolve, and you will certainly not be deceived. To the assembly: An ancient said, "Pick it up..."
When taken up, heaven revolves and earth turns; when laid down, grass bows and wind blows. Yet Yeshan was not like this:
when he took it up, heaven and earth were shrouded in darkness; when he laid it down, even tiles and rubble gave off light.

Suddenly, if one or two people were to abruptly strike their own cranial aperture open, the Dharma-lineage of Bodhidharma would not yet have reached its decline. To the assembly, he raised the example of Master Linji as follows:
Regarding the "Haozhi Brush" kōan, Xuedou commented: "Linji’s letting go was too precarious; his gathering back was too swift. The Master took up his staff and said:
"Linji acted according to the command, yet he did not realize he was betraying Huangbo.
Even though Xuedou carried this burden with all his might, he saw only one side. But tell me, where does the essential point of Jianfu lie? He then threw down the staff.
Holding up his staff, he addressed the assembly. He cited Fenyang: "If you recognize this staff, your journey as a wandering monk is finished.
The Master said, "Although Fenyang spoke with such clarity, how could he avoid falling into the 'second head'? [Suddenly] picking up the staff, he said:
'This cannot be called a staff; it is a lacquer bucket. Study! He then ascended the hall and cited Master Baoning Yong, who said:"
The Great Square has no exterior; the Great Circle has no interior. With neither interior nor exterior, the holy and the ordinary are gathered together.
The rubble emits light, and Mount Sumeru is pulverized. Regarding the immeasurable Dharma gates and the hundreds of thousands of samādhis, the Master picks up his staff and says:
"All are to be understood right here. *Sulu sulu, sili sili*. The Master then says: "Whether great or small, Bao Ning’s karmic consciousness is vast and boundless."

Unable to do anything with the boat, he smashed the bailer and showed it to the assembly, saying: "Why, even for a monk with clear eyes, has he lost his nostrils? Is there a crime here, or is there no crime?
A monk asked: "What is the first: 'The same, the same substance'? The Master said: "Torn asunder. The monk asked:
"What is the second: 'The same, the great matter'? The Master said: "Within a single hair-tip, one settles heaven and earth. The monk asked: "What is the third?"
[The student] asked about the "General Identity of the Companions. The Master said, "A shrimp, an earthworm, a lame turtle, and a blind tortoise.
[The student] asked, "What is the 'Fourfold Identity of True Wisdom'? The Master said, "One is not; two is not. [The student] asked, "What is the 'Fivefold Identity of Pervasive Universality'?

The Master said, "If you were to gather up the entire earth, there would not be an inch of soil left. [The student] asked, "What is the 'Sixfold Identity of Complete Fulfillment'? The Master said, "It still lacks one stroke."
[The questioner] asked, "What is the seventh: sharing gain and loss? The Master said, "Entering the mud, entering the water. [The questioner] asked, "What is the eighth:
sharing life and death? The Master said, "Unable to save oneself. [The questioner] asked, "What is the ninth: sharing the same sound and roar?
The Master said, "An octagonal millstone rolling in empty space. [The questioner] asked, "What is the tenth: sharing the attainment of entry? The Master said, "Hanshan meets Shigede."
[The student] asked, "With what kind of person does one enter together? The Master said, "Hū Zhangsan and Hē Lisi. [The student] asked, "With whom do they roar with the same voice?

The Master said, "The cat and the white ox. [The student] asked, "How do they share the same life and death? The Master said, "Deshan’s staff and Linji’s shout. [The student] asked, "What thing shares the same gain and loss?
The Master said, "Rolling in the grass. [The student] asked, "Which one shares the same [nature]? The Master said, "The one who rolls in the grass."
[The student] said, "Complete. The Master said, "When you pick it up with the hand of faith, every stroke is personal. [The student] asked, "What is this that is equally pervasive?
The Master said, "Riding a great Peng within the shadow of a needle-point; casually pushing down the moon at the edge of heaven. [The student] asked, "Who shares in true wisdom?"

The Master said, "A ghost cave on Black Mountain. [The monk] asked, "Who is it that shares the same realization? The Master said, "A lantern entering a pillar. [The monk] asked, "Which one is the same as the Great Matter?
The Master said, "The great elephant of Jiazhou and the iron ox of Shanfu. [The monk] asked, "What thing is of the same substance?
The Master said, "The bowl-shedding mound. He resided at Lingyin for six years; his Dharma path flourished ever more, and those who attained the Dharma were numerous. Suddenly—
Retiring to the Eastern Hermitage, he manifested a slight illness and composed a letter by hand to bid farewell to the various officials and nobles.
Furthermore, he offered two phrases to test those who had come to study under him, saying: "Why does a person of true power fail to lift their foot? When the mouth opens, it is not upon the tongue."
He also left a letter to his dharma heirs at Xiangshan Guangmu and Yunju Shancai, entrusting them with the preciousness of the Great Dharma.

He further wrote a verse, saying: "Coming, there is nowhere from which one comes; departing, there is nowhere to which one goes. With a sudden turn at the profound pivot, even Buddhas and Patriarchs are at a loss.
He passed away while sitting in the lotus position on the fourth day of the eighth month of the second year of the Jiatai era. He was seventy-one years of age. At the time of his death, he sat...

Guo moved to Guifeng. He ascended the hall and said: "The two words 'Buddha-dharma' are known by everyone. But how can one take a bite of such virulent poison and arsenic?
Even if you were to penetrate beyond the time before Aśvaghosa, you would still be wandering outside of folly and madness.

Five. The sky is half-sunny and half-rainy. How many travelers outside the gate fail to see the full moon directly before their doors?
This is both laughable and lamentable. How can they compare to this team of ancient Buddhas in a West Lake temple, who, having finished their meditation retreat, return to the hall to drink tea?
Entering the hall: The spring breeze fans east and west; the spring rain is neither sunny nor rainy. Pale greens and deep reds are in full bloom.

Spreading out brocade and embroidery, the warbling of orioles and the chirping of swallows play the lutes and pipes in harmony. Each and every thing reveals the wondrous gate of universal penetration;
at every turn, the treasury of the true Dharma-eye flows forth. Should one attempt to direct the mind toward it or settle upon it, the ten thousand waters and a thousand mountains remain as before;

yet, if one knows how to return directly beneath, one will immediately see the seven holes and eight apertures. Entering the hall, he said: "The rain and snow fall thickly; water drips from the eaves. O virtuous ones!

it topples over the silver mountains and the iron walls. The moon gives birth to two: the Earth-Dweller rides an ox through the bustling marketplace.
The moon gives birth to three: above the house, the secluded birds warble and chatter. This is neither a web of complications nor a mere formal proclamation."
Entering deeply into the principle, this is a profound discourse. At such a time, how do you speak the single phrase where guest and host interpenetrate?
"A single hand hangs over a precipice ten thousand fathoms high; amidst a thicket of myriad flowers, the udumbara blooms. Ascending the hall [he said]:

The cakes were burnt. He struck his knee once and said, "Good brother! Then he recited a verse on Lingyun’s stone: "The clouds come and the clouds go, yet they have no intention;

Chan Master Zuteng (Zijing) of Tiantong in Mingzhou was the son of the Gao family of Fuzhou. He first studied under various venerable masters, including Muguan Yong, Shuian Yi, and Huan'an Ti.
