Entering the water, he saw a tall man. The old man then shouted at him. Later, responding to the command of Chancellor Zhongxian Yuewang, he took up residence at Chongbao Temple.
He ascended the hall and said: "I have been lazy and indolent while living on this mountain, and nothing has been accomplished. Teaching is but redundant talk, and Chan is merely a forced name."
Striking the whisk, he said: "Last night my spring-slumber was deep; one awakening lasted until dawn. At Zhufoshi, he ascended the hall:
"Amidst a heap of red dust, four autumns have passed. Having thoroughly tested all quarters, the bowl has slipped from the hand. Suddenly, the prow of the boat is lightly turned around."
Returning to the house to hawk Yangzhou, one wears the robe inside-out and sings a song of returning home.
Cutting off all diversities, standing like a sheer cliff ten thousand fathoms high, the springtime light floods the eyes and the peach and plum trees of the old garden vie for beauty.

Auspicious vapors soar into the sky as the natural radiance of the original ground manifests. If you can suddenly open a thousand eyes, what prevents us from joining hands and returning together? Yet, if you have not yet...
However, once Sudhana departed, there has been no news of him; the gate of the pavilion remains open throughout the entire day. Entering the hall, [the Master said]:
"If one discusses this matter, it is like spring traversing the great earth—every single thing is spring. But if one is a withered sprout or a rotten seed, how can one blame anyone else?"
On his deathbed, he wrote a verse: "Sixty-three years before, sixty-three years after—when the mountain is consumed by fire in the twelfth month, the void itself reveals its ugliness.
He then passed away in the lotus posture.
Chan Master Suiqing Mengchuang of Shouguo Temple in Mingzhou was the son of the Yu family of Shanyin. He left the household life at Tianzhang Monastery in his home prefecture.
On the occasion of the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa, he ascended the hall and said: "The Buddha’s true Dharma-body is like empty space.

For what reason, then, on the fifteenth day of the second month, did he go beneath the twin śāla trees and put on the full display of death? After a long silence, he said: "Bamboo shadows sweep across the steps."
The dust does not stir; the moon pierces the bottom of the pond, yet the water leaves no trace. Ascending the hall, the Master raised the case of Master Baiyun Wenda, who said:
"If you can truly, once and for all, break into a sweat, then upon a single blade of grass, jade towers and crystal palaces will appear.
If you cannot truly, once and for all, break into a sweat, then even if there are jade towers and crystal palaces, they will be covered over by a single blade of grass. The Master said:
Do you wish to know where Old Man Baiyun has landed? Since undergoing fierce battles in the north of the pass, he dares to speak of battle arrays in Jiangnan.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Deshan would strike as soon as one entered the gate; Linji would shout as soon as one entered the gate.
To force a tortoise to reveal its markings will never make it truly auspicious. Here at Putuo, all is silent and unmoving, yet it responds and penetrates everything. After a long silence, he said:
"A horse that lacks the thousand-li stride cannot truly chase the wind. [The Master] ascended the hall and said: "I cite Cao Shan’s departure from Dongshan. Dongshan asked, 'Where are you going?
Cao Shan replied, 'I am going to the place of non-alteration. Dongshan said, 'In a place of non-alteration, how can there be going?
Cao Shan said, 'Going, too, is non-alteration. The Master said: 'Clouds hide the seamless robe; the bird finds its lodging.'"

The Unsprouted Branch. Entering the hall: The spring breeze is like a blade; the spring rain is like a balm. Where it cannot be cut or tailored, the color of the peach blossoms grows ever more exquisite.
Upon seeing this once, Lingyun departed without doubt; Xie Lang’s dancing oars further display their skillful maneuvers.
Entering the hall: Guizong slays the snake; Bimao holds up the forked staff; Heshan beats the drum; Zhaozhou offers tea. At the crossroads of the street, he opens [the gate].
[The Master] spread out his mats. "I trade for cash and do not accept credit. He ascended the hall and said:

"For thirty years I have sought the swordsman; how many times have leaves fallen and branches sprouted? Since the moment I first beheld the peach blossoms, until this very day, I have had no further doubts.
The Master continued: "Ordinary spring dreams hold nothing extraordinary; only Lingyun has spoken of them to others. Then, regarding what Xuansha said:

"It is true, it is most truly true. I dare say you, elder brother, have not yet reached the end. Furthermore, how would one know the lining of the quilt is worn through if one does not sleep in the same bed?
Ascending the hall, he said: "Ten thousand miles without a blade of grass—overhead, it stretches on and on. Stepping out the door is already grass—beneath one's feet, it stretches on and on.
Traveling by night, one simply covets the bright moon, unaware that one is crossing cold waters while still wrapped in one’s clothes."

Chan Master Bielu Fanzhou of Daochang Monastery in Huzhou, a successor of Chan Master Yuyang Yin, once composed a eulogy for Guanyin Carrying a Fish Basket, which says: "A crescent moon slants across the solitary sea gate;
Chasing the waves and following the currents, one is no true man. At the moment he lifts it up with both hands toward people, Yet..."
"Exchanging fish eyes for bright pearls.
Chan Master Wujiguan inscribed this on a portrait of the World-Honored One Emerging from the Mountains: "He would not stay in the royal palace—what a fool!
Climbing over the city wall at midnight was truly strange. Who would have cared for his six years of asceticism? When his resources were exhausted, he had no choice but to emerge from the mountains."
Chan Master Wuliang Chongshou of Ruiyan in Mingzhou, a successor in the lineage of Chan Master Duan Yuying, ascended the hall and said:
He cited the case where Layman Bai asked National Teacher Niaokuo, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? Niaokuo replied, "Commit no evil; practice all that is good."
The Minister said, "Even a three-year-old child can speak like this. Niaoke said, "Though a three-year-old child may be able to speak it, an eighty-year-old man cannot practice it.
He then offered this verse: Evil has no appearance; goodness has no form. Both are nurtured from within the field of the mind.
Without revealing a sharp edge, I lightly pierce through: Bodhi and afflictions are equal to empty space. The cause...
A monk asked the World-Honored One, "On the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month, before Mount Zhengjue, you beheld the morning star at night and awakened to the Way;
what was the meaning of this? The Master answered with a verse: "The moment the morning star appeared, my eyelids were pierced through. Han words and Hu words, tens of thousands upon ten thousands.
You destitute beggar who became rich overnight, stop talking in your sleep! In whose hearth is there no smoke from the fire?"
Chan Master Wujing Che of Tiantong Monastery in Mingzhou, a Dharma heir of the Tiantong lineage, ascended the hall and raised the following case:
A monk once asked Master Yantou, "In the midst of vast, turbulent dust, how does one discern the host? Yantou replied, "A copper cauldron filled with oil. He then offered this verse: One million...

The valiant general enters Han Guan; his majesty is like a fierce tiger and his formation is like a mountain. With a single blade, he takes the head of Yan Liang directly—had it not been for Lord Guan, this would have been most difficult indeed.
Chan Master Niaofeng Ding composed a verse in praise of Master Xuansha: "A green raincoat, unwilling to be exchanged for a golden seal— For all eternity, such refined elegance belongs to Xie Lang.
Having caught the scarlet-scaled fish, no one recognized its worth; On a cold night on the sands, he listened to the clanging of the oar."

Chan Master Wumen Can of Jianfu Temple in Raoyou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Yuyang Kanhui. Having received the Dharma from Yuyang, he accepted an invitation to reside at Jianfu in the sixth month of the third year of the Baoping era.
Subsequently, he moved to Kaixian, and in the fifth year, he returned once more to Jianfu. Entering his quarters, the mountain monk said:
"Today the gates of hell are opened. All people throughout the great earth are invited to perform the karma of hell and realize the fruit of hell.
If there should be even one person who attains Buddhahood and becomes a patriarch, I vow not to attain perfect enlightenment. Having ascended the hall and finished offering the incense, he said:
"Heaven is high and earth is deep; the sun reaches its zenith and the moon declines. To fully uphold [the Dharma] or to uphold it only partially is worlds apart. Chan Master Can—"

Throughout my life, I have done nothing but eat and wear clothes. When I heard others speak of the two words "Buddha-dharma," it was like the wind passing over the treetops or water poured upon a hard rock.
Today, having had my face torn open and being called an "Elder," I wish to discuss this matter with you all.
For no reason, I have braved the great heat of the fifth or sixth month and traveled three thousand li on a long journey; all at once—
"It has been struck down! Nevertheless, there is still this staff to rely upon. Holding up the staff, he said, "Staff, try to speak! He struck it once.
"In a world of pure peace, one must strictly avoid false speech. That evening, during the informal sermon (*xiao-can*), he said:
"Plying oars and hoisting sails, I steer a bottomless boat, sailing crosswise across the sea. With god-like heads and ghostly faces, I employ the Unwritten Seal to examine and verify all."
From as far as two thousand *li*, he has come to dwell in the mountains, single-mindedly upholding this matter.

He raises his whisk: look! The seal-pattern is already revealed. He draws a stroke: the seams of the brocade are already opened. Whether Buddha or Patriarch, whether sage or ordinary person—all are sealed and fixed within this very place.
It reaches such a state that the entire universe and great earth are filled with a whistling wind. Among the assembly...
Suddenly, someone from the assembly stepped forward and said, "Venerable Sir, do not be so alarmed or startled.
I realized this samādhi back in the era of Bhagavān Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja Buddha. What then? [The Master] struck the meditation seat with his whisk and descended from the seat.
He ascended the hall again and said, "Yunmen bestowed three blows of the staff upon Dongshan; Huangbo gave three blows of the staff to Linji. To diminish..."
The hearth adds to the soldiers' wounds; salt costs more than sauce. One does not make a single unit, nor two make a pair. How many reeds and flowers face the red dockweed?

People of this age look only at the fishing line. [He] ascended the hall and said: "The Dharma-gates of all Buddhas and the essential subtlety of the Patriarchs—last night, the rain from the four eaves spoke so that it was as leak-proof as a vessel filled with water. If you people can take responsibility for this here," [he continued].
Herein lies the guarantee. Shaking his hand, he said, "Waving it about, waving it about. Opening the furnace, he simultaneously thanked the elders for treading upon the field and ascended the hall.
Regarding Zhaozhou’s “Guest and Host” koan: one whose ground is stable and secure speaks the truth as soon as the mouth opens and treads with confidence as soon as the feet move.
If you cannot distinguish east from west or north from south, you will inevitably have your boundaries encroached upon by others.
Transcending boundaries. Those beneath the Jifu Gate are all people whose fields are secure and profound.
Picking up the incense ladle, setting down the fire tongs—each moment is authentically true. Why is this so? The official seal is clear. Ascending the hall:
Half a ladle from Linji, half a ladle from Moshan. The jade is naturally flawless, yet one vainly carves it. Having years but no virtue—Old Mul.
The Prefect. Without cause, he pressed down and broke Yunmen’s leg. On the Dragon Boat Festival, he ascended the hall. No talisman was written; no medicine was gathered.

He roused the dead and prohibited the inauspicious. Taking up his staff, he said, "Fortunately, this one is still here. With a sharp strike, he said, "Throughout the courtyard, the warm breeze blows as the summer days lengthen.
People dwell in a world of fragrant lotus flowers. At Kaixian, for the summer retreat, he gave a small *pratyaya* (private instruction): "The great Flower Treasury Ocean is vast and boundless..."
The Boundary: Rivers, streams, and brooks flow into it, all losing their original names; fish, dragons, shrimp, and crabs swim within it, all losing their original natures.
The Buddhas of the three periods attain equal and perfect enlightenment therein;
all sentient beings wander through birth and death therein; the great assembly present achieves effortless cultivation therein. [He] picked up his staff.
[The Master] strikes the staff once. Kaixian’s staff has been swallowed up in a single gulp.
Where, ultimately, do the Buddhas of the three periods of time, all sentient beings, and the assembly present here tread? After a long silence: "The waves of Caoxi are just like this;
countless ordinary people are submerged. Small-scale sermon for the Winter Solstice: "A drop of water, ice forms within it."
"You may rest now. The cliffs have collapsed and the rocks have split; this is precisely the moment to advance.

Even if you understand 'a single thread extending,' you have not yet understood 'the extension of a single thread. Even if you understand 'the extension of a single thread,' you have not yet understood 'a single thread extending.
Therefore, while the local dialects may be similar, the administrative jurisdictions differ. At Kaixian, it is otherwise: amidst the clamor and haste, the morning cock..."
The evening bell calls winter summer and calls summer winter; who can measure its length or brevity? Where snow and frost end, there is the spring breeze.
On the evening of my second stay at Jianfu, I gave this small *śāmaṇa* (sermon): "Going, going, yet truly not going; this Dharma abides in its own station.
Coming, coming, yet truly not coming; the marks of the world are eternally abiding. It has been five years since I last arrived, counting on my fingers.
At Donghu: The lotuses have withered, their rain-shielding canopies are gone; yet the spring breeze still lingers at the tips of the willow branches.
There is not a single thread of the marks of coming and going; there is not a single thread of the marks of new and old. If you see it, you see it together with all people;
if you hear it, you hear it together with all people. Suddenly, someone might come forth and say: "Wuwen is treating the property of the Sangha as his own."
"You have already used what you inherently possess. You are far too, far too [overbearing], eh? It turns out there was someone among the assembly. Again, he cited the case:
When Deshan gave a small lecture (*xiao can*) on "not answering questions," the hook was set in a state beyond doubt.
At that time, a monk stepped forward; Deshan struck him immediately. The monk said, "I haven't even asked a question yet; why do you strike me? Deshan replied, "Because you don't recognize it."
"O itchy fellow! Deshan said, "Where are you from? This was the second time he brought down the iron hammer. The monk replied, "A man from Silla. Deshan sent him out with that very sound.
Deshan said, "Had you not yet stepped onto the ship's railing, I would have given you thirty blows. Thunder rumbled loudly, yet there were no raindrops at all.
"Everyone, Master Deshan—great as he was—was headstrong and tail-weak; he instead led this monk toward..."
In the midst of the grassy thicket, they emerge and submerge. At that time, had he waited for him to say, "I have not even asked my question;

why do you strike me? he would have given him thirty blows right between the heels. Why? Because when acting for others, one must act thoroughly. Ascending the hall, [he said]: The wind whistles, the rain whistles.
Heaven is high and earth is deep; the waters are broad and the mountains are far. Master Bodhidharma wandered about for no reason.
During the Liang dynasty, which succeeded the Wei, the Great Master of the Second Patriarch lost an arm for no apparent reason. Master Shuilao was unworthy of receiving Mazu’s kick;
that great Chan master of the world ate it in vain. When one speaks of the "Four Strips of Rattan," it leaves people with resentment that cannot be extinguished.
Entering the hall [for teaching], he said: "Before the Buddhas and Patriarchs had yet arisen, there was a naturally present single phrase—neither East nor West."
Neither horizontal nor vertical. For the patch-robed monks, from morning until evening, they chew here and there; whether horizontal or vertical, there is nothing to be done.
(He strikes his knee once. If you can take a single step forward here, he will naturally deliver it with a voice and entrust it with both hands.
If you only learn it from the pages of books, it is merely cast from a mold.
As he was about to depart, [he noted that] the mountains had no fixed number of layers and the waters no fixed number of layers. At the opening of the summer retreat, he ascended the hall and said:

"I know nothing of a hundred things; I understand nothing of a hundred things. I eat my fill of rice and sleep soundly. If you wish to attain realization within a fixed period, you must realize such a samādhi.

The Master once wrote in a letter to his friend Zhiwu Wen: "What is there to say about presiding over a monastery? In recent years, appointments to monastic offices have been made by imperial decree."
What limit is there to this? How many people are there whose words are worth recording?
If I possessed a mouth capable of swallowing all the Buddhas of the three periods of time, I would never sit upon a curved wooden chair for the rest of my life—what regret could there be?

I have heard it said that when I first entered the monastic community, I observed that those who were literate often failed to cultivate refined conduct; consequently, I resolved never to serve as a scribe.
As for those elders who occupied positions and claimed the title of Master, he often looked down upon them; consequently, he had no intention of entering the world [of public monastic life].
Now, all have failed to fulfill their initial aspirations. Having resided in the monastery for ten years and being called an Elder, he remains nothing more than the former Chan-zhao.
His eating, drinking, and daily activities were no different from those of the monks in the hall. He was accompanied by over one hundred to one hundred and thirty disciples each year.

On every fifth day, he would strike the drum and ascend the hall, where he would expound upon the subtle and great Dharma-gates he had acquired while among the various elders during his ordinary times.
I have cut off all casual chatter, speaking here and there as the occasion demands. I do not dare to ensnare students with deceptive, empty words, nor do I dare to deceive them with hyperbolic talk.
When I reach the point where there is no handle to grasp and no flavor to savor, I smile to myself with joy;
those who listen need not understand this smile. Many among the scholar-officials know me well, yet what they know does not exceed—
It is said that he was capable of literary composition while reading, understood how to restore neglected works, and possessed a resolute backbone;
indeed, those who knew him were as few as the hairs on a goat's beard.
Chan Master Xuefeng Beishan Xin of Fuzhou, a successor of Chan Master He Shanqing, composed a verse on the Buddha’s Enlightenment: Six years of freezing have left his eyes without light;
A single glance at the morning star—snow after frost. Carrying water out of the mountains, he calls out repeatedly to sell it; He does not know that the rivers and seas are white.
Vast and boundless.
Zen Master Shantang Shanji of Huqiu in Suzhou, a successor in the Dharma lineage of Chan Master Guantong, inscribed this eulogy for the Fish Basket Guanyin: *Cloud-like tresses...*
Heavily made-up and forced to wear a smile, he enters the dusty world for the sake of trivial matters. Though he brings with him that which is truly alive, no one buys it;
they view it merely as an ordinary dead commodity.
Chan Master Wenwei of Tianyi Xiaoyan in Yuezhou ascended the hall and said: "Master Yunmen addressed the assembly, saying: 'Everyone possesses a luminous brilliance;
yet when one looks for it, it is not seen, shrouded in darkness. What is this luminous brilliance of yours? He then provided his own substitute answer:

'The kitchen, the storehouse, the mountain gate. He further said: 'A good thing is not as good as having none at all. He then offered a verse: Everyone possesses a luminous brilliance, Yet when looked for, it is dark and murky. What is this self-luminosity? The kitchen, the storehouse, the mountain gate. A good thing is not as good as having none at all.

Every person possesses radiance within; yet when looked for, it is not seen, shrouded in dark obscurity. When the mountain gate and the kitchen storehouse are kicked down, at that moment light and darkness are naturally distinguished.
Master Baiyan Ning composed a verse on the tattered robe, saying: "Fragmented and worn for many years, Picked up at random to drape over one shoulder.
At midnight, returning from meditation, it is folded and set aside; Who can transmit the message within this?"
Chan Master Shanjing of Huazang Chun’an ascended the hall and raised the story of the Sixth Patriarch regarding the wind and the banner. He offered this verse:

"It is not the wind, nor is it the banner; Where the white clouds end, the green mountains appear. How pitiable are those countless men of spirit and brilliance, Who open their eyes wide only to enter the Gate of Death."
Chan Master Jing-sou Ru-jue of Mount Jing in Hangzhou was a successor of Chan Master Tian-tong Ying. He was a native of Wuzhou. Initially, he went to see Chidu.
One day, in the meditation hall, [Chidu] posed a question: "What is the Buddha? The Master immediately replied, "A rotten melon. He then presented a verse, which began: "What is..."
The Buddha eats rotten melons; biting into them, the frost penetrates his teeth. Although the roots and stem have no storage pit, once a year they bloom but once.
He also composed a verse to present to Chidun, saying: "At Mount Zhong, I braved white blades with my bare body;
several times I have been nearly buried alive. Since the man was lost and the house destroyed, I have come to know there is no rank to be found."
Arrangements were made. After his stay, on the first day of the year, he ascended the hall and said: "A new year strikes a new drum, universally bestowing the fresh rain of Dharma;
all things are renewed, each and every one brought into accord with the rules. The Great Being Samantabhadra rejoices, seizing this opportune moment to open wide the gates."
He released the White Elephant King; it was nowhere to be found across the earth. [The Master] picked up his staff and said: "Only this one does not belong to the old or the new.
In a casual opening of the mouth, he swallows the Dharmakāya. He threw down the staff and asked: "What is it?
Within a peach pit of a thousand years, there is still that very same kernel of the past. Small Retreat Sermon: In this school of ours, the true command is fully upheld, like a sudden storm.
The wind suddenly rises and the rain drums on, surging forward without obstruction. A spark from a flint or a flash of lightning cannot catch up with their swift flight.

As soon as you form an intention, you lose the source; as soon as you lift your eyes, you have already missed it. This is not a dharma of the present moment; do not give rise to various kinds of thoughts.

Even if you were to cultivate the three modes of practice simultaneously and seek realization within a fixed period, you would be like a second head or a third neck—propped up by ten thousand pillars and a thousand supports, only to find yourself growing more frantic with every breath. It is utterly different.
They do not realize that before the skull is fully formed, one’s own eye must first be clarified; with a single "paw-di" cry, everything is settled once and for all.
Even though this is so, those who have attained direct realization are not one or two in ten thousand, while those who have misunderstood are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

A verse on the Buddha’s Enlightenment says: "Only after six years on the Snowy Peaks did he attain the Way; He struck out the ghostly eyes he had carried from of old. Covered in shame and confusion, there was no place to turn."
As for the place where he clings: to this day, I am terrified at the mere sight of the morning star.
Chan Master Deyin of Xuefeng at Mount Fuzhou composed a eulogy for the Monk with the Cloth Bag, saying:

Carrying a cloth bag upon his staff, he wanders through the red dust of the world. As for this matter, how has he ever seen it intimately? His karmic consciousness is vast and boundless, lacking any foundation; he does not know—
"Who is it that laughs with open mouth?

Master Gao Yuan Zuquan of Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou, a successor of Chan Master Qiji of Jinshan, cited the following account: One day, while Jingqing was at Xuefeng, they were engaged in communal labor (pǔqǐng).
Next, Xuefeng asked, "When Guishan said, 'As soon as you see form, you see the mind,' was there still any fault in this?
Qing said, "For what purpose did the ancients speak thus? Xuefeng said, "Even so, I wish to deliberate with you.
Qing said, "If it were like that, it would be better for me to go out and hoe the earth. The Master commented: "Xuefeng held the probing pole in his hand; the weeds followed the shadows."
[Shen] said: "If it were not for Jingqing’s communal labor, things would have been nearly ruined.
He further cited the Ninth Patriarch, Vajramitra, asking the Eighth Patriarch, Buddhanandi: "Parents are not my kin; who is the most intimate?
The Buddhas are not my Way; who is the ultimate Way? The verse says: "Parents are clearly not my kin."
The Patriarch pours out his liver and gall toward others. If you can directly realize this for yourself, the *udumbara* flower will bloom as spring within the fire.
A verse presented to Huang Hanling Kai upon his opening of a reception hall: The road winds around the crest of a ten-thousand-fathom precipice;
When travelers reach this point, they are filled with sorrow. Suddenly finding a place of rest, They wander at ease through layered mountains and passes.

Chan Master Wumen Huikai of Huanglong in Longxing Prefecture was a dharma successor of Chan Master Wanshou. He was a native of Liangzhu in Hangzhou; his clan name was Liang and his mother was surnamed Song.
He received the precepts from Venerable Tiantong Huihong and studied under Yue-lin at Wanshou Temple. Yue-lin instructed him to contemplate the word "Mu" (無).
Regarding the story of Zihu: For six years he made no progress at all. He then resolved with a vow, saying, "I shall rouse my will;
even if it takes the wasting away of this body through sleeplessness. Whenever he reached a point of exhaustion, he would walk along the corridors and strike his head against a pillar.
One day, while by the Dharma seat, he suddenly heard the sound of the meal drum and attained realization. He composed a verse, saying: "Under the blue sky and bright sun, a clap of thunder."
The eyes of all living beings upon the great earth were opened wide; the myriad phenomena of the universe bowed their heads in unison. Sumeru leaped and danced through the three stages.
On the following day, Lin entered the room intending to communicate what he had attained, but [Linji] suddenly said, "Where did you see gods and ghosts? At this, [the student] was at a loss.
The Master gave a shout. Lin also shouted. The Master shouted again. From that point on, their spiritual resonance and functional application became perfectly harmonized.

In the eleventh year of the Jiading era, he emerged from seclusion at Baoguo Temple in Anji. He subsequently moved to Tianning in Longxing, Huanglong, Cuiyan, Kaiyuan in Suzhou, Lingyan, Jiaoshan in Zhenjiang, and Baoning in Jinling.
In the sixth year of the Chunyou era, by imperial decree, he was appointed to open the mountain at Huguo Temple.

At Renshuang Temple, the Master ascended the hall and said: "If a person recognizes their own mind, there is not an inch of land in the great earth. When the ancients spoke thus, Huanglong was not like that. He said:
"If a person recognizes their own mind, the great earth is entirely soil. Ascending the hall again, he said: "Right and wrong, long and short—these are but the wind at one's ear.
Do not seek out differences or similarities therein. If you wish to remain unmoved by the eight winds, let them blow freely."
The mind-ground is equal to empty space. The Old Man of Cishou only knows how to set sail with the current;
he cannot hold the tiller against the wind. Huanglong, however, is not like this: having cast away both right and wrong, one must realize it within right and wrong. Why is that?
"Many times the black winds have tossed the great waves, yet I have never heard it said that the fishing boat has capsized. Ascending the hall, he said: "Two-thirds of one's life have already passed;
the ox of Huai Prefecture eats the grain. The single point of the numinous mind remains unpolished; the horse of Yi Prefecture suffers from bloating."
Driven by greed, they go about in trivial pursuits day after day; they search the world for a physician, yet when called, they do not turn their heads—what can be done?

By cauterizing the left shoulder of a pig, one may realize at this moment that the task of study is complete. If this is not yet so, I take up my staff and ask Elder Wood to explain it thoroughly for you all.
(He strikes the ground with his staff and descends from the seat. Entering the hall, he said: "Venerable Zhaozhou said:"
To those coming from the south, he unloads for them; to those coming from the north, he loads for them.

This is much like the worldly sentiment that watches for warmth and cold, where people’s faces follow the rise and fall of circumstances. Master Cishou said: "To those coming from the south, he gives him a smile;
to those coming from the north, he gives him a smile. This is much like joyful slaughter—there is a blade within the smile. If it were Jiao... [text ends]
Mount [Shan] was not like this. He treated those coming from the south with equanimity; he treated those coming from the north with equanimity. He did not become angry, nor did he smile.
He had no sense of inferiority and no sense of superiority. Why? Because in a world of pure peace, there is no need for weapons.
He composed the "Verse of the Rising Sun" (Chāoyáng gē), saying: "A thing most urgently needed in times of cold; Seize the warmth to apply a few stitches."
Suddenly, the twelfth lunar month has arrived; lest you find yourself with feet flustered and hands in disarray, I offer this verse to the moon:
"I have just begun to see a few glimmers of light, yet I wish to bring this final chapter to a close. If it were my 'fist of no door,' I would not strike such dull-witted fellows."
In his later years, the Master grew weary of wielding the mallet and whisk. He resided in a hermitage upon the West Lake, yet those who came to study under him remained numerous.

Emperor Lizong summoned him to the Xuande Hall to preach the Dharma; his prayers for rain were efficacious, and the Emperor issued an edict bestowing upon him a golden-embroidered dharma robe and the title "Fuyan" (Buddha Eye).

Chan Master Deshou of Nanshan Gufeng in Xinghua Prefecture was a native of the Chen family of Lianjiang, Fuzhou. He received the tonsure at Hanshan in Suzhou. Once, while presiding over the assembly, he raised the following case: A monk asked Xuefeng, "What is the first phrase? Xuefeng remained silent for a long time.

The monk reported this to Changsheng, who said, "This is the second phrase. Xuefeng then instructed the monk to ask Changsheng as follows: [The monk asked,] "What is the first phrase? Changsheng said, "It is not that there is no first phrase; it is simply that there is no one to speak it. Deshou then remarked, "Xuefeng’s silence was like a great ocean; Changsheng’s words were like a single drop of water. He added, "If you can understand this, you will see that the two masters were like a pair of tigers leaping together. If you cannot, you will fall into the pit of the 'four propositions' (catuṣkoṭi). He then quoted the verse by Changsheng: "The first phrase is like a sword hanging from the wall; The second phrase is like a dragon coiled in the deep. If you wish to know the third phrase, You must look directly at the fourth phrase. Deshou concluded, "If you can penetrate these four phrases, you will see that the Buddhas and patriarchs have all emerged from here. If you cannot, you will be lost in the weeds of intellectual speculation. He then descended from the seat.
"What is the first phrase? Sheng said, "Heaven! Heaven! The Master said, "Those two great elders shed tears like this because their hearts were pained;
as for the first phrase, you have not even dreamed of it yet. Suddenly, someone asked Yishan, "What is the first phrase?
He simply replied to him, "The sword has long since gone. [Later], while ascending the hall, he cited Master Zhenjing.
It is said: "The Head-Dhūta Rock is enveloped by moss; the Throwing-Pen Peak is entwined by *bìlì* vines.

Within Lóu-hàn Monastery, three practitioners are ordained each year; at Guī-zōng Monastery, one drinks tea after the formal meditation session concludes. Do you all wish to understand? Listen to this verse:
When the sky clears, the sun comes out; When it rains, the ground becomes damp. I have told you everything I know— I only fear..."
His faith was not yet sufficient.

Chan Master Zhuyan Miaoyin of Shishuang in Tanzhou was a native of Jinxian; his clan name was Wan. He received full ordination under Shaotan of Longtang and traveled extensively to consult masters throughout various regions.
Later, he arrived at Wanshou Monastery in Suzhou to pay respects to Yuelin. One day, he entered the master’s room for private instruction.
Next, Lin asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master replied, "A rat gnaws through a lamp bowl. Lin nodded his head in agreement.

He subsequently presided over several monasteries before moving to Shishuang, where he composed a verse titled "Reading Sutras While Gazing at the Moon": "The patterns and colors are revealed even before the tongue moves;
The five thousand scrolls are completed all at once. If one says they must wait for the moon to open the volume again, I dare guarantee..."
"In the year of the donkey, I have not yet reached the end. In his later years, the Master built a hermitage called Zixia (Purple Mist).

When Prime Minister Zhao Gong Kui was residing in his private residence in the village, he once invited the Master there to inquire about the Way. On the twenty-third day of the eighth month of the third year of the Baoyu era, the Master manifested illness.
He wrote a verse, saying: "Sixty-nine years—a single great dream. Return! Return! Be careful, be careful! Having finished writing it, he passed away.
He passed away peacefully, and his stupa was enshrined amidst the purple mists.

Chan Master Wuzhun Shifan of Mount Jing in Hangzhou,

the twenty-first-generation successor in the lineage of Great Mirror (Dajian) and the dharma heir of Chan Master Wolong Xian, was born in Zizhong, Sichuan, into the Yong clan. He was nine years old [when he entered the monastic order].
He left home life at Mount Ping under Master Daoqin. Upon merely glancing over the scriptures, he could recite them from memory.
In the winter of the fifth year of the Shaohui era, he received full ordination (*upasampadā*). The following year, he entered the summer retreat at Chengdu at the Zhengfa Monastery.

There he met the senior disciple Yao, the Head Seat of Xiatang, from whom he requested instruction on the method of seated meditation (*zuo chan*). Yao asked, "What is Chan? And who is it that sits? Through this, the Master received his guidance.
He investigated this day and night. One day, while using the toilet, he attained a realization. The following year, he went to visit Fozhao at Yuyang Monastery.
Fozhao asked, "Where are you from? The Master replied, "Jianzhou. Fozhao asked, "Did you bring the sword with you? As soon as the Master heard these words, he let out a shout.

Zhao Xiao said, "This fellow with the black head is acting recklessly. After some time, he returned to Lingyin. At that time, Po’an was serving as the First Seat (Dìyīzuò). They went together to visit Shísǔ Ān.

A practitioner at the hermitage requested instruction, saying, "I am like a monkey that cannot be caught; I pray you will grant me an opening for insight. Po’an said, "What is the use of trying to catch it? It is like wind blowing across water:
ripples form naturally. The Master [Zhaowen] said: [Note: The final sentence "The Master" appears to be a fragment or a concluding marker for the preceding narrative.]

While attending to him by his side, he attained a realization. Before long, Poban came to Tiantong to sweep the pagoda; the Master went with him. They further invited Yueshi Xi to travel together to Mount Tai and Mount Yan.
Upon reaching Ruiyan Yunchao, they requested the Master to occupy half the seat. That night, he dreamed of a person in magnificent robes and hat who presented him with a bundle of thatch grass.
The following day, a special messenger from Qingliang in Mingzhou arrived; the Master accepted the invitation and entered the monastery. There he saw—

The so-called Kālaṃkadeva (Gālánshén) was surnamed Máo; his attire and headgear were no different from what he had previously dreamed. He ascended the hall to expound the Dharma, offering a single incense stick to Pò’ān.
After three years, he moved to Jiāoshān; after one year, he moved to Xuědòu; after another three years, by imperial decree, he was transferred to Yùwáng;
and after another three years, following the dispersal of the assembly at Shàolín on Mount Sōng, the court appointed the Master to succeed him at Jìngshān.

The following year, the temple was destroyed. The Master had foreseen this event beforehand; he did not alter his countenance nor waver in his composure. In the tenth month of winter that year, an imperial decree summoned him into the inner court.
The Emperor presided over the Xuzheng Hall to receive him in audience. The Master’s responses were detailed and lucid, so much so that the Emperor’s expression changed.

He was bestowed with a gold-embroidered *saṃghāṭī* robe. Furthermore, an edict was issued for him to proceed to the Ciming Hall, where he ascended the seat to preach the Dharma while the Emperor remained behind a lowered curtain.
He granted the title of Chan Master Fojian to [the abbot]. Three years later, the temple was completed; six years after that, it was destroyed by fire once more.

Yet, with assistance arriving like clouds, it was restored to its former splendor within a few years. Forty *li* from the temple, he built a hall of one hundred bays to receive wandering monks, naming it "Wannian Zhengxu" (Ten Thousand Years of Orthodox Succession).
Several hundred paces west of Zhengxu, he constructed a small hermitage as a place of retreat.

The treasury was established with a multi-storied pavilion built above it, wherein the imperial calligraphies bestowed at various times were kept in secret storage. In the eastern and western wings of the spacious hall, the ancestral masters and the memorial tablets of previous generations were enshrined with incense offerings.
On the anniversary of the founder’s birthday, a meal was provided for the monastic community as a Buddhist service to augment his posthumous merit.

Because the Shu region was in turmoil, the ancestral sacrifices of the Master’s lineage were consequently cut off; the shrine was maintained to commemorate his filial devotion. When the Emperor heard of this, he sighed in admiration. A monk asked:
"The Venerable Zhaozhou said, 'Thirty years ago, while traveling in the south, at the head of my brazier, there was a saying about the absence of host and guest.
To this very day, no one has brought it up. What is the meaning of this? The Master replied: "The tongue."
[The monk] dragged his feet along the floor. The monk asked, "Ultimately, what is the 'no host and no guest' saying? The Master said, "Words fill the world.
The monk asked, "As for Xuansha, who upon hearing this said, 'This old fellow’s heels have not even touched the ground,' how do you explain that?
The Master said, "Bury them all in one pit. The monk said, "It can truly be called: struck by a red-hot brick, one freezes through to the very bottom. [The Master said: "Red!"
The eye bumps into the matchhead. The Master strikes once with his staff. He ascends the hall and says: "Under Wufeng’s gate, there is nothing whatsoever.
The meditation seat is cramped and the offerings in the hall are meager. Underfoot, one treads upon broken bricks and shattered shards;
before one's eyes, one encounters Wang Gela and Li Mahu. To dwell in the mountains with such meager merit is truly..."

"How could this old barbarian have been so deceived? [The Master] remained silent for a long while. "Even so, let me clarify it further. He ascended the hall and said: "One summer has already passed; there is nothing left undone.
Thus, I have taken up the bowl from Suizhou and the ceramic cup from Qiongzhou. He ascended the hall again and said: "At Vulture Peak they pointed at the moon; at Caoxi they spoke of the moon.
Passed down from generation to generation, they have taken a tortoise and certified it as a soft-shelled turtle. Chan Master Fan usually hangs his mouth open.
It is on the wall. Today, for no reason at all, those who enter through the door cannot help but bring forth this many years' worth of records to speak to you all.
This is simply so that Guo Da, Li Er, Deng Si, and Zhang San may understand: in Jiangnan and the two Zhe regions, spring is cold and autumn is hot.
To the assembly: if one were to discuss this matter, it is truly simple and essential. Yet, alas, you all create difficulties for yourselves.

It is difficult to create obstacles for oneself. Thus, when I usually see people on the eastern or western corridors bowing and exchanging greetings, I simply lower my head to receive them. There is truly nothing else behind this;
it is merely that I wish for everyone to recognize that this old monk is a native of Longqing Prefecture in Western Sichuan. If you can recognize me, I shall speak some of my local dialect with you.
Let us speak in our local dialect. For now, let us not yet discuss whether you recognize the Elder; rather, it is enough that each of you knows your own native place.
In the autumn of the Wushen year of the Chunyou era (1248), the Master built a dwelling by the Moonlight Pond and inscribed its name as "Retiring from Plowing.

He requested retirement from the court, and at that time his chronic illness flared up again. On the first day of the third month, he ascended the hall and addressed the assembly, saying: "This mountain monk..."
Now old and ill, I lack the strength to engage in idle chatter with you all here and there.
Today, I have exerted myself to come forth and shall, with all my heart, shake out before you all that which I have not yet spoken of in the past.
He then rose and shook his robe, saying, "How much is there? On the fifteenth day, he assembled the two orders of monks to arrange for his final affairs, writing this personally.
He left behind several dozen posthumous memorials and letters; his speech and laughter were as they had always been.
When his disciples requested a final verse, he took up his brush and wrote rapidly: "When coming, empty and bare; when departing, naked and stripped. If you wish to ask for the ultimate truth—"
There was a stone bridge at Tiantai where he passed away after traveling for a short while. His remains were kept in the shrine for fourteen days.
The Emperor dispatched an imperial messenger to offer incense and bestow ceremonial silk. He was buried with his entire body beside Zhengxu, and his stupa was named Yuanzhao.
Master Jiaci Ji’ān of Yunju in Jiangzhou ascended the hall and said: "I cite the case where King Min asked Xuefeng, 'What if I wish to build a Buddha hall?
How about that? Feng replied, 'Great King, why not build a Hall of the Empty King instead?
The King said, 'Please show me the master’s model. Feng then opened his two hands. Yunmen said, 'One gesture, forty [years of] work.'"
Nine. The Master’s verse says: The model for the Hall of the Empty King; Xuefeng spreads his two hands wide. Adding to the old Shaoyang, He makes one move and there are forty-nine.
All are facing south to look at the Northern Dipper. In praise of the Venerable Boatman, he spoke this verse:
"Over thirty years at Yaoshan— How could the livelihood of ghosts ever be transmitted? Had it not been for Old Jia Shan at that time, You..."
Furthermore, how vexing it is to prop up and patch a leaking boat! Regarding the story of Chan Master Xiangsheng of Ye County: A monk asked, "What is the place where one applies the secret mind?
Xiangsheng said, "Rolling a ball in the bustling marketplace. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of this? Xiangsheng said, "Everyone is invited to watch together. The verse says:
Rolling a ball in the bustling market, everyone watches; A gust of clear wind blows across the face, chilling. To settle the chaos.
"A double-edged sword is unnecessary; why must one who revives others rely on the Nine-Return Elixir? The Master once traveled to Yunju and stayed overnight at the Yaotian Estate.
In a dream, the God of Peace and Bliss told him, "The Master has but the karmic connection for a single bowl of gruel on this mountain.

The next day after noon, having arrived at the mountain and finished the evening discourse, he went to the guest hall. There, two monks were fighting, and according to the custom for newcomers, they were expelled.
As he pursued [the thief], the Master privately marveled at this. Several years later, the seat at Yunju was vacant; by imperial decree, the Master was summoned to fill the position.
He joyfully accepted the command and recalled his previous dream. Upon arriving at the Yaotian estate, he passed away.
Chan Master Duan’an Daocou of Daci Monastery in Mingzhou presented this verse to a shoemaker: "The work of reaching the bottom has already been perfected;

One must know that the secret place is transmitted from one's own mind. The heel follows along as it turns upon the ground; Even if one were to tread until the year of the donkey, the shoe would still not be finished."
Chan Master Shitian Faxun of Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou was the son of the Peng family of Meishan. From birth, he was exceptionally intelligent and sensitive;

when he was three or four years old, upon seeing a Buddha or a monk, he immediately knew how to pay them respect. At the age of sixteen, he went to Danling to enter the monastic life under Zhiming at Falu Bao Temple on Mount Shilong.
At twenty-two, he shaved his head and received full ordination. He then traveled to various regions until he reached Shi... [text ends]
When Frost Rite (Śrāvaṇa) moved the stupa of Thunder (Vajrapāṇi), he composed a verse, saying: "A single thought of compassionate countenance is fundamentally never separated;

why must you suddenly act with such reckless defiance? To level the high and accommodate the low, your compassionate heart is urgent; it vexes Thunder God so that he is busy all night long. Because of this, the Master’s fame became widely renowned.
Having heard of the spiritual reputation of Chan Master Pò’ān Xiàn of Qiónglóng, he went there to pay his respects. Upon seeing him, Pò’ān recognized him as...
A vessel of the Dharma. In his room, he raised the story of the World-Honored One holding up a flower and Kāśyapa’s smile.
The Master said, "A burnt brick strikes and freezes through to the bottom; red-eyed one bumps into a firebrand. Wuzu was struck by this;

in every daily activity, whether speaking or remaining silent, the Master never made concessions. Thereupon, the Master resolved to stay and rely upon him, sharpening himself daily with Wuzhun Fayan. After a long time...
He took his leave and traveled extensively to the gates of various masters. Lingyin’s Songyuan Yue, Jingci’s Kentang Chong, Huazang’s Dun’an Yan, and Xian all praised him.
Later, he appeared in the world at Gaofeng in Suzhou; subsequently, he moved to Hanshan. When the seat at Zhongshan became vacant, the imperial court petitioned for the Master to fill the position.
In the first year of Baoping, he moved to Jingci, and in the second year of Duanping, he returned once more.

He moved to Lingyin Temple. Ascending the hall, he said: "One path straight; two paths circuitous. If a patch-robed monk understands this, there are ten thousand distinctions and a thousand differences.
Gazing idly at the courtyard before him, spring has ended yet flowers still remain. It was not fitting for the Old Barbarian [Bodhidharma] to cross the shifting sands.

He struck his knee once and then descended from the seat. Ascending the hall again, he said: "The essence of the Great Way is vast; it is neither easy nor difficult. Buying a hat by measuring the head—this land is the West."
The Master ascended the hall and said: "If you recognize your own mind, mountains and peaks will sink away. Grasping gold, it becomes earth; grasping earth, it becomes gold.

Before and behind one's feet, it is already a ready-made commodity. Yet, before the Peak of Shaoshi, it cannot be handed over or pointed out. He ascended the hall again and said: "There is jade within the stone, but no oil in the sand.
Deshan and Linji have not yet emerged from the common flow. I instead recall the son of Hanshan as he stands at an ancient ford."
[The Master] ascends the hall. Seeing, hearing, perceiving, knowing, walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—before you even raise a single eyebrow, you have already missed it.
Barefoot, he sings a mountain song; on the road, there is no one to join him. Ascending the hall, he locks the heavy barrier:
the lives of all of you are in the hands of this mountain monk. When he opens a single thread, the life of this mountain monk is in the hands of all of you. And now...
Neither fixed nor released: the mountain monk is you all, and you all are the mountain monk.
After thirty years, do not say that Jiangshan has merely mixed mud with water. To the assembly: even turning one’s body upon the edge of a sword is still dull.
"Seeking directions at the edge of a roof is utterly groundless; a chicken from Chu is not a phoenix from Mount Dan. Why must one preen its feathers against the wind?

On the fifteenth day of the third month in the Jiachen year of the Chunyou era, he addressed his disciples, saying: "If you only obtain the root, do not worry about the branches. What do you call the root? What do you call the branches?
A pine or cypress remains green for a thousand years, yet it does not enter the minds of those who follow the trends of the age. The peony..."
"The sun is red; the young masters throughout the city are drunk. If there is anyone who does not agree with this statement by me, the mountain monk, they are my fellow practitioners.
Disciple Shi Jun painted the Master’s portrait and requested a eulogy, which included the words: "The final phrase is entrusted to Chushan."
The assembly marveled at this. Previously, the Master had established a reception hall at Xixi called Baoshou. The following day, he suddenly manifested illness;

the day after that, he retired to Baoshou and directed his attendants to prepare for his final departure. He bid farewell to the assembly and passed away. His entire body was interred behind the monastery.
He was seventy-five years of age and fifty-three years since his ordination. The Master had successively occupied five renowned monasteries, serving for thirty years.

For two years, he managed affairs with frugality so that resources were sufficient; he scrutinized measurements and calculated labor so effectively that, despite undertaking grand construction projects, not even a single hair’s breadth of expense was imposed upon others, yet temples with their earthen structures, timber, gold, and lapis lazuli were completed everywhere.
Chan Master Mingzhou Tiantong Mie’weng Tianmu Wenli was a dharma heir of Chan Master Lingyin Yue. He was a native of Lin’an in Hangzhou, surnamed Ruan.
His family resided at the foot of Mount Tianmu, and he was also known as Tianmu. When the Master was six years old, he accompanied his mother, carrying a basket, to gather [mushrooms].
Sang suddenly wondered, "Who is it that carries me? and thus conceived the aspiration to leave the household life. At the age of sixteen, he took tonsure under Zhìyuè at Zhēnxiàng Monastery.
He went to Jìngcí to study with Huòyuán; when Huòyuán raised the "ready-made" kōan regarding the story of "letting you off thirty blows," Sang did not reach a point of resonance.
He then visited Yùwáng, where Fózào asked him, "For one who comes in such a manner, which one is your master?"

The Master attained public renown. One day, when Zhao asked about the monk who said, "It is not the wind moving, it is the banner moving," the Master replied, "When the object sees the master, the eye stands upright.
Zhao said, "If it is neither the wind moving nor the banner moving, where do you see the Patriarch?
The Master replied, "Lift off the skull-cap. Zhao rejoiced in his brilliance and dispatched him to serve as the Secretary. After a long time...
Upon his return to West Zhejiang, he went to Upper Tianzhu to study the threefold contemplation in one mind under [Zhili]. At that time, Songyuan Yue was proclaiming the Way at Jianfu in Raozhou;
in his meditation hall, he would strike a monk with his staff as soon as the monk hesitated upon being asked, "It is not the wind moving; it is not the banner moving."
Upon hearing this, the Master suddenly forgot all intellectual understanding and went to see him. He received the seal of approval and attained the full realization of the teaching’s intent.

Taking his leave, he traveled to pay homage at the ancestral pagodas throughout the Jianghuai region. At that time, Zeweng Yan, who was presiding over Jiangshan, invited the Master to serve as the Head Seat for the ordained monks.
In the fifth year of the Jiading era, Lord Zhang Cai of Yuezhai requested the Master to open a Dharma seat at Huiyun in Lin’an. [He lit] a single incense stick...
He became the successor to Songyuan. Subsequently, he moved to Nengren in Wenzhou, but before long, he retired to Xiqiu.
When Lord Jiezhai Zhao, admiring the Master’s lofty conduct, visited him incognito, the Master did not inquire after his name or rank, conversing with him all day before he departed.

The following day, the Emperor issued an edict appointing the Master as abbot of Jingci. In his meditation hall, he would frequently cite the bamboo shoots of the Southern Mountains and the [fish] of the Eastern Sea.

The "Mudfish Talks. When a student attempted to deliberate upon this, the Master struck him; there was no one who could find a foothold therein. Later, he moved to Fiquan and was promoted to serve as the abbot of Tiantong.
He ascended the hall and said: "The Dharma does not arise in isolation; it arises by depending on conditions. Since conditions do not arise, from where could the Dharma be established?
The Dragon Pool pours forth a thousand-foot waterfall—this is certainly not the condition. The Wild Goose Peak towers ten-thousand fathoms high in its cold majesty—this too is not the condition."

Furthermore, this is not the Dharma. When a monk with clear vision arrives here, what should he do? Even if he were bold and discerning, this mountain monk would break his staff and still not let him go.
Why? Because it is the sword that kills and the sword that gives life. Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "In every matter there is no obstruction;
green mountains are reflected beyond the setting sun. In every dharma there is no discrepancy; ancient trees before the eaves are filled with swarms of birds."
Crows! Do you not see? The Venerable Fu of Taiyuan traveled to the ends of the earth; at the fifth watch in Yangzhou, he heard the painted horn blowing the plum blossoms to their fall.
Even until this very day, he has not yet reached home. Ascending the hall, he cited the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*:
"All things that can be returned belong naturally to others; that which cannot be returned—what else could it be but you? He then offered this verse: "That which cannot be returned..."
Whose is this? Withered red petals drift upon the fishing rocks. The sun slants and the wind has stilled, yet no one sweeps them up;
swallows carry them away as they fly toward the water’s edge. On the Winter Solstice, ascending the hall: when the Huangzhong note first arises, one begins counting from the number nine.

Soon the orioles sing in the secluded valleys, followed by the swallows’ chatter upon the carved rafters. The village elders sacrifice to Goumang, and the drums of the community shrine are struck. The farmers—

The father dotes on the cowherd boy; the village maiden instructs the silkworm women. The light and time exhaust all people of the world; from the winter solstice to the Cold Food Festival is one hundred and five days.

On the anniversary of Chan Master Hongzhi’s passing, he ascended the hall and said: "Beyond the night-bright curtain, before the precious mirror hall, there is fundamentally nothing of 'both-and' nor anything of 'partial-or-whole.
At this very moment, who ultimately occupies the central position? There is no one at the ancient ferry."
The frosty moon is cold; the wind stilled among the reeds, the herons sleep. Entering the hall: The long-necked bird does not perch in the lofty trees but flies crosswise beyond the heavens.
The snout-nosed ox, having finished plowing the mountain fields, goes straight up to the peak. The patch-robed monks of the world cannot look up to him even enough.
Why? Because at Jiazhou, he struck the Great Elephant. Entering the hall: Master Touzi said, "If you go forward to meet him, you do not see him."
As for its beginning, one follows it without looking back at its end; it is much like Xu Liu carrying a single plank. Tiantong, however, is not so:
the higher one looks up, the more lofty it becomes; observing downward, it is not far away. A heron from Hengtang takes flight obliquely;
several silver vases hang from the tree’s waist. Entering the hall: Sentient beings have never been deluded; when the night ends, the rooster cries toward the fifth watch. The Buddhas have never...
Zengwu said: "In the clarity of autumn, geese cross the vast sky and depart. He struck his knee once and said: "Last night by the western window, the moonlight was bright;
the pure breeze has already reached the wutong trees. On the occasion of the Lantern Festival, he ascended the hall and said:
"Last night, Dharma Master Mokṣala universally lit lotus lamps to assist the radiance of the Buddha, until even the True Man of Good Faith lost his luster. The Dragon King Taibai emerged..."
"Come, let me tell you. Since the time of the Buddha Dragon-Species Supreme Honored King, I have dwelt on this mountain, yet I have never heard such news.
Thereupon, a flash of lightning struck from the sky, transforming into a tempest of black winds and torrential rain filling the heavens. Do you understand?
"I saw the original auspicious light of the Buddha Lamp-Brightness was like this. A monk asked Niu-tou: "Before you had seen the Fourth Patriarch..."
"How is it? The Master said, "Ox-head. [The monk] asked, "What is it like after seeing him? The Master said, "Ox-head, Ox-head. A monk asked, "How was it when you saw Foguo?
The Master said, "There is jade within the stone. [The monk] asked, "What was it like after seeing Songyuan? The Master said, "Ox-head, Ox-head."
The Master said, "There is no oil in the sand. A newly arrived monk entered the abbot’s quarters and said, "I have come to submit a formal petition to the Master.
The Master asked, "Where is the defendant? The monk replied, "The Master himself is the defendant. The Master said, "What grievance do I have against you, old man?
The monk was speechless. The Master seized him and said, "Wretched fellow! Wretched fellow! [Addressing] the newly arrived one...

The Master asked, "What is your name? The monk replied, "Zhihu (Wisdom Tiger). The Master stepped back and made a gesture of fear. The monk hesitated, and the Master immediately returned to his quarters.
The monk asked, "Observing the directions, one knows where they go; yet the one who goes does not arrive at any direction. What is the meaning of this?
The Master said, "In front, it does not reach the village; behind, it does not pass the inn. Foguang Fazhao was the first to rely upon the Master during the Liang dynasty.
Zhu. The Master ordered him to go down to Zhuzhou to visit Beifeng Yingshi, giving him this verse: "I send you off to seek the Vulture Peak; In most places, you will fall behind.
Since the time when differences were opened to return to sameness, The perfect purport has grown weary of being discoursed upon even now.
Discerning the realm clearly is the wondrous medicinal prescription; All other conceptual discriminations must be further forgotten. The evening wind blows it down."

Fragments of withered red petals—do not seek their former fragrance on the branches. To this day, the monastic community continues to recite [his teachings]. The Master was particularly profound in his mastery of the *I Ching*.
During the Qiánchún era, when various Confucian scholars greatly expounded upon Daoxue (Learning of the Way), the Master associated with them and directly revealed the Dharma of the Mind.
When Zhū Húiān asked about "Sincerity Without Failure," the Master joined his palms to demonstrate it. When Yáng Cíhú asked about "the Power of Non-Deception," the Master replied:
The verse says: "This power is clearly manifest in non-deception; how many people can truly know this non-deception?

To clarify the phrase that fully encompasses both the elephant and the hare, look at the moment he ascends the steps with his formal tablet. Such was the nature of the Master’s understanding of humanity.
Throughout the five monasteries he visited, he spent no more than eight or nine years in total; during the many years of leisure he had, he wandered idly by the banks of the Liang River.

At Xiqiu, when the assembly of monks came to pay their respects, it was no different from when he led the community. As he was about to enter nirvana, he said to his attendant, "Who will build a seamless stūpa for me?
The attendant asked, "Please, Master, give us the model for the stūpa. The Master remained silent for a long while and then said, "Even with all one's might, one cannot paint it.
Thereupon, he passed away with a serene expression. His disciples performed the cremation and collected the śarīra and remaining bones, which they enshrined in a burial site.
To the left of the stupa of Ying’an, he lived for eighty-four years and reached sixty-eight *xiè* (years since full ordination).
Chan Master Hilián of Shíyán on Jiānxīn Island in Wēnzhōu was the son of the Mǎ family from Cháoyáng.

He ascended the hall and, citing the occasion when Chan Master Guǎnghuì Lián was engaged in a late-night conversation with Fúyáng Gōng, the Director of the Bureau of Sacrifices, said: "Director Fúyáng, with whom have you ever [discussed]..."
When the official brought up this story, he said, "I once asked Chan Master Liang of Yunyan, 'What is it like when two tigers bite each other?
Liang replied, 'A single unified form. I said, 'I have been watching this; I wonder if speaking in such a way is truly correct?
Huai said, 'It is not so here. The official requested, 'Please, Master, give me another turn of phrase. Huai [replied]..."
Making a gesture of pulling up his nose with his hand, he said, "This beast is leaping about even more! Under these words, the Official was suddenly liberated from doubt.
He spoke a verse: "An octagonal millstone runs through the void; A golden-maned lion transforms into a dog.
If you wish to hide your body within the Big Dipper, You must join your palms before the Southern Star. The Master said, "The Inner Secretary clings to the Southern Star and leans upon..."
The Northern Dipper: Broad Wisdom turns the celestial pivot and overturns the terrestrial axis. Vast and silent through the ages, who can know it?

A severed string must be mended with *luang-jiao* glue. A monk asked: "In the past, when Zen Master Fozhao Guang was questioned by Emperor Xiaozong of the Song Dynasty, 'What did Śākyamuni Buddha accomplish during his six years in the mountains?
Guang replied, 'I thought Your Majesty had forgotten. What is the meaning of this?"
"How is it? The Master answered with a verse: "Great root, great vessel, great cultivation; The pivot of the mechanism turns toward the ultimate.
Throughout ten billion years there is but one Buddha; The Snowy Mountains have never separated the Dragon Palace."

Chan Master Yunchao Yan of Ruayan in Taizhou composed a verse on the character “米” (mi) [composed of 木 + 八] as a title for a sutra, saying: “The character ‘米’ is not formed; the eight strokes are not there.
Held up directly before the sun, everyone knows it. Old Śākyamuni has no bone in his tongue; He takes yellow leaves to frighten small children.
He also offered a verse on the story of Lingyun seeing the peach blossoms, saying: “In the third month, the peach blossoms are in full, ruddy bloom. Lingyun..."
The clouds have struck down the master; following the heterodox and pursuing evil, the old man Xuansha was half sincere and half empty.
At the Qingmiao Assembly, Chan Master Juetong of Huazang ascended the hall and said: "Breaking open a single mote of dust, one brings forth the Great Sūtra."
The soaring hawks and leaping fish are even more distinct. Do not look with the eyes; look with the mind. This is already like repeatedly striking ice within fire.
Soaking black beans—this has obscured my lifelong practice. One must speak of a bountiful harvest beyond the kalpas. When the white snow is spun, the mulberry trees turn green again;
when the yellow clouds are harvested, the rice stalks are still green.
Chan Master Guoyuan Dao of Jingci Temple in Hangzhou cited the public case of Danxia Tianran’s initial visit to Shitou, regarding the weeding of the grass before the Buddha Hall.
He offered this verse: Shitou weeds the grass to test the heroes; Stupefied Danxia’s eyes were not high.
If one understands how to turn the body and walk the path of life, one should not trouble one’s descendants to this day.
Chan Master Wuxin of Beihai at Daochang Monastery in Huzhou cited the following:

Once, when Huangbo was prostrating before the Buddha in the hall of Yanguan, Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty, who was then a śrāmaṇera, asked: "Not seeking by relying on the Buddha, not seeking by relying on the Dharma, not seeking..."

Sengqiu said, "Venerable sir, when one prostrates, what is it that one seeks? Baizhang replied, "Do not seek by clinging to the Buddha; do not seek by clinging to the Dharma; do not seek by clinging to the Sangha.
Always perform your prostrations in this manner. Sengmi asked, "What is the purpose of performing prostrations?
Baizhang then struck him. Sengmi said, "That was too crude. Baizhang said, "What kind of place is this where you speak of 'crude' and 'refined'? He struck him again immediately after saying this.

The verse says: "Once he offered three handfuls of grain as tribute to the Sovereign; What inch of growth has the Buddha-Dharma ever shown? This coarse monk has sealed off the boundaries of the world;
To this day, there is no ground upon which to stand in shame. This recounts the story of the clam (*śukti*) involving Emperor Wenzong of the Tang dynasty. The verse says:
Mixing water with mud—how busy with such trivial matters! He has pierced through it all, yet remains utterly perverse.
Though he may indeed grasp the Emperor’s intent, alas, his entire body is plunged into the cauldron of boiling oil.
Chan Master Daxie Zhongqian of Xuedou in Mingzhou was the son of the Ying family of Yiwu.

In his youth, upon seeing the *Mind-King Inscription* by Master Fu Dashi, he resolved to leave the household life. He first visited Xianan, who, though recognizing his potential, suppressed him, saying:
"If you do not eliminate your scholarly habits as a Confucian, how can you study the Way? To reach the state of Great Rest and Great Cessation, you must be like a wooden puppet."
Having departed, the Master was inspired by this exhortation and redoubled his efforts, applying himself with unwavering diligence morning and night.
One day, he suddenly attained a realization and thereafter named his practice "Great Rest" (*Dàxiē*). Later, he relied upon Songyuan Yue;

one day, while in the meditation hall, Songyuan raised the koan of Bimozhe holding a fork, and the Master attained a sudden and great enlightenment. He then ascended the hall and, citing the words of Master Ying’an who asked Miaman, "What is..."
Regarding "The Eye of the True Dharma," Muzhou said, "A broken sandpot. He spoke in verse: "A white jade ball carved from clay, A golden iron K'un-lun cast from ore.
This merchandise of a thousand years no one buys; It cannot avoid burdening descendants today.
The verse for sending off the Rector says: "Xinghua struck Kebin in those days; The story remains a talk in the monasteries for a thousand years. The clouds are yellow..."
Set the staff aside for now; simply brew some tea and send it out the door.
Chan Master Zhao of Nuohan cited Songyuan’s instruction to the assembly: “Why do bright-eyed monks lose their nostrils?
This is like having a thief but no stolen goods. Verse: “One kills ten thousand, yet loses three thousand; Solely wielding the single-pointed pivot.”
Incomplete. "Ten thousand acres of blue waves on a bright moonlit night; a single blast of the short flute from a fishing boat.
The inscription for the Second Patriarch’s portrait reads: "Seeking the mind, finding no place—self-deception in vain. Willingly enduring the cold of snow waist-deep.

Rising after three prostrations and standing in his place—who would have known that the entire world is a surging wave? The verse for reminiscing about Huating says: "The entirety of one's livelihood..."

The Fishing Boat: As soon as the scaled fish enters the hand, the hook is withdrawn. I have come, yet I do not behold the Master’s personal instruction; Willow banks linger, dipping into the azure current.
Chan Master Yun’an Puyan of Daochang Monastery in Huzhou inscribed this eulogy for the portrait of Zhaozhou: "Pointlessly he raises it up..."
The Seven-Pound Coat. How many Zen practitioners have applied their minds to this? They all make their nests in Qingzhou, unaware that the spring colors lie in Jiangnan.
[The Master] cites the koan of Dongshan eating fruit on a winter night and offers this verse: Dongshan brought disgrace upon his family tradition;
The Head Seat buried his own potential. Together they embroidered the mandarin ducks, Yet for a thousand ages it remains unsupported.
Chan Master Jili Tan first resided at Yanqing in Siming. He subsequently moved to Qionglong, Zhenze Pujie, Ganlu in Zhenjiang, and Changlu in Zhenzhou.
Later, he arrived at Huqiu. Ascending the hall, he raised the following case:
A monk asked Xianglin, "What is the matter beneath the patched robe? Xianglin said, "In the twelfth month, fire burns the mountains. The Master said, "A rabbit..."
How could you ever leave this cave? If someone asks Yankeng, "What is the matter beneath the patched robe?

simply answer him: "The fish bought on the boat is especially delicious; the wine purchased while treading through the snow is doubly fragrant. Entering the hall, [he said: "In every thought-moment is the appearance of Śākyamuni;
at every moment is the descent of Maitreya. This instantly transcends the time before heaven and earth were yet divided. Not...
Having ascended the steps and overturned the treasure-store, if one simply proceeds in this manner, one can open immeasurable Dharma-gates and expound hundreds of thousands of wondrous meanings.
[The Master] suddenly picked up his staff and struck it once: "Immeasurable Dharma-gates and hundreds of thousands of wondrous meanings are all completely shattered here.
Do you know where Huqiu has landed? [The Master] leaned on his staff. Ancestor.
You do not understand; the calamity will extend to your descendants. Regarding the verse on Lingyun’s encounter with the peach blossoms, it says: "Peach blossoms bloom everywhere in the third month;
Lingyun’s two eyes are filled with dust and grime. Xie Lang readjusts his hands for catching the giant turtle;
He cannot avoid burying himself once more."
Chan Master Guangmu of Shaoshi at Ruiyan in Taizhou ascended the hall. He cited the case of Chan Master Xiang of Caoshan:
once, while a monk was standing in attendance, Caoshan said, "The Way-farer, it is quite hot. The monk replied, "Yes. Caoshan asked, "As for this heat, where do you go to avoid it?
The monk replied, "I avoid it within the boiling cauldrons and the burning furnaces. Caoshan then asked, "As for those boiling cauldrons and burning furnaces..."
"How do you avoid it from within? [The monk] said, "The various sufferings cannot reach him. The Master composed a verse: "The three eyes on the crown of the head are blinded;
One wanders freely amidst boiling cauldrons and burning coals. If one says the various sufferings cannot reach him, Where, in truth, has he ever had a place to stand?
He inscribed a eulogy for the portrait of the Fourth Patriarch: "Purple clouds fly atop Mount Pòtóu; Three times he declined the Heavenly..."
Inscription for Old Cuimei: "Though these stagnant goods have no practical use, they should not be handed over to a small child.
Chan Master Shan Kai of the Yanshi Hall at Mount Jinshan in Zhenjiang Prefecture ascended the hall and raised the story of Mian’s "Broken Sand Pot."
The Verse says: Fayan brought it forth and immediately deceived himself; Without cause, he mistakenly matched it to a broken sand-pot. Now it pervades the entire world, impossible to conceal;
It brings calamity upon the monastic grove and its descendants.
Chan Master Wuxiang Fan of Xuedou in Mingzhou ascended the hall and said: "Venerable Zhaozhou once remarked, 'As soon as there is right and wrong, confusion arises and the mind is lost.
Is there even any possibility of answering? A monk reported this to Luopu, who tapped his teeth."
He then recounted this to Yunju. Yunju said, "Why bother? The monk returned and recounted it to Zhaozhou.
Zhaozhou said, "In the south, many have lost their lives. The monk said, "Please, Master, give an example.

Zhaozhou was just about to repeat the previous story when the monk pointed to a monk nearby and said, "This monk, having finished his meal, speaks such words as these. The Master [Zhaozhou] composed a verse, which begins: "Sitting..."
Those standing see those sitting; those sitting see those standing. Alas, old Zhaozhou! Seeing ghosts with one's own eyes in broad daylight.
The Layman Lu You, styled Wuguan and nicknamed Fangong, was a native of Shanyin.
He once visited Master Songyuan at Lingyin Temple and asked with composure, "May I hear about the study of mind-to-mind transmission? Songyuan replied, "Since it is already..."
"How can the mind-transmission be obtained through hearing? Layman Dian nodded in silent understanding and presented this verse:

"Several times I have driven my carriage into the imperial capital, Meeting monks, my eyes were equally clear upon them all. Today, for the first time, I see the distinction of the Zen school: To speak of 'existence' or 'non-existence' requires one to listen with the eye."
Chan Master Chijue Daochong of Mount Jing in Hangzhou was a successor of Chan Master Jianfu Sheng. He was the son of Xun of Changjiang in Wuxin; his mother was Guo.

From birth, he was broad-shouldered and short-statured, and his natural disposition far surpassed that of ordinary men. When he grew older, he attempted the imperial examinations through the jinshi curriculum but was unsuccessful. Thereupon, he...
He received his formal training from Xiuzheng at Miaoyin Monastery in Zizhou. He traveled to the lecture halls in Chengdu to study the sutras and śāstras.
In the *Renzi* year of the Shaoxi era (1192), he left the gorges and traveled through the regions of Jing and Chu. At that time, Songyuan Yue was preaching the Way at Jianfu Monastery in Raozhou;
the Master went to pay his respects, but Songyuan would not accept him due to a famine. Later, when Caoyuan Sheng appeared in the world at Miaoguo Monastery, the Master went there to see him.

Upon hearing the words of instruction for entering the gate, he attained realization. He was assigned to serve as the incense attendant in the hall, where the Master’s morning and evening blows of the heavy fist and painful staff were never withheld.
Consequently, much of his lifelong views and knowledge became devoid of any lingering trace or influence. When Cao Yuan moved to Gui Peak, the Master attended him there.
After another three years, he took leave to travel to Zhejiang with a verse, which said: "I still have this pair of hands, the mark of a pauper; I shall now head toward all quarters."
He scratched where it itched. Upon arriving in the capital, he encountered Songyuan, who was presiding over Lingyin Monastery; the Master again relied upon him there.
In the Jia-di Ji-mao year (1219), having served as the first seat (*di-yi zuo*) at Mount Jing, he accepted an invitation from Guangxiao Monastery in Jiahe.
He became a dharma heir of Caoyuan. At that time, Cican Yuanjue, Jianfeng Yuanwuxiang, Fan Shixi Yue, and others were all present within the assembly. This news spread throughout the land.
In the morning, Zhongxian Prince Wei was appointed to the position at Jiangshan by imperial decree. The various estates of Jiangshan all border the river and are prone to flooding;

consequently, the low-lying fields frequently yield no autumn harvests. The Master endured hunger and proclaimed the Way, begging for alms to support his disciples. For thirteen years, he showed no sign of weariness.
In the Jiaxi year, the year Jihai (1259), Minister Dongquan Cao Bīn was the Governor of Fuzhou. Having heard of the Master’s reputation and spiritual influence, [he invited him].
Gushan sent an invitation, but before he could depart, a summons from Xuefeng arrived. Having served for half a year, the imperial decree for Tiantong was issued.
