The assembly gathered like the sea; as the seat at Yuyang was vacant, he assumed the duties of abbot. Moving between the two mountains, he ascended the hall and said:
"What Tiantong used here does not apply at Yuyang; what Yuyang uses there does not apply at Tiantong. Nevertheless..."

This is it. To act where there is no place for action to be applied is to have a surplus of function; a single arrow brings down two vultures, falling at the hand’s touch. Upon ascending the hall for the Summer Retreat:
in the monastery of Perfect Enlightenment (*Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*), every mote of dust has its own path. Seizing the coming and going, one suddenly empties past and present.
Where is that "thirteenth" beyond the "fifteenth"? Before and after do not differ by even a hair’s breadth. How laughable that the Yellow-faced Gautama remains, even to this day, unaware!
[The Master] ascends the hall. "There is one person who, in a single thought-moment, attains sudden realization and falls into the ranks of the Buddhas.
There is another person who, for kalpas on end, remains an icchantika and has no wish to become a Buddha. Tell me, which of these two is worthy of receiving the offerings of devas and humans?

After a long silence, he said: "A butterfly pierces the fragrant path, its two brows damp; a bee plunders the withered blossoms, its two thighs stout. [He] ascends the hall. "Throughout the entire universe and the great earth..."

"Not even so much as a hair's breadth. Yet you all carry your staffs across your shoulders and travel on pilgrimage throughout the four continents, claiming, "There is nowhere we have not been and nothing we do not know.
But tell me: what Dharma did the Master Śīlabhadra at Nālandā Monastery in India preach today?
Having said this, he descended from his seat. He ascended the hall. A monk asked: "Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—"
[The student asked: "There are three [minds], yet they are without distinction. What is the past mind? The Master said: "Set it down and wait for it to cool, then come look at it.
[The student asked: "What is the present mind? The Master said: "You ask and I answer. [The student asked:

"What is the future mind? The Master said: "I will tell you when I ascend the hall next time. [The student asked: "What is the Buddha of the past? The Master said: "Last year’s plum blossoms. [The student asked: "What about..."
"What is the Buddha of the present? The Master said, "The willows of this year. "How is the Buddha of the future?
The Master said, "His countenance and fragrance remain as they were. "What is the wisdom of differentiation of the past? The Master struck the left side of the meditation seat with his whisk.
"What is the wisdom of differentiation of the present? The Master struck the right side of the meditation seat with his whisk.
[The monk] asked, "What is the wisdom of future differentiation? The Master pointed a single dot in the center of his whisk.
The monk said, "Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings have no turning away; the oceans of lands in the ten directions are contained within a single hair. He then prostrated. The Master said:
The past mind cannot be apprehended; the present mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind cannot be apprehended.
Since the three periods of time are thus unapprehendable, what can be called "discriminating wisdom"?

If one perceives this thoroughly, the Buddhas of the three periods have never for a single moment not been turning the Great Dharma Wheel upon the crowns of everyone’s heads. Come here and test it further!

"Shoulders side by side, feet together—what is there to seek in a bowl? He descended from his seat and struck everyone at once with his staff to disperse them. Not long after, he was summoned by imperial decree to move to Mount Jing.
One day, he suddenly ascended the seat to take his leave of the assembly and cited the World-Honored One’s words as he was about to enter nirvana, saying to the multitude:
"You all should carefully observe my body, which is the color of purple-polished gold. Gaze upon it until you are fully satisfied; do not let yourselves regret it later.
Today there is, but tomorrow there will be no more. The Master said, "For forty-nine years, the World-Honored One exhausted every skill and artifice.
Yet when the time for his departure arrived, he could not find life when seeking it, nor could he find death when seeking it. As for this mountain monk, today when I wish to go, I simply go."
When it was time for his departure, he simply went; even the eight-armed Nātha could not stop him. At the hour of midnight, he rose from his seat and passed away within a short while.
He was eighty-two years of age and sixty-one years since his ordination. Upon cremation, there were countless relics of five colors.
In accordance with his final instructions, his remains were enshrined at Yushan Hermitage in Jinling. His disciples divided them, and half were interred in a stupa at Changpu Field.

Zen Master Qingxi Yuan of Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou, successor to Zen Master Tian Tong Jing, ascended the hall and said: "When Bodhidharma came from the West, he occupied the entire ground of one sitting mat.
After Shen Guang paid him three prostrations, it was all claimed at once. This has caused the descendants of later generations to each divide it up for themselves."
The boundaries are clearly demarcated. Monks of our tradition brush aside the weeds and observe the wind, traveling from Wu to Yue morning and evening; from South Tian Tai to North Wutai.
Have you ever trodden upon the tip of the staff or the sole of the shoe? After a long silence, he said: "Above all, do not tread upon it."
Chan Master Xixi Xi of Gong’an in Jingzhou ascended the hall and said: “Mind upon mind, where it seems shallow, is in truth most profound;

Way after way, so deep and remote, no one can reach it. If you walk too fast, you will not tread upon it; If you walk too slow, you will miss the mark. At Shaolin, he sat through many springs of flowering trees;
Yet he still yearned for the Western-come Hu Daomo.”
Chan Master Yuantong of Xichan Monastery in Fuzhou ascended the hall for the opening of the furnace. "Everyone guards the sky within the jar;
though earth may overturn and heaven may turn, I do not think so. With one direct blow, sparks fly forth; the Luojiang River has burned the boat of Master Xie. In praise of Monk Zhoutou, he said:
"Bloody and gory—this is the heart-mind of the ancient Buddha. How many times has it been raised up? Who is there to know?"
Yinming. Chan Master Jichuang Youzhao of Yuwang Monastery in Mingzhou was the son of the Deng family of Fuzhou, Min County. He received full ordination under Master Hui of Jiufeng Rong’an.
At that time, Kuchan was propagating the Way at Yishan; the Master went there to visit him. One day, Kuchan... [text fragment] ...said: "Chan..."
A questioner asked, "Ever since the first time I saw the peach blossoms, until now I have had no further doubts. Where exactly is it that he has no doubts?
The Master laughed loudly and walked out. Chanshen approved of this. Later, Chanyuan succeeded him at Lingyin Monastery, where the Master served as the head of the inner records.
Subsequently, he visited Dameishiyan, Huqiu, Jili, Maofeng Wuzhun, Jingshan, and Dayue; all these venerable elders held him in high esteem.
To care for his aged mother, he returned home to visit her. Xuefeng Chijue retained him to serve as the head of the secretariat (*kaji*).
The Governor of Min, Zhao Gong Ruyou, was well-acquainted with the Master’s reputation and invited him to open a Dharma seat at Dongshan Dacheng, later moving to Huangbo in Fuzhou.
At that time, Lin Xiyi, the Left Historian (Zuoshi), followed the Master to discuss the Dharma of the Mind. With sincere devotion, he took the teachings to heart. He composed a poem which says:
"In my old age, I have found a friend like the Master; having been parted from him for so long, who else could accompany me in my leisure? By imperial decree, I am now to be appointed to Jiangxin."
Later, when the Imperial Bed (Yujì) was moved and a natural disaster occurred, he exerted all his strength to restore it. He visited the Chancellor, Duke Jia, and petitioned the imperial court;
consequently, gold, silk, and bronze were granted to construct a precious *śarīra* stupa. A monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "The Eight Auspicious Ones.
The monk asked, "What is the Dharma? The Master said, "The Six Excellences. The monk asked, "What is the Sangha? The Master said, "Face and features."
Now, ascending the hall: The six sense-objects are not evil; they are identical to perfect enlightenment. The crow caws, "ka ka"; the magpie shrieks, "jiao jiao.
North of the river and south of the river, the tide rises and falls. In the third month, the spring breeze makes the flowers and grasses fragrant.
Where does Sudhana seek the pavilions? *Pah!* Ascending the hall: What is the Way? A piece of wood. What is Chan? A brick. The ancient masters...
What a marvelous instruction! Ten pairs of five [monks] remain placidly unconcerned, yet they do not realize that they are precisely scratching the itchy spot of Mount Mao.
Why? Because when constructing a temple, this is exactly what is required.
Chan Master Zhigu of Fashi in Quanzhou spoke these verses on mountain dwelling: "My saffron robe, dyed chestnut-brown, is tied with a thousand or ten hundred knots;

Leaning against a pine, I stroke my belly and watch the clouds fly by. When someone asks me about the purpose of my mountain life, I tell them: 'The spring is deep, and the bamboo shoots and ferns are lush.'"
Master Baoneng Taigu ascended the hall and said: "If one discusses this matter, it does not involve the workings of thought or intention;
it is not a matter of silent illumination or the forgetting of the self. To attain a state of transparent clarity, one must undergo a 'pouring of sweat.

But tell me, what is it like after the sweat has been poured? Suddenly, he called to his attendant, "Bring me the fan! He then ascended the hall [and continued]: "The night is cold and the frost is heavy; the wind..."
The coming cold will be even greater. As the seasons pass by in this habitual way, how is one’s own matter? [He] pats the meditation seat.

To those who are not true connoisseurs, how can it be presented to them? He ascends the hall and says: "Members of the monastic community travel abroad and wander on foot, parting the grass and observing the wind."
First, one must recognize the path; only then can one proceed. If the path is not mistaken, east, west, south, and north are all home.
Should one stray even slightly into detours, there will be single tablets every five *li* and double markers every ten *li*. "Where is it? Where is it?
Cast down the staff and look beneath your feet.
Chan Master Choun Weng’s verse on the Buddha’s Birthday says: The poisonous seeds of Vairambha wind have blossomed into toxic flowers;
They add but one more cup to Yunmen’s drunken draught. Today at Keqiao, the weather turns foul; Thin mist and sparse rain wash away the yellow plum. (Note:
This verse is recorded in the *Zadu hai* as being composed by Xiyuan, but that is an error.)

Chan Master Shuangshan Yuan of Tiger Hill in Suzhou, a successor of Chan Master Yinjing Rou, cited the account of Emperor Taizong of the Song dynasty who dreamed of a divine being exhorting him to arouse the bodhicitta.

The following day, the Emperor asked his court ministers, "How does one arouse the bodhicitta? None of the ministers could respond. Xuedou provided this substitute response on their behalf: "O Great Emperor, you have already aroused it."

It was said that this was truly something rarely heard in antiquity or the present. Biefeng Yin said in his time, "The words of the King are like a fine thread, yet what issues from them is like a thick cord.
The Master composed a verse: "Ten thousand miles of songs celebrate the Sage’s transformation; Gentle breezes and drizzling rain delight the woodcutters and farmers.
Were it not for the three cries at Mount Song, Who would know true peace in its formless state? Regarding the murals on the two corridors of Lingquan, he composed a verse: "One..."
Within a single mote of dust lies the firm and dense body; changing heads and faces, it transforms its spirit.
Who would have known that striking the west wall is none other than those who gathered on Vulture Peak?

Chan Master Xuanzhuo Yuanse Xingduan of Jingshan in Hangzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Fozhao Wuzhen of Mount Jing. He was of the He clan of Linhai, whose family had followed the Confucian profession for generations.
His mother was Lady Chen. From birth, he was exceptionally gifted; as a youth, he abstained from meat. At the age of twelve, he followed his paternal cousin, the Venerable Maoshang.
He received ordination at Huacheng Monastery in Yuhang at the age of eighteen. He mastered all written characters without being taught by a teacher.
Initially, he visited Zang-sou at Mount Jing; when Zang asked him where he was from, the Master replied, "Taizhou. Zang then gave a shout.
The Master spread out his sitting mat. The Old Man shouted again. The Master folded up his sitting mat. The Old Man said, "I grant you thirty blows; go to the meditation hall.
At these words, the Master attained sudden enlightenment. One day, while standing in attendance, the Old Man said, "There are no monks in Southern Quan.
The Master asked, "What about you, Preceptor? The Old Man struck him. The Master seized the staff and said, "Do not say there are no monks here! The Old Man nodded in approval.
He was appointed to serve in the Imperial Secretariat. Upon the passing of the Elder [Zhao Mengfu], the Master went to Jingci Temple to rely on Shilin Gong as his secretary (*jishi*).
The Master once referred to himself as a fellow villager of Han and Shi. When Hengchuan Yonggong resided at Yuwang Temple, he invited the Master with a verse, saying:
"Vast and empty between heaven and earth, there is only the son of Hanshan. The Master ultimately did not cross the river; instead, he visited Jue’an Zhen at Chengtian Temple.
Later, Tian went to Mount Yang to visit Xueyan Qin. Xueyan asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From the Two Zhe regions.
Xueyan said, "Why is your accent different? The Master said, "Shut that stinking mouth! Xueyan said, "The Tadaping Bridge is high and the Jiyun Peak is steep;
I do not yet recognize you as a secretary (monk). The Master clapped his hands and said, "A duck swallows a snail; its eyes pop out! Xueyan [laughed].

He smiled and looked toward his attendant to have fine tea brought. The Master said, "There is no need for this. After three years, Yan passed away, whereupon he returned to the region south of the Zhejiang River.
Jing Mountain requested that he occupy the position of First Seat. In the year of Great Virtue, Gengzi, he took up residence at Zifu Temple in Huzhou.
By special imperial decree, he was granted the title Chan Master Huiwen Zhengbian. He was sponsored by Zhang Lü, the Minister of the Secretariat.

He served as the Director of the Xingxuan Yuan. He was the first to recommend the Master for the position of Abbot of Zhongtianzhu. On the day of the opening of the hall, the Duke personally led his subordinates to pay their respects at the Master’s seat.
In the Renzi year of Huangqing, he moved to Lingyin Monastery; by imperial decree, a Water and Land Great Assembly was established at Jinshan.

He commanded the Master to ascend the seat and preach the Dharma. When the matter was concluded, he entered the imperial presence for an audience and was granted the honorary title "Buddha-Sun Shining Universally" (Furi Puzhao).

Taking his leave of the Emperor, he returned south to raise his parents in retirement at Xiqiu on Liangzhu. In the year of Renxu of the Zhizhi era, the seat of Jing Mountain being vacant, the Master was invited to fill the position.

The Master was thrice bestowed with the gift of gold-embroidered robes. For twenty years, his feet did not cross the threshold of his door, yet those who admired his Way gathered like fish scales until there was no room for them.
A monk asked, "What is the Eye of the True Dharma? The Master said, "A stone *gandang* at the crossroads.
The monk asked, "Is it just this? The Master said, "The moon is like a drawn bow; little rain, much wind. (From the *Wudeng Huiyuan*)
The Hall Master raised the case: A monk asked Zhaozhou, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature? Zhaozhou said, "No. Another monk asked, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature?
Zhaozhou said, "Yes. The Master said: "If you take 'no' as the ultimate, why did he later say 'yes'?
If you take 'yes' as the truth, why did he previously say 'no'? Here, one must seize upon it."

"Defeating Zhaozhou—this I grant you, heaven above and heaven below. Entering the hall, he said: "The mind is not the Buddha; rabbits and horses have horns. Wisdom is not the Way; oxen and sheep have no horns.
Suddenly picking up his staff and drawing a line with it, he said: "One night a rain of falling flowers; the flowing water fills the stream with fragrance.
Entering the hall, he said: "Autumn winds are cool; autumn nights are long. The traveler who has not yet returned thinks of his hometown. He struck the meditation seat.
The Bed: From this point on, there is no returning; once one returns, it is attained. Who can compete for the misty scenery of the Five Lakes?
Ascending the Hall: At the frontier garrisons, the horns blare at dawn; in the empty mountains, the evening bell answers. Everyone hears them together; where is there not universal penetration?

Ascending the Hall to thank the Supervisor of Collections, the Master of the Bath, and the Rector on the Lantern Festival: A thousand grains and ten thousand grains are born from a single grain. It is just this one...
From what place does a single grain arise? A thousand lamps and ten thousand lamps all originate from a single lamp; yet from where does that one lamp itself arise?

Once you recognize this one lamp, you will have no doubts regarding the lamp after lamp throughout a thousand and ten thousand lamps. Once you recognize this one grain, you will find no obstruction among the thousand and ten thousand grains.
A three-legged donkey trots about, kicking up its hooves and trampling through the boundless seas of fragrant water.
"Hai! [The Master] picked up his staff and struck once. "Even at the crown of your head, you cannot do without this one blow.
The Master once tested a newly arrived monk, saying, "Where do you come from, O Sage? From what place do you come, O Spirit? The monk said, "Lin-zhen-zen.
The Master said, "Ill-informed Chan practitioners are as numerous as hemp and millet. Go to the meditation hall! He also tested another monk, saying, "The Chessboard Rock will split you apart."
"Your skull! This bowl-basin will soak and rot your soles! The monk prepared to answer, but the Master gave a shout. Again, he interrogated another monk, saying:
"The Hua-yue Mountains split open, revealing their sky-reaching splendor; the Yellow River is released, flowing clear to its very bottom—let that be for now.
On the ground of plain reality, bring forth a single phrase! The monk prepared to open his mouth, but the Master struck him. The Master thus used scolding, rage, and abuse.

He offered compassionate and guiding instructions, acting contrary to worldly sentiment to practice the Way of Great Publicity. His benefit for others was entirely performed in secret; until the end of his life, he never spoke of it.

The Master was born in the year of Yimao (1255) during the Baoyu era of the Song dynasty. On the fourth day of the eighth month of the Xinsi year of the Zhi Zheng era (1361), he manifested a slight illness.
Having bathed and changed his robes, he wrote a verse of farewell to the assembly, saying: "Fundamentally, there is neither birth nor extinction."
How could there be coming or going? The icy river blazes with flames; the iron trees bloom with flowers. He cast down his writing brush, suspended one leg, and passed away.

His shrine remained for seven days, his countenance appearing as if alive. At the age of eighty-eight and with seventy-six years of monastic seniority, on the eleventh day of this month, his entire body was enshrined for burial in the Jizhao Pagoda Cloister.

Chan Master Yishan Liaowan of Jiangxin Temple in Wenzhou was a dharma heir of Chan Master Jingci Ying. He was of the Jin clan from Linchuan. Though his appearance was thin and frail, at the age of fifteen he gained renown for his proficiency in the formal examination essays;
nevertheless, his long-standing aspiration was to leave the household life. Upon reaching the age of twenty, he followed [Master Chang] at Changle Monastery in Jinxia.

When Sishi Ren shaved his head, miraculous *lingzhi* mushrooms suddenly grew from the pivot of his door. Later, when he traveled to various regions, he visited Yianxi Wen, Jing’ou Jue, and Jianweng Jing;
all these masters were in perfect accord with him. When Dong’ou took charge of Nanping, he appointed the Master as the head scribe (*shuji*).

Once, while passing by a shrine, he saw paper ashes rising up; he was suddenly liberated and forgot what he had realized. He immediately informed an elder, who questioned him, and he subsequently received his seal of approval (*inka*).
He traveled to Tiantai, where the assembly requested that he open the Dharma at Han Rock. He offered incense as the successor to Dongsou.

After more than three years, he moved to Zhituo in Xianju; ten years later, he moved to Shushan. When the local authorities discussed matters with him and they did not harmonize, he struck [the drum] and departed.

He retired. Not long after, the General Superintendent of Jianghuai convened the abbots of various mountains to welcome the Master to Kaixian. Upon his arrival, he took charge of the affairs, and the monastic community was renovated.
Ten years later, he ascended to the abbacy of Jiangxin. After a short time, feeling somewhat dissatisfied, he again abruptly departed.

Several hundred members of the monastery earnestly entreated him to remain; they followed him as far as Fenggong Ridge, each weeping as they parted. There, he met the Venerable Yuejian Ming of Mount Lu.
A boat was sent to welcome the Master back to Dongxi. When Master Ming passed away, the community at Kaixian requested him once more;

the Master initially declined, but the assembly pleaded so earnestly that they asked no longer for him to take charge of temple affairs, only beseeching him to instruct their disciples. He ascended the hall and said: "Silent and still."

In a state of great bustle, there is no involvement with the rungs of the ladder at all; one has already trodden the path that transcends. Ten thousand miles, not a single inch of grass—yet once you step out the door, it is all grass.
You collide with the wood-seller, who is none other than the old man who plants pine trees. Upon the crystal palace, the moon is full and round.
The sun shines brightly atop the coral branches. [He] ascends the hall and says: "If one encounters Yao or Shun, one presents the canons and maxims;
this is how one establishes a livelihood. If one meets Jie or Zhou, one employs execution and conquest; this is how one sweeps away all old nests and traps.
We people are dry and withered, firm and tough, pure and naked, bright and clear. When have we ever had so many complications? It is truly strange that Old Man Muzhou, upon seeing a monk..."
As soon as you enter the gate, I say that for this "ready-made" kōan, I grant you thirty blows. Look closely, however, and it is merely a desperate stratagem born of extremity.
Entering the hall, he took up his staff and said: "This staff—four or seven in India, two or three in this land."
The old monks of the world could not bring it forth; today it has fallen into the hands of Kaixian. Without beginning and without end, it can be released and gathered in;
detached from form and detached from name, it can be let loose and seized. Although this is so, it is only for those of middling and lower capacity.
What if a person of the highest caliber were to suddenly arrive? (He draws a line with his staff) and releases [the matter].
After one more year had passed, on the twenty-sixth day of the eleventh month of the first year of the Huangqing era, he fell ill. He sat upright and refused all medicine.
After seven days, he ordered his bath prepared, changed his robes, and wrote a final message to the assembly before passing away peacefully.
During the cremation, five-colored śarīras were collected, as numerous as beans and beyond counting; his eyes did not burn, and when melted in the fierce flames, they became even more crystalline.
Ying’s teeth, jawbones, and skull bones produced a resonant metallic sound when struck. At that time, the construction of the Wuzha Pagoda in Yuzhang was undertaken;
the Imperial Preceptor of the Jiangxi Provincial Administration, Qanich, commanded that the relics of the World-Honored One formerly enshrined there be interred within it.
He then dispatched an envoy to take the relics from the Master’s eyes and enshrine them in a silver casket as a secondary burial. The remaining skeletal relics were divided and buried in the east.
Xī. Chan Master Yùtáng Yì of Yuélín in Fènghuà, Míngzhōu, was a native of Wēnzhōu. He established the Dharma at Tiānníng in Wǔyì, then moved to Jiànfú.
Later, he presided over Tàipíng in Míng, and subsequently ascended to Zhāngshèng. In his later years, he resided at Yuélín. Upon ascending the hall, he said: "The Ancients..."

As for those who say, "In this place, I have no Dharma to give to people; I simply settle the case according to the facts," even in the realm of manifesting the sages, I likewise have no Dharma to give to people, nor do I settle the case according to the facts. [He] picks up his staff and asks: "What is the Buddha?
"Barefoot, treading upon lotus flowers. "What is the matter beyond the Buddha? "Carved beams and painted rafters. [He] throws down the staff and returns to the abbot's quarters.
[The Master] ascends the hall on the fifteenth day of the second month. He strikes his whisk once and says:
"Today, Zhangsheng shall take the black bean that burst forth from the cold ashes thirty years ago and exchange it for the eyes of the Old Barbarian. He lets out a shout.
"Even if there were a single dharma that surpassed nirvāṇa, this one shout of mine would not function as a mere shout. [He] ascended the hall.
"Lu Zu faced the wall; Ma Gu closed his door. Although these two great elders lived several hundred years apart from Tianning, today I cannot help but give each of them twenty blows of the staff.
Why? It is like making a lamp or candle out of oil and wax; it does not [shine] without..."
The fire will never be lit. Addressing the assembly: "Elder brothers, you cannot guarantee that your exhalation will be followed by an inhalation.

During the twelve periods of the day and night, do not divert your body and mind for other miscellaneous uses. Even if you were to wave your arms about, that would still be the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West."
Even from the tips of his toes, he kicks out an ancient Buddha. It is better to remain without affairs. He ascends the hall and cites the story of Huanglong’s Three Barriers.
The Master says: "The old fellow Huanglong has a flat head; that is why his accent of Zhangzhou, Quanzhou, and Fujian is so authentic.
He can deceive everyone in the world, but he cannot deceive the people of Zhangzhou, Quanzhou, and Fujian. He ascends the hall and, with his hand—
Pointing to the left, he said, "This is the incense burner. Pointing to the right, he said, "This is the flower vase.

One can take a single meaning and make it into immeasurable meanings, or take immeasurable meanings and make them into a single meaning. When the Venerable Chen wove straw sandals and Master Deng Shibai beat the earthen drum, they ascended the hall.
Step by step, this is the place where all of you bear witness; you must first attain self-acceptance before you can return home in peace.
He sat. "If it were not so," he said, "the *narcis* would have its belly for a crab, and the *jellyfish* would have its eyes for a shrimp.
He ascended the hall and said, "The five thousand and forty-eight fascicles are exhausted in a single phrase. He then rose and said, "Stand here and wait for everyone to grasp it!
He then descended from the seat. His verse at the time of death read: "Eighty-three years—what essence is there? Striking a tree and becoming a Buddha; empty space falls."
The site of his cremation was radiant with relics; his teeth, jawbones, and prayer beads remained unbroken.
Chan Master Zixian of Yunwu at Shuanglin in Wuzhou was the son of the Ye family of Kuocang and the ninth-generation descendant of Chan Master Xing of Wugu.
Initially, he studied under Jingcou Jue at Lingyin, and subsequently visited Dongcou Ying at Jing.
Cizhang Jishi once composed a preface for the *Buddha’s Enlightenment* (*Fochengdao shu*), in which he wrote: "The essence of vision (*jiàn-jīng*) arises at midnight.

The Old Man [Wuzhun Shifan] said, "Why not say that the essence of vision is extinguished at midnight? The Master was so startled that his thighs trembled and sweat poured from him as if a thick veil had been suddenly lifted;
he then clearly perceived the place where the Old Man acted freely for the sake of others. Later, he appeared in the world at Shuanglin and subsequently moved to Zhizhe. In the Renqing era...
On the twenty-fifth day of the tenth month, while conversing and laughing with his guests, he suddenly instructed his attendant monk to fetch a brush and wrote a verse,
after which he passed away.
He was a Dharma successor of Chan Master Wufang An.

Chan Master Kumu Rong praised the Third Patriarch with this verse: "Wind-illness entangles his body and life, beyond the reach of physicians; His family is poor and meets with robbery—how even more pitiable!
Who would have known that when one seeks the offense, it is nowhere to be found? This is precisely the moment the thief returns to an empty house."
Chan Master Huiji Yuanxi of Mount Jing, Fozhi Temple in Hangzhou, was a dharma successor of Chan Master Yuyang Guan. His clan was the Tang family of Yuzhang.

Both the Master and his elder brother, Yuanling, studied for the jinshi examinations. Once Yuanling had passed the examinations, the Master followed Master Ming of West Mountain to receive the tonsure.

He was about to travel abroad. His mother provided him with a full set of silver as travel funds. Fearing that he might lose his resolve once his resources were sufficient, she spoke to him with kind words.

Upon hearing that Master Wuchu had begun to propagate the teachings at Yujiji, he went there to rely upon him. When Wuchu first spoke with him, he was struck by his extraordinary nature and kept him in his service.

Later, he paid his respects to Dong-sou Ying at Nanping and was appointed to serve as the chronicler (*jìshǐ*). During the Zhìyuán era, the Imperial Commissioner Yang Liánzhēnjiā was commissioned by imperial decree to retrieve the relics from Yùwáng Monastery.
He personally visited the Master to request a record of the origins and details of the relics and invited him to accompany him.
The Master replied, "I have an elderly mother; her survival after the war is unknown. He subsequently declined the invitation and returned to Jiangxi. Yuan [Dynasty].
Lingxian had previously served as the Prefectural Commissioner of Linjiang, where he died in the cause of raising troops alongside Wen Tianxiang.

His mother alone remained at home, and Shifu served her with such filial piety that his reputation for it spread far and wide. In the second year of the Yuanzhen era, he ascended to the abbacy of Baizhang, remaining there for twelve years.
At the beginning of the Zhida era, he accepted the invitation to enter Jingci Monastery; when he arrived, the officials of the Zhongshu Sheng and the Xuanzheng Yuan all came out to welcome him.
"Please propagate our school's宗旨 (essential purpose). Monks from all quarters gathered like spokes converging at a hub. He ascended the hall and said:

"Yunmen spoke the single word 'Universal' (Pu), and yet the people of the entire world could do nothing about it. Little did they know that Yunmen was planting his feet squarely on all four corners of the ground.

At that time, had he simply let out a thunderous shout to rouse him, waiting for the other to flare up with indignation, [the master] would have slowly performed a bow and said: 'Do not take offense at my intrusion.'"

"Excellent! Not only will this old man be helped up, but his words shall surely circulate throughout the world. He ascended the hall and raised the case of Elder Fú of Táiyuán, who attained enlightenment upon hearing the sound of a horn.
He offered this verse: "The Lute-player enters the blue seas; The Grand Historian wanders the famous mountains.
From now on, along the road outside the city of Yángzhōu, The orders are strict: no gates are permitted to open early. He ascended the hall. "In the three realms there is no dharma..."
Seeking the mind within its abode: white clouds serve as a canopy, flowing water acts as a lute. From ancient times to the present, there has been no gap;
who here is a true connoisseur? (He strikes the whisk. One tune, two tunes—no one understands them. After the rain, the autumn pond is deep with water. Ascending the hall:
Sitting alone on the Great Hero Peak, cold ashes cannot be stirred to red. A single firefly emerges; a solitary crane flies past Liaodong. The retreat begins.
Ascending the hall, he made a gesture with his hands as if tying the mouth of a cloth bag and said, "Today, Nanshan has tied the mouth of the cloth bag shut.
You all must each dwell in the wisdom of equanimity, with body and mind at peace within it.
Should there suddenly be one who breaks through the azure sky and knocks over Mount Sumeru, do not say that the knot was not tied securely. After a long silence, he said:

A hundred thousand layers of nets covered the heavens. After residing there for seven years, he moved again to Mount Jing. Subsequently, he took up his staff and returned to the foot of Mount Nanping.
When the disciples of Baizhang and Dayang heard that the Master had retired from public life, they vied with one another to welcome and invite him.

The Master, having no choice, eventually returned to Mount Yang where he resided for three years. As he was about to pass away, he wrote by hand a letter of farewell to those with whom he had traveled, and further composed a letter.

He delivered his final verses to the assembly and passed away while casting aside his writing brush; this was on the seventeenth day of the intercalary eighth month in the sixth year of the Yanyou era.
He was eighty-two years of age at the time of his death. His entire body was enshrined and interred beneath the Jīnjī Stone.
His disciples residing in Hangzhou divided his fingernails and hair to erect stupas at Jingci and Xiyin.

Chan Master Yunfeng Miaogao of Mount Jing in Hangzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Wen of Jingci. He was a native of Changxi; his family had followed the Confucian profession for generations, and his mother’s surname was Yuan.

In a dream, he saw an infant sitting with palms joined upon the heart of a lotus flower on the surface of a pond; he reached out his hand and took hold of it. Upon waking, he was born as a master, and for this reason he was named Mengchi (Dream-Pond).
His spiritual brilliance was exceptionally clear and penetrating; he delighted in books and applied himself diligently to study, particularly cherishing the Buddhist scriptures.

He earnestly requested to learn the supramundane Dharma, and following Master Yunmeng Ze, he shaved his head and received full ordination. First, he attended upon Chijue; next, he visited Wuzhun. Wuzhun...
He was especially esteemed by him. Upon returning to Yuyang, he went to see Yanxi, who appointed him to oversee the library keys.
One day, Yanxi raised a koan: "It is like a cow passing through a window lattice; its head, horns, and four hooves have all passed through, but why can the tail not pass?
The Master suddenly attained realization and said, "The whale swallows the ocean's water until it reveals the coral branches. Yanxi gave his approval. At that time...
Master Xi Qian accompanied him to Nanping. Later, he emerged from seclusion to reside at Dalu in Yixing, followed by stints at Quanzhong in Jiangyin, Heshan in Zhezhou, and Heishan.
When the seat at Jiangshan was vacant, he was appointed to reside there by imperial decree. He remained for thirteen years, with his assembly exceeding five thousand members.
In the year of the Yi Hai cycle during the Deyou era, the temple was beset by military forces; a soldier pointed a blade at the Master, who extended his neck and said:
"If you wish to kill me, kill me; my head is not a whetstone for your blade. His words and expression were entirely devoid of fear.

The soldiers were moved by this transformation and cast away their swords and departed. In the gengchen year of the Zhizhi era (1340), he moved to Mount Jing. The temple had suffered from a fire, and only one-tenth remained in its original state;
yet within a few years, it was restored to its former splendor. Addressing the assembly, he said: "The preceding thought is ordinary; the succeeding thought is sacred—a single stroke."

Two sections. Do not hesitate further. Therefore, at the assembly of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the broad-faced butcher cast down his cleaver and immediately declared, "I am counted among the thousand Buddhas.
Although this is so, without the strength to lift the cauldron and pull the mountain, the black steed of a thousand *li* is not easily ridden.
To the assembly: Discern the meaning before words; clarify the essence beneath the phrase. Mount Dongji is ablaze.
Nevertheless, when preaching the Dharma, those who focus solely on its circulation are inevitably caught in a mutual stalemate.
If one still harbors the habit of observing and listening, one will remain in a state of restless agitation;

from the crowing of the rooster at dawn to the tolling of the bell at dusk, the very sounds and forms of the assembly hall become the lethal poison of non-arising, and sensation and perception become the pitfall for humanity. Who among you does not know such talk?
However, coarse food satisfies easily, while fine chewing leaves one hard to hunger. Entering the hall: Before the world had taken form, heaven and earth were in profound stillness;
before Buddhas and sentient beings were manifested, the body was entirely true. Without cause, the Great Being with a mirror-like countenance leaped forth from the eagle’s nest;
having already torn off his own skin, he was already being sketched by others. How much more so did that old barbarian with missing teeth, failing to abide in his proper station, gaze afar—
In the eastern land of China, there are those with the capacity for the Mahāyāna. Having come from afar across a hundred thousand *li*, their intent was to cut in line and snatch the market.
Now, the drums resound at the Phoenix Pavilion and the bells toll at the Azure Hall; every turn of the throat strikes a taboo, and there is no door through which to set foot.
The entire nation finds it difficult to pursue them, and they have once again been exposed. The new Jingshan, driven by necessity, has boarded another’s vessel and entered another’s domain.
Regarding the division of realms: a new official does not attend to old affairs. Ultimately, what is it? [The Master] struck the meditation seat once.

"The watchtowers of the borderlands quietly store the moon over a thousand peaks; the wild grasses of the frontier idly spread the autumn across ten thousand miles. He ascended the hall and said: "The five peaks stand steep and lofty;
those who reach them must be people of true caliber. A single mirror hangs in the sky; there is nothing that does not receive its illumination. The ancestral legacy remains as it was. Still...
Within the livelihood of a patch-robed monk, how has there ever been change? When there is no place to lay hands, it is precisely here that one must arouse mindfulness;

when there is no door for the feet to enter, it is only then that one is fit to tread. Until the mountain clouds are limpid and the mountain stream flows murmuring, until the single melody is impartial and the ten thousand realms enjoy peace—when this is so, where does the merit reside? From of old, the chariots and books have shared the same script and tracks.
"The four seas are now one family. In the spring of the Wuzi year, demonic disturbances suddenly arose.

There were those who slandered and defamed the Chan school. The Master said, "This is a matter of great importance for our Dharma gate; I shall struggle for it even at the cost of my life. He then hurried to the capital.

An imperial decree was issued to assemble the followers of all schools for a debate in the court. The Emperor asked, "What constitutes the essence of Chan? The Master replied, "Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect; its substance is fundamentally empty."
"Quiescence cannot be reached through seeing, hearing, perceiving, knowing, thinking, or conceptual discrimination.

After the master had been questioned repeatedly, he enumerated the patriarchs of India and China, as well as the causes and conditions regarding the staff and shouts of Deshan and Linji, totaling over two thousand words.

Furthermore, he was summoned before the throne to engage in repeated debate with the slanderer. The slanderer’s arguments were exhausted, and the Emperor was greatly pleased; he granted him food and he withdrew.

The Master took his leave at the palace steps and returned south. Addressing the assembly, he said: "I originally intended to remain deeply hidden in mountain caves, secluding myself until my time had passed.

I did not expect that the sun would shine upon me and Heaven would look down, making it difficult to escape this ultimate transformation. He further said: "With tattered robes covering one's head, all affairs come to rest."

At that time, the mountain monk could not comprehend it. When Mount Jing suffered a disaster and was destroyed by fire, the Master said to the assembly, "I have long been burdened by a debt to this mountain.
He then exerted every effort to rebuild; he filled in the pond at Huidian and constructed other buildings, which were completed one after another.
On the seventeenth day of the sixth month of the Gui-si year, he wrote a verse and passed away. The Master was born on the seventeenth day of the second month of the Ji-mao year of the Jia-ding era.
On this day, his secular age was seventy-five and his monastic seniority (*saṅ-lak*) fifty-nine. His stupa was erected at the western foot of the mountain at the temple.
Iron-Mirror Zhiming Chanshi of Heshan in Huzhou was the son of the Wang family of Changxi in Fudang.
He first visited Yao-sou Mingsu at Tianning Monastery in Jiahe; although he received encouragement and exhortation, he had not yet attained awakening. He subsequently went to see Yanxi at...
At Jingci, he paid respects morning and evening for a long time before finally obtaining certification. He then visited Qingxi Yuan and Zangsou Zhen.
In the *Xinsi* year of the Zhizhi era (1281), he took up residence at Heshan; subsequently, he moved to Damei. In the *Gengzi* year of the Dade era (1300), he was again invited to return to Heshan.
Ascending the hall, he said: "If you strive with focused intent, it will be like a donkey’s year before you see my face. If you let go completely, it appears in an instant.
Setting aside the story of Xiangyan hearing the sound of a bamboo strike and thoroughly seeing his original face, tell me:
when things are this heated, where can one find refuge? Return to the hall for tea. Ascending the hall again, he said: "In the autumn gloom of the plains and fields, the cricket sings; the maple..."
The leaves falling from the forest, each with its red heart, are the crown of the skull of Bodhidharma. A boneless descendant is like searching for a needle at the bottom of the sea.
When you suddenly find it, what then? Who says the palace of the Dragon King is deep? Ascending the hall, [the Master said]:

"If Bodhidharma had not come to the Eastern Land, the official roads would have few travelers. If the Second Patriarch had not stayed in the Western Heaven, many would have consumed the private wine. What mountain gate..."
Before you lies a great highway; how many have traveled it from south to north? Only a single stone in its midst has never been trodden by anyone.
Is there anyone among you who can tread upon it? Having said this, he threw down his staff.
Look under your feet. Entering the hall: Today is the twenty-fifth day of the eighth month. I remember Dongshan leaving Chadu; he fell into Yunmen’s net.
Having suffered this injustice, to this day there is nowhere to appeal it. [The Master] raises his whisk: "Master Yunmen is here!
Should he receive a blow from the hand of which mountain? Tell me, where does the fault lie? It was improper to beat the drum.
He played with the men and women of others. On the fifth day of the eleventh month of the Yanyou yimao year, he summoned his disciples to entrust them with his final affairs.
He asked for paper and wrote in large characters: "The net is cast aside; there is no more evasion. The waves of the great ocean are stilled; empty space is revealed alone."
He cast aside his writing brush and passed away in tranquility at the age of eighty-six.
Chan Master Zhihong Jian of Tiantong in Mingzhou first resided at Zhenru in Xinzhou and later moved to Tiantong. He ascended the hall and addressed the assembly:
The Buddhas are not real; they preach the Dharma to deliver all sentient beings. Bodhisattvas possess wisdom, yet their vision of the nature is not yet clear.
White clouds have no mind or intention, yet they shed rain upon the world. The great earth has no feelings, yet it can cause all grasses and trees to grow.
The ancient worthies’ proclamations in this manner were indeed skillful in opening the way for humans and devas within the Dharma of the Four Truths.
However, as for the realm of the patch-robed monks, it is more than ten thousand miles away from white clouds. [He] ascended the hall, took up his staff, and said: "One has many kinds."
The two are no different from one another. The withered mulberry tree knows the wind of heaven; the sea water knows the cold of heaven.
Hearing this said, the staff (zhuzhangzi) could not help but laugh joyfully and say: "To leave the body may still be easy, but to speak from the very essence is surely difficult.
He threw down the staff and descended from his seat. Entering the hall for the discourse, he cited the case where Chan Master Dayang Xuan asked Liangshan, "What is the path of formlessness?"

Chan Master Xuedou Yeweng Bingtong of Mingzhou was the son of the Zhang family of Xinchang. He studied under Dachuan.

He leaned on it, and the Master suddenly attained enlightenment regarding the essential meaning. Later, he bound himself with straw and took up his staff upon a peak, where he shut his door daily to transcribe the *Lotus Sūtra*.

He once composed the verse: "An old man comes; I am not weary of guests. In stillness, I wish to transcribe the sūtra. When Xuedou’s seat became vacant, public opinion requested the Master to fill it.

Chan Master Yue Tang Zu-yin of Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Shuanglin Peng. He was the son of the Zhou family of Nankang.

He once composed the *Fuzong Xianzheng Lun* (Treatise on Supporting the School and Manifesting Orthodoxy) and presented it to Emperor Renzong, who perused it.

The Emperor praised him and bestowed upon him a golden-embroidered *kāṣāya* and the honorary title "Huiguang Puzhao Wenming Tongbian" (Wisdom Light Universally Shining, Civilized and Penetrating Eloquence).

Upon retiring from his duties, he built a residence called Guixiu (Retreat) and lived there in tranquil repose. On the third day of the eighth month of the Wuyin year of the Zhizhi era (1318), he passed away at the age of seventy-nine.
