You youngsters and latecomers, you eggplants and gourds who eat ready-made meals—how could you possibly know what kind of bowl it is?
Ascending the hall: "The rocky gates are treacherous; the Jade Gorge flows murmuring. If you have not yet reached this place, it is natural to harbor doubts.
But once you have reached it—how do you express that single phrase of level unfolding? An ancient road where an iron snake lies across. Ascending the hall for the Buddha-Bathing Ceremony:
On the eighth day of the fourth month, Siddhārtha was born. Nine dragons spat forth water to bathe his golden body. Yunmen would strike him with a staff and beat him to death. Is it so?
"This great divine mantra, this great illuminating mantra, this unsurpassed mantra. "Do you all see the Old Man with the Yellow Face?
With his staff, he struck them all at once and dispersed them. He ascended the hall and said: "The cuckoo cries until its blood fills the flower branches;
In haste, it bitterly urges one to return home. Yet returning to one's native village, one remains but a guest; In every hamlet, the green is dark and the red is sparse. [The Box]
The phrase that covers heaven and earth; the phrase that follows the waves and drifts with the current; the phrase that cuts off the flow of all streams.
If you can realize it here, you will pass through it all at once. Yangqi’s donkey has three legs. Ascending the hall, [the Master said]:
"Just so, not just so—there is a source, there is no source. At the head of the Shili Rapids, Old Man Liao caught a pair of red-scaled, brocade-tailed fish. He released them.
"Down there is actually a loach. Why is it so? "Broken cliffs and a solitary boat. Entering the hall, he said: "The falling petals through the rains of the third month;
the lingering dreams to the bells of the fifth watch. Sound and form have all vanished; yet another layer of the Mysterious Barrier.
But one must not say this—there must be a direct overturning to the very bottom. Why? Because of Mount Sumeru. Entering the hall, he said: "Affirmation is cut away; negation is also cut away."
"Let the mandate descend without partiality; there are eyes upon the tip of the staff. Thinking thus, I recall the words of Master Huangbo:
"All of you who travel as monks like this—where could you have found such a day? This too was Muzhou carrying a single board. Entering the hall, he said: "Water does not wash water;
gold is not bartered for gold. Blue sky and bright sun from antiquity until now. When I, this mountain monk, arrive here, it is truly like planting [a pillar]..."
"The hand does not enter. Do you all still believe that you yourselves are Yangshan? "The waves of Caoxi are just like this;
countless ordinary people are submerged beneath the surface. [He] ascended the hall and said: "The Way is present in daily life, yet daily life is unaware of it.
When hungry, one simply eats; when cold, one simply adds clothing. Under a clear sky, the bright sun hangs over the withered pear tree, illuminating the plum trees by the stream."
Stealthily putting forth a southern branch while facing the sun. Entering the hall for discourse: The spring rain is misty and pervasive; the spring clouds are thick and heavy.

Suddenly, the bright sun appears in the sky—neither heaven can conceal it, nor can earth support it. At such a moment, setting aside the Zen of the Tathāgata, the Zen of the Patriarchs is not yet here.
Why is this so? It is permitted only to investigate, not permitted to understand. Entering the hall for discourse: Calling six "five."
He breaks two into three; the eyes look toward the northeast while the mind dwells upon the southwest. Under the gate of Mount Yangshan, however, such "tea and rice" is not required.
Why? Because the Buddha-dharma does not fear rotting. Ascending the hall, he said: "A fragrant breeze comes from the south, Bringing a subtle coolness to the halls and pavilions.
As for the place where the Buddhas manifest their bodies— One must strictly avoid deliberating on it wrongly. Even if you were to realize it before words, or grasp it beyond phrases..."
Yangshan accepted this, yet he dared to say it was not yet so. Why? "Tender bamboo strikes the wind, sounding like emerald birds;
lotus leaves toss in the rain, splashing like mandarin ducks. Ascending the hall, he said: "Pure clarity, free from a single speck—this is precisely the flow of the eternal.
But once the mirror is shattered, one cannot avoid a scene of total disorder. It is better to eat when you meet with food and drink tea when you meet with tea. Standing alone at dawn."
Outside the empty courtyard, he leisurely faces several blossoming trees of cold plum. Ascending the hall, [he says]: "The waters of the sea cannot be measured with a peck;
empty space cannot be gauged with a ruler; pure ground cannot be strewn with sand; and soft mud cannot support one's feet.
These four turning phrases each have a point of descent. Tell me, where do they descend? Within the Great Xiangguo Temple in the Eastern Capital..."
A plantain tree; when the wind blows and the rain beats upon it, it is just like a tattered robe. [The Master] ascends the hall and says: "A phrase, no phrase—like a vine leaning against a tree.
A white egret descends to the field: a thousand dots of snow. A yellow oriole perches on a branch: a single blossom of spring.
Having sold his cotton robe three thousand *li* away, he has come from no great distance. Why, then, does he set down his mud-platter? He lets out a great laugh. Vipaśyin.
"Śibi Buddha applied his mind early on, yet until this very day he has not attained the wondrous. Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The Zen tree cries out in clamor;
before the Gate of the Way, the wind sweeps vast and wild. Coldly reflecting upon this, it is truly laughable. But tell me, what is there to laugh at?
Carelessly picking up a pear from Zhengzhou, one looks closely and finds it is actually a jujube from Qingzhou. Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "This matter is fundamentally manifest."
Seek it, yet it cannot be seen. A white jade disk originally has no flaws; yet through polishing, it instead becomes marred by a blemish.
Grasping it as a substantial reality is like lightning flashing in the midst of emptiness. To view it as something trivial is to add a red thread beneath one’s feet.
Take heed! You who study the Way, look well! What is this skillful means? You must quickly turn your eyes to see the immortal; do not look at the immortal’s hand.

The Middle Fan. When the Master was among the assembly, there was a verse regarding the casting of a bell which said: "His entire body is but a single mouth; rolled out from within the furnace of a hundred refinements.
After sending the setting sun back to its rest, it further urges the bright moon up the tower.
On the anniversary of Wuzu’s passing, he offered incense, saying: "Everyone says that today the former master has died; who knows that today is actually his birthday? He did not know...
"But what evidence is there for this? [The Master replied: "Purple sandalwood and yellow sandalwood burn in one place.
A monk asked, "What is Deshan’s staff? The Master said, "It pierces through your skull. [The monk] asked, "What is Linji’s shout? The Master said, "Do you hear it?
[The monk] asked, "What is the meaning of 'One shout is like a Vajra King sword'? The Master said, "Above all, avoid wounding your own edge or injuring your hand. [The monk] said, "..."
"What is the one shout that is like a crouching lion? The Master said, "Truly pitiable.
"What is the one shout used as a sounding rod or a blade of grass? The Master said, "Neither in front nor behind.
"What is the one shout not used as a shout? The Master said, "You must investigate it before you can understand. Question: "What are the five houses?"
[The questioner asked about] the essential tenets. The Master said, "One who has a mouth is fit only for eating. [The questioner] said, "If one does not rely on inquiry, how can one reach the source?

The Master said, "I do not yet dare grant you permission. [The questioner] asked, "What is the school of Miu-yang? The Master said, "The father is compassionate and the son is filial. [The questioner] asked, "What is the school of Lin-chi?
The Master said, "A sudden clap of thunder leaves no time to cover one's ears. [The questioner] asked, "What is the school of Ts'ao-tung?"
The Master said, "At the third watch, one does not borrow the 'night-bright' curtain. [The monk] asked, "What is the Yunmen school?
The Master said, "The body is exposed to the golden wind. [The monk] asked, "What is the Fayen school? The Master said, "The mountains are naturally green and the waters are naturally blue.

The monk asked, "The five houses and their lineages have been pointed out by you, Master; as for the ultimate vehicle (*yāna*), what is it like? The Master said, "The head touches the heavens and the feet tread upon the earth."

Master [Dongshan] lamented that the fundamental principles of the school had lost their foundation; he therefore took up the task of providing guidance through *tihe* (pointing out) and *nian-song* (verses), using the dynamic interplay of "striking" and "singing" to inspire his disciples.
Through this, they attained direct insight and transcended the sect, whereby the spiritual style of the school was revitalized all at once.
He first resided at Longxing Temple in Tanzhou, and subsequently moved to Daolin, Nanming, Furi, Xianju, Husheng, and finally Guangxiao in Huzhou. This was during the Jisi year of the Xianchun era.
He resided at Mount Yang in Yuanzhou and was renowned in the world as the foremost among the "Dharma Caves. Emperor Yuan bestowed gifts and honored him with great ceremony.
In the Dinghai year of the Yuan era, he sent a bamboo rattle and a fly-whisk, along with the "Green Water and Blue Mountains" (Lüshui Qingshan) as a formal transmission, to Gaofeng Yuanmiao.
He presented them with a verse of praise, saying: "The Great Master [Wuzu] is now no more; Xueyan may be said to know the proper rites. Empty fame fills the world..."
He shattered heaven and earth and entrusted [the Dharma] to his attendant, Yuanmiao. At seventy-odd years of age, he passed away.
Chan Master Ling-sou Yuan of Guoqing Temple in Taizhou ascended the hall and said, citing a monk who asked Zhaozhou, "True Suchness and ordinary or holy beings are all dreams;
what then is the true word? Zhaozhou replied, "Oṃ phuḥ laṃ. The Master said, "This is Zhaozhou’s Chan."
"It is merely on the surface of the lips. To see him act like this is to mistake a bell for a jar. If someone were to suddenly ask Ling-sou, he would instead say to them:
"When hungry, simply eat your rice. Tell me, is this the same as the ancients, or is it different?
The Sanskrit language of India is the Tang language of this land. Entering the hall: Heat is heat; coolness is coolness. There is no duality in the Dharma; there is no need for it.
Consider this: if everyone’s nostrils were on their faces, they would certainly know it exists. But let me ask you further:
how does the fragrance of lotuses in a secluded pond compare to the fragrance of rice in a deep village? To illustrate the precept "guarding the mind as one would a city," he spoke this verse:

"The six gates are locked with the old boundaries; Already,攀缘 (pān-yuán) has ceased and ten thousand anxieties are forgotten. Last night, a poor household suddenly suffered a robbery; It turns out..."
Calamity arises from within the inner chambers. The verse on guarding the mouth like a sealed jar says: "Clearly it resides beneath the nostrils; To stir it is nothing but the gateway to disaster.
Relax directly so that you are like a wooden stump; Under the blue sky and bright sun, thunder rolls in fury."
Chan Master Bieshan Zuji of Tiantong in Mingzhou was surnamed Yang and was a native of Shunqing in Sichuan. At the age of fourteen, he received full ordination.
Initially, while listening to a monk reciting the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, he heard the passage about entering and then exiting the Maitreya Pavilion;
it was as if he had awakened from a dream. He then composed a verse on Lingyun’s seeing the peach blossoms, which begins: "A single red dot amidst ten thousand greens—how many people rejoice?"
How many who were joyful became sorrowful! He visited all the venerable elders of the lineage of Zhe-weng Yan, Wu-ji Pai, Gao-yuan Quan, Chun-an Jing, and Miao-feng Shan.
Finally, he met Wu-zhun at Xue-dou. Wu-zhun, recognizing him as a vessel for the Dharma, treated him with ever-increasing severity;

from time to time, he would deliver blows or shouts, withholding not a single word of concession. Whenever the Master attempted to respond, his mouth would immediately close and he was unable to utter a sound.
From this, his intellectual understanding was completely lost. After a long while, he rose and said, "All the skills I have cultivated throughout my life are but dead dharmas.
Only now, upon meeting this elder, do I see the path of life. Subsequently, when Zhuan moved to Jingshan, he invited the Master to share the seat with him.

In the Wuxu year of the Jiashih era, the throne at Tianwang on Mount Dongting became vacant, and they welcomed the Master to preside over it. In the Bichen year of the Baoyu era, Tiantong Monastery was destroyed by fire.

The provincial governor, Lord Wu Qian, memorialized the Emperor regarding Master Daoyuan’s conduct. The Master received imperial edict and arrived carrying only a single bag and a single alms bowl; he dwelt there, living in a thatched hut.

For a long time, Ning County had suffered from drought, but whenever the Master offered prayers, rain would fall immediately. Consequently, the people flocked to him, and within three years, all neglected matters were restored.
Tiantong Temple was thus returned to its former splendor. Entering the hall, he raised the topic: "When the World-Honored One was about to enter nirvana..."
Mañjuśrī requested that the Wheel of Dharma be turned once more. The World-Honored One rebuked him, saying: "Mañjuśrī, for forty-nine years I have never spoken a single word.
You ask me to turn the Wheel of Dharma once more; have I ever turned the Wheel of Dharma? The verse says: "This old man has always been a great liar;
He deceives the blind and the deaf by taking non-existence for existence. Only at the moment of departure does a single phrase become true."
Furthermore, this was the bell signaling the end of the meal for the *ācārya*. On the first day of the ninth month of the Gengchen year, he suddenly addressed the assembly, saying:

"The clouds are thin and the moonlight is fresh; the trees have shed their leaves and the mountains reveal their bones. Since heaven and earth came into being, how many have had their eyes truly open? When someone asked about his realization, he replied: [He remained silent].
The Master said, "We shall not meet again; each of you must strive with diligence. Ten days later, at the hour of midnight, he called his attendant and entrusted him with his final affairs.
With palms joined, he passed away peacefully. He was sixty-seven years old and had spent fifty-four summer retreats in the monastic life.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa to the right of the Mian (Mimoku-an) Stūpa on Mount Zhongfeng.

Chan Master Huanxi Yi of Xuefeng in Fuzhou cited the passage: "The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten eons, yet the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him, and he could not attain the path of Buddhahood. He then offered this verse: "The seal of Vairocana was cast at the beginning of the kalpa;
The ancient inscriptions, though worn like insects, remain distinct. How laughable and how tragic that people do not recognize it— They instead resent that the characters are not perfectly complete."
The inscription for the eulogy of the Baguā Héshàng (Cloth Sack Monk) says: "Whenever he meets someone, he begs for a single coin; Yet within his sack, he possesses the wealth of a rival state.
It is not that his descent into this world was late; He simply detested being a Buddha and refused to become one. Regarding the phrase "This very mind is Buddha," the verse says:
"This very mind is Buddha— It is arsenic and wolf-poison. To raise the dead and restore life, A single dose is all it takes."
Chan Master Duanqiao Miaolun of Jingci Temple in Hangzhou was the son of the Xu family of Huangyan in Taizhou. His mother was Liu.
She conceived him after dreaming of the moon. At the age of eighteen, he shaved his head at Guangci Monastery in Yongjia.

Initially, he went to Ruiyan to see Guyuan Dao, where he heard the master raise the koan of "Three Pounds of Flax" and became skeptical of it. He traveled everywhere to consult various masters until one day, while at Yunju, he encountered [Dongshan Shouchu].
In his mountain hall, while reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he came across the passage stating that even mosquitoes, insects, and ants can perform tasks without speech.
He attained a sudden realization and remarked, "Zhaozhou’s 'Cypress Tree' koan is truly direct. He then went to visit Wuzhun at Xuedou.
Zhun asked, "For what reason does a dog possess karmic consciousness? He requested the Master to provide a response, but after thirty turns of questioning, none were in accord.
The Master asked, "Is there no expedient means? Zhun showed him a verse by Zhenjing. The Master stood transfixed for a long while;

suddenly, upon hearing the sound of the wooden board, his entire body broke into a sweat. Thereupon, he was liberated from all doubt. Zhun later moved to Yuyang and Shuangjing, where he served as the Master’s attendant.

He shared his seat with all. He emerged into the world at Jiyuan Monastery, moved to Ruiyan and Guoqing, and later presided over Jingci. Ascending the hall, he said: "In the mountains of Jing there is jade;
those who obtain it do not find it within the mountains of Jing. In the waters of Chi there is a pearl; those who pick it up do not find it within the waters of Chi."
A patch-robed monk possesses the "True Person of No Rank. For one who has realized this, coming and going do not occur through the face-gate.
[The Master] suddenly took up his staff, held it crosswise, and said, "Do you understand? A stone man crouches at the mouth of the Yangtze River in Youzhou.

[He] ascended the hall and cited the case of Ciming, who kept a basin of water in his room. Across the basin he placed a sword, and upon the sword he set a pair of straw sandals. Whenever a monk came, [he would see this].
He pointed. As [the monk] hesitated, he struck him. The Master composed a verse: "Whips flash through the midst of a hundred flowers;
How much elegance and refined grace there is! The unexamined scholar peeks with sidelong glances; Full of heart, what can he do about his old sorrows?
Ascending the hall, he said: "Deshan lowered his head; Jiaoshan nodded his head; Juizhi held up a finger; Xuansha struck and broke his own toe."
[The Master] strikes the head [of the assembly]. He takes up his staff and says: "All of this does not go beyond the tip of my staff. How do you know this? He plants the staff on the ground:
"A single leaf falls, and the whole world turns autumn. Ascending the hall, he cites Chan Master Daguan Ying’s instruction to the assembly, which said:
"The Seven Buddhas are the subjects of nature; the myriad dharmas are the slaves of the mind. But tell me, where is the master? He then gave a shout himself and said: "Seven!"
The Buddha has already come down and poked his head out. He then personally assents, saying, "Each of you wait upon me. The Master says:
To call the Seven Buddhas "nature-slaves" and to point to the myriad dharmas as "mind-servants," Dahui claims he possesses a way to transcend them.

Yet, when he himself shouts and himself assents, these are still matters pertaining to slaves and servants. When has the true master ever been seen even in a dream? Does the great assembly wish to see him? [He] uses—
With a single sweep of his whisk, a spring breeze stirred at dawn; the hundred varieties of flowers throughout the gardens were in full bloom.

As he was about to pass away, he finished his session with the assembly. He then composed a handwritten letter bidding farewell to the various mountains and the Duke of Wei. When the Duke sent medicine as a gift, the Master would not accept it.
The Duke again sent a messenger to ask: "The Master was born at Tiantai; why did you die at Jingci? The Master replied: "The sun has risen."
In the east he fell at night and passed away in the west; he then wrote a verse and entered nirvana. His secular age was sixty-two and his monastic seniority (śrāmaṇeraka) was forty-four.
Chan Master Ming of Yuepo at Tiantong in Mingzhou cited a monk’s question to Yunmen: "When it has been raining for a long time and does not stop, what then?
Yunmen said, "Zha! The Master composed a verse on it: Yunmen’s single "Zha"— A hair-piercing blade, its luster shining through the scabbard. If it were not...
Zhang Hua: In vain, his eyes blink and blink. [The Master] cites the kōan concerning Liangsu’s meeting with Magu, and says in verse:

Carrying his hoe, he did not look back and simply went on his way. Who would dare say, "You are a lecturer"? [The Master] cites the saying, "Transcending the four propositions and cutting off the hundred negations," and says in verse:
Transcending the four propositions, Cutting off the hundred negations— Passing the blame back and forth, who has ever known? This monk carries a...
Carrying a state of dull-witted confusion, one returns with both ends muddied. Consider the public case: "The fragrant breeze comes from the south;
the halls and pavilions grow cool. The verse says: "The old woman selling fans shields her eyes from the sun; A single style of wind flows, the true heir to the house.
Tell this to the traveler who has not yet returned home: Why need you go outside to eat the *pōzhā*?"
Chan Master Zhizhi of Donglin on Mount Lu, in a verse for seeing off a monk returning to Chengdu, said: "Where wisdom does not reach, utter a single word;
A single word that hits the mark, and you have arrived home. Before the Heron Pavilion, the wind stirs the willows; Beside the city of Gansu (Jinguangcheng), the rain hastens the blossoms."
Chan Master Xuesou Hishou Shaotan of Mingzhou was a native of Western Sichuan. Having appeared in the world at Fulong, he ascended the hall.
A monk asked, "As for the matter of the supreme vehicle of the ancestral lineage, what is it like? The Master said, "The dripping from the eaves is distinct and clear. He then said:
"Floating upon the vast waters by the shores of Lake Xizi, One sees the willows drooping along the green embankment in the cold. Who would have known that the karmic debt is so difficult to escape?"
Avoid it! Opening your eyes wide, you enter the boiling cauldron with imposing dignity. Reaching this point, how can you possibly succeed?
If you intend to rot the yellow tubers in the fire while disregarding the purple clay seal, you cannot avoid treading upon the tracks of the ancients.

If you intend to lock the void, imprison dreams, block the roads, and break the bridges, you fear you will sit within a thicket of entanglements. It is better to accept things as they are, humbly conforming to the times.

"You should depart. [The Master] picks up his staff and says, "Vertically it exhausts the three periods of time; horizontally it spans the ten directions. He leans on the staff and says, "The blue-eyed, yellow-headed one cannot comprehend this.
Wild plum blossoms, the wind stilled, their fragrance floats darkly. He ascends the hall and says: "The third month, spring is said to be at its end; The brilliance of the season is as rich as wine.
The oriole sings in the willow rain; The butterfly dances in the sea-blossom breeze. If you understand this as an external object, you are like one who crosses mountains searching for ants."
Traces. Not forming a conceptual meeting with objects, one crosses the water seeking the tracks of fish. In the end, how is it? "The road home to my native land is far;

at sunset, I weep for my exhausted path. While at Xuedou, he ascended the hall. Yixiu Jue [carried] three loads of earth; before his feet had even crossed the threshold, his essential character was already revealed.
In taking a casual step, the perilous path is covered in frosty blossoms. With a stroke of color, he reveals a single pivot; a broken cliff.
The flying waterfall—though so, it is easy to cross the Gate of the Breast Peak, yet difficult to enter the Chamber of the Breast Peak.

Why? When the wild goose flies into the vast void, what does the hunter long for? Entering the hall, he said: "If one can give rise to a single vital mechanism and utter a single word that hits the mark, there will not be a single cloud for ten thousand miles;
the blue sky deserves a blow of the staff. Without waiting for the spring breeze to intentionally open it, the dark fragrance [is already manifest]."
[The verse] is already upon the plum blossoms. A monk asked Nanquan, "When you, Master, reside in the abbot’s quarters, what do you use as your guiding point?
Nanquan said, "Last night at the third watch, I lost my ox; when I rose at dawn, I had lost my fire. The verse says: With servile faces and cringing knees, he runs through the world;
Ashamed to see him in his sheepskin robe on Qili Tan. Though Wen-shu was noble as the Son of Heaven, Zi-ling remained [in his reclusive dignity].
Regarding him as an old friend, he sent a verse to Master Tiandong, which says: The old man of eighty has sprouted new teeth;
He chews the void thoroughly and spits out crabapples. Scattering them toward the trees by Linglong Rock, Every branch and every leaf is a *tánhuá* flower.

Chan Master Ning of Lingyin, Tui-geng, first resided at Chongsheng Monastery in Jiaxing. He subsequently moved to Ba’en, Huirì, and Chengtian in Suzhou, and later to Wanshòu before finally moving to Lingyin.
Upon ascending the hall for his formal discourse, he said: "No dharma exists before one’s eyes, yet the intent lies right before one’s eyes. After the rain, the mountain colors are verdant;
in the warm breeze, the birds’ songs are clamorous. He struck the meditation seat and said: "How laughable that the Old Barbarian (Bodhidharma) has no pivot to turn!"
Zhì sat for nine years before the peak of Shaoshi Mountain. He ascended the hall and, citing a case involving Xianglin, addressed a monk’s question:

"When the year has ended and the time is exhausted, what then? Xianglin replied: "The old Wang of the eastern village burns paper money at night. The Master said: "The old Wang burns money; his words are precise and his speech is exact.

It is like a jade stone wrapped in cotton, or a lump of mud encased in iron. He ascended the hall again: "The thousand peaks stretch before one's eyes; their verdant hues lock together, filling the void."
Willow catkins drift like cotton. Piteous indeed is the Unranked True Man, who has for long been sleeping in the grass and under the dew.
Silence! Another spring has passed; when will it be the year of our return? Raising the case where Yantou asked Qingshan, "What is the true word?
Qingshan replied, "Namo Buddhāya. The verse says: Responding to the occasion, he answered as the question arose. It is not Chan, nor is it not Chan.
"Xuan. This was translated without basis by later generations, who took Sanskrit terms and rendered them into Chinese (Tang language).

For example, there is the case where a monk asked Zen Master Zhaozhou, "What is your surname? Zhaozhou replied, "It is in Changzhou. The monk asked, "How old are you? Zhaozhou replied, "It is in Suzhou."
The verse says: There is one in Suzhou; there is one in Changzhou. In the third month, the partridges cry out across the Jiangnan region.
How laughable is this man of many years but no virtue, who, when pressed by others, tries to offer a forced explanation.
Chan Master Kexiang of Xuefeng’s Steep Bank in Fuzhou cited a monk asking Caoshan: "The snow covers the thousand mountains;

why does the solitary peak not turn white? Caoshan replied: "You must know there is that which is extraordinary within the extraordinary. The monk asked: "What is that which is extraordinary within the extraordinary?"
Mount [Shan] said: "It does not fall within the colors of the various mountains. The verse says: Within words, both this and that carry the profound and mysterious;
All seek to discern the correct and the biased within words. A solitary, neglected imperial post road— Vastly submerged before the bright moonlight.
[The Master] raised a case: A monk asked Guizong, "What is the profound principle? Guizong said, "No one can understand it. The monk asked, "How about before [one understands]? Guizong said:
Dongshan said, "To have a direction is to deviate. Xuefeng asked, "What of one who has no direction? Dongshan replied, "Who seeks the profound principle?
Xuefeng asked again, "Is there not a gate of skillful means to enable students to enter? Dongshan replied, "The wondrous power of Avalokiteśvara’s wisdom can save the world from suffering.
Xuefeng asked, "What is the wondrous power of Avalokiteśvara’s wisdom? Dongshan struck the lid of the cauldron.
The Master struck three times and asked, "Did you hear that? The monk replied, "I heard it. Returning to his quarters, the Master said, "Why did I not hear it?

The monk was speechless. The Master chased him away with his staff. He composed a verse, which says: "The three strikes lift the lid of the cauldron, the Universal Gate opens wide; In the bitter sea of toil, the weary wanderer cannot be called back.
Of the springtime's ninety days, half has now passed; Empty-flying petals fall, dotting the moss. The Verse for Receiving Guests at Yupu (Fisherman’s Harbor) begins: "Wu..."
Beyond the mountains and across the front of the peaks, there is food to satisfy hunger and a mat to sleep upon. Reaching this point, one can find rest;
yet the imperial capital remains separated by but a single tide of the boat.
Chan Master Xiyuan Liaohui of Tiantong in Mingzhou was the son of the Luo family from Pengzhou.

While still a young child with hair hanging down, he would invariably play with other children by kneading mud and sand to fashion Buddhist stupas and images. One day, Zudeng arrived at his home at Mount Yuzhang;

the Master joined his palms toward him, and because his parents perceived a karmic affinity between master and disciple from past lives, they allowed him to leave the household life. Zudeng bestowed upon him the *Banzhou* [Samādhi].

His aspiration was not with Samādhi. He took his leave to go to Chengdu to pay his respects to Guānzhào at Zhāojié. Guānzhào recognized his potential and directed him to travel south for further inquiry.
He then visited Zhèwēng Yán at Jìngshān. Hearing that Gāoyuán Quán was a person of straightforward character, he admired him deeply and went to seek him out.
Just as he arrived, Quán had departed for Ruìyán on Mount Tāi; the Master accompanied him there. One day, Quán asked about the great [expanse of] mountains and rivers.
When the Master was about to open his mouth to say whether the ground exists or does not exist, Yuan suddenly shouted at him. The Master then presented a verse. Yuan said, "There is no connection.

If you can discern and distinguish within this, then even a palace made of gold is not considered noble, nor is jade food.

Originally, there is no person who is deluded or awakened; it simply requires resolution this very day. Since there is neither delusion nor awakening, what is there to resolve? [He] strikes the meditation staff once.

"Not so. You all have spent the summer retreat here; I, this mountain monk, shall speak directly to you: the mouth is the gate of calamity. He then ascended the hall and cited Master Linji’s words: "There is one person who remains on the road for kalpas without ever leaving home; there is another person who leaves home and is no longer on the road. Which of these two is worthy of receiving the offerings of devas and humans? The Master [continued]: ...The Master said: "If you say they are one, you will fall into the pit of the common crowd. If you say they are different, you will be lost in the weeds of discrimination. If you can discern them clearly right now, then you may understand the meaning of Linji’s words. But even if you could distinguish them, it would still be like a dog gnawing at a dry bone. What is the use? If you can turn back and look within yourself, then you will see that the two persons are originally one. Since they are originally one, why do you seek outside? If you seek outside, you are far removed from the truth. If you can realize this, then you will know that the 'one person' is not separate from the 'other person. This is what is meant by 'the mouth is the gate of calamity. Do not let your own mouths deceive you.

If you can understand this, then you will know that the Buddha-dharma is not something to be grasped through words and letters. It is only when you let go of all conceptualizations that you can enter the gate of liberation. Therefore, I tell you: do not rely on words; do not rely on meanings; do not rely on the mind; do not rely on consciousness. Only when you are free from all these dependencies can you truly receive the offerings of devas and humans. The Master then descended from the seat.

Changjiang. Chan Master Jue’an Mengzhen of Chengtian Monastery in Suzhou, a successor of Chan Master Xuedou Qian, was a native of Xuancheng. He became a monk at the age of eight and received full ordination at nineteen.

He was fully equipped for his journey. Having traveled as a wandering monk (*yātrika*) for twenty years, he had encountered seven or eight venerable masters (*guruvṛddha*) but could not reach a definitive resolution.
Admiring the spiritual style of Wuzhun, he ascended Mount Jing to seek an audience with him. Each time he entered the meditation hall (*kōan-shitsu*), he was struck with trembling fear;

he could not even remember his *huatou*. From then on, he no longer entered the room for formal interviews. Day and night, he did nothing but practice seated meditation (*zazen*). One day, while walking along the corridor, he heard the fire-board (*hōban*) sounding. There was...

He had not yet finished speaking when the Master said, "Feel free to leap about as you please. Xie asked, "Where do you meet Yangqi? The Master replied, "You have missed it right before your face.

Gazing from atop the sandy mountain peaks, the west wind startles the geese into a slanting flight. Entering the hall, the Master raised up the verse of National Teacher Yao:

Chan Master Xutang Zhiyu of Mount Jing in Hangzhou was a successor of Chan Master Daochangyan. A native of Siming, he appeared in the world at Xingsheng Temple in Jiahe;
he subsequently moved to Guangxiao, Mingzhi, Xianxiao, Yanfu, Ruiyan, Baolin in Wuzhou, and Boyuan at Yuyang in Siming.
He resided successively at ten monasteries, including Jingci and Jingshan in Hangzhou. Within his quarters, he would offer this critical instruction:
"Why is it that those whose own eyes are not yet clear take empty space to wear as trousers? Why is it that they draw lines on the ground to make a prison and cannot pass beyond this?"
"Why enter the sea to count the grains of sand at its bottom? Why stand on tiptoe upon the point of a needle? A monk asked, "The single phrase before sound does not fall into the trap of permanence;
how do you manifest when shifting positions to accord with function? The Master said, "To inquire, one need not reach out the hand.
The monk said, "But tell me, what of 'Ten Thousand Years for the Son of Heaven'? The Master said, "Auspicious grass grows in times of great fortune; the numinous flower..."
[The Master] concludes the early spring. A monk said, "It would truly be like thunder shaking and wind blowing throughout the nine provinces and four seas.
The Master said, "When one goes out the door, one only fears not being the first to arrive. He ascended the hall and said: "The spring breeze is like a blade; the spring rain is like a balm.

Within the gate of the patch-robed monk, what use is there for such idle chatter? He ascended the hall and said: "If words are sufficient, though one speaks all day long, one has exhausted the Way. If words are insufficient, though one speaks all day long..."
Yet all things are exhausted within it. Furthermore, as for the Way and things: are they one or two? If the Way is one, why is the guest mountain high and the host mountain low?

If you can distinguish the black from the white within this, I will return to you the price of your straw sandals. If it is otherwise, I only wish that next year’s silkworms and wheat may ripen, so that Rāhula may receive a single coin.
Ascending the hall for the Summer Retreat: There is one person who consumes ten thousand taels of gold daily;
they are of the same nature as this sacred regulation, yet no one recognizes them. If there were someone who could recognize them, I would grant them [the merit of] a day’s consumption.
It would take ten thousand taels of gold to exhaust [the cost of this]. Entering the hall, he said: "Baolin has never had any gates or portals.

"Brothers who have long practiced and walk the true path—if there are those who cannot yet apply the 'Black Bean' method, the Way of Linji will soon perish and be heard of no more. How tragic! The Master continued:
"The Old Man of Vulture Peak is much like one leaning on a staff while riding a horse; though he avoids the danger of falling, he cannot escape the gaze of bystanders."

[The Master] Chou. Late in life, the Master resided at Jingci. On the day he entered the monastery, during the sequence of questions and answers with his disciples, an imperial messenger suddenly delivered an edict asking:
"Why did Zhaozhou travel as a pilgrim for eighty years? Why did Xutang reside in the mountains for eighty years?
The Master then cited the story of Zhaozhou’s pilgrimage to Linji and offered this verse: "Zhaozhou only began his pilgrimage at eighty; Xutang [resided] for eighty..."

He resided at Mount [Zhaoqing] once again. Possessing a distinct capacity, he revitalized the legacy of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; his influence moved the imperial countenance within the nine-layered capital.

when the Patriarch’s intent comes from the West, who else is there to ask? To accept it as a whole is to be the whole itself; atop the summit of Sumeru, one carries Sumeru.
[The Master] cited Chan Master Huichang, who was asked by the Imperial Historian Huang Shanggu about the shortcut to the Way, and requested the Master to point it out.
The Master said, "Tang, as for what Confucius said—'My disciples, do you think I am hiding anything from you?
I hide nothing from you'—how would you explain this, Taishi, in your ordinary state? Guo attempted a reply, but the Master said, "Not so, not so. Guo remained in a state of confusion and distress.

Listen idly to the cuckoo crying before the breeze. Ascending the hall, he said: "All day long busy, busy with that matter—it does not hinder the manifest, yet it is not revealed;

He subsequently went forth into the world at Wǔfēng on Yīn Mountain and later moved to Jīn'é. In the fifth year of the Hongwǔ era, an imperial decree was issued to summon eminent monks from throughout the land to establish [the Sangha].

They assembled at Mount Zhong; Master [Yuanxian] and Master Le Jitan were among them. Jitan was appointed by imperial decree to reside at Tianjie Temple, while the Master occupied the position of First Seat (*dìyīzuò*).

He upheld the essential principles and set an exemplary standard for the monastic community, earning contemporary praise for his propriety. The following year, he was selected to preside over Jinshan.
In the eleventh year, he ascended to Lingyin. On the occasion of the Buddha-Bathing ceremony, he ascended the hall and cited the story of Chan Master Yanyun of Yaoshan, who, due to Zhen...
While Puna was serving as the abbot of the bathhouse during the Buddha-bathing ceremony, Mount Yunmen asked him, "Can you bathe only this one, or can you also bathe that one?
Puna replied, "Bring me that one here. Yunmen then ceased questioning him. The Master said:
"This one and that one—each and every one has been bathed from the very beginning. Yunmen and Puna merely debated it; look closely, and it turns out to be so."

A slip of the tongue. A completed slip of the tongue. Turning into a confused error. [He] strikes the meditation seat. The spring in Wulin has already faded; the terraces and pavilions are filled with lush green shade.

On the occasion of the Buddha’s Birthday, he ascends the hall and says: When the World-Honored One was first born, he pointed one finger toward heaven and one finger toward earth, walked seven steps, and looked around in the four directions, saying, "In the heavens above and the earth below, I alone am honored. Truly, he became a great man.
[The Master] said, "This is no child’s play. Yunmen said, "If I had seen him at that time, I would have struck him dead with a single blow and fed him to a dog, so as to bring peace to the world.
If you wish to belong to the lineage of the Old Barbarian, you must act exactly like this before you will succeed."
Fachang said, "What a fine blow! But it is far too late. Before he had even left the soles of his feet beneath the Tuṣita Heaven, a single thrust of the awl would have sufficed;
how could it wait until today? Even so, it is much like drawing one's bow after the thief has already fled. One might have thought his beard was red."
Furthermore, there is the "Red-bearded One" and the "Yellow-faced Old Man," who are surely showing off their cleverness at the very end; they seem as if they were unconcerned by anyone else.

[The Master] drew a line with his staff and called to the assembly, saying: "Do you understand? A tangle of willow threads cannot be gathered up."
Mist blends with smoke as it rests upon the jade balustrade. Entering the hall: Today is the first day of the intercalary fifth month;

the sun continues to rise from the eastern side. Every monk understands how to appreciate the sound; whether in short or long verse, all remain in harmony with the musical laws. The plum rains have cleared.
Strolling leisurely beneath the dense shade of the forest trees, what gain or loss could there be? The "True Person of No Rank" is but a lump of red flesh; at any moment, one may topple Vimalakīrti.
On the day of the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*, he ascended the hall and said: "Nirvāṇa and birth-and-death are equally like flowers in the sky;
'Buddha' and 'sentient beings' are both superfluous words. At this point, how do you all understand it? After a long silence, he struck the meditation seat.

One merely sees fallen blossoms drifting away with the water, unaware that they carry the springtime out from within the cave. On the occasion of the Buddha-Bathing Ceremony, the Master ascended the hall and cited the Venerable Xiangyan:

An old mistake! Today is the eighth day of the fourth month, the Buddha’s birthday. How can one raise this public case on such a day?

When asked which faculty he possessed, none among the assembly could respond in accord with his realization. Before long, he encountered the calamity of false accusations and was arrested.

Some urged the Master to devise a plan for himself early on, but he paid them no heed. With a serene countenance, he went to the authorities; before the interrogation had even begun, he recited a verse beneath the corridor eaves and passed away while sitting upright.
This was the twenty-third day of the sixth month in the nineteenth year of the Hongwu era. He was sixty-nine years of age at his death.

Chan Master Fanchi Chu-shih of T’ien-ning Monastery in Chia-hsing Prefecture was a native of Hsiang-shan in Ming-chou. His secular surname was Chu.

The divine monk Master Mo said, "This child is the Sun of the Buddha. In the future, he will surely uplift the Buddha-dharma and illuminate the dark alleys of the world.
He therefore named him Tan Yao. Having lost both parents early, he was raised by his grandmother.
At the age of seven, he was able to compose verses; far and near, he was hailed as a prodigy. At nine, he entered Yongzuo Temple to study under Master Ne. Soon thereafter—

He followed his ancestral master, Jin Weng Xun Yuhu, at Chong'en Temple. When Zhao Wengong saw him, he regarded him with high esteem and purchased a *sengqie* (monk’s certificate) for him so that he could receive ordination.
At the age of sixteen, he received the full precepts (*upasampadā*). When Jin Weng moved to Daochang, the Master served as his attendant and subsequently took charge of the library keys.
One day, while reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he reached the passage: "When seeing depends on conditions, then because of clarity, darkness becomes non-seeing. He did not understand it.

When one clarifies that which arises from within, all dark appearances can never again obscure it. Because he attained this realization, he perused the various scriptures and felt as though they were in accord with what he already knew from a former life.
At that time, Yuansou was propagating the Way at Shuangjing. The Master went there to seek instruction and asked:

"What is it that when speech issues forth it is not sound, and before form appears it is not an object? Yuansou immediately said: "Speech issues forth but is not sound; before form appears it is not an object. Speak quickly! Speak quickly!"
As the Master was about to offer a word in response, the old man let out a thunderous roar of a shout. The Master was struck with astonishment.

Later, when Emperor Yingzong summoned eminent monks to transcribe the Great Canon in gold, the Master responded to the imperial decree and entered the capital. One night, having risen from sleep, he heard the sound of a drum and attained great enlightenment; sweat poured from him like rain.

He was named Shijushi Haiyan Fuzhen. In the Wuchen year of the Dali era, he moved to Tianning Monastery in Zhuozhou; in the Yihai year of the Zhiyuan era, he moved to Baoguo Monastery in Hangzhou.

"Where are you, sir? The Master said, "Blinking one's eyebrows. [The student] said, "Thank you for answering my question. The Master said, "It happens that my staff is not here.
[The student] asked, "Since the entire earth is this Buddha-body, where does one dwell and observe the retreat?"

The Master said, "This is like adding another layer of flowers upon brocade. [The student] asked, "The bamboo is dense, yet it does not hinder the flowing stream from passing through; the mountain is high, yet how could it obstruct the white clouds from flying?
The Master said, "You are generating interpretations based on mere words. [The student] asked, "What is 'first illumination, then function'? The Master said:
Splitting open Mount Taihua, it reaches the color of heaven; releasing the Yellow River, its sound flows to the sea. [The student] asked, "What is 'first using, then reflecting'?
The Master said, "The sword leaves its precious scabbard because of injustice; the medicine comes from the golden jar to save the sick.
[The student] asked, "What is 'reflecting and using simultaneously'? The Master said, "Dingguang beckons from afar at Jindi; Zhiyi [signals] secretly at Jiangling."

[The Master] nodded his head and said, "What is meant by 'illumination and function do not occur at the same time'? The teacher said, "For three months, I have been too weary to travel the road beneath the blossoms;
my entire household sits in sorrow with the door closed in the rain. The monk bowed. The teacher said, "Would it not be well to ask one more turn?
[A monk] asked, "For what purpose does the Great Compassionate Bodhisattva employ so many hands and eyes? The teacher said, "The spring wind does not wrap the head. [Another] asked.
"What is the lion in its cave? The Master said, "Its head touches the heavens. [The student] asked, "What is the lion emerging from its cave?

One day, while Fengshan was entering the provincial capital, High Chancellor Gao asked him, "Chan is divided into five schools and the Teachings are arranged in three vehicles. I do not ask about the Teachings; what is Chan? The Master replied, "It is precisely the time for the New Year’s banquet. The Chancellor said, "Bodhidharma came from the West not to establish written texts, but to point directly to the human mind so that one may see one's nature and become a Buddha. Where is the Buddha? The Master replied, [and pointed]. The Chancellor looked at his hand. The Master said, "Do you understand? The Chancellor said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "If you had understood, you would have been a Buddha. The Chancellor said, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "This very thing is the Buddha. The Chancellor said, "What is this very thing? The Master said, "The Chancellor himself is it. The Chancellor said, "How can I be it? The Master said, "If you were not it, how could you be the Chancellor? The Chancellor said, "I still do not understand. The Master said, "If you do not understand, you will surely fall into the pit of doubt. The Chancellor said, "I am deeply grateful for your instruction. The Master said, "If you are grateful, you must practice accordingly. The Chancellor said, "I shall practice accordingly. The Master said, "If you practice accordingly, you will surely attain realization. The Chancellor said, "I am afraid I am too dull-witted. The Master said, "Dullness is precisely what is needed to break through the barrier. The Chancellor said, "I am truly grateful for your great compassion. The Master said, "Great compassion is not something to be grasped. The Chancellor said, "I do not know where to begin my practice. The Master said, "Begin by letting go of all thoughts. The Chancellor said, "But how can I let go of them? The Master said, "If you try to let them go, you are already clinging to them. The Chancellor said, "I am at a loss. The Master said, "There is no need for a loss; simply be as you are. The Chancellor said, "I am still confused. The Master said, "Confusion is the very state of enlightenment. The Chancellor said, "I am deeply moved by your words. The Master said, "Words are merely empty sounds. The Chancellor said, "I wish to receive your seal of approval. The Master said, "A seal is just ink on paper. The Chancellor said, "Then how can I prove my attainment? The Master said, "Attainment is not something to be proven. The Chancellor said, "I am truly fortunate to have met such a master. The Master said, "Fortune is not something to be sought. The Chancellor said, "I shall cherish these instructions for the rest of my life. The Master said, "Cherishing is itself a burden. The Chancellor bowed deeply and withdrew. The Master said, "Go and reflect upon this. The Chancellor departed. The Master said to his attendants, "That man has a sharp root of capacity; he will surely benefit many in the future. The attendants asked, "Why did you say that? The Master said, "Because he knows how to put the teachings into practice. The attendants said, "We do not understand. In the ninth month of autumn in the first year of the Hongwu era, an imperial decree was issued to convene more than ten eminent monks from Jiangnan at Mount Jangshan to establish a Great Dharma Assembly.

The Master was commanded to ascend the seat and preach the Dharma, which greatly pleased the Emperor. In the spring of the second year, he again summoned him according to the precedent established in the first year.

The Master preached the Dharma. An imperial banquet was granted for him below Wénlóu, where he personally received the Emperor’s inquiries. Upon his departure, the Inner Treasury was opened to bestow white gold upon him.

In the autumn of the third year, the Emperor, considering that the manifestations and conditions of ghosts and spirits are profound and subtle and difficult to fathom, believed that the lost scriptures must contain clear explanations regarding them.
He summoned those among the monks who were extensively versed in the Tripiṭaka to question them; thereupon, the Master, along with Mèngtáng Ē and Xíngzhōng, [were selected].
The Venerable Ones and their colleagues responded to the imperial summons and arrived at the capital, where they were quartered at Dàtiānjiè Temple (Great Heaven-World Temple).

The Emperor ordered the Ministry of Rites to provide them with hospitality and commanded the Ministry of Food to distribute firewood and rice. Shortly thereafter, he instructed them to submit a detailed analysis of the questions posed to them.

The Master drew upon the sūtras and śāstras to compose a treatise intended for presentation; however, he suddenly manifested slight illness. After four days had passed, he summoned his attendants, bathed, changed his robes, and requested a brush.
He wrote a verse, saying: "The true nature is perfectly luminous; fundamentally, there is neither birth nor death. A wooden horse neighs at night; the sun rises in the west.

It was the twenty-sixth day of the seventh month. The Emperor heard of this and lamented for a long time. At that time, cremation was prohibited;

Five-colored *śarīra* were scattered throughout the skeletal remains. His disciple Wensheng enshrined the bones and the unharmed items in the pagoda at the Western Quarters. As for the Master’s worldly lifespan...

He was seventy-five years of monastic seniority (śrāmaṇera-vassa) and sixty-three years of age. Master Ren of Zhong composed a biography of his conduct, and Master Song Lian, the Wenxian, wrote an inscription for him.

His extant works include the *Recorded Sayings of the Six Assemblies*, *Pure Land Poems*, *Verses on the Rebirth Above of Maitreya*, the *Beiyou Ji* (Collection from the Northern Tour), the *Fengshan Ji* (Collection from Feng Mountain), the *Xizhai Ji* (Collection from the Western Studio), the *Poems in Response to the Three Sages*, the *Yongming Hermitage Poems*, and translations of the poems of Tao Qian and Lin Bu.
His collected poems comprise several volumes, all of which circulate in the world.
