Chan Master Xiling of Xubai Valley at Mount Jing in Hangzhou was a native of Yiwu in Wuzhou. His surname was He.
At the age of nineteen, he shaved his head at Zishou Monastery in Dongyang. Upon receiving full ordination, he visited Xuzhou Yuan at Shuanglin.
He subsequently relied upon Dongsou Ying at Jingci Monastery, where he served as the inner record-keeper (*naiji*) and later as the attendant (*shizhe*) who succeeded Shilin to the master’s position.
One day, he went to visit Xueyan at Beijian. Xueyan cited the karmic connection between Huanglong and Ciming to question him;
the Master was praised as being exceptionally sharp and capable. When Xueyan moved to Dayang, he sent a letter inviting the Master to serve as the head of the first seat.
One day, Xueyan asked: "Linji received sixty blows of the staff from Huangbo three times; why did he then go to Daoyu?"
[The Master] struck downward with his fist. Yunyan said, "This will surely leave people dull-witted. Yunyan then struck him. The Master shook out his sleeves and departed.

In the *wuchen* year of the Yuan era (1266), as Yunyan was about to pass away, he patted the Master’s shoulder and said, "I entrust this burden to you. The Master replied, "I shall certainly not let myself be buried alive here. Not long after, Yunyan passed away, and the assembly requested the Master to succeed him on the seat.

He once offered three statements for instruction: 1. "The Great Way is not difficult; it simply avoids picking and choosing. 2. "The Great Way is not difficult; it simply avoids being attached to anything. 3. "The Great Way is not difficult; it simply avoids having preferences."

Fàn’s standards were rigorous and he would not grant any concessions. When Tièguānshū was traveling on pilgrimage, he once visited the Master. It happened to be the Small Assembly (xiǎocān) for the Winter Solstice;
the Master raised the kōan concerning Yúnmén’s "millet cake" (húbǐng). Guān presented four verses as an offering. The Master asked, "Who are you?"
Guankui said, "Venerable Shuzhang. The Master asked, "Where have you come from? Guankui said, "Yunmen.
The Master said, "Are you mad? Are you crazy? Guankui said, "Where are your eyes, Master? The Master then gave a shout. Guankui also shouted. The Master struck out a punch.
Guankui stepped forward, met him head-on, and said, "Setting aside the blow for a moment, what is the meaning of the 'Yunmen cake'? The Master—
He lunged forward with his hand and snatched away Guan’s cap. Guan said, "A mistake. The Master struck several more punches in succession. Guan said, "Your fists have no eyes;

you will be scrutinized by others later. The Master paid him no heed. He went on, tripping Guan’s seven-striped robe so that he fell to the ground, and delivered nine blows across his waist, saying, "This is to let you know my methods.
Guan said, "These methods are superior to those of Linji and Deshan."
The Master summoned Zhigong, the keeper of the locks, and sent him to the treasury office. He was not released until nightfall.

I shall answer them all. After a moment, the drum sounded, but Guankui waited for a long time and the attendant did not arrive.
During a year of famine, the Master always shared his food with the community. One day, he conversed with a guest until past midnight.

Halfway through, he was overcome by hunger. His attendant requested that he take a spoonful of grain to make a drink. The Master said, "It must not be so. How can the permanent property of the monastery be used privately by the abbot?
In the year of *Xingyu Bingchen*, the Provincial Administration submitted a petition to the Imperial Court to invite the Master to preside over Mount Jing. A monk asked:
"The past mind cannot be apprehended; the present mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind cannot be apprehended. What does this mean?
The Master said, "One does not give to those who are already close. In his youth, the Master once dreamed of wandering through the Hall of Arhats at Jingci Temple.

Summoned for an audience, he preached the Dharma to the Emperor’s satisfaction. He was granted the title Chan Master Fojian. During the Dade era, he was further bestowed with the title Dayuan.

Upon becoming the abbot of Jingshan, Renzong added the titles Huizhao and Dabian. On the twelfth day of the fourth month in the Renxu year of the Zhizhi era, he personally wrote a letter entrusting his external protectors and admonishing his disciples.
He spoke a gāthā to bid farewell to the assembly and passed away at the Budong Xuan Hall. (From the *Quan*)
His body was interred in a field of achyranthes (chāngpú). His secular age was seventy-six, and his monastic seniority (*saṃgha-rakṣa*) was fifty-seven.

He left behind the *Bàoyán jí* (Collected Works from the Waterfall Cliff) and several volumes of recorded sayings (*yùlù*). Iron Mountain Qióng, a Zen Master of Cíhuà in Yúzhōu, left home at the age of eighteen and first visited Xuěyán at Dà...

Chan Master Tianyin Muchuan Yuanzhi of Nengren Monastery in Jianchang Prefecture was a native of Gaoyang. His surname was Yao, and both his father and elder brother were renowned jinshi (metropolitan graduates).
The Master aspired to the school of emptiness; at the age of nineteen, he went to Chan Master Huirang of Yangshan to undergo tonsure and ordination.

After serving him diligently for several years, during the Yuanzhen era, he emerged into the world at Nengren Monastery, where he and Gaofeng both upheld the legacy of National Teacher Changqing Huichong.

Sometimes the wind moves them so they lean against one another repeatedly, as if fighting incessantly before the steps. (A shout.

Until the cultivation of the mind reaches the groundless state, ten thousand kinds and a thousand variations follow the flowing water. Baoning’s informal sermon upon entering the monastery: Sitting grandly in the hall, a hundred layers and a thousand folds;
with a single phrase fully raised, it encompasses heaven and contains earth. Even the Buddha-eye cannot see it; even the ocean-mouth [cannot describe it].
Difficult to proclaim! Ancient and modern follow different paths; both ordinary beings and sages cannot fathom it.

It is only when the qilin manifests its auspiciousness and the phoenix arrives in person, when mountain colors present their blessings and human dwellings cluster together—yet even so, Master Bao of Liang missed the mark regarding Bodhidharma.
Although he was called the Great Being Avalokiteśvara who transmitted the Buddha’s mind-seal, in the end he did not recognize this very message. This is for all of you...
Have you not yet had a moment of sharp realization? (He strikes the meditation staff. "If one does not sleep in the same bed, how can one know that the lining of the quilt is worn through?

A small *can* (informal sermon). He cites Master Sīxīn’s address to the assembly: "High-ranking practitioners on pilgrimage must untie their alms-bowl bags, take off their bundles and hats, and cast aside their dietary taboos.
They must reach the place where one person goes; they must reach the place where half a person goes; they must reach the place where no person goes."
"To exist, one must personally arrive there. The Master said, "Such talk is like black rock candy; it is sweet both inside and out.
Nevertheless, were it not for the wild geese at nightfall, how could one see the autumn at the sea gate? The Small Sermon on New Year’s Eve: "Tonight, as the year ends, has it ever truly ended?
Tomorrow, as the new year begins, will it actually come? Thirty-six hundred breaths turn like a carriage wheel; how many times have the tides gone out?"

Furthermore, as the tide turns and the wheel of the mechanism revolves, even a flash of lightning would leave one bewildered. When the Great Function manifests before you, who can discern its true mark?

Eradicate the dust of emotions before they arise; forget the ultimate principle through verbal explanations. Every person’s nostrils reach toward the heavens; every individual dwells in peace and joy.
Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, should they give rise to views of Buddha or Dharma, shall be banished to the two Iron Ring Mountains. The lantern...
The dew-pillar protrudes its adamantine eye. Ha ha! Great laughter! "Three pounds of flax," "a dried-up dung pellet.

If you attempt to deliberate upon these as matters of Buddha-dharma, you will enter hell as swiftly as a shot arrow. Here, words and thoughts are cut off; the sphere of mental activity is extinguished.
In a state of uniform equanimity, all things subside of their own accord. At such a time, what is it like? The east wind blows yesterday...

The night’s remaining snow has melted away; blossoms have once more appeared upon the branches of the withered trees. This is the small *sīmā-bandha* (summer retreat) *śamaya*. Tomorrow, the summer retreat begins and you shall arrive.
You simply pass the days in idle indolence, yet when the drum is struck and you ascend the hall, you truly find yourself unable to conceive of a response.
As you all crowd forward together, you cannot help but mistake south for north. Before the Seven Buddhas, there was never such a thing as this "melting away."

Rest. Although there have been those with this news since the time of the Seven Buddhas, they were ultimately unable to fully awaken to the unsurpassed Bodhi of the Tathāgata, nor were they able to enter the monastery of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-vijñapti*) and dwell in the wisdom of equanimity within body and mind.

Consequently, for ninety days, these people concerned themselves only with their mouths and bodies rather than with cultivation; they turned their backs on awakening and conformed to the dust of the senses. In vain...
"Stretching out the months and years. The Fifth Patriarch, the Venerable Master, said: "Master Bodhidharma came with his feet believing and spoke with his mouth believing;
the descendants of later generations, however, turned it into mere calculation. Through such calculation, heaven becomes clear and earth becomes peaceful.
Yunmen’s fan leaps up to the Thirty-three Heavens, striking the nostrils of Śakra, while the carp of the Eastern Sea is struck once with a blow, and the rain falls like..."
The basin overflows; the chicken of Chu is no phoenix from Mount Dan, yet it loves to cry out atop the wutong tree.
The Master once gave this instruction: "There is still more beyond this. He reveals the claws and fangs of the lion; within this, there is another matter for deliberation.

One cannot help but brandish a sword at the gate—before this sharp blade of spirit, who dares to propose a comparison? His verbal prowess is steep and lofty; his hand-eye coordination is extraordinary.
Master Ying'an was likely the foremost among his teachers; he once continued the *Zongmen tongyao*. Later, he passed away at Baoning.
Chan Master Tianyi Dujiang Jue'en of Yuezhou was tall and thin in stature, possessed pure integrity and firm resolve, and was compassionate by nature.

Xi Gu was a member of the Gu clan. In his youth, he relied upon Yunmen Guangxiao to receive the tonsure. He followed Master Wen at Yanqing Monastery in Mingzhou to study the *Sijiaoyi* (The Ritual of the Four Teachings).
Within seven days, he mastered it; Master Wen was so astonished and marveled at his extraordinary talent that he sent him to attend Huixiang of Yangchuan in the quarters of Yuyang Monastery.

His spiritual resonance was as intimate as being held in the palm of one's hand, and his virtuous deeds became manifest day by day. At that time, all the worthy scholars and gentlemen delighted in associating with him.
He emerged from the world at T'ien-p'ing in Su-chou; later, he moved to K'ai-yüan, then to Pao-fu in Ming-chou, and finally to T'ien-i in Yüeh-chou.
One day, while the assembly was standing in attendance within his quarters, he suddenly leaned on his staff and said: "This old monk stands hollow and empty, leaning upon his rustic staff."
He clearly depicted Subhūti, looked left and right, and asked, “Do you understand? After a long silence, he cast down his staff, leaned against his meditation cushion, and passed away.

[This is] the portrait of Zen Master Yuejiang Yin, inscribed [by another]: An eighty-year-old Chan elder whose vision empties the four seas. His face bears the ancient hue of Mount Kuanglu; his body is like the wondrous peak of Zhuobi.

Hearing his proclamations, even Nanyue Huairang would have nodded in agreement. Observing his life’s course, how could Daomei not have shared the same wind? A wild goose flies across the vast sky, its shadow sinking into the cold water. He succeeded to the ancestral tradition of the furnace and bellows that smelt gold, like the moon in autumn or the frost on a winter night.
"Zhong: I shall see that the Way of this hermitage will become luminous and magnificent, extending perpetually through infinity.

Chan Master Dongyu Dehai of Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou was a successor of Chan Master Gong of Jingci Monastery. He was the son of the Chen family of Linhai in Taizhou; he was fourteen years old [when he entered the monastic life].
He left the household life under the Sichuan monk Anshi and went to visit Shilin Gong at Chengtian Temple.

Shilin asked, "What is your own self? The Master hesitated, and Shilin immediately pushed him out. The Master was immediately filled with doubt. One day, while entering the inner quarters, Shilin asked, "The entire great earth is the true body of the Vajra;
where would you place yourself, Upāsaka? The Master was about to respond when Shilin struck him. From this point on...

This was Chemezhen. Lin Qian appointed him to the position of Attendant Director at Jingci Monastery. One day, in the meditation hall, he raised the story of the National Teacher’s three calls to his attendant.
The Master said, "It is not that the cat is lost; it is certainly that the dog is lost. Lin said, "Is this betraying [the truth], or is it not betraying it?
The Master said, "Deceiving others and deceiving oneself. Lin struck him with his bamboo staff and said, "Excessive!"
My lineage is that of Hai Zi. In the twenty-seventh year of the Zhizhi era, he appeared in the world at Hanyan on Mount Tiantai.
In the *yisi* year of the Dade era, he moved to Hanshan in Gusu. In the *jiyou* year of the Zhide era, he moved again to Dongchan in Kunshan.

In the *xinhai* year, he was granted a golden-embroidered dharma robe by imperial decree. In the second year of the Huangqing era, he moved once more to Zhongzhu. In the second year of the Yanyou era, an edict appointed him as the abbot of Jing...
Cizhi arrived at the mountain gate and said: "The Pure Gate of Compassion is like the autumn waters of a single lake.
Whether one can enter it or not—tigers bite tigers; snakes swallow tortoises. When the assembly numbered in the tens of thousands, he uttered a pivotal phrase from within his room:
"A hand grasps a sharp sword; why does the monkey not die? One bites through iron-acid dumplings; why are there hungry people on the road? Wave upon wave.
He remarked, "One expects to remove one's hat to bite into the sweet head of a sugarcane. He asked, "Fish take water as their life; why then do they die within the water?

None of the assembly’s answers accorded with his intent. In the second year of the Taiding era, he moved again to Lingyin Monastery. In the ninth month of the fourth year, the Dingmao year, he manifested a slight illness.

Having summoned his disciples and finished his final instructions, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. His secular age was seventy-two, and his monastic seniority (śrāmaṇeraka) was fifty-seven.
He was posthumously granted the title Chan Master Mingzong Huiren. He left behind recorded teachings from six assemblies. His stupa was erected at the foot of the rear mountain of Yewang Monastery.
Chan Master Zhuyun Jingtan of Tiantong Monastery in Jiaxing was the son of the Yan family of Putian.
Having long relied upon Shilin, he later resided at Zhiping in Wuzhou, Beichen in Suzhou, and Tiantong in Huzhou. Upon ascending the hall, he said:
"The golden crow rises in the east; the jade hare sinks in the west. Clever patch-robed monks search here and there. Suddenly, they smash through empty space—throughout kalpas..."
"Only right now. [Zhaozhou] struck his staff and descended from the seat. A monk asked, "The Three Worthies have not yet attained it, and the Ten Sages find it difficult to know.
What is this school? The Master said, "A holeless flute and felt clappers."
Chan Master Shouyong of Dongzhou at Suzhou Huqiu sent a verse to a departing monk, which says: "Whether moving or still, how could one ever be entangled?
Why need one further penetrate that which is prior to birth? The ancestral garden is a thousand li away; now you return— On land there is the journey, on water there is the boat.
He then spoke words for Layman Zhang Yi of Juezhai regarding his entry into the Way, and offered this verse: "A single blow of the staff reaches the ears as the bell tolls."
The root: the ocean of three thousand worlds is simultaneously darkened. The thief departs from the side of the lump of flesh; tomorrow it remains as before, not leaving the gate.
Dharma successor of Chan Master Du of Jing Mountain.

Chan Master Jingfu of Huarong at Mount Jingshan in Hangzhou was a native of Huai’an. During the Zhizhi era of the Yuan dynasty, he was summoned to the imperial court and presented an ode to the Emperor.
Its brief contents state: "The Tathāgatas of the past dwell securely within the secret treasury; the Buddhas of the present in the ten directions have realized the Way and turned the wheel of Dharma;
as for the World-Honored Ones of the future, they are all sentient beings themselves—due to the grasping of deluded thoughts."
Attached to the fetters, afflictions, hindrances, and entanglements, they are deluded into taking on bodies within the six realms and undergo the sufferings of the three miserable paths in vain.
They think only of the Buddhas of the past and present, yet fail to revere the Honored Ones of the future; thus they bind themselves in enmity with the Buddhas.

Some even slaughter and butcher [living beings], failing to realize that the characteristics of sentient beings are entirely the body of *dharmatā*. In the past, there was one named Never-Disparaging who prostrated to all, saying, "I do not disparage you."

"You! You all shall become Buddhas. If you can mindfully regard yourself and others as equally being future Buddhas, you will increase your merit and longevity in the present life, and be born in the Buddha-lands in every lifetime.
Upon reading this, Emperor Bì was greatly delighted and asked whether there had been anyone among the emperors since God (Shàngdì) who observed the precept against killing.
The Master replied: "In the past, Emperor Rénzōng of the Sòng dynasty once said to his ministers: 'Last night I was very hungry and thought of eating a rabbit.'"

He had sacrificed a sheep, but fearing the consequences for those who would follow, he subsequently established this as a permanent rule. He would rather endure a temporary hunger than bear witness to endless killing.
The ministers all cried out "Ten-thousand-year Emperor! The Sovereign praised and accepted his counsel; he then immediately received the precepts from the Imperial Preceptor.
A monk from Tiantong Zhuxi Tan Chan Temple in Mingzhou came for an audience. The Master asked, "From where have you come? The monk replied, "Jinge (Golden Goose).
The Master asked, "How high is Jinge Mountain? The monk said, "Its peak cannot be seen. The Master rebuked him.

One day, as the Master ascended the seat, he raised the koan of the World-Honored One holding up a flower. At these words, the monk attained realization. (This is the eulogy for the Master’s portrait composed by Chan Master Yuejiang Yin: "River-like eyes, sea... )

His mouth was eloquent; his heart was like brocade and his inner being like embroidery. He possessed the vast capacity to swallow the Great Lake, and his brilliance shone with the radiant luster of the Great White Star (Tàibái). When he scolded or reviled, he embraced all with the spring-like nurturing of the sea; when he manifested compassion, he was as fierce as the midday sun or the autumn frost.

He cited the words of Xuansha regarding "not yet having reached the end," which was like Zhēnjìng testing Jìyīn’s gold that has been refined a hundred times. He brought forth Dōngshān’s "three blows of the staff," comparable to Címíng producing the fragrance of nine-fold refined cinnabar from Jīcuì.
His spontaneous wit was unyielding and his martial array was majestic. This is what is called the cooling shade of the great tree of five generations at Zhōngfēng.

Chan Master Baoye Yuan of Dingshui in Yuezhou, a successor of Chan Master Yushan Yu, recounted the karmic occasion involving the World-Honored One and the five-attainment immortals. He offered this verse:
"Which one attainment? You ask, I answer: 'The mouth is the gate of calamity. To invite causes and carry their fruits—this is the great Dharma of shame and compassion."

"O King! Although *bing* and *ding* are associated with the trigram *li*, they do not belong to the element fire. [The Master] ascended the hall and related the case of the scholar Zhang Zhuo, who visited Shishuang.
Shishuang asked the scholar, "What is your noble surname? He replied, "I am a disciple surnamed Zhang, named Zhuo. Shishuang said, "In this place, even 'cleverness' (*qiao*) cannot be found;
from where does 'clumsiness' (*zhuo*) come? At these words, Zhuo attained great enlightenment. He offered this verse: "Advancing forward, there is a precipice three thousand feet high; Retreating..."
Beyond lie a hundred thousand layers of precipices. Revered by the Old Man Zhang Zhuo of the Great Tang: the seamless iron hammer dances in the spring breeze.
Chan Master Xianji Yun of Suzhou’s Tiger Hill had long relied upon Xutang; he served as the First Seat at Mount Jing.
One day, Baoye Yuan requested instruction from Xutang regarding the "final word" of Deshan. [Yuan said,] "If one says it exists, how could Deshan have failed to understand?
If one says it does not exist, yet Yantou remarked that Deshan had not yet understood. I beg the Master’s compassion to provide me with guidance.
Xutang said, "I do not know; go and ask the Head Seat. Yuan went to the Master [the Head Seat], only to find him away on a mountain excursion.

Returning, Yuan sought water to wash his feet. Xuanzang hurriedly brought him water, and Yuan again prostrated himself for the Master to rub and massage him. Thereupon, looking up, Yuan raised the previous conversation to question him.
The Master then scooped up some water and splashed it on him, saying, "What is that ultimate phrase? Yuan did not attain realization.
He went up again and saw the Hall Master. The Hall Master said, "How would you explain this to the Head Seat? Yuan recounted the previous conversation.
The Hall Master said, "That fellow understands it; I will tell you how. At that, Yuan was relieved and grasped the meaning.

He then related the story of the karmic connection between Master Xinghua and Emperor Zhuangzong of the Tang, offering this verse: "The treasure of the Sovereign is naturally difficult to price; Xinghua..."
How could I ever dare borrow it to look at? Since Heaven and Earth have no partiality in their covering and supporting, it remains to this day to stabilize the Central Plains.
Master Lu Geng asked Nanquan: "In my home, there is a single stone; I have sat upon it and I have lain upon it."
He proposed to carve [the words] "Is it attained? Chanquan said, "It is attained. The Grand Master asked, "Is it not attained? Chanquan said, "It is not attained. The verse says:
Sitting and reclining through many springs, Half-sealed by moss, half-enveloped by clouds. Without edges, without seams, difficult to grasp;
In vain one offers one's innermost heart to others.
Chan Master Nan-sou Mao, a successor of Chan Master Yue of Jing-shan, recounted the story of Master Yan-tou, who served as a ferryman on the shores of Lake E-zhu. He hung a wooden board on each bank.
Whenever someone came to cross the river and struck the board once, Yan-tou would ask, "Who is it? or sometimes say, "I want to cross over."
One day, a woman carrying a child approached. [Zhao] Yan said, "I do not ask about presenting oars and dancing with paddles;
tell me, from where did the child in the woman’s arms come? Yan struck her. The woman said, "I have given birth to seven sons;
six did not meet with those who understand them. This one alone is not even worth keeping. She then departed.
He threw it into the water. A verse says: "The destitute ghost-child at the ferry of E-zhu, His entire skill was misplaced at the moment he tapped the boat’s side.
How much better it would have been to offer another turn of phrase, To rescue the seventh son of the old woman. [The Master] brings up the story of Jia-shan’s visit to the Boatman Monk.
A verse says: "Without form and without flaw, he immediately turned his spear back; It was simply because he trusted lightly the Zen mendicant Zhi. If...
He had not yet reached Huating when he was struck by an iron boat-paddle; what could it do to you? Pang Jushi sold his fish-trap fence and fell while crossing a bridge.
When Lingzhao saw him, she also went and collapsed beside her father. The Master asked, "What are you doing?
The daughter replied, "Seeing my father fall, I went to support him. The Master said, "Fortunately, no one else saw this. The verse says: Filial piety conceals rebellion.
"Conversely, one should not conceal the ugliness before others. Those who are close kin in this life were enemies in past lives.
Master Dongsheng Deming of Yuyang, Mingzhou, a Dharma heir of Master Miyuan of Yuyang, was born into the Liu family of Yongdong. At the age of sixteen, he relied upon [the Sangha].
At Xiyuetan, Chenggong shaved his head and received full ordination. He first visited Xisou Tan at Xuedou, and subsequently studied under Wanji Mi.
Mi raised the question: "Manjusri is the teacher of the seven Buddhas; why was he unable to bring the woman out of her samādhi?"

Wangming asked, "How did you manage to get out? The Master said, "In the spring colors there is no high or low; the branches of the flowers are naturally long or short. Mizhi was appointed to oversee the treasury and keys;

he appeared in the world at Yuyang Monastery and was granted the honorary title *Furi Puguang* (Sun of the Buddha, Universal Radiance). Regarding the koan of Chuanzhi’s capsized boat, the Master composed this verse:
"The clear world is vast and boundless as he occupies the vital ford; A single oar is his livelihood, moving with the weight of a thousand *jin*. At Zhu Jing..."
Travelers on the road were few; the depths of his inner mind could not be matched by the vastness of the blue sea. Later, he passed away and was interred in Dongyun Pagoda.
He was eighty-four years of age and sixty-seven years since his ordination. Yuan Yue, a Hanlin Academician, composed the inscription for his memorial stele.
Jingshan and Chan Master Kongsou Xinwu of Lingyin Temple in Hangzhou were dharma heirs of [the aforementioned master]. Chan Master Xinwu was the son of the Niu family of Wuxian County in Suzhou.

At the age of nine, he entered Longxing Temple in the prefectural city to take refuge with Baiyun Xian and received the tonsure. In the Wuxu year of the Zhizheng era, he went to Jingde Temple to study under Yuan'an.
Cizhu asked, "What is the essential meaning of Yongming? The Master replied, "I am but a newcomer; I see only a lake.

Cizhu approved him and subsequently admitted him into his room. In the year of Renyin, he was appointed to the second seat. In the year of Guiyou, Lan’an of Zhuzhu invited him to share the seat and preach the Dharma.
The Imperial Preceptor bestowed upon him the title Yuan Ci Zheng Ji. In the year of Gengxu of the Hongwu era, he resided at Zhe.

In the eighth year of the Chongning era of the Jiang dynasty, he was transferred to Zhongzhu. At that time, the seat at Lingyin was vacant, and the Monastic Registrar included the Master’s name among those recommended;

he was selected. Scholars of the day all packed their provisions and followed him. Not long after, due to past affairs concerning his former tenure as abbot, he was summoned to the capital and died of illness on the road.
On his deathbed, he wrote a verse: "I am fifty-five years old; I have trampled the path of death."
On the third day of the fifth month in the twenty-fourth year of the Hongwu era (the Xinwei year), at midnight, his disciples Duanjing and others performed the cremation according to the dharma.
His tongue and rosary remained unburnt. They enshrined his remains and interred them on the eastern ridge of Lingyin;
subsequently, they divided the remaining bones and buried them at the site of Jiuqu in Xixi. There are three records of his discourses.
Biography.

Yao Guangxiao, the Junior Preceptor, was a native of Changzhou. He styled himself the "Recluse Who Flees Emptiness" (Taoxu zi). At the age of fourteen, he entered the monastic life at Miaozhi Hermitage;
his dharma name was Daoyan, and his courtesy name was Sidao. During the military chaos at the end of the Yuan dynasty, he wandered through the rivers and lakes, deeply concealing his talents.
Huì studied under Yúān of Jìngshān, where he inquired into the essentials of Chan until he fully grasped its core essence.

He served as the inner record-keeper for three years, after which he emerged from seclusion at Pùqìng and was subsequently transferred to Tiānlóng. He once inscribed his own portrait, saying: "Having seen through the *bājiāo* plant and the staff."

In his ordinary moments, he revealed his refined elegance to the very marrow of his bones; at times, he would brandish a whisk made of tortoise-hair, which caused even the void to laugh and nod its head.

During the Hongwu era, he was selected as a high monk to attend upon the Emperor Wen at the Yan residence. Later, during the Yongle era, the Emperor wished to grant him an official rank for his merit in assisting the founding of the dynasty, but he would not accept.
One day, the Emperor summoned him for an audience and secretly had someone drape him in ceremonial robes and a crown.

Tǐ was promoted to the rank of Imperial Uncle Junior Master (Taizi Shàoshī). An imperial decree was repeatedly issued for him to express his gratitude; having no choice but to accept the command, he ultimately did not grow out his hair.

When his wife and concubines were bestowed upon him, he refused to accept them. He composed a poem on living in seclusion which says: "The spring swallows, their fledglings grown, abandon their old nests;

the midday rooster, its crowing finished, pecks at the shaded steps. This may serve as a glimpse into the character of the Junior Master. Later, when his illness became critical, the Emperor visited his residence to inquire after him.

Regarding his final affairs, [the Emperor] asked, "As one who has left the household life, what more is there for you to be attached to? He was urged repeatedly, yet he remained silent until the end. He passed away peacefully;

his secular age was eighty-five. He was posthumously granted the title of Duke of Rongguo with the posthumous name Gongjing (Gongjing). He authored one scroll titled *Daoyulu* (Records of the Remnants of the Way).
Chan Master Wanshou Ren’s Dharma heir was Chan Master Nanshi Wenxiu of Jing Mountain in Hangzhou. He was the son of the Li family of Kunshan.

He left the household life at Shaolong Hermitage, taking Master Zhixing as his teacher. When Master Xingzhong Ren resided at Yunjing, the Master went to follow him; their minds met like a needle and its eye.
He first resided at Pumen Monastery in Suzhou, then moved to Lingyan, and thirdly presided over Wanshou Monastery.

At the beginning of the Yongle era, an imperial edict was issued for scholars, Buddhists, and Daoists throughout the realm who were proficient in literary and doctrinal matters to compile the *Yongle Dadian*. The Master responded to this summons.

Upon the completion of the work, he took his leave of the Emperor and returned south. Finding that the seat of Mount Jing was vacant, the Director of Monks (Senglü) recommended him to fill the position. He ascended the hall at Pumen Monastery and delivered a formal address.

A monk asked, "The Dharma assembly has already been opened; the Dharma drum has already sounded; the fourfold assembly has gathered like clouds. We pray that the Master will offer a benediction for the Emperor.

The Master said, "The sun and moon serve as the celestial eyes; Mount Sumeru serves as the mountain of longevity. The monk asked, "When the World-Honored One appeared in the world, the heavens rained down the four kinds of flowers.
When the Master appears in the world, what auspicious signs are there? The Master said, "One ox drinks water, and five horses do not neigh. The monk said, "In that case..."

Thus, his joyful and radiant intent was transmitted through the ages, and the spiritual wind of his silent illumination spread in all four directions. The Master said, "Better that such good things had never happened.
He then declared, "The Tathāgata’s appearance in the world was like a man carrying dung; the Patriarch’s coming from the West was like a fortune-teller."

As for the rest—Deshan, Linji, Yunmen, Guishan, Xuefeng, Xuansha, Nanquan, and Zhaozhou—each displaying their own sharp wit and alternating between illumination and function, they were all nothing but smugglers of private salt. Here in this New Pumen, I shall sweep them all away at once. Why?
"Fortunately meeting the age of Yao and Shun, one naturally ought to rejoice in non-action. Again, he cited Yangqi: [The verse follows]
Furthermore, when a monk asked, "What is the Buddha? Qi said, "A three-legged donkey prancing on its hooves.

The monk said, "Is it not just this very thing? Qi replied, "Elder of Hunan. The Master said, "Great as Yangqi was, he could not avoid having his hands and feet fully exposed by that single question from the monk.
He then ascended the hall and said: "The ten directions have no divergent paths; why then do you seek them to the south?"

"Seeking the Five Terraces (Wutai) north of the Heavenly Capital, there is not a single blade of grass before one’s eyes that is not it. Why, then, is the peach blossom red and the plum blossom white?
After a long silence, he said: "Break through the barrier of the Patriarchs; it is all your own. Lingyan ascended the hall and said:
"The entire great earth is oneself. From where do the myriad phenomena arise? For those who cannot understand this, thirty blows of the staff. For those who can understand—"
He also gave thirty blows with his staff. In all other places, the assembly ascends the hall after the morning gruel; at Lingyan Temple, they ascend the hall after the formal retreat to drink tea.
Ascending the hall: "Today is the first day of the seventh month; before the gate, the golden wind whistles.
For no particular reason, the drum is struck and we ascend the hall. Not a single word can be uttered. The pillar bows to Śākyamuni; the lantern greets Mañjuśrī."
Accumulated. There is only the "unconcerned" monk, whose eyes remain askew and nose straight. I dare ask the assembly: which one is the unconcerned monk?
After a long silence, he said: "Three feet tall. At Wanshou, upon taking leave of the head officers and praying for rain, he ascended the hall.

A nimble monk turns with effortless ease. Facing his guests, he stands with his body slightly turned to one side. He gathers the conditions for the community, transforming wood into charcoal and straw into grain.
He listens as the rooster flaps its wings and crows; he watches as the tea ladle leaps from the ground. He plants his staff: "Last night on the river, the rain fell;
it has divided into the streams of ten thousand homes. Upon returning from the summer retreat, he ascends the hall: "The *Avataṃsaka* (Perfect Enlightenment) can give rise to all dharmas."
All phenomena have never been apart from Perfect Enlightenment. Ants know the coming rain and seal their burrows; the stone pines respond to the seasons and lift their blossoms.
How many times has one’s hands and feet become sticky? How many times have the ten directions been traversed crosswise and lengthwise?

Upon the conclusion of the retreat, he ascended the hall and cited Master Chan Master Cuiyan, who at the end of the summer addressed the assembly, saying: "Throughout this entire summer, for the sake of you elder brothers..."
The younger brother speaks of the east while talking of the west; look and see whether Cuiyan’s eyebrows still exist. The Master said, "He sells flour along with the bran.

Ascending the hall, he cited an ancient worthy who said: "When the sun rises, the light of the mind shines forth; when the sky is overcast, the nature-ground grows dark. Those who do not know heaven and earth..."
The Way of the Firm has Heaven and Earth. To speak thus, those who have attained thorough enlightenment throughout ancient and modern times are as numerous as rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds;
those who have misunderstood it are likewise as numerous as rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds. (With the whisk, he draws a line: The Lake Anavatapta is forty *zhang* deep and forty *zhang* wide.
A small *chan* lecture on New Year’s Eve: Nāgārjuna filled his bowl to the brim with water; Kātyāyana cast down a brocade.
The Needle. When Deshan beckoned from across the river, Gaoting strode away crosswise. Morning bells ring and evening drums beat;
the wind stirs, dust rises, magpies screech, and crows caw. There is not a single place that is not this very moment.
Now, on the thirtieth night of the twelfth month, I dare ask you all: do you understand? Only boundless clouds and billows can contain it.
A fish that swallows a boat requires a wind of ninety thousand *li* to carry it; a bird with wings that hang from the heavens requires the same.
When the Buddha ascended the hall for his *nirvāṇa*, Śākyamuni—the Old Man—descended from Tuṣita Heaven and took birth in the womb of Māyādevī.

Even within the womb, he was already infected by the grave illness of birth and death. Upon his birth, he immediately pointed one finger toward heaven and one finger toward earth. This can clearly be seen.
That which cannot be grasped by gathering it together, when the morning star appeared, was suddenly realized as the Way; this was precisely like a diseased eye seeing floating flowers.

Throughout forty-nine years and over three hundred assemblies, whether speaking extensively or briefly, directly or indirectly, openly or secretly—was this not merely the delirium of one in a deep sleep? Even at the very end, he rubbed his chest and addressed the assembly, saying:
"You all should carefully contemplate my body, which is the color of purple-polished gold. Gaze upon it until you are fully satisfied, lest you later feel regret.

Whether one says that my parinirvāṇa means I am no longer your disciple, or whether one says that my not entering parinirvāṇa means I am no longer your disciple—it is like a disease that has reached the vital organs (gao-huang), beyond the power of any cure.
Not only would worldly physicians fold their hands in helplessness, but even the divine physician Jīvaka himself could do nothing."
He has retreated three stations. Today, I, the distant descendant of the Northern Mountain, must treat him.
If I cannot treat him, future generations will forever lose their reliance and support.
If I can treat him, then the body of purple-golden hue—majestic, dignified, and resplendent—will manifest everywhere. (He strikes the whisk. The color of the willows is yellow.
The golden buds are tender; pear blossoms are white snow with fragrance. [He] ascends the hall and says: "Study only the living word, not the dead word.
To manifest it at every head and clarify it in every object is a dead word. To step forward and tread upon the Southern Star, or turn around and overturn the Northern Dipper, is a dead word.
What is the living word? 'After the rain has passed through the streets of Suzhou, she puts on her embroidered shoes. The assembly hesitates.
He cast down his whisk and descended from the seat. At Jingshan, he ascended the hall and said: "The myriad phenomena of the universe are all sealed by a single Dharma.
Before you is Bowu Peak; behind you is Lingxiao Peak; in between is the Buddha Hall. What do you call 'the single Dharma'?
After a long silence, he said: "National Teacher Guoyi was originally a native of Kunshan. He then ascended the hall and said: "Master Mazu said..."

"Since the time of 'huluan' (the chaotic period), thirty years have passed without a lack of salt and sauce. There is not even two ounces of gold in this place; the common man buys three *shēng* of wine.
He ascended the hall and said: "There is no dharma before one's eyes; the intent lies within the present moment. It is not a dharma of the present moment; it is beyond the reach of ears and eyes.
At the head of the inkstone pond, the clouds drift slowly; atop the chicken grave, the grass grows lushly. — Master [Fayan Wenyi]
Once, while speaking from within his room, he said: "The source of the Way is not far off; where is it? For what purpose did the Patriarch come from the West?
There is no tree of Bodhi; who established its name? A monk asked, "What is the guest within the guest? The Master said, "Leaning on a staff, one stands by another's gate.
The monk asked, "What is the host within the guest? The Master said, "Leaning against a pillar in front of the hall. The monk asked, "..."
"What is the guest within the host? The Master said, "One's nature and life belong to another. He asked, "What is the host within the host? The Master said, "Holding a vajra in one’s hand.
The layman asked, "What is the matter within the gate of the patch-robed monks? The Master said, "You are a layman;
how could you understand the matter within the gate of the patch-robed monks? He asked again, "What is the matter within the Gate of the Patriarchal School?"
[The Master] said, "I am busy today and have no leisure to discuss matters of the Zen school with you. The scholar was about to offer a response when the Master shouted him out.
One day, seeing a monk passing through the courtyard, the Master said in a stern voice, "The eaves of the roof are collapsing!
The monk looked up, and the Master said, "A hawk has flown to Silla. As soon as the Master saw a monk enter the gate, he said, "You there, who are treading upon the state!"
Xian Han: "Thirty blows are well-deserved beneath his heels. The monk said, "I have not even asked a question, yet I have already received these blows.

The Master said, "What is the use of waiting for you to open your mouth? The monk hesitated, and the Master immediately shouted him out. Another monk came forward and performed the formal salutation with his sitting cloth (*zuoju*).
The Master said, "In my place, there is no leftover soup or stale rice; there is no need to use up your worn-out cooking cloth."
The monks said, "Out of compassion, O Master. The Master replied, "I laugh until the green stone pillar before the gate collapses.

He occupied four seats of the Dharma, each leaving behind achievements worthy of observation. In his later years, he withdrew from public life, divined a site to the left of Jizhao Pagoda, and built a hut there to dwell.
He passed away at the age of seventy-something.

Chan Master Xibai Lijin of Tiantong Monastery in Jiaxing Prefecture was a dharma successor of Chan Master Ming of Mount Jing; he was the son of the Yao family of Suzhou and, in his youth, relied upon Baoji Monastery.
He left home to become a monk at the monastery. Seeing an ancient tripod inscription, he was reminded of the karmic conditions between Deshan and Longtan, which he presented to his teacher;

after a long time, they reached a profound accord. In the *dingyou* year of the Zhizheng era, he took up residence at Rui Guang Monastery. Encountering the disaster that destroyed Tian Ning Monastery, the Master again undertook its restoration.

The Imperial Preceptor conferred upon him the title Yuan Tong Pu Ji. Having lost his father in childhood, the Master had no one to rely on for his aged mother; he therefore built a residence east of the city to provide for her care.
At the beginning of the Hongwu era, he was transferred to Jingci Temple. In the spring of the fourth year, an imperial decree ordered him to reside at Tiantai Temple.

In the winter of the fifth year, an edict was issued to establish a Great Unrestricted Assembly (*amogha-mahāpariṣad*). The Master was commanded to ascend the seat and expound upon the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*). The Emperor’s carriage arrived in person;
from the dukes and marquises downward, ten thousand people gathered to listen, and every individual attained a state of joy. One day, he suddenly said to his attendant monk: "I have..."

"Since past causes have not yet been exhausted, they must be repaid. He then manifested a slight illness and passed away in accordance with the natural course of things. His stupa was erected to the west of the city of Jiaxing.
Chan Master Xiangyuan Renshu of Jing Mountain in Hangzhou was a native of Taizhou. One day, he hurried toward the gate and cried out loudly.
He said, "They have come to kill me! They have come to kill me! How can one evade them? Thereupon, he passed away while seated.
Zen Master Jueyuan Huitan of Tianjie in Jinling was a successor of Zen Master Longxiang Yin. He was a native of Tiantai, of the Yang clan. His mother dreamed of a bright moon.
She swallowed it while still in her womb and subsequently became pregnant. When she was born, her appearance was strikingly majestic. As she grew older, she did not associate with other children.
Following the custom of Yue, she entered the monastic order under the nun Guo Da-jun; at the age of sixteen, she received the full precepts as a bhikṣuṇī.
Hearing that Xiaoyin was presiding at Zhongzhu, the Master went there to pay his respects and exhaustively set forth the intensity of his quest for the Way.

Xiaoyin rebuked him, saying, "That which enters through the gate is not the family treasure. Since the Way resides within yourself, why do you seek it from others? The Master withdrew and attained realization.
One day, upon hearing the story of Baizhang’s wild fox, he experienced a sudden and great enlightenment, exclaiming, "The Buddha-Dharma has fallen into my hands!"
"It is simply because it is too clear that what is attained is delayed. Yunyan said, "What principle do you see?
The Master spread his two hands and said, "Not worth half a penny. Yunyan nodded in approval. One day, as the Master entered the gate, Yunyan asked, "Where have you come from?

The Master replied, "I have come from traveling the mountains. Yunyan asked, "If your hat were crushed under the feet at Luopu, what would happen to one who has traveled everywhere seeking instruction?"
The Master said, "When you had not yet entered the gate, you already presented yourself to the Abbot. Yinyuan said, "Why do you not bring it forth right now?

As the Master hesitated, Yinyuan gave a shout. From this, the Master was suddenly liberated. On another day, Yinyuan spread out both hands and showed them to the Master, saying, "It has been opened wide like the character 'eight' (八).
Why do you refuse to accept it? The Master said, "Stop; do not weary me with your dullness."

[The Master] set it aside. [Zhao] Yun said, "Come closer, and I will explain it for you. The Master covered his ears and departed. Later, when Zhao Yun presided over Longxiang, he invited the Master to share the seat with him.
In the twentieth year of the Zhishun era, the Master took up residence at the Patriarchs' Hall of Niushou for three years;

subsequently, he moved to Qingliang Guanghui. Upon ascending the hall, he said: "A single phrase is pitch black; it has no handle, yet it possesses a standard. After a long pause, he asked, "Do you understand?"

The pestle pounds toward the southeast; the millstone grinds toward the northwest. Entering the hall: "Regarding the Sūtras, there are masters of the Sūtras; regarding the Śāstras, there are masters of the Śāstras.
Today at Longhe, I shall let loose a single thread of the Way to divide the sections and arrange the segments. He picks up his staff and strikes it once. "Tell me, what chapter or verse is this?
Entering the hall: "This is a ready-made case. Among the assembly, there are many who claim to understand it, yet they are all mistaken."
Those who have gathered here are not few; yet they fail to distinguish gold from brass and jade from stone.
Here at Long River, we shall distinguish them directly: "Venerable Zhang! Venerable Li! One has long arms, the other has large eyes.
If everyone were like this today, what would the Dharma-gate of Bodhidharma be left for? (After a long silence) He lets out a single sigh.
Descending from his seat, he addressed the assembly: "The spring breeze sweeps on; the spring days linger long. A yellow oriole sings upon the branches of a hundred blossoms.

Within this, there is infinite meaning—whose message will allow it to be known? Before he had finished speaking, a monk suddenly asked, "What should one do when the mind, intellect, and consciousness cannot be suppressed?
The Master shouted fiercely, "Who is there to suppress? He then said to the monk in the room: [continue as requested].
He said, "During the twelve periods of the day and night, you have no share in pecking and swallowing; you have no share in seeking and advancing. Do you understand? The monk was at a loss.
The Master said, "If you do not clarify three, eight, and nine, it will be difficult to avoid brooding over yourself.

In the fifteenth year, the Imperial Preceptor conferred upon him the title of Chan Master Jingjue Miaobian. In the sixteenth year, when the imperial army settled Jianye, the Master went to visit him at the imperial camp.
Upon first seeing him at the gate, [the Emperor] sighed in admiration, saying, "Truly a monk of great merit. He was appointed to preside over Jiangshan.

After more than a year, the Longxiang Monastery was renamed the Great Tianjie Temple, and by imperial decree, the Master was appointed to head it. He established a grand memorial Dharma assembly and was commanded to ascend the seat and preach the Dharma.
The Imperial carriage graced his presence, and the favors bestowed upon him were most abundant and thorough. The Emperor personally inscribed the characters "The World’s Foremost Zen Forest" for him.
In the first year of the Hongwu era, he was granted purple robes and a golden-embroidered square cassock.

By imperial decree, he was conferred the title of Chan Master Yanfan Shanshe Liguo Chongjiao and appointed as the Abbot of the Great Tianjie Temple, with authority over all Buddhist affairs across the various mountains. At that time, [the Emperor] carefully selected...

The selection was orderly and the evaluation most impartial. Those from the royal house and the ancestral altars who were intent on their aspirations, as well as scholars dwelling in the mountains and forests who embraced the Way, rose up together like horses yoked side by side.
In the sixth month of summer in the third year, the court deliberated upon the Western Regions, which had not yet submitted.

The Sovereign, noting that those kingdoms highly esteemed the Buddha-vehicle, issued a special edict for the Master to go there. Receiving this command, the Master set out that very day; traveling from Yang in Min, he passed through all...

Throughout the kingdoms and cities, there were none who did not hear of his reputation and come to seek refuge. In the seventh month of the autumn of the fourth year, he arrived at the kingdom of Harikela (Hala) to proclaim the majesty and virtue of the Son of Heaven.
He took up residence at Fo-shan Temple (Buddha-mountain Monastery), where its king received him with the etiquette due to a teacher, attending upon him from the early hours of the night.

The officials and commoners of the entire realm all came to gaze upon him in reverence. In the ninth month, the Master manifested a slight illness; the king and his ministers all came to offer their condolences. In a brief moment—
Having bathed and changed his robes, he said to those around him, "My karmic conditions have come to an end; I cannot return to my life. He sat upright in the full lotus posture.

At the half-hour of the night, the Master asked, "Is the sun about to rise? He replied, "Not yet. After a while, the Master asked again, and after repeating this four times, [the disciple] said, "The sun has risen.
He passed away with a serene countenance. His secular age was sixty-eight, and his monastic seniority was fifty-three.

After five days had passed, his countenance remained as if alive. The King was filled with great reverence and admiration. He carved fragrant wood to form a shrine, constructed an altar, and performed the cremation.

The King and his hundred officials personally escorted him to the base of the altar. When the firewood and flames were extinguished, the *śarīra* relics were beyond counting; his tongue, jawbone, and teeth remained uncorrupted.
They collected the *śarīra*, the sacred bones, and the uncorrupted remains, enshrining them alongside the *śarīra* of the World-Honored One for burial in that kingdom.

In the seventh year [of the reign], in the ninth month, he returned to the capital with his companions and presented a memorial regarding these matters. The Emperor sighed with lamentation and sorrow.

He issued an imperial decree that Zongle, the abbot of both Tianjie and Jiangshan Monasteries, and others should enshrine the Master’s remaining robes to the left of the Rain Flower Terrace (Yuhua Tai).
There are also the *Dharmagāthās* from his five assemblies.
Chan Master Quan-shi Zong-le of Tianjie Shan-shi in Jinling was the son of Zhou of Linhai in Tai.
He was born on the seventeenth day of the seventh month in the Wuma year of the Yan-you era. At the age of eight, he followed Xiao-yin at Zhong-zhu to receive his training;

upon merely glancing at the scriptures, he could recite them from memory. At fourteen, he shaved his head; at twenty, he received full ordination. One day, Zhong asked him about the National Teacher’s three calls.
"Attendant, attendant," [Zhaozhou] called out three times. "What do you think of this? The Master said, "How can you dig into your own flesh to create a wound?

Zhuhong said, "I thought you were extraordinary, but it turns out there is nothing to be gained. The Master gave a shout. Zhuhong prepared to raise his staff, but the Master shook out his sleeves and departed.

Thereupon, he traveled abroad to visit various regions and study under all the venerable masters. When Yuansou resided at Mount Jing, he invited him to remain and take charge of the administrative affairs.

The Secretary. Later, he appeared in the world at Xuancheng Water-West. In the first year of the Hongwu era, he moved to Zhongzhu. On the fifteenth day of the fourth month, he entered the temple and ascended the hall.
With the sword of the Vajra King brandished horizontally, a thousand demons vanish; with the eye of Śakrāloka piercing through, the myriad things conceal their forms.

Reaching this point, the rolling up and spreading out are within one’s own power, and killing or giving life are applied according to the occasion. It is truly a matter for those of a thousand years’ standing.
The celestial [star] Pei leaps and bounds in the midst of the crags; the waters of Qiantang flow backward toward the Eastern Sea. Do you all know whether this exists or not? (He raises his whisk.
The stone shoot before the courtyard has sprouted its branches; one who understands will see a phoenix roosting upon the high boughs.
Again, when Nanquan first entered the monastery, the assembly escorted him into the abbot’s quarters. A monk asked: "When you sit upright in the abbot’s room, with what do you instruct people?"
Nanquan said, "Last night at the third watch I lost my ox; when I rose at dawn, I had lost the fire as well.
The Master said, "Great Nanquan not only deceives others, but he deceives himself as well. Xintianzhu’s application of the Dharma must also be known by all. Suppose someone were to ask:
'When you sit upright in your chamber, what do you use to instruct people? You would strike them across the spine with your staff immediately. Furthermore—"
"Is the Way the same as or different from the ancients? Zhuo struck his staff and descended from the seat. In the fourth year, the Xinhai year, he moved to Shuangjing.
That winter, an imperial decree summoned ten Buddhist monks of the Way from Jiangnan to the capital to establish a Great Memorial Dharma Assembly at Taiping Xingguo Temple;
the Master was ranked first among them. The Emperor observed the fasts and abstinences, personally composed the ritual petitions, and presided over the imperial carriage.

[The Emperor] approached. Wearing the *píbiàn* robe and holding a jade *guī* tablet tucked into his girdle, he faced north to pay homage to the Buddha. The various ministers each donned their ritual robes to follow him.

Prior to this, the Emperor had commanded the Master to compose musical pieces for the offering to the Buddha, which were presented for imperial review. The Emperor inscribed the titles of eight chapters:

"Shanshi" (Benefiting the World), "Zhāoxìn" (Manifesting Faith), "Yáncí" (Extending Compassion), "Fǎxǐ" (Dharma Joy), "Chányuè" (Meditative Bliss), "Biànyìng" (Universal Response), "Miàojì" (Sublime Salvation), and "Shànchéng" (Virtuous Accomplishment). He then decreed that the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (*Tàicháng*) perform these with song and dance.

He regulated the proceedings with rhythmic precision. He then commanded the Master to ascend the seat and preach the Dharma. His discourse exhausted all principles and perfected all natures, penetrating the fruit while encompassing the cause;

whether manifest or esoteric, shallow or profound, there was no capacity that it did not reach. The Emperor was greatly pleased. Not long after, Grand Master Xibai Jin Gong requested retirement on the grounds of his mother’s advanced age and recommended the Master as his successor.
The Emperor then decreed that the Master should preside over Tianjie Monastery. On one occasion, the Emperor wished to command the Master to grow a beard.

He was summoned to serve as an official by virtue of his hair. The Master pleaded earnestly twice and was granted exemption. Later, he was convicted for associating with the Hu faction and sentenced to labor at Chafeng Mountain in Fengyang, where he built a temple over three years.
He was subsequently recalled to court; the Emperor bestowed a poem upon him containing the lines: "The Elder Le has departed from here—ask who now practices Chan?
Morning and evening, I constantly think of him as if before my eyes. When Empress Gao passed away, a sudden storm of wind, rain, thunder, and lightning broke out during her funeral.
The Emperor was displeased. He summoned the Master and said, "Now the Empress Dowager is about to proceed to her tomb; recite a verse for me to see her off. The Master replied at once:
"The rain falls as heaven sheds tears; Thunder rolls as the earth raises its lament. All the Buddha-sons of the Western Heaven Together escort the Tathāgata Māra.
The Emperor’s mind was somewhat relieved, and he bestowed upon him one hundred taels of white silver. The Emperor [noted] that the celestial realm was intermingled with the dwellings of commoners.

Not being cautious with fire, he wished to select another secluded and superior site. The Master submitted a memorial regarding the current location, stating that all matters concerning its planning and construction had been conceived and designed by his own hand;
he further requested that the Master continue to lead the affairs of the monastery. Later, the Master sought retirement due to old age and was granted leave to return to Chafeng Peak.
Dùjiāng passed away at Shìfó Temple on the banks of the river. Addressing his attendants, he said: "The birth and death of a person is like a bubble upon the water.
A bubble arises and a bubble perishes, yet both return to the water. Where, then, is there not the state of quiescent extinction?

Having finished speaking, he looked again at his attendant and said, "What about this? The attendant was bewildered. The Master said, "Suffering," and then passed away. This was during the second year of the Hongwu era.

The fourteenth day of the ninth month in the thirteenth year [of the Hongwu era]. At seventy-four years of age, his cremation yielded immeasurable śarīra relics, which were enshrined in a stūpa to the right of the stūpa of Xiaoyin Yun.

The Emperor Wen (the Yongle Emperor) composed an inscription for his portrait, stating: "The Imperial Ming has begun its auspicious course; scholars gather like clouds. To quell disorder, one relies on martial might."

Governance is regulated by culture; how much more so when we know that beyond these walls there were likewise great men. One transmitted the robe at Pushe Monastery; another assisted the teachings at Xianjin. One discussed the sutras at Jinma Gate; another presented his fu-poems at Zichen Palace. Chosen with favor by the Emperor’s heart, their honor surpassed all peers.

Both served as masters for the world—preeminent artisans and high ministers—to support the royal ordinances and to edify our people. Having renewed the *Yunhan* hymns, they have now carved [their names] upon the Green Peaks. Unstartled by honor or disgrace, they have transcended the root and the dust. The Huai River flows vast and deep; the Cha Peak rises rugged and steep. I compose this eulogy; who can truly capture their likeness?
Chan Master Yongzhang Lanweng Tingjun of Zhongzhu, Hangzhou, long relied upon Xiaoyin before entering the world at Mingzhou.
Longfeng. He subsequently moved to Ruiyan and later presided over Zhongzhu. Taking up his staff while seated in the hall, he said:
"If there were no one in this hall who could realize the truth upon the tip of my staff, I would swear that this staff would never be called a 'staff.

Is there such a person? [He then said: "The imperial decree summons the flying dragon; the lame turtle pokes its head out. On the day of the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*, he ascended the hall. An ancient worthy said: "There is [something] after *nirvāṇa*..."
"The marks of a Great Man—Old Śākyamuni has entered nirvana. Where are the marks of a Great Man now?
Holding up his whisk, he drew a circle and said, "Do you see? His countenance was most wondrous; his radiance illumined the ten directions.

I have previously made offerings to him, and now I come once more to behold him in person. Ascending the hall, he said: "Lately, there are many among the assembly who are intelligent and quick-witted."
There are not few who have reached this depth. Each of them claims to have attained it within their own mind and applied it with their hands;

when encountering circumstances or objects, they kick it forth, lively and agile, without expending the slightest bit of effort. Yet, upon arriving at the gate of Longfeng, they must be subjected to a thorough examination from the very beginning.
[Longfeng] took up his staff and struck it once, saying: "It is like making a lamp or candle out of wax."
A lamp will not become bright unless it is lit with fire. [The Master] ascends the hall and says: "Master Zhenjing said: 'The Heavenly Mind attains freedom;

even in the height of summer, it is cool and refreshing. If a patch-robed monk can realize this, he is a true King of the Dharma—cherish this! Now, the first day of the Middle Autumn month has begun."
The intense summer heat has receded and refreshing coolness has returned. Let me ask you all: has the Heavenly Mind attained its sovereign freedom yet?
Even if it has attained such freedom, you must further recognize the King of the Dharma before you can truly succeed. If this is not yet so—*huṃ huṃ*! There is still great heat ahead.
[This was said] upon ascending the hall to thank the Head Seat, the Guest Master, the Attendant, and the Steward, while requesting the rhinoceros-horn fan.
Son, do not raise waves where there is no wind. A sword hangs between the eyebrows; weapons lie upon level ground. Do not involve yourself with either. There is another principle:
smash the glass cup and take up the handleless hoe. Shallowly dig for the bright moon and plant deeply in the white clouds.
From moment to moment sing of the era of Yao and Shun; day after day rejoice in the transformation of Fuxi and Huangdi. Furthermore, know how to repay kindness.

Regarding the phrase "The grace—how do you speak of it?": "The nine-tenth-thousand-li Peng bird has just spread its wings; the ten-thousand-year-old crane immediately soars. Ascending the hall, [the Master said]:
"Encompassing heaven and earth, the light of heaven shines back. Cutting off all streams, I pray you accept this offering.
"Following the waves and drifting with the current—I grant you one thread of the Way. If you can apply words in this manner, will you still be able to accord with the intent of Master Yunmen?
"Ma! [The Master] picks up his staff and says: "One is three; three is one. Fire burns within water; a stone stands from within the void.
He strikes once with the staff and lets out a shout. Entering the hall, he says:

"Śākyamuni Buddha had already committed seven errors and eight mistakes before leaving Tuṣita Heaven, let alone Bodhidharma’s voyage across the sea to the East—his mistakes were even more severe. Upādhyāya Jun," [the Master continues].
Since they are already his own descendants, one can only take the wrong for right.
Grasping the staff, he brings forth the supreme pivot and points to the matter within, desiring only that all people clarify their own fundamental mind and realize their own fundamental Dharma.
Suddenly, if one or two among them forget both mind and Dharma, they will be able to say: "At the mountain-crossing ferry, a tiger bites a tiger; before the moon-clipping pavilion, a snake..."

"Swallowing the turtle's nose. If it were so, then all the Buddhas of the three periods and the patriarchs of successive generations would collectively be begging for their lives upon the tip of Xingruyan’s staff. Nevertheless, consider this:

when the broad-foreheaded butcher set down his cleaver and said, "I am counted among the thousand Buddhas," tell me, did this manifest from his original mind, or did it manifest from the fundamental Dharma?
Yes. [The Master] drew a line with his staff: "In the heavens, all stars bow toward the North; in the human world, there is no water that does not flow toward the East.
On the eighth day of the twelfth month, he ascended the hall: "By day one sees the sun; by night one sees the stars. Among the sentient beings of this great earth, who does not know this?
Old Śākyamuni rubs his eyes and sees flowers where there are none, yet he insists that within this there is a place of awakening. On the twenty-first day, Du...
"Your mouth does not speak, yet you are pitiable enough to live. For forty-nine years you have uttered empty and deceptive words;
what is this desperate hurry for death? He let out a single sigh and descended from his seat. Ascending the hall, he took up his staff and struck it once. "Does the assembly understand?

After a long silence, he said, "If you wish not to incur karma of the Avīci Hell, do not slander the True Dharma-Wheel of the Tathāgata. He then descended from his seat. Ascending the hall again, [he said]: "The spring mountains..."

Layered and tangled greens; spring waters shimmering in empty azure. Vast and silent between heaven and earth, standing alone, what limit can one’s gaze reach? Listen well, you virtuous Chan practitioners:
without experiencing a single matter, one does not grow a single bit of wisdom. At this small *can* (sermon) for the summer retreat, I have tied the mouth of the sack shut.
The Buddhas of the three periods, the patriarchs of the six generations, and all the old masters of the world—none may look upon these eyes with presumption, nor may they listen.

Do not listen recklessly. Your mouth must not utter false words, and your feet must not take reckless steps. When one restraint holds you firmly without the slightest movement, it is called the Monastery of Perfect Enlightenment (*Yuanjue Jialan*).
For ninety days, when even the insects in a jar of vinegar are restrained, what possibility is there for them to emerge?
Yet you do not realize that this Way is like the pure solar disc ascending into the great void, illuminating no hidden corner that it does not reach. It is like...
A poison-coated drum: a single light strike causes all who hear it to perish. Nevertheless, if one dwells in existence, existence is destroyed;
if one dwells in emptiness, emptiness is destroyed. When both illusions are empty, even the "middle" does not stand.
Ultimately, what can be called a poison-coated drum? What can be called the pure sun-wheel? (He lets out a shout. A man of great capacity ought to walk freely, following his own feet.
Trampling over the cave of views and knowledge. A Small *Xichan* (Retreat) *Canshan* (General Instruction). When the autumn river is clear and shallow, white dew mingles with the mist.
Originally there is no person who is deluded or awakened; it simply requires resolution today. Since there is originally no one who is deluded or awakened, what else is there to resolve?
Well, all you venerable Chan practitioners: let the true eye atop your heads illuminate the past and the present; let the divine light behind your heads be without interior or exterior.
Externally, although this is inherently possessed by every person and is fully manifest in each individual, alas, due to deluded thoughts and attachments, one cannot realize it.
Now that the sacred retreat (varṣā) is about to conclude and the monks wish to perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, let us settle this matter today.

It does not matter if it is pierced through in seven ways, penetrated in eight, or traversed in ten directions. If you do not resolve it now, thirty years from now you will beat your breast with your hand in regret.
Do not say you have not heard it. A Small Lecture on the Eve of the New Year: The night when the year is nearly spent; A person who has not yet returned from ten thousand miles.
*Du!* (A shout) What is this drowsy chatter? Right now, you all come forward in a crowd, standing there dazed, looking at one another, face to face, eye to eye.
Which of you is the person who has not yet returned? On the tower above, the horn for the New Year has already been blown—listen to that which cannot be heard as sound.
Listen clearly: "The lamp before the window still burns from the old year. To see without transcending form—to see this directly—is to be one who has blood beneath the skin.
In whose household is there no smoke from the hearth? What need is there to speak of arriving or not arriving, returning or not returning?
Although it is true that misfortune turns to fortune, you must all grasp the single phrase at the point of connection.

[He] paused. Holding up his staff, he struck it once and said: "The fragrance of plum blossoms spreads as the spring valley warms; the sound of pines in the wind carries through the night hall’s chill.
He then cited the kōan of the Five-Abhijña Rishi questioning the Buddha, adding: "Since that one abhijñā was not recognized, I dare say his five abhijñās have not yet been fully penetrated.
Have you not heard it said: 'When shooting at a man, shoot first at his horse; when capturing a rebel, you must seize the king'? He then cited another [kōan].
Dowen asked the Buddha, "I do not ask about words of existence; I do not ask about words of non-existence. [The Master] held up his staff and said:

"The outsider is hungry and seeks the royal banquet; the World-Honored One presents the entire dish. Ānanda seeks a flaw, yet fails to reach the deep spring; he instead falls prostrate within the shadow of the whip.
He then cited the public case of Fu Dashi lecturing on the sutras and held up his staff, saying: "When Dashi lectured on the sutras, he struck once with his measure-stick, and hundreds..."
The thousand samādhis and immeasurable wondrous meanings have already been clearly manifest. As for Master Zhi’s public lectures on the sutras, his words were often far removed from the Way.
To illustrate this, he cites the public case of Panshan acting as a street monk and says: "Singing voices and weeping voices exist everywhere;
why was it that when Panshan heard them, he immediately attained realization? One does not wait for the moon to open the pond; once the pond is formed, the moon comes of its own accord."
Come. He brings up the story of Dongshan eating fruit, and offers this verse: "Ordinary etiquette for hosting guests should be respectful, How much more so when dividing the winter months?
The fruit table is brought forward and then withdrawn; Dongshan greatly lacked a master of the house.
In the first year of the Hongwu era, while residing at Mount Zhong, he sat upright and passed away. His cremation yielded countless relics, which were enshrined in a stupa south of Hangzhou.
Ping. Chan Master Ji’ān Yòngzhēn Fúlíang of Línghyìn in Hángzhōu was a native of Wúxiàn in Sū. He was a tenth-generation descendant of Wén Fànzhènggōng.
From childhood he was intelligent; the classics and histories seemed as familiar to him as if he had practiced them all his life. At the age of fifteen, he followed [Master] Yíngfú.
At the age of twenty, Yuan Shoumi shaved his head and received full ordination. Moved by a sense of earnest resolve, he traveled to various regions to seek instruction.

During the Tianping era, Master Baoyun Biao directed him toward Xiaoyin. The Master subsequently went to Longxiang; in the brief space of a question-and-answer exchange, his intellectual attachments were suddenly cast away.

Shi Shi, the eminent master of Yuyang Monastery, held him in the highest esteem and appointed him as the keeper of the monastery’s treasury. In the Renwu year of the Zhizheng era, he emerged from seclusion to serve as abbot at Zisheng Monastery in Jiahe, where he passed through successive stations.
After thirteen years, he moved to Tiantong in Mingzhou; subsequently, he transferred to Zhongzhu in Hangzhou, and finally took up the abbacy at Lingyin.
He once addressed the assembly, saying: "The school of Bodhidharma has declined until it is nearly extinct. You must exert yourselves with the urgency of one whose hair is on fire."
The immeasurable and wondrous meanings of hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates can be fully known upon the tip of a single hair;
if one knows them as such, one may transform the great earth into gold and accept it without hesitation. Otherwise, to whom shall the blame for the shame of eating the public’s salt fall?
Time flows like a flash of lightning; regarding the matter of the Ultimate, I pray that each of you will quickly turn your gaze upward. The tenth day of the first month, the fourth year of Hongwu.
On the fifth day, he personally attended to his final affairs and said to those around him, "At the hour of the snake (10:00 am) tomorrow, I shall pass away.
When the time arrived, he bathed, sat upright, wrote a verse of farewell, and entered nirvana. His worldly age was fifty-five and his monastic seniority forty years.
During the cremation, his teeth, gums, and tongue remained unburnt, and countless *śarīra* relics were produced. They were interred within the Guiyun Pagoda.
Chan Master Chongzhi Yuan of Lushan was a native of the Chen family of Piling. He went to visit Xiaoyin Ju and was interrogated with the koan regarding the "True Person of No Rank.
Without realizing it, the Master felt a sense of liberation and prostrated himself. Xiaoyin asked, "What did you see that you prostrate? The Master replied, "There is no second person.
Xiaoyin said, "One who enters through the gate does not possess the family treasure. The Master... [continued].
He said, "Preceptor, please take care not to suppress the noble and degrade them to the lowly. Later, he resided at Nanchan, and subsequently moved to Yuancong and Yuyang.

In the autumn of the fifth year of the Hongwu era, the Emperor summoned eminent monks to hold a great assembly on Mount Zhong. The Master responded to the imperial decree and arrived at the private hall.

The Emperor asked about the general meaning of the Buddha-dharma, and the Master answered him with a verse. The Emperor was greatly pleased and granted him food before him. At times, the Master would...
While he was sleeping, his breathing made a sound. His neighbor, sitting beside him, pulled at his robe to wake him. The Master smiled and said, "This old man has no artifice in his heart;
he is truly a good spiritual friend. Later, when he manifested parinirvāṇa, he was interred in a stupa on Stone Ear Peak.
Chan Master Gufeng Mingde of Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Xuedou Lin. His clan was Zhu, and his family lineage was from Changuo in Mingzhou.

His mother dreamed that a monk named Jie sought lodging with her, and upon awakening, she became pregnant. From childhood, he did not enjoy playing; he would frequently sit in meditation with his legs crossed and his posture upright. All...

The senior monk Fuming was amazed by him. He took him along to Jinge Temple and had him serve as an attendant to sweep and clean. At the age of seventeen, he received ordination and became a full monk.
Carrying his staff, he traveled to visit various teachers, first paying a call on Zhuxi Tan. Upon hearing the words from the high seat, he attained realization.
He then went to Jingci Temple to see Huiji. Huiji asked, "What thing comes in such a manner? The Master replied, "Hū Zhangsan and Hē Lisi."
The Master took up his staff; the monk shook out his sleeves and went straight out. Later, he arrived at Shuanglin to see Mingjue Jun.

When the Japanese government dispatched an envoy to invite Jun, the Master escorted him as far as the seashore. There, he happened to meet Zhutian in Mingzhou, who then invited the Master back to Xuedou to serve as the First Seat.
One day, while Zhutian was ascending the hall, he raised the koan of Yishan’s “Mud Ox Entering the Sea.”

His voice was like thunder. The Master’s myriad doubts were suddenly dispelled. He composed a verse and presented it to Tian, who sighed in admiration, saying, "The Eye of the Human and Heavenly Eyes remains resplendent.
From then on, he proclaimed the vehicle of the school, speaking in accordance with its true nature.

He once built a hermitage with Master Lun Zhongfang in Peach Blossom Ravine, where they mutually stimulated and refined their understanding. For five years, his feet did not cross the threshold of the hut; his reputation spread far and wide.

I have heard that he was invited by the Xingxuan Yuan to reside at Dongchan Temple in Songjiang. He subsequently moved to Baoning Temple in Jiqing—the Dharma-center of Lake Daochang—and then to Jingci Temple in Hangzhou.
The Imperial Preceptor conferred upon him the title "Yuanying Dinghui" (Perfectly Enlightened Concentrated Wisdom).
