In the fifth year of the Hongwu era, he retired to Zhulin Hermitage at Daochang. One day, manifesting a slight illness, he exhorted his disciples, saying: "You all are the one true [nature]..."
"The nature of perfection is equal to that of the Tathāgata. The arising and ceasing of worldly phenomena are no different from sparks from a flint or a flash of lightning.
Practice diligently day and night; do not give rise to regression. After my passing, you should follow the Buddha’s regulations and perform the cremation according to the Dharma;

do not have me dressed in hempen cloth while wailing. Having finished speaking, he wrote a verse and passed away peacefully. His secular age was seventy-nine, and his monastic seniority was sixty-two.
When his skull was cremated, indestructible *śarīra* relics were found scattered throughout the ashes. A stupa was erected to enshrine them on the eastern ridge.

Tianchi Xìn, the Dharma successor of Chan Master Tiěguān Fǎshū of Tiānbǎo Monastery in Fúzhōu, was the son of the Lin family from Píngyáng in Wēn. He was seventeen years old [when he entered the monastic order].
He went to Huazang Temple in Wuchang to pay respects to Master Zhuxi Tan and receive formal training. At nineteen, he received the tonsure; at twenty, he received full ordination.
He first visited Master Zhongfeng, and subsequently called upon Master Jikan, but found neither of them to his satisfaction.

Hearing that Master Yuanweng presided over Shimen on Mount Xiuzhi, he traveled there to seek instruction. The Master showed him the koan of Nanquan’s "Three Nots. After three years had passed, one day...
He attained enlightenment. He composed a verse, saying: "It is not mind, Buddha, or thing; I have squeezed out the very bones of space.
A golden-maned lion cub— How could it linger in a wild fox den? With a shout, he cried, "Ho! Ho! Ho! Then he went straight to the abbot’s quarters.
The Master asked, "What are you doing? The teacher replied, "Nanquan has been caught by me. The Master said, "Not mind, not Buddha, not a thing."
"What is this? the Master said, "A set of teeth made of bone; two flaps of skin for ears. The elder said, "Not it, not it! Speak further!
The Master said, "The warbling of the oriole, the chatter of the swallow, the cawing of the magpie, the cawing of the crow.
The elder said, "Wrong. The Master also said, "Wrong. The elder asked, "Where is Nanquan now? The Master then gave a shout. The elder said, "Apart from..."
"Regarding that one shout of Nanquan, where exactly does it ultimately reside? The Master shook his sleeves and departed. Thereupon, he traveled extensively to visit various masters.
He saw Xuguleng at Dayang and later visited Haiyinru at Zhai Fu in Raozhou. As soon as he entered the abbot’s quarters, Ru asked, "Who is there?
The Master replied, "I have come briefly to pay my respects. Ru asked, "Where have you come from? The Master said:
Jiangxi. Yinyuan asked, "What has happened in Jiangxi recently? The Master said, "The rattan staffs beneath Mount Jiyun have been snapped by someone.
Yinyuan said, "Do not speak such nonsense. The Master said, "If it were not for this nonsense, how could I have reached this place?
Yinyuan said, "Tell me then, what is the matter here? The Master stepped forward with his hands joined and said, "This very day."
I respectfully wish that the Abbot, the Venerable Monk, enjoys ten thousand blessings in your daily life and activities. Yin asked, "What is the phrase that does not involve mud or water?
The Master gave a shout and said, "The wind follows the tiger; the clouds follow the dragon. Yin asked, "How is it that this one shout does not function as a single shout?
The Master said, "Two earthen oxen fight their way into the sea; even until now, there has been no [trace of them]."
Xiaoxi said, "Wrong. Yunmen also said, "Wrong. Yunmen called to his attendant, "Bring some tea. The Master said, "I do not accept offerings.
Yunmen said, "If you do not accept offerings, then which offering do you accept? The Master said, "I thank the Master for the offering.
Yunmen asked, "Whom have you ever met? The Master said, "I have never met anyone. Yunmen said, "Since you have not..."
"Where did you get this news from? The Master replied, "If one were to see people, there would be no such news.
Thereupon, he served diligently as a *jingtou* (sanitary attendant). Yinzong once said to the assembly, "The Attendant Shu of Yongjia is gold that has been fully smelted.
Later, he traveled to Donglin to study under Zeshan Xian. He encountered Xian opening his room for the assembly and raising the topic of the bamboo staff.

Regarding the "Bamboo Rake" (zhubi) incident: Before the words had even ceased, the Master snatched the bamboo rake away, stepped over to the left side, and stood there, saying, "What would you call this?
All replied, "A mere empty gesture, Master. The Master struck them once with the bamboo rake, broke it in two, and departed.
The following day, Xuansha again opened his room for instruction and raised the case of the Great Sage of Sizhou, asking, "Why did he manifest in Yangzhou? He then said, "The South Mountain rises..."
"Clouds rise on the northern mountain, and it rains on the southern mountain. The Master again seized the bamboo staff and asked, "What is the meaning of this?
Xian gave a shout. The Master said, "That is merely a livelihood within a ghost cave; what, after all, is the true meaning?
Xian replied, "A bit of empty talk, you fellow! The Master struck him once with the bamboo staff and said, "I have heard that the flowers of Luoyang..."
[The Master] looked like brocade; he shook out his sleeves and departed. Later, he returned to Shimen.
As soon as the Old Man [Baizhang] saw him, he asked, "Where has Nanquan gone? The Master said, "Why mention Nanquan? Even Śākyamuni Buddha would have come.
The Old Man said, "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing—what is it? The Master said, "The sword has long since been lost. The Old Man said, "Zhaozhou!"
"Is there not? The Master said, "A dragon gives birth to a golden phoenix chick that pierces through the azure lapis lazuli.

The Old Man said, "The ancients spoke thus, 'Dao, Dao, Dao. The Master gave a shout. The Old Man said, "Wrong. The Master shouted again. The Old Man said, "Wrong, wrong. The Master then prostrated himself.
The Old Man said, "I grant you thirty blows," and then instructed him, saying, "Guard and maintain this well for yourself. The Master then remained hidden among the assembly for ten days.
In the fifth year [of his tenure], in the *wumao* year of the *Yanyou* era (1318), he took up residence at Tianbao Monastery in Fujian.

The Imperial Preceptor bestowed upon him the name of the monastery and conferred upon him the title of Great Master Miaojue Zhenkong. He subsequently moved to Songxi, where he ascended the hall and said: "A single phrase facing the sun cuts off the very source.
Holding fast and letting go, the entire mechanism is laid bare. Seizing the summit of a thousand sages, he gouges open the eyes of the patch-robed monks. *Ji*. (Swiftly.)
The flames pass, the winds rush, and the torrent flows across the blades. Directly attaining the wondrous peak, the waves of the ocean of wisdom surge and leap.

At such a time as this, tell me: how do you express the single phrase for the congratulatory praise upon opening the hall? (He strikes the whisk. "When the dragon’s sleeve is swept aside, the entire body is revealed;
where the Elephant King walks, there is no trace of the fox. Small Assembly: The Diamond Seal pervades all lands.
Returning [to the source], the Buddhas and Patriarchs wield their tongs and hammers while devas and humans are left at a loss. No rungs are established; intellectual understanding does not exist.
Deshan’s staff reaches from the highest to the lowest; Linji’s shout cuts off what came before and shines after. One being enlightened, all are enlightened; one being employed, all are employed.
A great man wields the "blow-off" sword and hangs the "arm-pit" talisman; releasing both and gathering both, he kills completely and brings to life completely.
[The Master] held up his staff: "A crane has nine gao of its flight; a horse lacking a thousand li’s distance merely chases the wind.
On the occasion of the Buddha’s Birthday, he ascended the hall: "Born in the Lumbinī Garden, endowed with eighty minor marks, he walks with the gait of an elephant king and roars the roar of a lion.
[The Master] held up his staff: "Master Yunmen is coming! He struck it once more: "Father! Father! [The Master] then ascended the hall.
Sansheng raised the question: "The golden fish that has passed through the net—what does it eat? Xuefeng said, "Wait until it comes out of the net, and then I will tell you.
Sansheng said, "Even you, a teacher of fifteen hundred people, do not recognize the point of this inquiry.
Xuefeng said, "The affairs of an abbot are many. The Master said: "Sansheng was much like a venomous dragon stirring the sea, where white waves surge in flood."
"O Celestial One! Had it not been for Xuefeng’s habitual entry into the surging waves, how could he have secured the dragon pearl in his grasp?
[He strikes the whisk. [Addressing the Hall Master, he ascends the hall. "What is that which is within the Buddha Hall? *Siri sulū sulū siri.* The spring breeze of the river realm cannot stir it;
the partridge cries out amidst the deep flowers. [He strikes the whisk. [He ascends the hall and lifts up the incense.]

Regarding the story of Yanguan climbing the tree: Head Seat Houtou came forward and asked, "I do not ask about having climbed the tree; I request the Master to speak of the time before he had climbed it.
Yanguan laughed heartily. The Master said: "Whether having climbed the tree or not having climbed the tree—iron snakes lie across the ancient road."
Meeting face-to-face, he laughs heartily. "The bitter gourd is bitter from root to tip. Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the example of National Teacher Linji’s address to the assembly:
"Upon this ball of flesh there is a True Person of No Rank who constantly enters and exits through the gates of your faces.
Those who have not yet attained verification—look, look! At that time, a monk stepped forward and asked, "What is the True Person of No Rank? Linji descended his seat and grabbed the monk.
The monk twisted the bed and said, "Speak quickly! Speak quickly! As the monk hesitated, Linji pushed him away and said, "What is the 'true person of no station'?
It is a dry piece of shit. The Master [Wuzu] said: "The 'true person of no station' is a dry piece of shit. Linji was not yet a 'white-handed thief.
For a thousand ages it flies like a long white silk ribbon, a single line that divides the color of the green mountains. He ascended the hall and raised the example of the ox crossing the river.

The window lattices. The head, horns, and four hooves have all passed through; why then can the tail not pass? The verse says: The waves are calm and the wind is still, yet the meaning grows ever more extraordinary.
The stars and constellations fill the sky, while the lunar disc stands solitary. People of this age, do not linger by a single pool of water; Come aboard a light boat and sail upon the Five Lakes.
After residing there for three years, he took leave to return to Tiānbǎo, where he succeeded Fǎshàn Chóu as the abbot of the temple.

In the eighth month of the sixth year of the Zhizhi era (1269), he manifested a slight illness. He wrote a letter by hand inviting those with whom he had been close associates to enter the mountains, and they met as scheduled.
When seekers came to request the Dharma, he fulfilled their desires without the slightest sign of weariness.
At noon, he bathed, sat upright, and wrote a verse which said: "Fundamentally there is no coming or going; a single phrase is fully raised. Red clouds pierce the azure void; white [light...]"

He circumambulated Mount Sumeru once per day. He passed away after casting down his writing brush; his lifespan was sixty-three years and forty-five *lǎ* (years). His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at Ruiyun Yuan.
He was a Dharma successor of Chan Master Yimeng of Monsan.
When Master Jizhou Guzhou was serving as the First Seat under Master Zhong of Yueting at Jiangshan, Zhu Yuan went to the First Seat’s quarters to visit him.
The Master asked Yuan, "Mongshan once said that the man who planted pine trees did not grow them from two conditions.
After Bodhidharma was buried at Xiongeri, his single sandal returned to the West. Was this due to supernatural power?"
"Subtle function is simply the nature of things. Yuan said, "Form and spirit are both subtle. The Master rebuked him, saying, "Not so.
You shall know this for yourself in the future. Later, when Yuan visited Wuneng and recounted the Master’s words, Neng said, "It was because you did not understand them.
At these words, Yuan was suddenly and greatly enlightened.

Chan Master Longchi Yiyuan Yongning of Yixing, Changzhou, was a dharma successor of Chan Master Tuhai Kuan. His courtesy name was Xuhuanzi. He was surnamed Zhu and was a native of Tongzhou in Huaidong.
His family had been an official lineage for generations. When he was six or seven years old, upon hearing the name of the Buddha, he immediately fixed his ears and stood up straight.
He was permitted [to enter the order]. At nine years of age, he earnestly requested to leave secular life, but his parents would not grant permission. The Master then refused to eat.

He subsequently took the master Yuanmo as his teacher at Guanghui Temple, which was formerly the site where Chan Master Zhaofa of Huaihai preached the Dharma. On the eve of this, the community of monks at the temple dreamed that they were welcoming Zhaofa;
on the following day, the Master arrived, and those who recognized him marveled at the coincidence. At twelve years of age, the Prince of Henan appointed him as a Record Keeper of Monks (*senglù*).
He was granted a certificate for tonsure and soon thereafter received full ordination. He traveled extensively throughout various regions, visiting Zhongfeng Hai at Wanshou Monastery in Suzhou.
He subsequently entered Qionglong to pay his respects to Keweng Shao; observing that the Master’s aspirations were extraordinary, Shao appointed him to oversee the library.
At the age of nineteen, he once wished to return home to visit his parents; upon reaching Pilin, he again made an appointment with Mingji Cai at Mount Jiaozishan.
After practicing meditation for five years, Jiexiu said, "Master, your understanding is merely like this; you ought to go quickly to see other teachers and not remain stagnant here.
The Master nodded in agreement. He then traveled to Wutai Lake in Huaixi to visit Wuyong Kuan. Wuyong’s gate was strictly austere;
as soon as the Master entered the gate, Wuyong shouted at him with a stern voice. The Master performed his prostrations outside the gate, and only after a long time did Wuyong grant him entry.
He entered to see him and asked, "Where are you from? The Master said, "Tongzhou. The man asked, "How have the tides of the Huaihai been lately—rising or falling?

The Master replied, "The waters drench the sun and overflow the heavens; not a single drop remains. He struck him with his staff and sent him out. The Master withdrew and did not sleep all night long.

One day, while listening to Master Yongjue’s presentation of Yunmen’s “Mount Sumeru” koan, before the sound had even ceased, he attained realization. He hurried forward, and Yongjue struck him, saying, "What about Zhaozhou’s ‘No-character’? The Master immediately replied, "Zhaozhou’s dog has no Buddha-nature; the myriad phenomena all beg for their lives. A bottomless basket filled with dead snakes—adding to the many and subtracting from the few. Yongjue said, "You have not yet seen Zhaozhou. The Master then said, "I have seen it. Yongjue struck him again. The Master said, "If you strike me again, I will hit you. Yongjue laughed and said, "You’ve got some spirit! The Master then composed a verse: "The Great Matter is like a bright mirror; The entire world is one single body. When the sound of the staff strikes the ear, The whole universe is overturned. The thousand peaks are all shattered; The ten directions are completely destroyed. The moon’s reflection in the water is clear; The fisherman’s boat is empty. The three worlds are all within the eye; The four seas are contained in a single drop. The ancient road is wide and level; The white clouds are high and distant. When the wind blows through the pine trees, The sound fills the valley. Yongjue said, "This is indeed the work of a true man. From that time on, his reputation spread throughout the land. Later, when he was staying at Mount Shuangfeng, the Master went to visit him. As they were conversing, Yongjue asked, "How is it when the staff is held up? The Master said, "The staff is the staff. Yongjue said, "How is it when the staff is put down? The Master said, "The staff is the staff. Yongjue said, "How is it when the staff is neither held up nor put down? The Master said, "The staff is the staff. Yongjue said, "You have attained the Way. The Master said, "I have not attained the Way. Yongjue said, "Why do you say you have not attained the Way? The Master said, "If I had attained the Way, I would not have come here. Yongjue laughed and said, "You have attained the Way. The Master then composed a verse: "Attaining the Way is not difficult; Difficult is not attaining the Way. If you attain the Way, You will not have come here. Yongjue said, "You have truly attained the Way. The Master then took his leave. One day, while traveling through the mountains, he encountered a tiger. He did not move, and the tiger eventually left. Later, he composed a verse: "The tiger’s roar is like thunder; My mind is like a mountain. The tiger leaves and I remain; The mountain is always there. He then returned to Mount Shuangfeng. One day, while sitting in meditation, he heard a monk reciting the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*. When the monk reached the passage where Vimalakīrti asks Mañjuśrī, "What is the meaning of the Tathāgata’s coming into the world? the Master suddenly leaped up and shouted, "The Tathāgata has never come into the world! The monk was startled. The Master then composed a verse: "The Tathāgata has never come into the world; The myriad phenomena are all the Buddha's body. If you seek the Buddha outside of form, You will wander for a hundred thousand kalpas. Later, while staying at Mount Donglin, he heard a monk reciting the *Lotus Sūtra*. When the monk reached the passage, "The Dharma-body is eternal," the Master suddenly leaped up and shouted, "The Dharma-body is eternal! The monk was startled. The Master then composed a verse: "The Dharma-body is eternal; The myriad phenomena are all the Buddha's body. If you seek the Buddha outside of form, You will wander for a hundred thousand kalpas. Later, while staying at Mount Huangbo, he heard a monk reciting the *Diamond Sūtra*. When the monk reached the passage, "Form is emptiness, emptiness is form," the Master suddenly leaped up and shouted, "Form is emptiness, emptiness is form! The monk was startled. The Master then composed a verse: "Form is emptiness, emptiness is form; The myriad phenomena are all the Buddha's body. If you seek the Buddha outside of form, You will wander for a hundred thousand kalpas. Later, while staying at Mount Nanquan, he heard a monk reciting the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. When the monk reached the passage, "The nature of the mind is originally pure," the Master suddenly leaped up and shouted, "The nature of the mind is originally pure! The monk was startled. The Master then composed a verse: "The nature of the mind is originally pure; The myriad phenomena are all the Buddha's body. If you seek the Buddha outside of form, You will wander for a hundred thousand kalpas. Later, while staying at Mount Yangshan, he heard a monk reciting the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. When the monk reached the passage, "All dharmas are ultimately empty," the Master suddenly leaped up and shouted, "All dharmas are ultimately empty! The monk was startled. The Master then composed a verse: "All dharmas are ultimately empty; The myriad phenomena are all the Buddha's body. If you seek the Buddha outside of form, You will wander for a hundred thousand kalpas. Later, while staying at Mount Jiashan, he heard a monk reciting the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. When the monk reached the passage, "All dharmas are without self," the Master suddenly leaped up and shouted, "All dharmas are without self! The monk was startled. The Master then composed a verse: "All dharmas are without self; The myriad phenomena are all the Buddha's body. If you seek the Buddha outside of form, You will wander for a hundred thousand kalpas. Later, while staying at Mount Guishan, he heard a monk reciting the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. When the monk reached the passage, "The Buddha-way is not difficult," the Master suddenly leaped up and shouted, "The Buddha-way is not difficult! The monk was startled. Chan Master Duanya Liaoyi of Tiantu Mountain in Hangzhou was the son of the Tang family in Deqing, Lake District.
At the age of seventeen, he heard a practitioner reciting the words from High Peak’s formal discourse: "If you wish to exhaust the view for a thousand li, climb yet another story."
The Master said, "There is a great spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) who will surely be able to pull out nails and remove wedges for others.

He then went to pay his respects and attended at the Dead Gate (Sīguan) under Master Feng. Feng instructed him to contemplate the koan: "All dharmas return to One; where does the One return? Consequently, he was named Congyi.
On another day, Dayfeng raised for the assembly the story of the ox passing through the window lattice. Upon hearing it, the Master felt doubt and investigated it throughout the day and evening.
By chance, while passing by Bawutang, he saw snow falling from the pine branches and attained realization. He went to Dayfeng and presented a verse, saying: "I ask not of north, south, east, or west;
the great earth, mountains, and rivers are all one sheet of snow. Before his voice had even ceased, Dayfeng struck him with a severe blow of the staff and drove him out. No [other words were spoken].
Jue fell from the cliff. The precipice was sheer and vertical, and everyone thought he would surely die.
His fellow students climbed up by grasping at creepers and scaling the steps to rescue him, but the Master felt no pain. He then vowed that within seven days he would attain realization.
Before the period had even ended, he suddenly attained great enlightenment. He rushed back to Siguan and cried out, "Old Monk, today you cannot deceive me anymore! He then...
He spoke in verse: "The great earth, mountains, and rivers are a single expanse of snow; As soon as the sun shines upon them, their traces vanish.
From this point on, I no longer doubt the Buddhas and Patriarchs; There is no longer north, south, east, or west. Feng then ascended the hall and said:
"For over twenty years, I have spread my all-encompassing net to capture phoenixes and ensnare dragons, yet I have never encountered so much as a shrimp or a crab. Now...
One day, a tiny gnat flew into a net; it was truly unfitting for the eyes to behold. Thirty years later, he raised his voice and shouted loudly from the peak of a solitary mountain.
But tell me, what did he shout? Raising his whisk, he said: "The great earth, mountains, and rivers are all one sheet of snow.
The Master said to his fellow students: "Throughout the entire world, there is but one person who has set forth in truth to return [to the source]..."
Yuancong knew all of this from the beginning. Feng sighed in admiration of his brilliance and quick wit. Soon after, he returned home to visit his parents;
taking his mother with him, he entered Shangbo in Wukang and built a thatched hut to dwell in. People saw him mingling with the mundane world and could not fathom his intent.
Later, when he returned to the mountain to see Feng, Feng said, "Many people have seen you trailing mud and water. The Master replied, "Two eyes facing two eyes," and then...
He underwent tonsure and was renamed Liaoyi. After Feng had entered nirvana, the Master became even more reclusive, remaining humbly in a subordinate position.
Despite repeated requests from the fourfold assembly, he was eventually persuaded to reside for one year at Shizi Zhengzong Chan Temple. Addressing the assembly, he said:

"If you wish to transcend the mundane and enter the sacred, forever liberating yourself from worldly toil, you must strip away your skin and change your bones, passing beyond death to be reborn anew—like cold ashes catching fire."
"A withered tree blooming again in flame—how can this be taken lightly? I was at the old master’s place for many years;
every time I was struck with his great staff, it pierced through to my very marrow, yet I never once harbored a thought of leaving.
Even now, when I am touched upon that painful spot, tears flow involuntarily. How could I be like you, who leap for joy at the mere taste of a small morsel?"
Upon encountering a bitter taste, one immediately turns the head away and disregards it; yet one fails to realize that this bitter taste can eliminate a hundred ailments.
Generally speaking, when one’s practice reaches the stage where effort is effortless—like a boat sailing downstream with the current—the helmsman must simply hold the rudder firmly.
Should even a hair’s breadth of a divergent thought arise, one can be certain of losing one's life. If one reaches the state of pure unity, one must not give rise to [such thoughts].
With a single thought of diligent effort, you must not give rise to a single thought of indolence; you must not give rise to a single thought of seeking enlightenment;

you must not give rise to a single thought of gain or loss. As soon as a thought arises, all manner of demons enter your heart and viscera, causing you to become deranged and to speak nonsense and delusions, forever becoming a member of the demonic family—such that even a Buddha would find it difficult to save you.
"I save you. Be cautious, be cautious! On the eve of the New Year in the first year of the Yuansheng era, he said to his attendant, "There is one matter as vast as heaven;
do you understand it thoroughly? After a long silence, he said, "Tomorrow is the seasonal assembly.
On the sixth day of the first month, go to the west of the Fayun Pagoda and point to a vacant space, saying, 'It would be even better to erect a seamless pagoda here. That evening, together with...
The Chan master conversed and laughed as if nothing were amiss. At midnight, he said, "I, the old monk, shall go to Tiantai tomorrow. The attendant said, "I will follow my teacher.
The master replied, "Even if you were to gallop like a horse, you could not catch up with me. The following morning, he sat in the full lotus posture and passed away.
His secular age was seventy-two, and his years as a monk were forty-nine. His entire body was interred at Yunsen Monastery.

On the day of his transformation, thunder crashed and rain lashed down until midday was shrouded in darkness. At the time of the funeral, snowflakes fell in profusion and the trees were draped in white.
Several thousand mourners attended the burial; their cries of grief and longing resounded through the mountains and valleys.

Initially, during the memorial feast following the master’s passing at Zhongfeng, the Master said to the assembly, “Twelve years hence, there shall be another gathering for this old monk. The assembly did not yet...

His profound faith was finally vindicated at this point. In the seventh month of the second year of the Zhishun era, the imperial court, in admiration of the Master’s spiritual conduct, issued an edict bestowing upon him the posthumous title:
Great Master Fohui Yuanming Zhengjue Pudu (Buddha-Wisdom, Perfectly Enlightened, Rightly Awakened, Universal Deliverance).

Chan Master Dajue Bunan Zu Yong was a native of Ninghai in Mingzhou. He served Gaofeng for the longest period of time, personally attending to tasks such as pounding grain and cooking, until his appearance became very dark and emaciated.
He was blunt and lacked literary refinement. Initially serving as the head of the monastery, he later presided over the assembly; his expositions of the Dharma were exceptionally outstanding.
After Gaofeng passed away, the community invited Zhongfeng to occupy the position at Dajue, but Zhongfeng firmly declined and recommended that Master Zu Yong take charge.
It is a pity that he did not remain long in this world. I once saw his verse on mountain dwelling, which says:
"Under trees I bind thatch to form a house; I gather thorns to weave my door by the stream. Because I, Lanzan, lack any spiritual efficacy, I have provoked the Celestial Book to descend three times.
His lofty character and distant resonance can generally be imagined from this. Later, at the Guizitang Hall in Zhongzhu, he wrote a verse while sitting in meditation:

He passed away. (Master Zhongfeng’s eulogy for the Master’s portrait reads: "The mountains of East Zhejiang, the waters of West Zhejiang—his countenance remains solemn and present; the true mechanism does not rely on anything. Lotus Flower Peak towers abruptly halfway to heaven; Guizi Hall stinks of the world for ten thousand *li*.
Who would say that crystal is not a family treasure? Deep and profound, the Dharma-ocean has no bottom.
According to the *Chandeng Shipu* (Genealogy of the Lamp of Chan), under the successors of Gaofeng, there is Zhongkong Jia. This is recorded in the *Wudeng Xulu Ji*.
There was the provisional Chan Master Baiyun Kong of Chuzhou, who received the Dharma from Gaofeng.

He resided at Mount Baiyun, and when the reputation of his teachings spread, Chan practitioners from all directions came to visit him until shoes were piled outside his door. In the summer of the *wuxu* year of the Zhizhi era (1276), one day he took up his brush and wrote this verse:
"Earth, water, fire, and wind—the Buddhas of old have already prophesied them. Dig deep into the earth and bury the primary principle. One.
"First, it spares the donor several pieces of firewood; second, it avoids the criticism that there are no śarīra. Having finished writing this, he sat in the lotus position and passed away.

I, the humble one, consider that throughout his life, the Great Ancestor Gaofeng remained firmly shut within the "gate of death," rarely granting audiences, let alone giving permission [for cremation].
At that time, as can be clearly verified from beginning to end in the biographical inscriptions, Master Yunwu Bunan followed this precedent.
I have not yet heard of anyone who has succeeded his predecessor in the lineage of this Dharma.

While it is not necessarily the case that there are none among the others who have attained awakening through inquiry and consultation, those who possess only a partial understanding merely maintain their practice so as not to let their resolve perish; I therefore dare not arbitrarily list them among the Dharma heirs.
Now, in the Linji (Ji) school, there remains only the single line of the Patriarch. Although this may be of no concern to later students, it is nonetheless sufficient to serve as—
Nowadays, those who follow superficial influences and engage in forced interpretations act like practitioners of acupuncture and moxibustion.

Chan Master Shisheng Juexue, a Dharma successor of Chan Master Lingyun Ding, addressed the assembly: "Those with resolve should take advantage of the dry firewood and flowing water within the community."
It is well. When the Sangha hall is warm, one may make a vow not to step outside for three years; there will certainly be great benefit to be gained.
Yet there are those who, as soon as they begin their practice, feel a sense of lightness in their chests and clarity before them, whereupon they immediately abandon their efforts.
They compose verses and hymns with a quick tongue and ready speech, imagining themselves to have achieved great realization. Thus they waste a lifetime; what a pity!
Many have come with clever schemes, only to abandon their practice midway. When the three-inch breath is severed, what will they rely upon for protection?
Brothers, if you wish to transcend birth and death, you must practice authentically and attain authentic realization; only then will it be achieved.

Chan Master Zhuyuan Zhengyuan of Jingshan in Hangzhou was a successor of Chan Master Ling of Jingshan. He was a descendant of the illustrious official Ouyang Wenzhonggong. His family had resided in Nankang for generations.
At the age of twenty-seven, he left home to become a monk and received full ordination. He traveled to various regions to seek instruction, first visiting Xugu. Xugu raised the case of Long...
In the story of "Blowing Out the Paper Candle at the Pond," the Master said, "A heated stone can break through layers of ice. Gu said, "What is it like after it has been broken?
The Master said, "One knows it by searching for it. Gu asked, "What is that which is known? As the Master was about to respond, Gu struck him across the back with his staff.
The Master was startled and realized the essential meaning. Later, he appeared in the world at Guanyin Xingsheng Monastery, and subsequently succeeded to the abbacy at Daofang Lingyin. Afterward...
He moved to Mount Jing. He was granted the title Chan Master Fohui Cizhao Puying. Later, he passed away. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at Mount Jing.
His disciples divided his fingernails, hair, and *śarīra* relics and enshrined them at Daochang Monastery. His secular age was seventy-two, and his monastic seniority (*saṃghavarṣa*) was forty-five.
Chan Master Shaodai of Baolin in Wuzhou was the son of the Wu family of Yanzhou. His family had resided in Tongjiang for generations, and he took this as his sobriquet.

In his youth, he entered Fengshan Temple in his hometown to leave the household life and receive tonsure. Having received full ordination, he went to Jingshan to study under Xugong, where he received the seal of the mind.
He traveled extensively throughout the Jianghu region, visiting and studying under all the renowned masters wherever they were located.
One day, he sighed with profound realization and said, "From this day forward, I have finally come to know that the Dharma has no diverse flavors. Thereupon, he ceased formal inquiry (*chán*).
He personally perused the Tripitaka three times; his mastery of both Buddhist and secular learning was such that he thoroughly comprehended their essential principles.

While residing at Dongyu, he was requested to take charge of the library keys at Jingci Monastery. In the *Renshen* year of the Zhishun era (1312), he emerged from seclusion at Wulong in the prefecture, and later moved to Baolin at Yunhuang.
At one time, the Dharma assembly was said to be at its greatest prosperity. One day, he manifested a slight illness. He struck the drum to assemble the congregation and expressed his gratitude.
When the assembly requested a verse, the Master took up his brush, threw it to the ground, and said, "Even if I were to write until Maitreya descends to be born, I shall never depart from this place.
He then passed away with serene composure. His secular age was seventy-four, and his monastic seniority fifty-eight. Upon cremation, the *śarīra* relics were like deep blue pearls.
His teeth did not decay. He authored three collections of recorded sayings (*yulu*).

Chan Master Wumen Sichong of Xiangyan in Ruzhou was a successor of Chan Master Tieshan Qiong; he was a native of Xiangshan. Initially, he studied under Dufeng, who instructed him to contemplate: "Do not..."
Regarding the saying, "This mind is neither Buddha nor a thing," Yunfeng, Yueshan, and five others established a covenant to investigate it together to its ultimate conclusion.
Subsequently, they went to Huaixi to see Wumen, who was teaching the "Mu" (No) kōan. One day, they met their fellow practitioner, Zen Master Jing.
Jing asked, "In these six or seven years, what realization have you attained? The Master replied, "Day after day, I do nothing but look at..."
There was not a single thing before him. Jing said, "Where did this string of yours come from? The Master was at a loss.

Jing asked, "Ultimately, when one seeks to clarify this great matter, how should one act? Jing said, "Have you not heard it said that if you wish to know the essential meaning, look southward at the Big Dipper?
Having said this, he departed. The Master was so struck by this that for a time he could neither walk nor sit.

Not knowing where to sit, for five or seven days he did not bring up the word "Mu. He simply looked back at the meaning of wanting to know the ultimate point, like looking at the Big Dipper facing south.
One day, while visiting the head of the purification hall and sitting together with the assembly, his state of doubt could not be resolved.

After about the time it takes to eat a meal, he suddenly felt a lightness and clarity within his chest; his conceptual thoughts shattered, and all people and things before his eyes vanished. He attained realization.
As he approached, his entire body was dripping with sweat. Upon seeing him, [Zhaozhou] held up a fan and said, "Speak quickly!
Speak quickly! The Master suddenly replied, "Lift it up clearly; how wondrous! The pure breeze blows everywhere, penetrating one's breast. Within this, there is not much of a message."
He attained such wholehearted joy that from then on, his speech and verse-making were entirely free of obstruction.
Yet, when it came to the path beyond, he could not yet achieve a sense of liberation. He then entered Mount Xiangyan to spend the summer retreat, single-mindedly upholding the "Mu" (No) koan.
One day, he suddenly felt as though his body and mind were like a house whose four walls had collapsed; there was not a single dharma to be grasped.
Qing then visited Wufang Pu. Pu asked, "The myriad dharmas all return to the One; to what does the One return? The Master said, "The nose stands upright and the eyes look sideways.
Pu said, "That is something learned. The Master said, "When the rooster is cold it climbs the tree;
when the duck is cold it goes into the water. Pu said, "I am not asking about that. What is your original face before your parents were born? The Master raised his fist.
[The Master] said, "Look! Fupin said, "Very well; I shall give you thirty blows with my staff. The Master shook his sleeves and departed.
It happened that at that time, Iron Mountain Wenheshang was returning from Goryeo and had arrived at Shishuang. The Master went to visit him. Iron Mountain asked, "Where is your native province?
The Master replied, "Ruizhou. Iron Mountain asked, "What is the countenance of the Ancestor of Fengxue like? The Master explained it thoroughly, recounting twenty years of his diligent practice.
Yi-byeon held him by the throat and asked, "What is the word 'Mu'? The Master said, "I have recently come from Tanzhou;
I have had no news from Hubei. Yi-byeon said, "Not yet—speak further. The Master said, "When did you leave Goryeo, Preceptor?"

Mount [Shishuang] said, "Not yet; speak further. The Master gave a shout, shook out his sleeves, and departed. Mount Shishuang said, "These brothers are all well, but they have only one great illness:
they claim they have attained realization. Upon hearing this, the Master was deeply moved and sought a definitive resolution.
He entered the mountains of Guangzhou again and only after seventeen years did he finally achieve liberation. He once addressed the assembly, saying: "The Dharma has no fixed form;
it accords with the source as conditions meet. Grasping the Vajra Sword, one swallows the thorny jujube fruit and cuts off the tongues of the monks.
One sits upon the crown of Vairocana’s head and erects a single blade of grass as a sixteen-foot golden body. Taking that sixteen-foot golden..."
Make your body a single stalk of grass; simply ensure that not even an inch of thread hangs upon you.
When the moon is cold in the autumn sky and the cold ashes flare into flame—reaching this point, if you call it "Buddhadharma," you will enter hell as fast as a shooting arrow;

if you do not call it "Buddhadharma," you will likewise enter hell as fast as a shooting arrow. How, O virtuous ones, do you ultimately understand this? Have you not seen what the Boatman Master said?
Where the body is hidden, there is no trace; where there is no trace, do not hide the body.
Even so, when viewed with the true eye, all of this is merely idle furniture. From the perspective of a patch-robed monk, it is simply of no concern.
Chan Master Shiwu Qinggong of Fuyuan in Huzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Daochang Xin. A native of Changshu in Suzhou, his secular surname was Wen.

He was born at the beginning of the Xianchun era of the Song dynasty. In his youth, he relied upon Xingjiao Chongfu Temple to shave his head and receive full ordination. He first studied under Gaofeng.
He was shown the saying, "The myriad dharmas return to the One; where does the One return? He served diligently for three years without attaining any realization.
When he took his leave of Feng, Feng said, "There is a blind donkey in Wenzhou and Ji’an in Huai; you should go see them. Consequently, he went to Jianyang to visit Ji’an.
Ji’an asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From Tianmu. Ji’an asked, "What instructions did you receive there? The Master replied, "The myriad dharmas return..."
“Where does each one return? Yun’an asked, “How do you understand this? The Master was speechless. Yun’an said, “This is a dead word.
Why did someone suffering from a feverish illness make you speak like that? The Master bowed and requested further instruction. Yun’an said, “‘Where there is a Buddha, do not dwell;
where there is no Buddha, run past quickly. What is the meaning of this? The Master did not attain realization. Yun’an said, “This...”
"This too is a dead word. The Master was so startled that he broke into a cold sweat. One day, while entering the room for instruction, Yuan'an brought up the previous conversation again.
The Master said, "One sees the road once one has mounted the horse. Yuan'an rebuked him, saying, "How long have you been here, and yet you still hold such a view?
The Master left in a fit of indignation. On the way back, he suddenly looked up at a pavilion by the wind and had a sudden, clear realization. He then returned.
Yu’an said to him, “Today I have understood the ‘live word. Yu’an asked, “How do you understand it?
The Master replied, “On the Qingming festival, when the rain has just cleared, the yellow oriole sings clearly upon the branch. Yu’an nodded his head in approval.

Thereupon, the Master remained to study under him for several more years before taking his leave. As Yu’an saw him off at the gate, he said, “In the future, we shall share the same reliquary stupa. Not long after, Yu’an...
When the Master of the Dharma Hall was transferred, he again entrusted him with the keys to the treasury. Yue Tang Yin, the abbot of Lingyin, invited the Master to serve as the Second Seat.
After concluding his formal training, he established a hermitage on Mount Xawu by Lake Dongting, where he personally performed all manual labor, such as gathering firewood and vegetables.

He delighted in composing and savoring poetry; several of his verses on mountain life circulated throughout the monastic community. The Guangjiao Prefecture dispatched an official summons inviting him to take up residence there.
At Fuyuan of Danghu, the Master lay firm and refused to rise. Although he was visited back and forth as many as twice, the Master only reluctantly consented to enter the monastery.
Ascending the hall, he said: "When held fast, not even a glint of the blade is revealed; when let go, the ten directions are crisscrossed.
Meeting in the depths of water and clouds, one is actually atop a thousand peaks; meeting atop a thousand peaks, one is actually in the depths of water and clouds. This day..."
At Fuyuan Temple, I opened the hall to expound the Dharma. Yesterday, by the side of Tianhu Hermitage, I broke ground and tilled the earth amidst the mist.

Thus it is said: "The Dharma has no fixed abode; when conditions meet, the essence is realized. This allows the true stillness of the wind to be transmitted and assists the unconditioned transformation from above.
At such a time as this, what is there to say? He brandishes his staff and strikes once: "The nine-thousand-li Peng bird has just spread its wings."

A crane of ten thousand years suddenly soars into flight. [The Master] addresses the special envoy, as well as the Head Seat and Chief Administrator of the Three Pagoda Monastery, from the Dharma Hall:
"Muzhou’s inciting Linji to take a blow was not a kind intention. Yangqi’s pressuring Ciming during the evening session was not a kind intention.
Zhaozhou’s visiting Daowu was not a kind intention. This special envoy from Fuyuan is forcing me to take charge of this monastery."
Now tell me, is this a kind heart or not? "Two rows of tears upon the coral pillow; half are for missing you, half are for resenting you.
The Abbot of Xie Temple ascends the hall: When one body is pure, many bodies are pure;
when one world is pure, many worlds are pure. The foul odor from the latrine and the dust and weeds within the Buddha Hall.

Tell me, from where did it come? [The Master] covered his nose with his hand and said, "Yet another drop. On the occasion of the Mid-Autumn Festival, he ascended the hall to thank the Librarian, saying:
"In the heavens the moon is perfectly full; on earth the moon is but half-full. I fear you have not yet understood this."
Strike the drum and all are invited to look! It is said to be the *maṇi* jewel within the *tathāgatagarbha*;
it is also like the lapis lazuli bowl in the hands of Venerable Piṇḍola. It cannot be compared, nor can it be debated. The celestial wind blows, moistening the osmanthus flowers;
their fragrance soaks the Hall of Broad Cold at the edge of the clouds. Entering the hall, I have a single phrase I wish to give to all of you.
People say it is exposed. Furthermore, fearing that others might revile me, I do not expose it for them; yet fearing that others might doubt me, I remain silent.
But tell me: is it now spoken, or is it unspoken? Rubbing his knee, he said: "Whether you understand me or find fault with me, I have no words to offer.
He then ascended the hall. Huangmei had old Lu tread the pestle; Shitou criticized Yaoshan for not doing so. There was...
A ten-foot sail can harness the winds from all eight directions; without a three-foot whip, it is difficult to control a thousand-li horse.
An *ilāṇa* grove does not produce sandalwood; how could one seek honeyed fruit at the top of a *huángbò* tree? Ascending the hall, he said: "Movement is like drifting clouds;
stillness is like the valley-spirit (*guǐshén*). The salty taste in water; the blue lacquer within color. When fine rain wets one’s clothes, it cannot be seen."
"Silently listen to the falling flowers upon the ground. Entering the hall, he said: "That which is heard cannot be heard; that which is seen cannot be seen.
Last night at the fifth watch, the wind blew down a petal of peach blossom; crimson clouds arise upon the surface of the blue moss. The hundred birds do not come, yet spring is in full bloom.
Entering the hall, he said: "To eat is to satisfy hunger; to drink is to satisfy thirst; to wear clothes is to avoid the cold."
Returning home, one must reach the destination; studying the Way, one must reach the place where the Buddhas of the three periods cannot open their mouths;
practicing Chan, one must reach the place where the patriarchs of successive generations cannot set foot.

If you do not act thus, relying on others' gateways and leaning against others' walls, listening to the commands of others and swallowing the spittle of others, you are in no way a true man. Thus speaks Fuyuan.
Saying: "Good medicine is bitter to the taste; loyal words are harsh to the ear. Entering the hall: Whether saint or ordinary person, you see them as soon as you enter the gate.
The Persian’s nostrils—you see them as soon as you open your eyes. The clam’s heart and liver—you see them as soon as it opens its mouth.
All of you have two eyebrows hanging horizontally above your eyes; why then do you fail to see them? For those with clear eyes, there is darkness at a distance of three feet. Entering the hall.
The first day of the twelfth month: bones emerge from the water. Empty clarity illuminates itself of its own accord, requiring no exertion of mental power.
White gulls and cold geese—amidst the reeds, there is nowhere to seek their traces. Waiting until the sun grows warm and the ice melts, the surface of the water widens;
as before they fly back, piercing through the lake’s emerald light. On this day, Master Pingshan ascended the hall and said: "‘This very mind is Buddha’ is not it; ‘not this mind’ is not it either."
It is not the Buddha, nor is it not. It is not the mind, not the Buddha, and not a thing; yet even so, it is not. Neither is it "not so," nor is it "not so.
Neither "so" nor "not so"—it is not any of these at all. Look closely, and you will find no place for the mind to rest;
this is precisely where you must apply the mind. (He strikes the meditation staff. A lotus root pierces the level ground to become a lotus flower.
[He lived at] Ye-sun, where he passed by the eastern neighbor’s house to create a bamboo grove. He resided there for seven years, after which he retired due to old age and returned to Tianhu.
During the Zhizheng era, the imperial court bestowed incense and ceremonial silk, and the Empress granted him a golden-embroidered Dharma robe.

Among those who heard of the reputation of Tianhu, there were none whose hearts were not refreshed or whose spirits did not yearn for him; they considered that he had truly attained the legacy and model of the ancient masters. One day, he manifested...
Suffering from a slight illness, he then gathered the assembly to bid them farewell. When the assembly requested instructions for his final affairs, the Master sought out a brush and wrote a verse:
"The green mountains are not startled by a stinking corpse; Once dead, what need is there to dig and bury? I, too, possess no fire of samādhi;

A single pile of firewood, ending one era and beginning another. Having finished writing, he threw down the brush and passed away. His cremation yielded relics of five colors, which were enshrined in a stupa at Tianhu.

The origin [of this] is such that it includes the stupa at the hermitage, arranged in accordance with the intention of not forgetting their shared dwelling in the same niche. He lived to the age of eighty-one and had been a monk for fifty-four years.

The State Preceptor of Goryeo, Taegu Yugong, once attended upon the Master and received his instructions. When the King heard of him, he revered him with deep longing and reported the matter to the court.

An imperial edict was issued posthumously bestowing upon him the title "Zen Master Buddhic Compassion, Wisdom, and Illumination" (Bucihyeojō Seonsa). Furthermore, he requested an official letter be sent to Jiangzhe to invite [the Master].
The Master returned his relics to his home country to be venerated. The Master lived in the mountains and spoke much; a summary of his words is as follows:

Someone asked me, "In what year did you come to dwell here? Only after sitting for a long time did I realize it: Outside my gate, I personally planted the green peach trees; Twenty times has the spring light caused them to bloom.

I loathe the toil and labor of worldly affairs and cherish peace and leisure. How could one such as this fail to dwell in the mountains? —Baizhang *Note: This passage is a famous verse attributed to Baizhang Huaihai (749–814), the founder of the Chinese Chan monastic system.*
In former times, those who dwelt in mountain caves made their entire livelihood from the edge of their mattocks. Having finished planting winter melons, they would plant eggplants;
they made their living through physical toil and bitter hardship. If others wish for the kitchen hall to be well-stocked, the garden master must always remain at home.
A thatched cottage, lowly and consisting of only three or two rooms, is encircled on all sides by green mountains. The bamboo bed allows no lingering clouds to rest;
before the sun has even slanted, the door is closed. Clearly seeing is not seeing another; clearly knowing is always knowing without a separate knower.
I remember last year, amidst the rain and mist, a monkey came and stole away a pair of pears. Moving my home deep into the mountains—
To the west of the jagged peaks, smoke and trees layer upon layer, separating one from the distant stream. Old in years and at ease in mind, I covet a sound sleep;

I grow weary of hearing the tolling of bells and the crowing of roosters. An iron head is added to the hoe, and it hangs from the roof of my hut. When vigorous, I plow the clouds; when weary, I sleep.
At the zenith of the red sun, the yam (*huangdu*) ripens; its sweet fragrance does not reside by the hearth. Again, he addressed the assembly, saying: "Before thought has arisen..."
It is like a false awakening; if even a single thought arises in a flash, one immediately harms others. When your practice reaches this point, you must take heed:
there are many who stray along the path before the withered tree at the crag. It is said that profound words and secret phrases are truly obtained through the samādhi of mastery.
Chan Master Chulin Pingshan of Jingci Temple in Hangzhou was the son of Wang Shi of the Renhe family in his native prefecture.

National Preceptor Mengchuang Zhihao of Japan was a dharma successor of Chan Master Gaofeng Rujing. His secular surname was Minamoto; he was originally a native of Kii Province and a ninth-generation descendant of Emperor Uda.
He entered the monastic order at the age of nine and became a full monk at eighteen. He frequently dreamed of traveling to China.
Having resolved to travel to visit various masters, he first met Yishan Ning and fully expressed his sincerity in seeking the Dharma.

Yishan said, "In our school, there are no words or phrases, nor is there a single dharma given to anyone. The Master asked, "Is there not some expedient means? Yishan replied, "The original vast emptiness is itself the great expedient means.

The Master recounted his previous words. Feng shouted in a stern voice, "Why do you not say that the Master has leaked no small amount?
At these words, the Master attained realization. He redoubled his efforts, and one night after sitting for a long time, he suddenly leaned against a wall and collapsed.
He experienced a sudden, great awakening. He composed a verse containing the line, "Casually striking through the very bones of empty space," and presented it to Feng. Feng [approved].

He granted his seal of approval and then presented the *Yuanyuan* (Source and Flow) by Master Wuxue Yuan to define its boundaries. Thereafter, he widely propagated the teachings and traditions of the religion in his own country, where he was bestowed the honorary title of National Preceptor Pujie.

[The Master] walked about. "Good assembly! Previously I said that this dragon was stubborn and would not believe; indeed, he has now won back the embroidered banner. He ascended the hall and said:
"Zen practitioners say, 'There is nothing I do not know, there is nothing I do not understand. Yet when someone suddenly asks, 'What is the matter of traveling on pilgrimage?
their mouths hang down like a flat pole. Where does the sickness lie? It lies in having too much knowledge and too many explanations. It is thus..."
Studying the Way is not as good as being a farmer in a village of three households. Suppose someone were to ask, "How are the crops this year?
One would describe them one by one, like water pouring from a jar. This is because such a person has no intellectual understanding and no discrimination.
As the autumn air turns cold, each returns to his hall. Take care. [Ascending the hall: Having left one's kin, severed attachments, shaved one's head, and donned the dyed robes, one enters...
To what purpose does this gate come to be joined? If one knows this, then gradually recognizing the wondrous is true renunciation:

first, leaving behind the worldly home of affection and love; second, leaving behind the home of the burning house of the three realms; third, leaving behind the home of coarse delusions and afflictions;

and fourth, leaving behind the home of subtle delusions and ignorance. Only upon leaving these four homes can one be called a member of the *nàsēng* (patch-robed monk) family. But tell me, what is this *nà* (the patch)?
The Monks: "We have run into a kinsman with foul-mouthed talk. The Master ascends the hall and says: "The mind is like an actor; the intellect is like the director.
The five consciousnesses are their companions, and deluded thoughts watch the performance. O Great Assembly, do you yet recognize the Mind?"
If one recognizes the mind, one immediately recognizes the manas (the thinking faculty). If one recognizes the manas, one immediately recognizes all the consciousnesses (*vijñānas*).

If one recognizes all the consciousnesses, one immediately recognizes deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*). When deluded thoughts cease, all the consciousnesses cease; when all the consciousnesses cease, the manas ceases; when the manas ceases, the mind ceases;
when the mind ceases, everything ceases. Therefore it is said: "When the mind arises, all phenomena arise; when the mind ceases..."
The various dharmas cease. [He lets out] a shout. What fault is there in the mountains, rivers, the great earth, the sun, moon, and stars?
Descend from the seat. Entering the hall: "The single, firm, and dense body manifests within all dust motes. Holding up his staff, he said: "Śākyamuni the Old Man has arrived!
His three hundred and sixty bones and joints, and eighty-four thousand pores, each and every one emits a great radiance."

It shines through and penetrates lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Within them, whether they be noble or ordinary, sentient or insentient beings, all who are touched by this light realize Great Nirvāṇa, attain Great Peace and Bliss, and obtain Great Enjoyment. Leaning on his staff, he said:

"If you do not investigate the root source at this time, you must wait until the future to question Maitreya. To the assembly, he showed: "In the deep spring of the mountain temple, the grass grows tall."
The tree is lush. How many times have I intentionally opened the wicket gate? The traveler remains only beyond the green mountains; the cuckoo calls again and again, yet he does not return.
Entering the hall, [he said]: "Upon this mass of red flesh there is something—vivid and intelligent, yet hazy and indistinct."
Adapting to circumstances with total freedom, one must clearly know the source from which things come; it does not depart from the very lifting and setting down of the feet.
Nowadays, when one hears such talk in the monastic communities, people immediately dismiss it as "old woman’s Zen.
Little do they realize that clouds emerge from mountain clefts without intention, and water flows after filling its hollows; it stops before encountering high mountains, yet reaches the great ocean.
Just as he was about to stop, he struck the meditation seat and said: "The Buddhas appearing in the world is the second head;

the Patriarchs coming from the West is the third head. Even if you were to establish a separate livelihood beyond the realm of Vipaśyin, or fully manifest the power of killing and giving life among the tips of the hundred grasses—yet the old crow in the sack still does not know there is a path for emerging. Now tell me, what [is it]?"
"What is the path for emerging from the body? On this day, as no one came forward to ask a question, the Master said: "Today there is no one to ask a question;
this is not a matter of the lineage being neglected, but rather a matter of the lineage being brought to glory. Why is this? If we discuss this reality, it truly does not reside in words and phrases.
If it were to reside in words and phrases, the Elder Śākyamuni would have been speaking for forty-nine years."
The entire Great Canon of scriptures—what is it other than "zhi-huo-ye"? How could it be that there are no words?

Why, then, at the very end, before the assembly of hundreds of thousands on Vulture Peak, did he single-handedly hold up a single flower? Only Kāśyapa alone nodded his head, knowing the tail from the head;
suddenly breaking into a smile, since this was a transaction where the goods were rightfully valued, he immediately said: "I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye."
It was entrusted to Mahākāśyapa, and from him it has been passed down through successive generations until the present day.

At that time, were there not those who could gather flowers and cluster brocade, possessing eloquent and sharp rhetoric, such that one question would elicit one answer, fitting together perfectly and harmoniously, before the entrustment was finally made?
O practitioners of Zen: if you wish to succeed to this very gate, [you must do so].
Wind! There is no need to seek extensively for textual meanings, nor is there any need to cease thought and return to emptiness.

Simply grasp it all at once—at the moment before the World-Honored One held up the flower, and before Kāśyapa smiled. It is like a commoner being appointed as a high minister; it is like ascending to immortality upon level ground.
Without traversing the rungs of a ladder, one overturns the conventional tracks and sits with majestic freedom, securely established in the ancestral hall. The five desires and the eight...
The wind has no door through which to peep; the four modes of birth and nine realms of existence cannot cage it.
Thus one sees that no kindness goes unrequited and no virtue goes unrewarded. One also sees that this mountain monk has traveled far from Siming, wandering restlessly until he arrived here.
To sit upon the curved wooden seat and scatter sand and dust is not considered an extra burden. Grasping his staff, he reveals [the truth] atop the peak of Mount Zhurong.

Dripping from ten-thousand-year pines, incense is offered on the anniversary of the founder’s passing. Had one not yet seen Yantou, whose mouth was like a stone millstone; now that one has seen Yantou, his eyes are like wooden stakes.
Since the fundamental principle supports the earth and props up the heavens, what need is there to pose a question? The master of the house calls out and beckons, yet remains lacking in alertness.
[The officiant] inserts the incense. When meeting, do not dismount from your horse; each shall hasten toward their own path. Dismissal.
On the anniversary of the Master’s passing, he ascended the hall and said: "The Dharma does not arise in isolation; it arises only by relying on conditions.

Today is the morning of the Great Parinirvāṇa of the founding patriarch, Master Kōjō. I shall take unspeakably, unspeakably many worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and make them into a single banquet.
I shall take ten billion Mount Sumerus and make them into a single bowl of rice. I shall take ten billion seas of fragrant water..."
A single bowl of soup is offered as a modest act of供养 (pūjā). At this very moment, tell me: upon what is this banquet spread?
If it is spread upon the world, the phenomena of the world already constitute the banquet.
If it is spread within empty space, how can empty space be spread upon? Do not be vague or superficial; simply let it rest just as it is.
"Is there no one among this assembly who will step forward to take charge? If there is none, I, the mountain monk, shall take action myself. He raises his whisk.

"The worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the ten billion Mount Sumerus, and the ten billion seas of fragrant water—all these, with their clusters of flowers and clusters of brocade, are entirely upon the tip of this whisk.
Neither wide nor narrow, neither lacking nor excessive. O Great Assembly, consider this!"
"Does the Way, which is empty illumination, come back to receive this offering? Whether it receives it or not, set that aside for a moment.
Tell me, where does it establish its dwelling and sustain its life right now? [He strikes the whisk. "Before every door, the sun and moon blaze;
in the Great Peace, there is no need for the majesty of a general. Small Retreat Session *Small Ch'an*: "The *Garuḍa* Monastery of Perfect Enlightenment is possessed by everyone."
Sufficient. In heaven they are as heaven; on earth they are as earth. From this point on, people have probed too far and been unable to grasp it.

Thus, Śākyamuni, the Tamer, toiled to open the gate of skillful means, setting periods and limits like pressing a living snake to transform it into a dragon, requiring you to personally realize and personally awaken.
Master Pang said: "The ten directions gather together; every single one..."

Study non-action; this is the field for selecting Buddhas. With an empty mind, one returns having passed the imperial examination. Well done, great assembly! An arrow is never fired in vain—when fired, it must hit the mark.
A word is never uttered in vain—when spoken, it must be entirely true. I shall not ask about the needle-eyed fish swallowing the Great Elephant of Jiazhou;
but tell me, was it truly so when the Master Ke received the marrow after three prostrations? (He slaps the meditation seat.)
The bed. Another spring has passed; the terraces and pavilions are filled with lush green shade. Ascending the hall: Meeting face-to-face, one does not bring it forth;

Zhaozhou and Wenyuan compete in inferiority rather than superiority. These elders have no shame; they join the feast and follow its rules, causing those with clear eyes to have no way to distinguish the heterodox from the orthodox.
Since the orthodox and the heterodox cannot be distinguished, it leads further and further to the development of faults. Ruishan—
A hundred cannot do it. Using a love-measure with no stars on the scale, one weighs up the great void; not even a grain’s weight is lacking or remaining.
Taking this as an auspicious omen, taking this as a pit and a trap, it severs the throats of the monks and continues the wisdom-life of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Entering the hall: Those who sit in a deep well do not know the vastness of the great void; only those who forget their biased views [can truly see].

He overturns the great ocean and shatters Mount Sumeru; yet on level ground, why can he not lift his foot? His gaze pierces through the four worlds;
yet though his own eyebrows have fallen away, why does he not see them? In his preceding and succeeding utterances, they mostly fail to accord with the truth.
His spiritual acumen was steep and transcendent; no student could fathom or deliberate upon it. One day, he retired from his duties and entered Songyan (Pine Rock).

This rock was the secluded retreat of Master Qiu Jiangzhan, situated atop ten thousand mountains where human traces were rarely found. The Master sent away all his disciples and remained there alone amidst the jagged crags.
The assembly wept and entreated him with great sorrow, but he resolutely refused to leave. In the summer of the seventh year of the Hongwu era, the Kingdom of Japan...
He dispatched envoys to present tribute and submitted a memorial requesting that the Master convert his country. He offered a crystal rosary and a stone inkstone from Mount E as gifts.

The Emperor summoned him to the palace, but the Master declined on account of his old age and illness. The Emperor took pity on him and did not send him away, instead retaining him at Tianjie Monastery.
Master Le of Quanshi invited him to his own quarters. At that time, Song Jingliao was serving in the Hanlin Academy.

He visited his teacher and engaged in profound discussions on the subtleties of the Way; among the court officials of that time, there were none who did not revere and admire him. That winter, he received an imperial decree to return east.
In the seventeenth year, his disciple Jūding resided at Cui Mountain in Yīn and welcomed the Master there to provide for his needs.

Those who came to pay their respects from all quarters were never absent for even a single day. Monks from Jīnzhi and Dàlǐ arrived at the capital and specifically entered Cui Mountain, numbering more than fifty people.

They prostrated at the foot of his bed, each requesting a verse before departing. One day, he manifested a slight illness and earnestly exhorted the assembly to hold themselves in high esteem regarding the ancestral Way.
He asked for a brush and wrote a verse, saying: "In seventy-eight years, there is no dharma to be preached; the final phrase—let the pillar speak!
*Du!* Having finished writing, he sat upright and passed away. This was the seventh month of the year Bingyin, the nineteenth year of the Hongwu era.

It was the tenth day of the month. He was seventy-eight years of age and fifty-nine years since his ordination. His final instructions were that he should be cremated and the ashes scattered among the bamboo groves;
however, [his disciples] did not dare to follow this, and instead enshrined his remains in a burial mound on the plain of Tangxia.

By nature, the Master was pure and sincere; he treated his monastic disciples like a compassionate mother. Whenever there were those within the Dharma gate who rebelled against the teachings or betrayed their principles, he would certainly...

He rebuked others with direct severity, never showing them leniency. He served his master with the utmost reverence; once he attended Master Jizhao until the third watch of the night, never daring to withdraw unless commanded.

His writings include the *Two Assemblies of Discourse*, a re-evaluation of one hundred ancient cases from Xuedou’s *Niangu*, one hundred and ten supplementary verses on Dahui and Zhuan’an’s *Songgu*, the *Miscellaneous Records of the Mountain Hermitage*, and poems on the Pure Land. [Four Ming...]

"The three mysterious spears and armor are all gathered up at once. The Master said, "A mistaken use of names and phrases. A monk shouted.

[The student] asked, "Names are false, dharmas are false, persons are empty, and dharmas are empty. I pray the Master will point directly. The Master said, "How many people have you questioned about this? [The student] replied, "Rootless."
"Where should the tree seed be planted? The Master said, "It is still bearable at nightfall, but after midday it causes people more sorrow.
[The student] asked, "It is right before one's eyes; why is it that one does not see it again and again? The Master said, "A thousand-year monastery lasts for but a single day of a monk."
Chan Master Dazong Xing of Mount Jing was a native of Taizhou. He once traveled with Shuzhong and Muan as companions to visit various regions.

After their travels, they settled at Zituo; subsequently, he visited numerous renowned monasteries before eventually moving to Mount Jing. At the time of his death, he suddenly sighed, saying, "The husband is thirty years old, while the wife is six;
in the end, we have failed to become a match. Thereupon, he sat upright and passed away.
Chan Master Nan Tang Liaoyan Qingyu of Lingyan in Suzhou was a dharma heir of Chan Master Baoning Moshan. His clan name was Zhu, and he was a native of Linhai in Taizhou.
Having received the Dharma from Gulin, he first appeared in the world at Kaifu in Zhongshan, subsequently moved to Benjue, and thrice presided over Lingyan.
