If you do not understand it, You have never seen the Buddha and the old woman as the Sun of Truth. If you can understand it, Then you have seen the Buddha and the old woman as the Moon of Dharma. If you do not understand it, You have never seen the Buddha and the old woman as the Moon of Dharma. If you can understand it, Then you have seen the Buddha and the old woman as the Cloud of Mercy. If you do not understand it, You have never seen the Buddha and the old woman as the Cloud of Mercy. If you can understand it, Then you have seen the Buddha and the old woman as the Rain of
The Buddha’s body radiates the light of purple-polished gold; all the spirits of the great earth together revere it.
From birth, my two eyes have had no wish to behold it; this old woman truly possesses the heart of a man. Mañjuśrī and Vimalakīrti each expound the Dharma-gate of non-duality. The verse says:

Having passed through the land of Abhirati to inquire after his illness, he discerned the old Vimalakīrti before the first movement of thought. Within the atoms of every buddha-field, he constantly speaks of emptiness.
Listen in silence. A single moment of silence in response is already much. To cite the passage where Mañjuśrī instructs Sudhana to gather medicinal herbs, the verse says:
"When this medicine is brought forth, do you understand it? This divine prescription need not be asked of Jīvaka. If one says its skill in killing and reviving is entirely artful,"
The ailments of the masses throughout the great earth have increased greatly. [Dongshan] raised the case of Mazu sending someone to deliver a *yuanxiang* (circle) to Jingshan, with this verse:
"Sealing it back and returning it is a special expression of gratitude; The ocean moon and mountain clouds are intimate wherever they are seen.

Do not take offense at Nanyang’s excessive talk; Who in heaven and earth is a person free from doubt? [Dongshan] raised the case of a monk asking Mazu about "departing from the four propositions and transcending the hundred negations," with this verse:
It is said: A single piece of ice-silk, five colors new; a jade shuttle skillfully weaves the spring of the Phoenix Pond.

The embroidery of mandarin ducks is for you to behold; the golden needle is not passed on to others. Baizhang was once traveling with Mazu through the mountains and fields when a flock of wild ducks flew past.
He offered this verse: "A flock of wild ducks flies past in haste; Mazu’s vision was nothing but ordinary. Even if..."
Twisting until his nose was broken—this too was a medicinal pouch behind a funeral carriage. When Shigong raised his bow to receive Sanping, the verse says:
What did Shigong ever know of drawing a bow? To him belongs the strength that achieves complete success. He need not employ a golden arrowhead from the mugwort;
He shoots through the hundreds of thousands of layers of Mount Sumeru. With one bow and two arrows, he finished his life. Before the trigger has even been pulled...
The poison has already sprouted; to kill or to bring to life, one must strike the vital point with personal penetration. Three plucks of the bowstring are but empty sounds.

When Linquan saw the peach blossoms, Xuansha said he had not yet reached the ultimate. The verse says: All head toward Chang’an to tread the early spring; Purple steeds follow the fragrant dust everywhere.
Year after year, amidst the songs and pipes of the east wind— How many are there who truly recognize the peach blossoms? Hongwu.
In the first year [of the reign], he was summoned to the capital as an eminent monk. He was granted a meal in the inner court, and the honors bestowed upon him were most generous.

Coinciding with the convening of a great assembly at Mount Zhongshan, the Emperor issued an edict for the Master to ascend the seat and preach the Dharma. Furthermore, he commanded Prince Chun of Shu to follow the Master and inquire about the Way.

In response to the Prince of Shu’s questions regarding the essential points of the Chan method, the Master said: "The true lineage of the Chan school transmits mind-to-mind; it is presented directly and pointedly."

Directly ascending to the superior faculties, one does not involve oneself in verbal explanations nor dwell upon conceptual understanding. It is like the spark struck from flint, like a flash of lightning.
To see is simply to see; to realize is simply to realize; to attain is to attain forever. Upon hearing it once, one awakens to a thousand truths and acquires the Great Dharani.

When employed, it is inexhaustible; its essence cannot be fathomed. If one instead engages in discursive deliberation, grasping and rejecting, or making conceptual distinctions, these all belong to heterodox meditation and heterodox paths;
they are not the wisdom of Bodhi. When birth and death arrive, none of these will be of any use.

Therefore, one must investigate with true investigation and realize with true realization. This is because realization comes from within oneself and does not depend on seeking elsewhere. For this reason, Bodhidharma came from the West.
Not relying on words and letters, but pointing directly at the human mind so that one may see one's nature and become a Buddha—this is called the "Separate Transmission Outside the Teachings.
When he met the Great Master Huik'e, the Second Patriarch, he merely pointed out the substance of the mind to enable him to awaken to it himself.

When Huik'e was questioned regarding what he had attained, he said, "It is clearly and constantly known, yet words cannot reach it. Only then did Bodhidharma grant him certification, saying, "This very thing is your own [Buddha-nature]."

The nature of the mind is pure; do not harbor further doubts. The word "knowing" (*zhi*) spoken by the Second Patriarch at that time precisely refers to the direct realization of the substance of the mind.
For "mind" is the name, while "knowing" is its substance. This knowing is the knowing of numinous awareness (*ling-zhi*); it encompasses all wonders. Its nature is inherently spiritual and liberated;
it does not depend on conditions for its arising nor is it triggered by external objects. It is not a matter of deliberate mental effort, conceptualization, or discursive thought.

It is through deliberation that one knows. This is simply the true, pure, luminous, wondrous, empty, penetrating, and spiritually unimpeded, responding universally and without end, clearly and eternally aware.
Sentient beings, due to delusion regarding this awareness, give rise to the mark of self. If one realizes this awareness, one attains Buddhahood in a single instant.
Generally speaking, from antiquity to the present, spanning the mundane and penetrating the sacred, there is no other dharma; it is solely this One Mind. This mind is...
Within all phenomena there is no mind apart from them; these very phenomena are the mind, and there are no phenomena apart from the mind.
Do you not see how Mañjuśrī told Subhūti Bodhisattva: "Within the three realms, the mind is sovereign. Those who can contemplate the mind attain ultimate liberation;
those who cannot contemplate it remain ultimately submerged in saṃsāra. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* also says: "Sentient beings are bewildered and distressed..."
Turning one's back on awakening and conforming to the sensory dust, one gives rise to worldly toil and the manifestations of the mundane world.

I, however, unite my wondrous clarity—neither arising nor ceasing—with the Tathāgata-garbha; and this Tathāgata-garbha is solely wondrous, enlightened clarity, perfectly illuminating the Dharma-realm.

Therefore, within it, the one becomes the infinite and the infinite becomes the one; the small manifests the large and the large manifests the small, all without moving from the site of enlightenment.
Pervading the worlds of the ten directions, his body contains the inexhaustible voids of the ten directions;
upon the tip of a single hair he manifests jewel-king lands, and within a speck of dust he turns the Great Dharma Wheel. Thus one knows that to realize Bodhi is simply the mind itself.
Apart from the mind there is no Buddha; apart from the Buddha there is no mind. To clearly recognize the mind is to wakefully behold the Buddha. This is truly the wondrously luminous true awakening.
Perfectly illuminating and unimpeded, it cannot be fathomed by ordinary cognition; only through direct realization can it be known.

Generally speaking, when practitioners of the Way apply their minds daily but fail to clarify the essence of mind, they are turned about by external objects and give rise to deluded inversions. If the essence of mind is clear, it is like seeing forms in broad daylight—distinct and free from doubt.
Therefore, the former masters said: "If the mind wanders and scatters, you must immediately collect it back and cause it to abide in right mindfulness. As for that right...

One who reflects should know that there is only mind and no external objects; furthermore, this very mind lacks any intrinsic nature (*sva-lakṣaṇa*), for it cannot be apprehended in any single thought-moment.
It is further said: "In delusion, the person pursues phenomena; upon awakening, phenomena arise from the person.

This means that in delusion, one takes the mind to be the object and is thus robbed by the object, such that phenomena appear in a thousand variations. Upon awakening, one realizes that the object is none other than the mind. Dust...
Dust and the Way merge; dharma after dharma is entirely true. Appearing and disappearing, unfolding and rolling up—all is governed by me.
This is because, since the time of the ancient masters, the Chan school has been transmitted as a direct pointing and single-minded holding, possessing none of this many verbal explanations.

One simply realizes that "the mind is Buddha," and suddenly inherits the ancestral position, sitting at once upon the site of enlightenment. It is like the kalaviṅka bird within its egg, whose cry already suppresses all other birds.
It is like a fine, sturdy tree that rises high above the ground, towering over all other trees.

For instance, for one who practices the sudden teaching of the Mahāyāna, the moment a single thought does not arise, they are called a Buddha. How could it be said that they must wait to realize the fruit through the gradual accumulation of merit over kalpas?
This is because the mind of all sentient beings is fundamentally the Buddha; it is only because deluded thoughts arise that [it appears otherwise].
For the sake of sentient beings: if even for a single thought-moment a deluded mind does not arise, why would one not attain Buddhahood?
Furthermore, as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "O Son of the Buddha, there is not a single sentient being who does not possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata;

it is only because of deluded thoughts and attachments that they do not realize it. If one is free from deluded thoughts, then all-knowledge, spontaneous knowledge, and unimpeded knowledge will immediately manifest."
This is what my ancestors called "perfect understanding and perfect cultivation, entering directly and transcending all at once," achieving a merit that surpasses many kalpas.
Could this be mere deceptive speech? It is simply that people nowadays mostly lack sufficient faith; they do not see it, do not practice it personally, and thus do not reach it.

If one can truly believe, truly see, personally practice, and truly reach it, then day and night the mind will be without interruption, and waking and sleeping will be as one, reflecting back upon oneself.

The true nature of the spiritual source manifests; there is no dharma it does not penetrate and no principle it does not harmonize. Its spontaneous application is all-pervasive, traversing freely and functioning effortlessly.
Once one reaches this stage, there is no need to worry that the Buddha will not understand one’s speech. Though remaining within birth and death, one constantly enters nirvana;
though dwelling amidst worldly toil, one always resides in a pure land. In every thought-moment, Śākyamuni appears in the world; with every step, one is Maitreya.

Descending into birth, awakening is spontaneously perfected without cultivation; afflictions are naturally eliminated without being severed. Subject and object both vanish, and conceptualization is entirely forgotten.
In its very essence, it is the True Suchness; the one mind is unmoving. Now, Your Highness has long possessed right faith, and the conditions for the Buddha-dharma have matured.
Your discernment is profound and your vision transcendent; the substance of your mind is already clear. You possess great power and do not need to remain dull or stagnant.
Throughout the day and for the rest of one's life, one should simply practice perfect understanding and perfect cultivation.

Whether entering or leaving, rising or sitting, speaking or remaining silent, moving or still—even when responding to affairs, interacting with others, or issuing commands—at all places and at all times, one must awaken as soon as a thought arises, maintaining constant awareness without obscuration.
By clarifying the mind and forgetting worldly emotions, one will naturally attain realization after a long time. This is what the Third Patriarch meant by "empty clarity arising from within."
Illumination does not require the expenditure of mental effort. It is further said: "Without leaving this very place, it is ever serene; seek it and you will know it cannot be seen.

If one can directly realize and penetrate this at once, then it is acting without action, practicing without practice, attaining without attainment, achieving without achievement, and realizing without realization. This is most appropriate and most essential. In the past...

The King of Min invited Chan Master Xian of Luoshan to ascend the hall and expound the Dharma. As the Master ascended the seat, he gathered up his *saṃghāṭī* robe and said, "Take care," then descended from the seat.
The King of Min stepped forward, took hold of the Master’s hand, and said, "How is this assembly on Vulture Peak any different from today?
Observe how the masterful Luoshan did not rely on words or speech; yet the King of Min possessed innate discernment.
This transcends ordinary sentiment. Later, Dongshan Cong said: "Luoshan could not restrain his impatience; he fully displayed the family style with a single roar.
Though paper and ink are as vast as mountains, they cannot exhaust the writing. Monks, do not seek within conceptual meaning. This is the point where the ancients gave direct instruction;
their eye of the school was clear and distinct from the crowd. It is truly what is meant by "meeting someone, do not pick up [the brush]."
It emerges; as soon as the intention is raised, it is known to exist. How could it depend on raising eyebrows, blinking eyes, moving lips, or stirring the tongue?

This poor monk’s lamentation is already like painting legs on a snake or adding feet to a serpent, yet I have presumed to intrude upon Your Majesty’s sagacious hearing. Nevertheless, having been granted this inquiry, I cannot remain silent.
I hope that amidst the leisure of state affairs, you will deign to glance briefly at this within the Great Perfect Mirror. It may also serve to reveal the long-cherished vows made at Vulture Peak.
That you have not forgotten the ancestral Way is a most supreme blessing. Furthermore, in response to the Prince of Jin’s inquiry regarding the essentials of *dhyāna*, he replied:

"On the twentieth day of the second month, I respectfully received your gracious decree concerning the Dharma of the Buddha as realized within one's own mind. How could I dare not reveal my humble thoughts and venture to present even a fraction of them?
Your Highness is a Bodhisattva appearing in an emanation body, returning by the power of your vows to propagate and protect the Buddha-Dharma."
He benefited the world and aided sentient beings. In the intervals between attending to state affairs, he constantly and earnestly investigated the "Great Matter" of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
this was truly because he did not forget his original vow. Yet, in his daily life, he relinquished all external conditions and rested from the myriad thoughts.

Whenever a thought arose, he was immediately aware of it, maintaining constant awareness without obscuration, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, eating, drinking, or attending to his duties.
In engaging with beings, observe whether you are effective or ineffective; do not allow yourself to be turned by external things or to enter into the objective realms of others.
For all the myriad affairs and principles of the world arise from the mind. When the mind is fully realized, there is no phenomenon that is not realized.
Thus it is said: "When the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease. Therefore, know that the mind has no self-nature, being merely a condition.
Arising is itself emptiness; it is most essential and economical not to employ excessive effort. The *Lotus Sūtra* states:
"Worldly speech and activities for livelihood are all non-contradictory with the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"Without destroying worldly appearances, one accomplishes the supramundane Dharma. A former master said: "Do not deliberate at all upon any good or evil, and you will naturally attain [it]."
Enter the essence of the pure mind. This is the place where the Buddhas and Patriarchs directly point out the Way to people.
Regarding the activities of daily life and the objects before you—do not concern yourself with whether they are good or evil, adverse or favorable, pure or defiled.

It is like a precious mirror set upon its stand, clearly reflecting both the beautiful and the ugly; as things come, it responds to them, but when they depart, it leaves no trace. Do not give rise to a single thought.
Regarding the mind that discriminates through mindfulness and discernment: there is no need to inquire whether it is during times of stillness or clamor, or suffering or joy.
Simply exert yourself to the utmost and practice with sincerity. If you reach a point where there is no rational understanding, this is actually good news; at that moment, let go all at once.
Suddenly, when both knowledge and understanding are forgotten and both person and phenomena are extinguished, this is the great rest and the great... (enlightenment).
This is the season of sovereign great bliss. Formerly, there was a king who asked the Venerable Prajñātāra, "What is the Buddha?
The Venerable replied, "To see one's own nature is the Buddha. The King asked, "Does the Master see your own nature?
The Venerable replied, "I see the Buddha-nature. The King asked, "Where does this nature reside? The Venerable replied, "The nature resides in its functioning. The King said, "If it were so..."
"At what times and in how many places does it appear? The Venerable One replied, "When it appears, there are eight instances.
The King said, "Please explain to me these eight instances of its appearance. The Venerable One then spoke: "In the womb, it is called the body; in the world, it is called the person;
in the eye, it is called seeing; in the ear, it is called hearing; at the nose, it is called smelling fragrance; at the tongue, it is called speaking; in the hand, it is called grasping; in..."
The movement of the feet rushes on; manifestations appear everywhere, encompassing all *sāhasra-lokadhātus*, yet they are withdrawn into a single minute atom (*paramāṇu*).

Those who recognize this know it to be Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*); those who do not recognize it call it the vital spirit (*saṃskāra*). This is precisely the model for thoroughly investigating one's own nature (*svabhāva*). Your Highness has long possessed the seed-wisdom of *prajñā*;
you will surely be able to illuminate and realize this—what need is there to rely on my humble words? Only within the Great Perfect Mirror [of the mind]... with the mind.

He sealed [the transmission] in the mind. It was a great blessing for all sentient beings and a great blessing for the Buddha-dharma. Later, he was arrested due to his association with the Hu party and received the ultimate punishment;
at that time, he was over seventy years old. Public opinion lamented his innocence. Alas! Was his fixed karma such as this?
Among his writings are the *Puanji* (Collected Works of Puan) and the *Puan Waiji* (External Collected Works of Puan).
Chan Master Xiuan of Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou, successor to Chan Master Ming of Lingyin Monastery, was surnamed Li and a native of Linhai in Taizhou.
At the age of twelve, he followed his younger uncle, the śramaṇa Zhongzhi, at Shimen Temple. At nineteen, he received full ordination and became a bhikṣu.

He attended upon Pujue at Lingyin. During a brief exchange of questions and answers, his doubts were suddenly dispelled. In the sixth year of the Zhizhi era (1340), he emerged from seclusion at Ansheng in Taizhou.
After five years, he moved to Long'en; two years later, he was appointed to Zhenru. The following year, by selection of the Xuanzheng Yuan, he became the abbot of Longhua.
He occupied this seat for thirteen summer retreats. In the sixth year of the Hongwu era (1373), he was invited to become the abbot of Zhongzhu in Hangzhou.
The Prefect and the Marquis issued a mandate requesting that he serve as the abbot. Upon his arrival, the veteran monks of Jingci Temple all joined in a vigorous dispute against him;
though they repeatedly refused him, he would not listen. Having no choice, he was forced to remain for two years before beating the drum to announce his retirement.

One day, manifesting illness, he summoned those around him and said, "I am about to pass away. When his attendants brought ink and brush, the Master waved them away, saying, "Our school is fundamentally without words or explanations."
He passed away in profound stillness. His secular age was sixty-nine, and his monastic seniority (śrāmaṇeraka) was fifty. Upon cremation, his teeth and bones remained intact, threaded like pearls;

the śarīra were brilliant and translucent, with a color like refined gold. His disciples collected these remains, along with his skeletal relics, and returned them to the Longhua Pagoda for enshrinement.
Chan Master Lichong Cheng of Puming Temple in Hangzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Zufanglian. He was a native of Qiantang in the prefecture and surnamed Sun.

At the age of thirteen, he left home to become a monk under Ruoshan at Ciguang Temple. He first visited Chan Master Zufang, who one day, within the meditation hall, raised the koan of the "winter solstice fire."
*Shanhua*. The Master presented this verse: "The white clouds obscure my former tracks; In the twelfth month, the mountain fires burn a brilliant red.
Suddenly, the breeze of compassion fans them forth; Where it was cold and stark, it now blazes with warmth.
Later, he established Puming Temple in Beiguo to welcome those from afar. Not long after, he was invited to return to Ciguang. The sixth year of the Xington era (1431).
On the thirteenth day of the month, he ascended the hall and spoke this verse: "This year I am eighty-one; old and ill, I pass the days according to conditions.

This year I shall record the matters of next year; next year I shall record the events of this very day. He passed away sitting in meditation on the day of Guiyou (October 23, 1153), exactly as predicted, at the age of eighty-three.
His cremation and distribution of relics were beyond measure, and a stupa was erected at Puming Temple.
Chan Master Zhaoyuan Zongjing of Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou was styled Tixuan Seng. He was the son of the Gao family of that prefecture.

Having tonsured himself at his home mountain from a young age, he came to rely upon Grandfather Fanglian when the latter took charge of the monastery’s affairs; after a long time, he received the master’s seal of approval. Subsequently, he served as the keeper of the treasury.
In the *Xinmao* year of the Yongle era, he was selected by appointment to preside over Huguo Monastery. Shortly thereafter, he was transferred to Xuedou. Not long after, the monks...
Upon the vacancy of the abbotship at Jingci Temple, the Master was nominated to fill the position. In the year Dingmao, the imperial court bestowed the Tripitaka upon him;
the Master went to the palace to express his gratitude and stayed at Mita Temple. Suffering from a slight illness, he said to those around him, "My karmic conditions have come to an end.
He bathed, changed his robes, sat upright, and passed away peacefully. His secular age was seventy-six, and his years as a monk were sixty. His stupa was enshrined at Ouhua.
His ancestral teacher was Master Qiu. He has a *yulu* (recorded sayings) titled *Sanhui*.
Master Tai-chu Qi-yuan of Hu-long, Ruian, Wenzhou, was a Dharma successor of Master Wu-shi Yu Chan-shi. He was a native of Japan; his surname was Minamoto (Genji), and his father was...

He was an official of the Imperial Secretariat. At the age of nine, he entered Kenchō-ji Temple to become a monk. At eighteen, he requested imperial permission to travel south in search of the Dharma.
After three years, he arrived in Fuzhou. It was the second month of the Bingwu year of the Wu Yuan era; he entered the capital to present tribute items.

Upon completing his offerings and receiving alms, he was granted an audience with National Teacher Ledeng (Jitan Lekong), who instructed him to travel extensively to visit various masters. Later, he visited Wushi Jiefeng. One day—

Xuefeng ascended the hall and said, "The snow covers the thousand mountains; why then is the solitary peak not white? A monk from the assembly stepped forward and said, "The thunder rumbles, yet there are no drops of rain.
Xuefeng said, "The thatched hut is roofed with lapis lazuli tiles; within the stone chamber is hidden a carnelian vase.
The monk said, "A tiger has mounted the tiger of the South Mountain. Xuefeng said, "A tiger gives birth to seven cubs; which one is it?"
"Which one has no tail? The Master said, "The seventh. Feng said, "I shall grant you thirty blows for that. Thereupon, he permitted the Master to enter the inner sanctum.

Later, taking his leave, he went out into the mountains to build a thatched hut on Mount Lu. He subsequently moved to Shilong, entered the world at Guangdu, transferred to Sanfeng in Luoyang, and later moved again to Hulong.
He once set forth the "Three Barriers" (Sanguan yu): "Why is it that the Śūnyatā-deva..."
On level ground, one drags through mud and water. Why was the King of Golden-Winged Birds (Garuda), who split the ocean to seize and swallow dragons, himself swallowed by a mudfish?
Why is it that the Buddhas of the three periods cannot speak of it, yet the "tame cat" and the "white ox" recite the *Mahā*?
One day, he assembled the multitude and spoke this verse: "Born with an iron face, Dying with an iron face. One.
He struck [the ground] with a hundred fragments of miscellaneous objects. At midday, he circumambulated the Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*), cast aside his brush, and passed away while seated.
The Chan Master Wuyi (Non-illusion) Wuya of Linggu Temple in Jinling was a native of Xi'an in Quzhou.
At the age of twelve, he entered the monastic order under Master Jiefeng at Mount Wushi. When Jiefeng asked him, "Where have you come from? the Master replied instantly, "Empty space."
There was no turning away from him. Feng pointed to the bell to indicate it to the Master. The Master spontaneously composed a verse, saying:
"Rolled out from the furnace of a hundred refinements, Empty space has never been stained by dust. Now it hangs upon the heads of men; When struck, its great sound pervades the nine realms.
Feng marveled greatly at this and immediately shaved his hair for him. He resided on the lower platform, serving with diligence for a long time until all doubts and obstructions were exhausted.

Shi De attained unimpeded eloquence, and Xuefeng certified his realization. During the Yongle era, he was promoted to the rank of Right Director of the Buddhist Registry (Senglü You Chanjiao) and commanded to reside at Linggu Monastery.
At that time, the imperial court established a Great Assembly for Offering (Dazhahui), and the ritual officials overseeing the affairs were extremely strict.

When the Master appeared to pay no heed to them, those around him questioned him in astonishment. The Master replied, "I have a matter of great importance of my own; I have no leisure for anything else."

He then bathed, changed his robes, sat in the lotus position, and wrote a verse, saying: "Life and death drift on; I sever all worldly ties. Having received this grace, I shall enjoy eternal peace for years to come.
This time, casting off my hands, I return to the void. The snow has cleared and the clouds have vanished; the moon is perfectly full. Having set down his brush, he passed away.
Upon hearing of this, the Emperor dispatched an eunuch to offer sacrifices. His body was cremated, and his relics were distributed everywhere.

Compiled by the Chan Master Tongwen of Eastern Wu, a successor to the Patriarchs.
Compiled by the Layman of Lize, Shipei of Huating,
of the twenty-fifth generation under Dajian of the Linji School.
Chan Master Wanfeng Shiwei of Mount Dengwu in Suzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Fulong Chang. He was the son of the Jin family in Leqing, Wenzhou.
From his infancy, whenever he saw a monk, he would immediately smile and join his palms. At the age of thirteen, he followed Dharma Master Yan Qingsheng to receive instruction; at sixteen, he...
He attained liberation. At nineteen, he went to Hangzhou to receive full ordination. There, he studied under Master Zhiyan of Hupao, who presented him with the koan:

"It is not the mind, it is not the Buddha, it is not a thing. He subsequently traveled to Fozhi Temple on Mount Dapeng in Mingzhou, where he pitched a hermitage and practiced intensive meditation day and night.
One day, upon hearing the temple master cite the koan of Guishan kicking over the water pitcher, he was suddenly enlightened.
He spoke in verse: "Mad, upside-down, and old Nanquan, you have caused me to toil for half a year.
Had you personally realized it at that very moment, why would he not have struck you with a fist right through the chest? He then went to visit Wujian at Huading;
Wujian instructed him to reside in the mountains, so he returned to Dapeng. Later, hearing of Qianyan’s teachings, he went directly to Fulong to pay his respects.
Yan said, "What have you brought to meet this old monk? The Master raised his fist and said, "I meet the Abbot here.
Yan said, "When one is dead and burned, where does one find a place to dwell and establish one's life? The Master said, "The bubble arises and the bubble perishes, yet the water remains;
the wind ceases and the waves subside, and the moon is reflected in the pool. Yan said, "Do you not wish to request further instruction and receive the precepts?"

"Ma! The Master covered his ears and went out. The next day, while everyone was being asked to help cut pine trees, the Master picked up a round stone and made the gesture of offering a pearl, saying, "I request the Abbot to set a price.
Yunyan said, "It is not worth half a coin. The Master said, "Blind!

Yunyan said, "I am blind too; you are blind too. The Master said, "Blind! Blind! He then presented this verse: "The daughter of the Dragon Palace brings a pearl as an offering; The man of the mountain valley takes it back again."
"Something worth three thousand or even a great trichiliocosm was instead shattered by a bystander; who would have known it was not worth half a penny?
Yun'gan said to his attendants, "Master Wusun possesses the true breath of a monk," and he subsequently appointed him to the first seat. One day, as Yun'gan ascended the seat, he cited the saying:
"The lotus leaf moves though there is no wind; there must surely be a fish swimming. The Master stepped forward from the assembly.
Zhen-sheng let out a single shout, shook his sleeves, and departed. Zhuo-an resided at Mount Song in Lanxi for nine years. Yán once sent him a verse, saying:
"Deeply verdant chrysanthemums fill the eyes with autumn; Baizhang sits upright atop the azure peak. Lightly he brings forth the 'no host, no guest' phrase;
With a single shout, the waters of a thousand rivers flow backward. Three times Yán personally wrote letters to summon him, showing great esteem and affection.
When he arrived, [the Master] turned around and showed him his Dharma robe and the *uṣṇīṣa* on his head. A monk asked, "What is the realm of Mount Song?
The Master said, "Fine mountains on all four sides support the sun and moon; a lake of autumn water drenches the blue sky. The monk asked, "What is the person within the realm?"

When the assembly requested a verse, the Master said, "The entire Tripitaka has no one to look upon it; what use are these few idle words? He then sat in the full lotus posture and passed away.
His cremation yielded countless relics, which were enshrined in a stupa at Dongwu. He was seventy years of age and fifty-five years of monastic seniority. [End of] National History.
Hu Gong Yong, the Grand Master of Libation, composed an inscription for him. Later,
when Chan Master Da-chan of Xuegu at Tianjie Monastery in Jianning Prefecture— a successor of Chan Master Lai of Futian— was attending to his studies, the Master asked him from where he had come.
Dajian came forward. Changchuan said, "It fills the void; there is no coming or going. The Master said, "If there is no coming or going, who is it that drags this leather bag here?
Changchuan said, "When both the internal and external are empty, how can there be a leather bag? The Master asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
Changchuan said, "When he came from the West, how could there have been any 'meaning'? The Master said, "What about when the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives?"
"Where do you come from, and where will you establish yourself? [The monk] replied, "With a step of faith, I have overturned heaven and earth, standing alone revealed.
The Master then showed him a verse, saying: "This is truly the golden-haired lion emerging from its den; The wheel of Dharma is turned to enter the marketplace.
A single roar suddenly echoes through the vast sky; When the wild jackal hears it, its head splits open."
Chan Master Chushan Huanzou Jingbi Shaoqi of Touzi in Shuzhou was a successor of Chan Master Dongpu Wu. He was the son of the Lei family of Tang’an in Shu.
At the age of nine, he received instruction from Master Xuanji Tong. He first visited Master Wujie; one day, upon hearing the sound of the wooden board, he had [an awakening].
He returned to visit and consult various elders, including Yuexi and Haizhou, all of whom praised him highly. In the sixth year of the Zhengtong era, he again attended upon Wuji.
Wuji asked, "Where have you been staying for the past few years? The Master replied, "Vastly open and without a fixed location.
Wuji asked, "What have you attained? The Master said, "Originally there has been nothing lost; what is there to attain? Wuji remarked, "This is study."
Ji said, "I have attained it. The Master said, "If not a single dharma exists, from where does learning come? Ji said, "Does this not fall into emptiness? The Master said, "I am not even 'I';
who could fall into anything, and what could be empty? Ji said, "Ultimately, what is the matter? The Master said, "The water falls and the rocks appear;
the rain clears and the clouds vanish. Ji said, "Do not speak in confusion. Even if the Buddhas and Patriarchs were to come, they would not be permitted [to enter]."
"Even if you were to swallow the ocean of the *Tripiṭaka* whole and manifest hundreds of thousands of supernatural powers, here you shall not be permitted.
The Master said, "Although you, Preceptor, hold fast at the vital ford, it is nonetheless a great strain on your spirit. Xijì snapped his knee once. The Master then let out a shout.
Xijì said, "One who can uphold the family must be one who breaks the family; doing so to manage the household affairs is truly effortless. The Master covered [his ears].
He left through the ear. When evening came, [Zhaozhou] summoned the Master again and interrogated him, saying, "Recite for me the sequence of how you previously attained enlightenment.
The Master answered truthfully and in detail. Jì said, "Give me back the meaning of the word 'No'.
The Master presented this verse: "This monk’s question was full of complications; How could Old Zhao have ever engaged his thoughts? With one word spoken offhand, everything was revealed."
[Zhaozhou] replied, "On the contrary, it merely causes people to have doubts. Guizong asked, "What is that place where you have no doubt?
The Master said, "Green mountains and blue waters; swallows warbling and orioles singing—everything is vividly clear; what more is there to doubt? Guizong said, "Not yet; speak further."
The Master said, "The head reaches toward the void; the feet tread upon solid ground. Ji then struck the bell to assemble the assembly and presented him with a *kāṣāya* robe and a whisk.
Later, he appeared in the world at Tianzhu. A monk asked, "What is the realm of Tianzhu? The Master said, "The mountain stream is wide;
clouds return as evening falls. The mountain is high; the sun rises late. The monk asked, "Who is the person within this realm? The Master said, "Eyebrows cover the forehead."
[The Master] has eyes; his cheeks reach his ears and his shoulders. He asked, "What is the house style of Tianzhu?
The Master said, "A cloud-steamer cooks pine powder; an ice-cauldron boils moon-discs. He asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, "The Sea God has cast out a night-bright pearl. He said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Mañjuśrī has lost his glass cup. He asked, "As for suchness..."
"What is the Buddha? The Master said, "A cast-iron scale weight. "What is the Dharma? The Master said, "A stone or a clod of earth.
"What is the Sangha? The Master said, "A black-lacquered staff. In the fifth year of the Jingtai era, he moved to Touzi. He ascended the hall and addressed the assembly.
A monk asked, "Having come from Mount Xuan, you now occupy Touzi. As the assembly gathers before the dais, we request the Master to offer prayers for the Emperor.

The Master said, "The eternal characters within the cauldron; the ageless pine atop the peak. The monk said, "I have already received the Master’s direct instruction regarding the prayers for the Emperor.
But as for the 'house style' of Touzi, what is it like? The Master said, "Passing through the marketplace with a water jar; not the oil-seller. The monk said, "Just as it is..."
The Patriarch said, "I do not permit traveling by night; one must arrive before the light of dawn. Is this truly so?

The Master said, "Though there be sinews in the eyes, what can be done about the tongue having no bone? [The questioner] asked, "Zhaozhou said, 'I am already white as a monkey; he is even blacker than a monkey. What is the meaning of this?

The Master said, "Were it not for the exhaustion of arrows and bows, he would not yet have raised his banner of surrender. [The questioner] asked, "What about Harmony (He)? The Master said, "He is like a man who, having lost his way, asks for directions from a stranger."
"Furthermore, today you have ascended the seat to preach the Dharma; I wonder what auspicious signs there were? The Master said: "The Qilin strides beyond the realm of painted scrolls;
the Utpala flower blooms amidst the fierce flames. [The monk] asked: "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said: [He remained silent.]
The snow melts and the mountain peaks are revealed; the wind passes and the treetops sway. [A monk] asked, "What is it like when the precious sword has not yet emerged from its scabbard?
The Master said, "Gods cry out and ghosts wail. [The monk] asked, "What is it like after it has emerged from the scabbard? The Master said, "Buddhas and patriarchs swallow their voices.

[The monk] asked, "What is it like when it has emerged and when it has not yet emerged? The Master said, "A hairless lock of chain rattles at both ends. The monk lifted up his sitting cloth (*kaṣāya*). The Master—

He then shouted. As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him and said, "To rub an itch on the head of a venomous snake or to thrust one's body into the mouth of a fierce tiger—this must be done by such a person as this. That monk just now was much like a seasoned warrior."
To dare come here to seize the drum and snatch the banner—what a pity! To have the head of a dragon but the tail of a snake is to die beneath the staff.
Had you known how to turn back for a living path, you would naturally have avoided the edge of the blade. Thus it is said: "To handle a snake, one must be a master of handling snakes."
"One who does not know how to handle a snake will be bitten to death by it. Again, Faideng addressed the assembly:

"This mountain monk originally intended to hide deep within a rocky cave to pass my time in seclusion. However, because the Elder Qingliang has an unfinished case, I cannot help but come forth to settle it for him.
At that time, a monk asked, "I wonder, what unfinished case did the Elder Qingliang have?"
Fadeng took up his staff and struck him, saying, "The patriarchs failed to resolve it, and the calamity has reached their descendants. The monk asked, "Where does the fault lie?
Fadeng said, "The fault lies with me; the calamity reaches you. The Master [Zhaozhou] remarked, "Generally speaking, when a master appears in the world, he must first set forth his own insight;
only then can he adjudicate the teachings of the past and present. Observe how Fadeng employed such a strategy."
"It is beautiful indeed, yet it is not yet resolved. Today, this illusory old man also has an unresolved case for the Elder of the Silkworm Bones;
come forth and resolve it for him! If anyone asks, 'What unresolved case does the Elder of the Silkworm Bones have?'—at that very sound, give a shout!
If their eyes flicker or they move, strike them out with a staff! "O Great Assembly, when the mountain monk acts in this manner—"
"Hold fast! Tell me, is there any difference in the application between this and the use of Fandeng?
If you, whether monastic or lay, can resolve this, I will grant that you are a fellow student. He ascended the hall, took up his staff, and said: "This very thing is a source of confusion.
How many monks have reached this point and been unable to open their mouths, unable to conceive of it through thought, and unable to bring it forth for proclamation? Right now, it falls upon..."
In this mountain monk’s hands, whether held horizontally or vertically is up to me; lifting it, setting it down, rolling it out, or drawing it back—killing or giving life—all is entirely up to me.

Pointing once into the air with his staff, he said: "At such a time as this, from the Buddhas and Patriarchs of old to the elder monks of the world, upon reaching here, they can do nothing but beg for their lives. Among the assembly, was there anyone who could...?
"Is this the Buddha and Patriarchs letting out their breath? After a long silence, he struck his staff once, saying, "I blind the true eye of Vajra;

I topple the precious throne of the Sovereign of Space. You people, what bowl are you looking for? He then descended from the seat. Ascending the hall, when the assembly had gathered, the Master adjusted his robes and took his seat.
After a long silence, he said, "Great assembly, take this clearly to heart. He then descended from the seat. He addressed the assembly, saying: "Select..."
The Buddha-field opens the pivot of the Patriarchs; distinguishing the heterodox from the orthodox within the tongs and hammer.

The waves warm at the Dragon Gate and wind and thunder stir—this is precisely the time for fish and dragons to undergo transformation. Is there anyone among the assembly who can surge through the waves and stir up the billows?
After a long silence, he drew a circle with his whisk. One move prior to the pivot, he presents it fully face-to-face. He struck the meditation seat once. Beyond the phrase...
A single word, a harmonious tone, is revealed; no room for lingering thought or hesitation. There is no allowance for deliberation or analysis.
By the time you blink an eye, the sword has long since departed. Even if a Buddha or a Patriarch were to arrive, they would only have cause to knit their brows. Why is this so?
This is because it is not a path where words can be communicated, nor is it something that can be fathomed by the conscious mind.

If a truly eminent monk were to nod his head and break into a smile before the words were even raised, he would still have some measure of excellence. In recent times, however, the human heart has not returned to its ancient state;
students do not strive for genuine inquiry and authentic realization, but merely pass on echoes and inherit empty claims, taking mere scholarly knowledge and intellectual facility as awakening.

They take the pursuit of intellectual dissection as their means of investigation, the violation of monastic discipline as their liberation, and the manipulation of circumstances to secure positions as their transcendence of the world.
Consequently, the ancestral wind has withered and decayed while demonic doctrines blaze forth;

they block the level path of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and blind the true eye of humanity, causing the Way of our Ancestors—the separate transmission outside the teachings—to be cast to the ground at this time. Greatly Awakened World-Honored One...

More than two thousand years ago, the Honored One already understood the mental afflictions of sentient beings. He therefore established numerous expedient means and unconventional rules. Thus he said:
"Do not allow sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) age who aspire to attain the Way to seek awakening;

it will only increase their learning and grow their self-view. He further asked: "Since sentient beings have not yet awakened, what skillful means can be used to cause them all to open to awakening? For this reason—
During the retreat of the *kṣetra-bandhana* (the summer rains retreat), one strives to realize the goal within the fixed period;

once the three-month term has passed, one may depart without hindrance. Thus, we know there is a specific time for the "untying" of the retreat. Venerable sirs, during these ninety days, have you ever attained realization?
Let us set aside those who have already realized it for now; if you have not yet realized it, then this entire period has been spent in vain. If...
These are the true descendants of the Way. They take the ten directions and the dharma-realm as the site for their period of intensive practice (*yuánjué qítáng*).

Whether it be a hundred days or a thousand days of formal retreat (*jiézhì*) and its conclusion (*jièzhì*), they simply take the raising of the *huàtóu* (critical phrase) as the beginning. If one does not awaken within a year, one continues the investigation for another year.
If you do not awaken after ten years, continue for ten more; even if it takes twenty, thirty, or your entire life, do not waver from this resolve.
You must directly seek that ultimate, thorough, and true state of realization before it shall be the day of "dropping the study.
As it is said, "A single thought lasts ten thousand years"—how could this be empty talk? (He raises his whisk. All of you...
"Virtuous ones, do you know where it has fallen? Today, this illusory old man will not refuse to be loquacious;
let me provide another commentary for all of you: A golden ball forged in a fierce fire—when struck at the critical moment, it is crushed yet remains perfectly round.
Carelessly discarding both gain and loss, the wind carries the sound of the tide out through the sea gate. When the Master reached the vegetable garden, he saw a winter melon and asked the gardener:
The Head said, "This fellow has no mouth; why has he grown so large?
The Master said, "Has the Lord of the House exerted any effort on his behalf? The Head said, "I rely entirely upon his strength.
The Master said, "Bring him here to meet me, old monk. The Head then prostrated himself. The Master said, "This is still merely..."
The slave and the servant were there; they turned their heads and picked up bamboo strips to bind the frame.

The Master then laughed heartily and, looking back at his attendant, said, "There are insects in the vegetable garden. The Head Seat Xingkong requested instruction on the Three Barriers of Mount Meng, saying:
"A gnat sucks dry the vast ocean; where shall the fish, dragons, shrimp, and crabs find a place to dwell and establish their lives?

The Master said, "A golden-haired lion lies on the road to Chang'an. [The student] asked, "The water-jelly flies up to the Ultimate Heaven (Akaniṣṭha), enters the eye of Mahesvara, and performs a dance—why is it not seen?
The Master said, "Iron horses neigh before the Five-Phoenix Pavilion. [The student] asked, "At the Lotus Lake Bridge..."
[The student] asked, "Why did a person of direct insight fall into the well? The Master said, "The bright moon illuminates the traveler at night.
[The student] said, "I beg the Master to provide a verse on this. The Master said, "A good chance for a severe beating. [The student] said, "I am willing to accept the beating;

I beg the Master not to be sparing with the verse. The Master laughed heartily and composed this verse: "When the opportune moment seizes the ford between sage and ordinary, If one hesitates, he knows [the truth]."
His path was still unyielding and his purpose unfulfilled. If you wish to know the ultimate meaning of Mount Meng, it is like casting a hook with the intent to catch a golden-scaled fish.
In the first year of the Tiānshùn era, he returned from Mount Lú to Shǔ. Duhòu Hán established Yúnfēng Monastery on Mount Fāng and invited the Master to serve as its abbot.
On the fifteenth day of the third month in the ninth year of the Chénghuà era, he manifested a slight illness. When the assembly requested his final words, the Master extended both hands.
He asked, "Do you understand? He spoke again: "On this very day this year, pushing a cart, he crashes against the wall; he shatters empty space, and a thunderbolt strikes the blue sky.
A-ha-ha! The earthen ox swallows the old dragon’s pearl; the tranquil ocean of nature stills its foam-flowers. Then, with serene composure, he passed away.
His secular age was seventy, and his years as a monk were sixty-one.
Chan Master Shanjian of Guting in Yunnan Prefecture was a native of Kunming in his home province. He first studied under Wuji, who posed the koan:

"The myriad dharmas return to One; to what does the One return? The Master applied himself with great diligence, and only after ten years of exhaustive investigation did he attain complete penetration.
Later, he sought certification from Long'en. Long'en asked, "How is your realization different from mine? The Master unfolded [his hands].
Liangshou said, "This is nothing other than this. Xijì nodded his chin in agreement. One day, as the Master was taking his leave, Xijì asked, "Where are you going?
The Master replied, "I am going to the crossroads to revile the Buddhas and scold the Patriarchs. Xijì asked, "Will you return?

The Master said, "I shall not fail to pay my respects to the Honored Countenance of the Master," and having prostrated himself, he departed. Initially, he traveled to Jintai and stayed at Mount Dayong; subsequently, he returned south and took up residence there.
At Tianjie Monastery in Jinling, [Zhaozhou] moved to Fushan in Wanshan, Tongcheng. There he addressed the assembly, citing Chan Master Wuye of Fenyang:
"After the ancients who were true men of the Way attained realization, they lived in thatched huts or stone chambers, cooking their meals in broken-legged cauldrons for twenty or thirty years.
Fame and profit did not disturb their minds; wealth and treasures were not a concern. They utterly forgot the world of men and concealed their traces among the mountain crags."
"When a sovereign summons us, we do not come; when feudal lords invite us, we do not attend.
Is this not the same as our own kind, who greedily pursue profit and crave fame, wallowing in the worldly path? We are like petty peddlers who, having small desires, forget the great fruit.
The Master said, "Truly so! We merely plunder empty titles and arrogantly exalt ourselves. The three poisons of ignorance are secretly bound within our hearts."
When encountering adverse and evil conditions, one knows there is no liberation. To speak according to reality: for now, let us set aside whether you are a man of knowledge or not.
Setting aside all conditioned activities—whether movement or stillness, speech or silence, and even words and texts—when birth and death arrive, how will you ultimately escape them?
You must not cling to a state of dead stagnation, nor dwell in deluded thoughts during long intervals of silence. Do not do so.
To grasp at something that rolls and turns, and to wander recklessly in a state of superficial liveliness—

so long as there remains even a hair’s breadth of discriminatory view or intellectual awakening, then even if one’s backbone were forged of cast iron and one’s eloquence flowed like a cascading torrent,

one could not avoid being cast by Old Yan into the *āpapa* and *aṭaṭa* hells, through the eight cold and eight hot realms, undergoing ten thousand deaths and ten thousand births. This is most certainly so.
He struck the whisk. "Last night, a gnat swallowed the six realms; empty space was smashed to pieces and fell before the cliff. He again called to the assembly, saying, "Be careful!
Afterwards, he returned to the Ancient Courtyard of Kunming to pass away. The Ancient Courtyard stands south and north, side by side with Panlong.
To this day, the physical remains of these two great adepts (dàshì) are preserved.

At the assembly held by Chan Master Yigan Zhen, a dharma successor of the Great Adept Tian Su’an, he addressed the congregation: "The green mountains rise in layers; the clear waters flow on and on. At this very moment..."
Attained! He strides alone, soaring far above. Nevertheless, it is but ordinary tea and rice. An ancient said, "If you wish to exhaust the view for a thousand li, climb one more story higher.
If the pivot does not leave its station, one falls into a sea of poison; if the words do not startle the crowd, one sinks into vulgar convention.
If you can discern the black from the white within the spark struck from flint, and clarify killing and giving life within a flash of lightning, then you may [attain it].
Seated, one cuts off a thousand differences; standing like a sheer cliff ten thousand fathoms high. Brothers, do you know if there is such a time?
Nowadays, the various quarters speak of Chan in a great clamor, all claiming their heels touch the ground and their nostrils reach toward heaven.

Yet, in the end, those who truly possess the right eye are rarely heard of, being few and far between. Consequently, views of partiality and correctness are not uniform, each establishing its own heterodox path and clinging tenaciously to it.
Although you have attained some understanding, you have not yet penetrated the true principle. As it is said: "When the True Dharma is difficult to uphold, heterodox teachings arise in competition.
An ancient master said: "If one has ten parts of faith, one will have ten parts of doubt; if one has ten parts of doubt, one will have ten parts of awakening.

You should take all that you have seen with your eyes and heard with your ears throughout your life—those evil interpretations and understandings, those strange words and wondrous phrases regarding Chan and the Way—and [cast them away].
Completely cast off all arrogance, conceit, and other such mental states regarding the Buddha-dharma; do not retain even a hair’s breadth of them.

Focus solely upon a kōan that you have not yet understood or resolved, planting your feet firmly and straightening your spine. Without distinguishing between day and night, practice where there is no place to practice, and doubt where there is no room for doubt.
Continue until you reach a state where east and west cannot be distinguished and north and south cannot be told apart; remain in a state of total, simple stillness.
It is like a living corpse; the mind transforms according to its environment, yet it still knows upon contact.
Once the skull is shattered, one does not obtain [realization] from another. Is this not a source of lifelong celebration?

Chan Master Haizhou Yongci of Yishan in Jinling, a successor of Chan Master Dongming Chai of the twenty-eighth generation under Dajian, was a native of the Yu clan from Chengdu. He was born in Hong... [text truncated]
In the twenty-seventh year of the Wu era, [Zhaozhou] was an orphan from childhood. Whenever he saw a monk, he would feel joy.

One day, hearing that the matter of birth and death is of great importance, he resolved to leave the household life. With determined will, he sought out a spiritual teacher. He first met Taichu, who asked him, "Before your parents were born, what is your original face?
The Master immediately walked from east to west and stood with his hands folded. Taichu said, "That is not it."
"No," the Master said. "Two eyes facing two eyes. In the second year of the Xuande era, he left the Gorges to travel to the capital, Beijing.
On his return south, he arrived at Wulin to visit Dongming. He asked, "Who is worthy to wear the formless *fútián* robe? Dongming struck him with his palm.
The Master said, "What is this? Ming struck him again. The Master said, "If one blow does not serve as the function of one blow, what then?

Ming struck him once more. The Master said, "The old monk's reputation is not in vain. Ming then fully spread his sitting cloth and prostrated three times. Not long after, he traveled again to Jinling.
In the second year of the Zhengtong era, the eunuch Yuan Cheng, admiring the Master’s virtue and realization, invited him to open a Dharma hall at Yishan.
On the twenty-ninth day of the fifth month in the fifth year, a monk from Dongmyeong arrived to deliver robes and a whisk. He offered this verse:
"Entrusted to the boat of Compassionate Sea, Seek me, for I have no recompense. On the first day of the following year, The west wind smiles and nods its head.
The following year, Dongmyeong passed away exactly as predicted.
Chan Master Juejing Shuixin Yuejiang was the son of the Shen family of Gusu. At the age of fifteen, he went to follow Guzhuo to receive the tonsure.
In the *Renyin* year of the Yongle era, he visited Xianshan Zong; later, he met Dongming, upon whom he relied most intimately for the longest period.
One day, he asked Dongming, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Dongming said, "Where have you come from? The Master stepped forward.
Bowing deeply, [Ming] asked, "Where have you come from? Ming then gave a shout; the Master also shouted. Ming then struck him. Later, he lived in seclusion at Tianmu.
During the Tian-shun era, he moved to Shuixin in Li. On the nineteenth day of the first month of the Jihai year of the Chenghua era, he exhorted his disciples and passed away while reciting a verse.
He was seventy-nine years old by secular age and fifty-one years since his ordination.
Chan Master Da’chan Huītong of Jūnfēng Peak in Shàowǔ Prefecture was a dharma successor of Chan Master Tiānjiān. He was the son of the Shào clan of Jiān’íng.
Having shaved his head at Dòufēng, he went to study under Xuěgǔ Zhōng. One night, he attained realization and spoke this verse: "Holding the axe of pure wind in hand, I..."
The crown of Lu’s head burst open. The Buddhas and patriarchs of the three thousand worlds were strung together on a single thread and brought before him.
Upon entering Master Zhong’s quarters, Zhong said, "Return my *huatou* to me. The Master again spoke a verse: "Severing the world of Ganges sands, The whole mind is devoid of a single thing.
Floating clouds have all dispersed; A solitary wheel shines alone. Zhong certified his realization. Later, he resided at Junfeng.
On the seventeenth day of the second month in the fourteenth year of the Hongzhi era, he gathered the assembly and spoke this verse:
"Human life reaching seventy years is rare since ancient times; To add another year is even more extraordinary. If you ask where this old monk goes, The void alone is revealed, smiling broadly.
Having bathed and changed his robes, he sat in the lotus posture and passed away.

Chan Master Guxi Juecheng of Gaosuo, Jinling, was a successor of Chan Master Touzi Qi. A native of Weizhou, he received the tonsure under Yunzhong Tianhui Chang and spent five years and six seasons reading the Tripitaka.
Upon encountering the "Mu" (No) koan in the records of Dahui, he gained a preliminary grasp of its meaning and subsequently sought further instruction.
Yuexi then went to Touzi to see Chushan, where he remained in close attendance for a long time until he fully grasped the master’s essential teachings.

He lived in seclusion on South Mountain in Guoshi for many years. During the Tianfu era, he resided at Gaozuo Monastery in Jinling. At the opening of the retreat, during the *xiaocan* (small private instruction), he said:
"Sitting beneath these three rafters, I hold fast to body and mind like cold ashes; yet from within the hearth, I stir up a spark of fire that startles the world."
Heaven shakes and earth trembles with a single clap of thunder. Is there anyone here who does not spare their eyebrows? After a long silence, he said:
"There are times when the Buddhas of the three periods preach the Dharma to the brazier; seeking the fire, one finds it along with the smoke.

There are times when the brazier preaches the Dharma and the Buddhas of the three periods listen intently; carrying the spring water and returning with the moon. If you can realize this, a mustard seed will contain Mount Sumeru."

It is so. It is also possible for Mount Sumeru to contain a mustard seed. Viewed through the True Eye, both fire-pits have had the Buddhas of the three periods of time bound within a Qingzhou cloth robe;
a single grain of mustard seed has brought ten billion Mount Sumers back into a Yunmen sesame cake.
The assembly of monks in the two halls may pierce it again and again, yet they cannot pierce it; they may chew upon it again and again, yet they cannot chew it. O Great Assembly! Truly...
"At such a time, what is it ultimately like? Do you understand? The vajra-flames are squeezed out from between the eyebrows; the lamp-stands and lanterns all emit light.
On the ninth day of the eighth month in the Gui-si year of the Chenghua era, he bathed, changed his robes, assembled the assembly for a final farewell, and passed away while sitting upright.
After a short while, as the assembly wept, the Master opened his eyes again and said, "There is no need for this," and then [passed away].
[The Master] closed his eyes.
Chan Master Dayunxing of Xiangyang Prefecture had long attended Chushan. One day, as Chushan was returning from the prefectural seat, the assembly went out on the road to welcome him.
Chushan said, "I have never descended the mountain, nor have I ever left the prefecture. Tell me, where have you come from? The Master [closed his eyes].
The Master said, "The great assembly has been standing for a long time; I request that the Abbot return to the temple. Yunmen said, "Where is the temple?
The Master replied, "The sound of the bell rings well. Yunmen laughed heartily. The Master then prostrated. Later, Yunmen bestowed upon him a verse, saying:

"In person from Xizhou, you have settled the fundamental tenets; From Touzi yourself, you have received the *kāṣāya*. In years to come, when you appear in the world to uphold the essential principles, Do not establish [a fixed doctrine]."
"Solitary peril is the true artist.
Chan Master Jinshan Bao of Zhuozhou went to visit Chushan. Chushan asked, "Facing south, you look at the Big Dipper;
tell me, what matter do you see clearly? The Master said, "Master, please shut your mouth. Chushan said, "Not yet. The Master said, "To deceive [you]..."
The other person immediately attained it. Chushi asked, "What is the eye that penetrates the barrier? The Master let out a thunderous shout. Chushi asked, "And what about the single pivot beyond?
The Master said, "The sun at high noon in a clear blue sky. Chushi said, "I have not even dreamed of it yet."
The Master said, "The wooden boy holds the jade thread; the stone woman passes the golden needle. Cui said, "Speak quickly, speak quickly—a turning phrase!
The Master said, "The rain makes the mountain colors more exquisite; the wind comes and the bamboo shadows shift. Cui picked up his staff.

One day, during a private interview, Chushan asked, "What is the single word of ultimate principle? The Master replied, "There are lips, but they cannot speak.

While Chan Master Shijing Haiju was in seclusion behind closed doors, one day Chushan arrived before the gate, struck it once, and said, "I request an audience with the master within the gate.

Mount [Shan] asked, "Why can he not speak? The Master said, "He has no mouth. Mount [Shan] said, "And yet you say he has no mouth.
