Cuiwei Wukong Chan Master was a native of Guansi who had long relied upon Chushan.

One day, while entering the inner chamber for instruction, Chushan asked, "When you have trampled over the great earth until not an inch of soil remains and you have thoroughly exhausted the source, what is it like? The Master replied, "All stars bow toward the North;
all waters flow toward the East. Chushan asked, "Is there still any need for the function of practice and realization? The Master said, "Practice and realization."
"Then it would not be that effortless [action] is unattainable. Shanshan said, "Even this very 'unattainable' place is unattainable;
what else would you do? As the Master was about to offer a word in reply, Shanshan let out a thunderous shout. The Master said, "Your great kindness is difficult to repay," and prostrated himself.
Zen Master Xiantong Dawei Jinglun of Mount Wutai was a successor of Zen Master Jian of Yunnan. He was a son of the Kang family of Yunnan and was born in the Dingwei year of the Xuande era.
During the Zhengtong era, he received the tonsure under Master Tai at Wuji. Later, when Guzuting resided at Fushan, the Master went there to seek instruction in his room.
The middle capacity was harmonized. Later, while residing at Xian, he ascended the hall and said: "A holeless iron hammer is hurled right before your face;
a black-lacquered Kunlun sits blocking the road. Is there anyone who can strike through it and grasp its essence?
Come forward and speak! A monk asked, "What is the realm of Mount Tiantai? The Master said, "It is nothing other than fine weather or rain. The monk asked, "What is..."
A person from Jingzhong asked, "Master, [who are] the ten thousand bodhisattvas within the Vajra Cave? The Master said, "I do not know what Dharma you usually preach.
The person asked, "How is it that the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma is expressed? The Master said, "This year the rains are timely;

the farmers' spring wheat will flourish. The person asked, "What is the Patriarch? The Master said, "A clear breeze blows through the secluded pines; the closer one listens, the more exquisite the sound."

[The monk asked: "What is the meaning of the Master’s coming from the West? The Master said: "Wait until I have finished my meal on Mount Xian; once I turn my body, I shall tell you. He then continued:
"There have indeed been those who took arsenic and made it into clarified butter (amṛta). Who would not treat scattered pearls like shards of tile?
To open one's eyes and climb a tree is to needlessly lose one's entire self. Dreaming of ascending to Tuṣita Heaven is merely exposing one's family disgrace—before even a single thought has moved."
He transformed the demonesses entirely into vessels for Bodhi. Without exerting physical effort, he pointed toward the Sahā world and made it the Pure Land of Wondrous Joy.
Longshui and Junyue came like surging waters; Langye and Jue departed like melting ice. With a step of faith, he overturned the lapis lazuli pit;
with ease, he smashed the coral branches. He ascended the hall. The Three Sages let out a thunderous shout; the True Dharma...
Scattering sand into one’s eyes; Nanquan brandishes his white blade aloft. The ancestral style of the ancient Buddhas has been swept away like dust.
Whether it be "necessary" or "unnecessary," how could the probing pole ever be held by human hands? From south of Xiang and north of Tan, he brings forth the very model of the stupa.

Spring returns upon the branch that never buds; a single snowflake flies amidst a mass of blazing flames. One who possesses such a strategy may truly be called a man of his caliber—whose house is this?

In the bottom of the well there is no sky; everywhere, within the waves, there is a moon. Ascending the hall: The three greatnesses—essence, characteristic, and function—are manifested simultaneously.

Every particle of dust is subsumed; the five cycles of cause, effect, and wisdom are realized all at once. All phenomena are perfectly interfused. The misty waters of a hundred cities do not go beyond a single hair’s breadth;
the ten ages of past and present do not shift from the present moment. When the red lotus blooms, its fragrance touches the mosquito.
The insect has a nose on one side; where the green mountains are low, the sky unfolds vast and wide—a single stalk of brows for a gaunt mosquito.
A hundred rivers compete to pour forth, yet the substance of water does not flow; ten thousand apertures cry out together, yet wind is fundamentally still from the start.
The golden lion need not labor to crouch upon the ground; the water buffalo accepts its portion as it is. Every movement fills the eyes; the home mountain remains as ever, a clear blue sky.
A Bright Day. At the Winter Solstice, he addressed the assembly: "The five peaks are mounds of jade and snow; the thousand pines are branches of pearls and gems.
All the springs, rocks, mist, and clouds of Mount Tai, along with the soaring pavilions and surging halls—these are all the true radiance of Mañjuśrī’s single eye of wisdom.
You people are constantly within it, walking, sitting, and lying down; yet do you know that you have never once touched it?"
"Does it have eyebrows? If you can see it in this way, then you will gather the great trichiliocosm within a single hair-tip and expand the sands of dust throughout the Dharma-realm.
If this is not yet so, you must by all means avoid guessing east and west. For all of you, I, this old monk, give you this true report:
today is the winter solstice, and the first yang has arisen. Take care. (Addressing the assembly: "The mountains are high and the seas are vast; the moon..."
The bright wind is clear; the pines are dark green and the rocks are white; summer is hot and winter is cold. Thus, everything is distinct and clearly manifest, one by one.
But tell me, within the sphere of a patch-robed monk, what kind of matter can be accomplished? Is there anyone who can say it?
"Come forth and speak; if you cannot, I, the old monk, shall speak for myself. He took up his staff and descended from the seat. Addressing the assembly, he said:
"The Master Yan spoke of a most extraordinary cause and condition to illustrate it to all of you. If one wishes to explain it, one is hindered by the very act of explaining;
if one does not explain it, one is hindered by the non-explanation. Great Master Yan was truly like a sacred tortoise dragging its tail—a single word [that leaves no trace]."
"Once it has fallen upon people's ears, how can it be concealed? This old monk also has a most extraordinary karmic cause;
I shall straightforwardly present it to the Great Assembly, so that those who merely lean against the door or peep through the window may each stand like a cliff rising ten thousand feet.
He then descended from his seat and addressed the assembly: "In this place of mine, I do not speak of Old Man Li of the East Village being too stingy, nor do I speak of..."
The two elder sisters of King Xishewang were excessively extravagant; they neither knew how to trim the horns of a rabbit nor how to add legs to a painted snake.
At dawn there was a bowl of white congee, and in the afternoon a cup of clear tea.
Who cares about this old, rotten vine blooming in the cold? He spreads his two hands and says: "You people, what dry goods are you seeking here?"

Mujaku. The Master had a poem titled "Verses on Dwelling in the Mountains": "In my mountain cottage, there is nothing to do; the door remains unopened. On the earthen steps, spring rains have caused green moss to grow.
I thought this mind would remain entrusted to no one, Yet from where does the cry of a solitary bird come? Later, he passed away at his native mountain.

Zen Master Dufeng Benshan of Tianshen in Hangzhou was a successor of Zen Master Cheng of Dagang. His ancestral lineage was the Wu clan of Fengyang; he was born while his father was serving as an official in Leiyang, Guangdong.
At the age of seventeen, he left home to become a monk. Initially, he encountered Master Yuanming, who showed him the koan of the "Wordless" (Wuzi).
The Master immediately understood this and related it to Ming. Ming said, "For twenty years I have been contemplating the word 'Mu' like a mosquito on an iron ox.
You, however, as soon as you began practicing, already possessed so many intellectual views.
He further remarked, "I observe that your faculties are extraordinary; do not let yourself be deceived by others along the way and go astray by becoming an elder."
"You have a great matter. Upon receiving this instruction from his teacher, he made a vow to practice with single-minded devotion, swearing that in this life he would take awakening as his only goal.
Admiring the boundless reputation of Master Wuji, he traveled to Sichuan to seek instruction. Later, when Master Wuji was summoned to the capital, he subsequently shut himself in retreat.
He did not prepare a bed, but kept only a small stool; when drowsiness set in, he even discarded the stool. One day, he heard the sound of a bell.

He had an awakening. He spoke a verse, saying: "Profoundly still and utterly silent, all activity ceases. Upon contact, it roars like thunder without cause. With one sound that shakes the earth, all news is exhausted;
The skull shatters to pieces, and the dream finally returns. He went again to visit [Zhao] Ji, but just then Ji had passed away.
He then sought certification from Yuexi, who said: "The Buddha-dharma is not fresh fish; one fears it will rot. One day—
He would only strike from the east and hit from the west, secretly setting up examinations.

One day, while sitting in the garden by the stream, Xī said, "You have had no particular *huatou* (critical phrase) until now. The Master replied, "The word 'Mu' (No). Xī asked, "What is this word 'Mu'?
The Master said, "Looking at it now, it is like the Vajra-Wheel King’s Precious Sword. Xī asked, "What is the Vajra-Wheel King?"
“Precious Sword. The Master said, “Its cold radiance blazes forth, shining through antiquity and surging into the present.
Xuefeng said, “Give me back my sword! The Master said, “If you move to do so, you will strike against its edge. Xuefeng said, “What about when it is held horizontally across the hall?
The Master said, “I would kill even a Buddha; I would kill even a Patriarch. Xuefeng said, “What about when the old monk comes? The Master said, “I will not spare you either. Xuefeng said—
"After he was killed, what happened? The Master said, "For now, let us rejoice that the world is at peace. Xuefeng asked, "Ultimately, what is the meaning of the word 'wu' (no)?
The Master said, "The culprit is clearly identified. Xuefeng said, "Setting aside the culprit for a moment, give me back my stolen goods!
The Master said, "Six times six is thirty-six. Xuefeng said, "Not yet; speak further. The Master said, "The nights are short and sleep is insufficient; the days are long."
Ji said, "There is a surplus. Xī asked, "When an ox passes through the window lattice, its horns, head, and four hooves have all passed through;
why is it that the tail cannot pass? The Master replied, "There is not a single dharma that stands before the mind; in a flash, the whole body is revealed.
Xī asked, "Where do you now establish your dwelling and maintain your life? The Master replied, "Where could one not be honored? Later, he took his leave of Xī.
While traveling through Zhejiang, he retired into seclusion at Wanfeng Monastery on Mount Tianmu. Yuesi was also granted imperial permission to return to Daga in Jinling;
he sent a letter summoning the Master to entrust him with his final instructions. At that time, the Master had gone elsewhere on business.

Yuesi came in person to transmit his final testament and presented him with his robe and whisk. The Master resided on the mountain for over forty years. During the Tianfeng era, he established [the West Lake...].
He visited these three pagodas. Subsequently, he went to Chaoming at Mount Tianmu, Baolian on Mount Wu, and Ganglu at Mount Nan.
At the beginning of the Chenghua era, he closed his retreat in Shiwu; later, he resided at Tianzhen. A monk asked, "What is the master’s house style?

The Master replied, "The tide is swift in the river ahead, so the fish swim with difficulty; the peaks are high on the ridge behind, so the birds find it hard to alight. The monk then requested further instruction regarding Gaofeng.
The Master addressed the assembly, saying: "The mud ox at the bottom of the sea chews the moon as it runs; the stone tiger before the cliff sleeps while cradling its cubs.
An iron snake drills into the diamond eye; the Kunlun man rides an elephant led by a heron.
Within these four lines, there is one phrase that can kill and can give life, can let go and can seize. If anyone can discern it, their lifelong study will be complete."
“I do not yet know which phrase that is. The Master said, “I will tell you when you have attained realization.
The monk said, “I do not understand. The Master said, “Have you not heard it said: ‘If you have a staff, I give you a staff;
if you have no staff, I take your staff away’? The brief general discourse says: “The precious sword is fully raised within daily life; wield it high.”
Da Mo Ken was composed and at ease. When he rolled up [his robe], his soul and gallbladder were lost to the wind; when he spread it out, skulls lay scattered across the ground.
Disregarding life and death through ten thousand trials, he achieved success with a single spear and a single horse. Zhaozhou’s very life-force was clearly revealed therein.
A blood-stained blade reaches the heavens, yet its edge is not revealed. With a whisk, he sweeps once: the void is vast and transparent, without a trace of news;
ten thousand *li* are cloudless, and the Milky Way is azure. He forces Mount Sumeru to enter a lotus fiber; Maitreya and Śākyamuni both cry out in protest.
Riding backward upon an iron horse, he chases the western wind; it startles the earthen ox to emerge from the sea. O worthy ones, if you take this as...
If you understand this as something extraordinary, you betray your own spiritual nature; if you do not understand it as something extraordinary, you harbor a grievance while crying out for injustice.

But how, then, do you understand it? Only when you can conceal the whole world within the world will you first see the horned sheep hanging from the treetops. On the *Ren-yin* year, he passed away at Tianzhen, and his stupa was built on the mountain where he resided.
Chan Master Guyue Jingcheng of Pujisi on Mount Wutai was the son of the Zhang family of Xihe. He first studied under Yuexi, who instructed him to contemplate the "Mu" (No-thing) koan of Zhaozhou.
After three days, he attained realization, which caused Yuexi to marvel at him. He subsequently traveled to Sichuan to visit Guangfu.
Fú asked, "When one who has undergone the great death returns to life, what is it like? The Master said, "The eyebrows lie across the eyes;
the nostrils are large and the head hangs down. Fú asked, "What is the meaning of the word 'wu' (no)? The Master said, "The wind blows and the grass bends; the water flows and the channel is formed."

Before one's eyes, there appear illusory objects of conceptualization; unaware that these are entirely a dream, one regards them as truly existent.
With a deluded mind of thought and recollection, the spiritual consciousness flutters about, taking these objects to be real. This is what is meant by "both waking and sleeping are dreams."
It is like dreaming within a dream. The person of ultimate attainment knows the realm of their own mind as it truly is;

therefore, regarding the illusory phenomena appearing before them, their wondrous function is coolly lucid, penetrating and unimpeded, while even sleep and dreams are known with clarity and they remain vividly awake—this is what is meant by "waking and sleeping are one and the same. Thus, the person of ultimate attainment has no dreams.

From childhood, he was outstanding and unconstrained; he often sighed, saying, "In this world, all that is sought brings suffering; it would be better to seek an exit early."
At the age of twenty-five, he shaved his head at Dongfeng. Initially, upon meeting Dachen, he received no inspiration.
Next, he visited Xingkong, the abbot of Guanzhuang, where he encountered the veteran monk Jinghuang sitting beside him. One day, Huang was reading the *Record of Ancient Plum* (*Gumei yulu*).
In it, there was a passage concerning a monk who went to the abbot’s quarters and said, "I have a point of entry. Plum then struck him out. The monk stepped forward again.
The abbot struck him again with his staff. Huáng laughed and said, "This monk truly has a place of awakening; it is simply that he has not yet clarified the Great Dharma.
Upon hearing Huáng’s words, the Master rose, performed a prostration, and requested instruction on the essential points for entering the Way.

Huáng said, "Although the Buddha-nature is inherently present in every person, if one does not cultivate and transform it through wisdom, one remains merely a common worldling. Now, if you wish to achieve..."
To accomplish this matter, you must completely sweep away all entanglements and branches.

Take up a single phrase of "tasteless" *huatou* and, through self-doubt, self-inquiry, self-pressing, and self-squeezing, refuse to seek someone else to explain it for you, and refuse to rely on intellectual interpretations or forced analysis.

One must decisively sever the life-root and personally realize and awaken to it. Thus, pressing on three times by day and three times by night, after a long succession of years and months, suddenly the flower of the mind will burst forth in brilliance like the sun appearing through the clearing of clouds.

One will then thoroughly penetrate every ancient kōan; only then will one know that there is no Zen to be studied and no Buddha to be made, and that realization occurs at every head and upon every object.
"Penetrating [the truth] is like a person who has reached home and no longer asks for directions. Having received this instruction from the Master, he devoted himself to deathless study of the koan:
"The myriad dharmas return to One; where does the One return? He subsequently traveled south to Yunnan to visit Shoutang. Upon arriving at Jimingtan, he suddenly attained great enlightenment.

When he met Shoutang, their minds met like a needle and its eye; he was immediately granted the seal of transmission. He then returned to live in seclusion at Shuangfeng. This is the correct [account].
In the year of De-renchen (1752), he moved to Ruiyan. Addressing the assembly, he said: "A student of the Way should sever all external conditions and still all miscellaneous thoughts.

They must single-mindedly maintain the original *huatou* of their inquiry. Amidst walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, and throughout all circumstances—whether of suffering or joy, adversity or favor—they must not allow it to be forgotten.
Whatever wholesome or unwholesome objects and conditions appear during periods of stillness all arise from improper reflection. Simply..."
With eyes closed and sitting in stillness, the mind lacks vigor; the consciousness follows the flow of objects, half-dreaming and half-awake.
Or, by craving a state of quietude, one may encounter various visionary realms. If you are a patch-robed monk practicing with the correct cause, when it is time to sleep, you should simply sleep;
upon waking, you must shake off your lethargy, rub your eyes, clench your teeth, and tighten your fists.

Focus your mind with single-mindedness and right mindfulness, pressing on with earnest inquiry as doubt arises and passes away. When you reach the point where the water is exhausted and the mountains end, the mass of doubt will suddenly burst apart.
You will then suddenly perceive your own original ground and its natural brilliance, which is not obtained from without.
Reaching this stage is what is called "entering the gate and attaining the ground. Yet, one must still seek a clear-eyed master to provide definitive discernment;

one must not stop here. If even a single dharma is not understood, it must be thoroughly investigated until clarified. If even a single principle is not penetrated, it must be mastered until it is fully realized.
Even if one has attained awakening, if one cannot penetrate the gates of transformation, the ancients called this "sitting atop a hundred-foot pole.
One cannot thereby reach the ocean of all-knowledge. To let go of one's hand over a precipice and take responsibility for oneself—only after death to be revived again;
this cannot be faked before the Master. Take care.
Chan Master Wansong Huilin of Mount Jing in Hangzhou was a successor of Chan Master Jintai Jue. He was the son of the Shen family of Renhe County.

Having received the essential points of the mind from Pingshu of Tianmu, he later traveled to Jinling, where he heard a monk reciting the words of Chan Master Danxia from his formal lecture hall discourse.
He then attained great enlightenment. At that time, Funiu Konghuan was staying at Guangde; the Master went to visit him and presented his realization, immediately receiving his seal of approval.
Later, while residing at Jingshan, he took leave of the assembly one day and wrote this verse: "For seventy-six years, what reliance has this floating life had?"
"Fundamentally there is no coming or going; one merely responds to conditions. Having finished writing this, he passed away.
He was a Dharma successor of Chan Master Tianqi Rui of the thirty-first generation under Dayuan Jingzhen (Dajian).
Chan Master Zhengcong Wumen Jue of Guanziling, Longquan, Suizhou, was a native of Shaowu. His clan name was Xi and his mother’s surname was Wu.
He entered the monastic life in his childhood and received full ordination at the age of twenty. He studied the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā-śāstra* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.
One day, an elder monk questioned him, saying: "The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat upon the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas, yet the Buddha-dharma did not manifest."

"Previously, you could not attain the Buddha-way. What was your intention? The Master answered according to the text. [The guest] departed with a reproachful air. From this point on, the Master was spurred to exert himself;
his doubts suddenly arose, and he remained restless whether sitting or lying down for six years. One day, hearing the neighing of a horse, he attained great enlightenment.
He then went to see Tianqi, whereupon he received certification (*inka*). Later, while presiding over the assembly in the Dharma hall, he raised the following case: A monk asked Yunmen...
The monk asked, "What is the teaching for this one era? The Gatekeeper said, "It is spoken in response to each individual. Longquan, however, was not like this.
If someone were to ask me, a mountain monk, "What is the teaching for this one era? I would strike them across the spine and say, "Shut that dog's mouth!
A monk asked, "What is my original face? The Master said, "The Stone Incense Pavilion. The monk asked, "If I go away just as it is..."
"What? the Master said. "It has been lost. A monk asked, "Today is the eighth day of the fourth month;
all the monasteries throughout the world celebrate the Buddha’s birthday. I wonder, where was the Tathāgata born? The Master drew a circle on his desk and showed it to him.
Xiaoyan Bao was practicing meditation. One day, while they were sitting around a brazier, the Master said, "Every person has their original parents.
Where are your parents now? Xiaoyan replied, "A single fire has burned them away. The Master said, "In that case, you have no parents?
Xiaoyan replied, "They exist, yet even the Buddha-eye cannot see them. The Master asked, "Can you see them? Xiaoyan... [replied].
He said, "I do not see them. The Master asked, "Why do you not see them? Yank replied, "If one were to see them, they would not be the true parents.
The Master said, "Excellent! Yank then presented a verse: "The original true parents have never been separated throughout kalpas. In rising and sitting we rely on their power;
in cold and warmth we share their knowledge. When meeting, we do not see them; when seeing, we do not recognize them. For this reason, I ask now—"
"Where is it? [The student] clearly presented it to the Master. The Master then bestowed upon him a verse, saying:

"Your mind is my mind; my mind is fundamentally no-mind. No-mind is identical to the Buddha-mind; the Buddha-mind is not my mind. He further instructed him, saying: "You must protect and uphold this."

When the conditions for his passing were ripe, both the wise and the foolish crossed over [to the other shore]. On the first day of the seventh month in the year of Ren-shen, the Master manifested a slight illness.
He bid farewell to the assembly, spoke a verse, and passed away while sitting in the lotus posture. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa to the right of the temple.
Chan Master Guyan of Mianzhou lost his sight in both eyes during middle age. When Xiangyan came to visit him, the Master asked, "Where have you come from?
Xiangyan replied, "I have come directly from Guanziling. The Master asked, "Is your elder brother Wumen doing well? Xiangyan said, "He is well. The Master asked, "How do you know he is well?
Xiangyan replied, "In his old age, he is robust and healthy. The Master asked, "How can you see that he is healthy? Xiangyan—
[Yaoshan] said, “Dressing, eating, sitting, lying down, walking, and practicing meditation. The Master said, “If that is so, then you do not transcend ordinary circumstances.

"Is the Master well-versed in learning? The Master said, "I am not well-versed in learning either. Yankou said, "If that is so, then we are the same.

Chan Master Daxiu Shishi of Fu-niu Jie-an was the son of the Li family of Xinzheng. As a child, he suffered from chronic illness;

Qichu asked, "Before your parents were born, what did you shout at? The Master was speechless and departed.

I knew you had come to meet a true master in person. Xuyan then gave a shout. After a short while, the Master asked again, "What about my old man?"
"Brother, it has been forty years since we last met; I do not know how your nostrils have been lately. Yuan said, "They are just like the Master's nostrils.
The Master said, "Upādhyāya, do you see this old monk’s nostrils? Yuan said, "I see them. The Master said, "Where do you see them?
Yuan said, "Below the two eyes and above the mouth. The Master said, "There is a secret phrase; have you ever heard it?"
The Elder asked, "Did you say something? Yanguan replied, "I did. The Master said, "Try to repeat it and see. Yanguan said, "Shut that stinking mouth!

Chan Master Daju Yuan of Xiangyang Prefecture was a dharma heir of Chan Master Tiantai Susu. A native of Hanchuan, he possessed a robust and imposing physique and a voice like a great bell.

Having visited and questioned Master Jing’an until attaining silent realization, Jing’an bestowed upon him a verse of transmission, which said: "A single branch of the True Dharma Eye has been transmitted successively by the patriarchs. It was thus conferred.
"You must wait for the time to come; then your fragrant reputation will pervade the nine realms. After receiving these instructions, the Master retired to live in seclusion west of Xiangyang.

When Xiaoyan and Shuang'an came to pay their respects and seek his guidance, the Master said, "The Senior Monk has made a mistake. This old, clumsy fellow has lived his life content with mere warmth and full bellies;
I have no other special talent. Shuang'an replied, "For us, the matter of birth and death is of great importance. Before he had finished speaking, the Master laughed heartily.

[The Master] said, "I, an old fool, also have birth and death; why should you alone be exempt? Sang replied, "I regret that, having entered [the path] late, I lack constant resolve. How could the Master reject anyone?
The Master said, "Those who have left the household life are fundamentally without affairs. Why do you create affairs where there are none?
After a short while, he said, "Only when you prepare your own rice gruel and meals will it be right. The Master’s skillful means were unfathomable; he most detested mistiming his opportunities.
"Not sincere. One day, in the meditation hall, the Master raised the case of the outsider who asked the Buddha: "I do not ask about speech, nor do I ask about silence.

After the World-Honored One remained silent for a long while, the outsider attained great enlightenment. The Master said, "Since the question did not involve existence or non-existence, that long silence was merely an idle name.
At such a moment, what did the outsider realize? As Yan was about to offer a word in response, the Master suddenly reached out his hand.

[The Master] covered his mouth and said, "It still hangs between the lips and teeth. Yunyan was then relieved and said, "One could say that the patch-robed monks of the Eastern Land cannot match the non-Buddhists of the Western Heaven.
He then recited a verse: "I laugh at myself for the patterns I drew in those years; Several times red, several times black.
Now, having thanked my master, I return to my old home; Who cares whether I attained it in my lifetime or not? The Master praised him.
Later, he passed away without illness. His secular age was seventy-three, and his monastic seniority (*saṃgha-rakṣā*) was fifty-three.
Chan Master Wuqu Ruokong of Jiaxing Prefecture was a successor of Chan Master Yeweng Xiao; he was the son of the Shi family of Xiushui in the same prefecture, born during the Hongzhi era.
On the eighteenth day of the tenth month of the Xinhai year, at a young age I took a deep interest in the vehicle of the patriarchs and devoted myself to investigating its essence.

For several years, I traveled with Fazhou Ji to visit various masters. Later, I encountered Yeweng, who reached the very bottom of the Dharma source. He opened the gate to instruct the assembly, saying:

"I have bound the profound gate myself; I have buried myself alive. By myself I close it, and by myself I open it. With a single blow of the fist, break through the aperture of the profound gate and release that which was there from the beginning."
The Han monk arrives. On the Lantern Festival, he addresses the assembly: "If you can realize it amidst the sound of the painted horns, even Avalokiteśvara is not yet a master.
If you know where to return within the shadows of the colored lanterns, Śrīmati may boast of her skillful hands.

To announce this to all of you in such a manner, one must surely laugh until the void’s own mouth splits open. If you have not yet had a sudden flash of insight, look again at the Turtle Mountain tumbling upside down. [End] Small Session."

The assembly stood in formal posture. The Master let out a shout and said, "Calamity arises from within one's own house," and then returned to his quarters. He addressed the assembly, citing the *Sūtra* teachings:
"To attempt to fathom the realm of the Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment with the conceptualizing mind is like trying to burn Mount Sumeru with a firefly.
The Master said, "I shall ask you all: since the realm of the Tathāgata is something to be fathomed..."

"I have not attained it. Ultimately, how should one bring it to a decisive conclusion? He let out a shout. "Do you see the meaning of the teaching? Then he descended from his seat and addressed the assembly:

"If you can realize it before words, you are already at the edge of the world; If you accept it upon a phrase, the path grows ever more remote. A single blow shatters the Iron Ring Mountains as if they were powder;

The sea and sky are vast and open, the geese fly in a slanting line. On the eve of the year, during a small *ch'an* (meditation) session, he said: "When time is exhausted, how does it compare to when the day is exhausted?"
"Good. If the month is exhausted, it is the same for the coming year. When the thirty-six weeks have passed, the old King of the Eastern Village burns paper money at night.
The old man possesses not a single thing; he merely responds to the conditions of the occasion. [He] picks up his staff and says:
"There is only this, which is inexhaustible through kalpas and years. Tonight, I shall send it forth according to the season, so as to avoid entangling complications."
He drew [the staff] and cast down his whisk. "What has been acquired through kalpas is now brought to an end; with empty hands clapped together, he receives the New Year. He addressed the assembly:
"The Buddha is one who has settled all matters within the house of sentient beings; sentient beings are those who have not settled their matters within the house of the Buddha."
If you wish for things to be as they are, simply let go of both the Buddha and sentient beings at once; then there will be neither that which is realized nor that which is not.

(He strikes the meditation staff. When one penetrates the phenomenal world through non-phenomenality, seeing forms and hearing sounds does not require deafness. [This was spoken] to the assembly on the Dragon Boat Festival.
How could this auspicious Festival of the Double Fifth have been pre-arranged? On the fifth day of the fifth month, it strikes us year after year.

The wind shakes the sword-like *pú* leaves, shimmering with green; the sun shines upon the *liú* flowers, glowing with crimson. Since the Way resides within the conditions of the seasons, why discuss whether it is the True Dharma or the Final Dharma?
In the past, you sought it with focused intent, yet your entire being was nothing but weeds. Today, when you pick it up at random with the hand of faith, there is nothing that is not [the Way].
"This is the medicine. [The Master] held up his whisk. "Tell me, Great Assembly, what illness does this medicine cure? [He] struck the whisk. "Not only did old Vimalakīrti take a dose;
even Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata took a dose. He addressed the assembly: "Open wide the eye at the crown of the head, illuminating the great trichiliocosm.
Having become the King of Dharma, one attains mastery over all phenomena. One night, the Master walked by moonlight along the lake.
He encountered a monk. The Master said, "The bright moon and the clear wind; the water and the sky are of one color. Everyone is within this very state, yet none can emerge.
The monk asked, "Why do you 'strike the grass to startle the snake'? The Master said, "And what about you, Venerable One? The monk said, "Look beneath your feet.
The Master laughed heartily and said, "I thought the red-bearded ones were rare, but here is another with a red beard!"
Hu. In the second month of winter in the *jīmǎo* year of the Wanli era, the Master said to his disciple Xingchong:

Chan Master Fahui of Yungu at Xushan in Jiaxing Prefecture was a successor of Chan Master Tianning Ji. He was the son of the Huai family of Huaisian in that same prefecture. He received the tonsure and ordination at Dayun Temple.
At that time, Chan Master Fazhou was secluding himself in his room at Tianning; the Master went there to seek instruction, and [Fazhou] instructed him to practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name.
"Whose words are these? One day, while at a meal, his eating vessel fell to the ground, and he suddenly attained realization.
A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "Where there is water, it contains the moon; where there is no mountain, it does not bear clouds.

The monk asked, "Is there perhaps something even more extraordinary? The Master said, "One must by all means avoid calling a tortoise a turtle. [The monk] asked, "How can I, this humble one, directly..."

Regarding the point of swift mental application, the Master said: "If you do not look back upon what has been raised, you will err; if you intend to deliberate through thought, when will you ever awaken?
The Master never provided himself with bedding while residing there; he sat upright day and night for over forty years, remaining as if it were a single day.
On the fifth day of the first month in the third year of the Wanli era, he passed away. He was seventy years of age and fifty-six years since his ordination.
Chan Master Fangze of Jingyan Dongxi in Jiaxing Prefecture was a native of Jiashan in the same prefecture. His clan name was Ren. He first visited Fazhou at Tianning Temple.
One day, during a private interview, the Master raised the koan of Longtan seeing Emperor Huangtian. Upon reaching the line, "Where did he not point out the essential heart?

Fangze attained realization. Later, he received formal certification of his enlightenment. At the conclusion of the retreat, he held the whisk and presided over the assembly. Thus, the Buddha-dharma...
Although it pervades all worlds, there has never been even a hair’s breadth of leakage; how can it be bound?
Although there has never been even a hair’s breadth of leakage, there has likewise never been even a hair’s breadth of concealment; how can it be unbound?
Therefore, one should know that Great Master Baizhang’s indirect guidance for beginners is merely a skillful means, words used to deceive and alarm them; in reality, there is nothing [to be grasped].

It can be tied, yet none can untie it. Suppose there were a fellow like Meng Bala who came forth and said, "I can tie a single knot where Great Master Baizhang could not tie one, so that all the monks in the world would lose their bearings and find no way out.
He could likewise untie a single knot where Great Master Baizhang could not untie one.
"Open! It would be truly extraordinary if it were to leave the monks of the world in such a state of total disarray that they had no place to hide their bodies.
You venerable ones, since he is already a man of such caliber, how could I not be so? (After a long silence) He strikes the whisk once and says: 'HŪṂ!'"
The Venerable Fupeng Puen, a successor of Chan Master Tianchi Ju, was the son of the Jin family of Shanyin. At the age of ten, he went to Yanfu Monastery on Lake Jian to receive instruction.

When he reached the age of nineteen, he suddenly realized that the matter of birth and death was of great importance and resolved to seek out a teacher. He first arrived at Daci Monastery and knocked [at the gate].
Wuji. The Head Seat showed him the saying, "When the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise. At that moment, the Master attained a realization. He spoke a verse:
"Returning to the root and restoring the source is arriving home; There is no mystery or marvel to be praised.
A vast expanse of the single nature of True Suchness— All loss and confusion stem from a single thought gone astray. He later met Fazhou at Tianning Temple.
He presented his insights. Zhou approved of them. He then went to pay his respects to Wansong Xiu at Wushifeng.
Wansong asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From Tianning. Wansong asked, "What words or phrases did they speak there? The Master recounted the previous conversation.
Wansong said, "Not so, not so. The Master said, "Tianning says it is so; why does the Master say it is not? Wansong said, "Tianning is correct, but as for me—"
"No. The Master remained in doubt and could not resolve it. Later, he visited Yuzhi and again raised the previous dialogue.

Yuzhi said, "To say 'it is' or 'it is not' does not transcend ordinary sentiment; both are liable to receive a blow of the staff. The Master asked, "What is the phrase that transcends ordinary sentiment?

Yuzhi gave him a slap on the face. At that moment, the Master attained sudden enlightenment; the blockage that had long obstructed his chest was instantly dissolved. Yuzhi said, "Since you have already..."
Thus you should skillfully guard and uphold this. Furthermore, he entrusted him with these verses: "Do not study the tributaries to distinguish the turbid from the clear;
where right and wrong are exhausted, one transcends ordinary sentiment. When the iron whip shatters the coral moon, you shall see the waters of Dongshan flow uphill."
Chan Master Tianzhen Daojue of Doupeng in Jianning Prefecture was a dharma successor of Chan Master Shuangfeng Qin. He was the son of the Zhang family of Jian’an in his native region.
While contemplating the phrase, “All dharmas return to One; where does the One return? for a long time, he attained realization. He composed a verse, which begins: “One hand claps, and...”
Hand drum. The person of no station performs an extraordinary dance; from his mouth he sings a tuneless song.
The three thousand Buddhas share the same mother. He went to see Gu Yin to seek verification; Yin praised him.
Chan Master Yuexin Xiaoyan Debao of Beiping Shanguo was a descendant of the thirty-second generation under Dajian (Baizhang). He was of noble lineage from Jintai; his father was from Wumen.
Her mother was Lady Ding. She was born on the full moon day of the twelfth lunar month in the *Ren-shen* year of the Zhengde era.

Having lost both parents at an early age, she reached the age of twenty when she happened to attend a lecture series to hear the Great Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra. Upon reaching the chapter on the Ten Stages (*Daśabhūmi*), her body and mind suddenly became vast and empty, beyond all perception.

He sighed, saying, "All things throughout the ages are but a single illusory dream. He then resolved to leave the household life. Over a year later, he went to follow Guanghui Daji Neng to have his hair shaved.
The following year, he received full ordination. He attended the morning assembly and knocked at the door in the evening;

though he possessed deep faith and understanding, he refused to rest content with mere knowledge, vowing instead to seek personal realization. He visited various masters, including Dayong, Yuezhou, Guchun, and Guzhuo, before finally arriving at [the master’s place].
Guan Ziling went to visit Chan Master Wumen. He asked, "The Ten Sages and Three Worthies have already fully realized sage-wisdom;
why do you say they do not understand this principle? Wumen then spoke in a stern voice, "You already know of the Ten Sages and Three Worthies.

What is this principle? Speak quickly! Speak quickly! The Master uttered several words in succession, none of which accorded with the Master's intent. Thereupon, he became filled with indignation and abandoned both sleep and food.
One day, he took a basket to the edge of a stream to wash vegetables. A single leaf fell into the water and spun around;
he tried to catch it but could not hold it. Suddenly, he had an awakening. Carrying his basket, he returned home with great joy. Wumen was standing under the eaves and asked, "What is that?

The Master replied, "A basket of vegetables. Wumen said, "Why do you not say something else? The Master said, "Please ask me something else, Reverend. That evening, he entered the inner room [for private instruction].
When Wumen heard that Xuansha had remarked, "I dare guarantee that you, elder brother, have not yet reached the ultimate," the Master said, "A thief has entered an empty room.
Wumen said, "This public case must not be treated with casualness. The Master gave a shout, shook out his sleeves, and departed.

Not long after, he went again to visit the venerable masters Jie'an, Guyan, and Dajue, all of whom held him in high esteem. Later, he returned once more to attend upon Wumen, who then conferred [upon him]...
He received a formal prediction of his future enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). He remained in close attendance for over a year before taking his leave to travel through the regions of Xiang and Han.
Later, he arrived in Jinling (Nanjing) and resided at various sites including Jinghai, Niushou, and Gaozuo. After several years, he returned to Jintai. Initially, he stayed at Yuantong;

subsequently, he moved to Nan Temple, Luyuan, Ciguang, and Shanguo monasteries. On the Dragon Boat Festival, he ascended the hall and cited the discourse given by Master Dahui upon ascending the hall.

[The monk] said, "This morning is again the fifth day of the fifth month. The great ghosts clap their hands and the little ghosts dance. Suddenly they run straight into the deity of the peach-wood talisman;
with both hands they beat their breasts, crying out in grievous suffering. The Master said, "Old man Dahui looks very much as if he were lacking a certain restraint."
In every direction, under the blue sky and white sun, people see gods and ghosts. Xiangyan, however, was not like this: "Today is precisely the fifth day of the fifth month.
Clouds follow the dragon; wind follows the tiger. This mountain monk wishes to gamble with all the great sages and ordinary beings present here.
Picking up whatever comes to hand from the tips of a hundred blades of grass—what is sweet is sweet, what is bitter is bitter. He picked up his staff and struck out.
However, there is one thing that stands out, piercing through all the Buddhas and Patriarchs above. You people here before me possess it in a hundred ways;
why then is it that you alone lack this one thing? Suddenly, someone who sees the meaning and acts with courage might step forward indignantly and say:
"Preceptor, do not suppress the noble by treating them as base. If we speak of this one thing, I dare say—"
"Everyone lacks nothing by even a hair's breadth. Putting down his staff, he said: "You truly do not know.

What harm is there in adding a point to an arrowhead, or piling more earth upon a mound? Ascending the hall, he said: "A man of spirit may indeed harbor ambitions to pierce the heavens, yet it is better to let them fall from the very start.
Directly seize the skull and let it wither away; then cause the dead eyes to open wide. Ascending the hall, he raised an example.
One day, National Teacher Nanyue Huairang asked the assembly, "Has Daoyi preached the Dharma for the people yet? They replied, "He has already finished preaching the Dharma for the assembly.
The Master said, "I have not yet heard any news from him. He then secretly dispatched a monk to scout him, instructing him:
"Wait until he ascends the hall to teach; then go out and ask him, 'What is this? and see what he has to say."
"What words did he say? You must remember them for me. The monk went and reported exactly as instructed.
Mazu said, "Since the time of chaos, for thirty years there has been no lack of salt and sauce. When the monk returned and recounted this, Baizhang deeply approved.
The Master said, "Only one who, like Great Master Mazu, has had no lack of salt and sauce for thirty years is fit to gather disciples and preach the Dharma. Here in my place, for thirty..."
"I have not seen a single grain of salt or a drop of sauce for years. What kind of bowl are you all looking for here? With his staff, he drove them all away at once.
He then ascended the hall and said: "A single arrow right at the gate; those who come must observe the skillful means. If you intend to step forward and ask 'How is it?'"

[The Master] threaded them through the skull-face. A monk came forward to inquire: "From among the seventeen hundred old cold fellows, I have today strung them all together on a single thread to present to you, Master.
I humbly request your judgment. At that moment, the sound of a dog barking was suddenly heard outside the gate.
The Master immediately looked at his attendant and asked him to see what guest had arrived. The attendant went out; the questioning monk was left bewildered. The Master said:
"Venerable Elder, what was it you were just asking? The monk intended to repeat his question, but the Master struck him with a continuous blow of his staff and drove him out.
One day, two nuns came to pay their respects; as they rose, each stood to the left and right. The Master said, "The woman entered meditative absorption before the Tathāgata.
She had money but did not know how to spend it. The old woman of Mount Tai went straight ahead; she knew how to spend it, yet she had no money. Tell me, which of these two..."
"How can one make this 'housewife Chan' exactly right? The two nuns walked from the left to the right, and from the right to the left;
they joined their palms facing each other and each let out a single sigh.

The Master said, "In this way, you not only understand housewife Chan, but you also know how to drum up the steam of rice gruel. The nuns said, "Master, please take care of your eyebrows. The Master said, "The mountain..."

Let us set aside the matter of the monk’s eyebrows for a moment. I shall ask you this: when Zhou Jingang bought oil-cake pastries as refreshments and was about to eat them, he had them snatched away by an old woman.
When Liu Tiemo invited Guishan to attend a great assembly at Mount Tai, Guishan did not go.
These are both instances of the same occasion; tell me, why were their choices so different? Two nuns acted [as follows].
Liyue said, "If we had not come to pay our respects, how could you have seen the great functioning of the ancient masters' supernormal powers?
The Master said, "Excellent! Thirty blows for each of you. Just then, his staff was not where it usually was, so he said, "For now, let us return to the tea hall to drink some tea."
A monk asked, "What is the Samādhi of Universal Vision of Mañjuśrī? The Master said, "The eyes of a dead man.
The monk asked, "What is the Samādhi of Universal Hearing of Avalokiteśvara? The Master said, "The ears of a dead man. The monk asked, "What is the phrase that exhausts the bottom of the single path?
The Master said, "The mouth of a dead man. Another monk requested instruction on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* passage concerning being "despised by others. The Master said:
"Do you have doubts? The monk said, "I have doubts. The Master said, "If you have doubts, you will be held in contempt by others;
if you have no doubts, you should fall into the evil realms. The monk hesitated. The Master said, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not understand.
The Master said, "Bring forth that which you do not understand and let me see it. The monk said, "Since I do not understand, what am I supposed to bring forth? The Master said, "You..."
Their karmic offenses were instantly eradicated. The monk departed with joy, bowing in gratitude. He asked, "Xuansha did not cross the ridge; Baoshou did not cross the river.
To which of the 'turns' (ji) do these belong? The Master said, "Both fall into the second turn. The monk asked, "What is the first turn?
The Master said, "Xuansha did not cross the ridge; Baoshou did not cross the river. The monk asked, "Ultimately, what was attained?"
"What? The Master said, "Truly, after all, what have you actually obtained? Question: "What is 'taking away the person but not the environment'?
The Master said, "A single coin and a large fried pancake. Question: "What is 'taking away the environment but not the person'?"
The Master said, "Once it has been eaten into the belly, one is immediately satiated and joyful. [The monk] asked, "What is 'both the person and the environment being simultaneously negated'?
The Master said, "Even if you have not a single coin, you must still endure hunger. [The monk] asked, "What is 'neither the person nor the environment being negated'?
The Master said, "Yunmen’s sesame cakes and Niu-tou’s rice; coming with an empty stomach, one returns with a full belly. A monk asked.
"Are the meaning of the Patriarchs and the meaning of the Teachings the same or different? The Master said: "Willow shadows stretch across the pond as fish climb trees;
locust-tree shade covers the earth as horses mount branches. The monk said: "If that is so, then form and shadow are divided, and right and wrong manifest of themselves.
The Master said: "You have not yet eaten your fill of Luling rice; you merely take your meditation cushion to be the sky. The monk, having asked his question, departed.
"The Buddhas appear in the world for the sake of one great matter. The monk asked, "Master, what is this great matter?
The Master replied, "Putting on clothes, eating food, defecating, and urinating. The monk did not accept this; he did not prostrate and departed.
The Master called him back and showed him with a verse: "The Buddhas appear in the world, Solely for the sake of the Great Matter. Defecating and urinating..."
Urine. Eating when hungry and sleeping when exhausted—these are urgent matters before one’s eyes. Yet people only wish to ascend to heaven;

they discuss the profound and speak of the wondrous, only to encounter calamity and pay fines. The monk, filled with shame and alarm, bowed and departed. One day, two officials were touring the mountain.
Upon entering the gate, they recited: "Lush pines and tall bamboos. Looking back, they saw the Master and asked, "What is a man of the Way?"
Regarding the family style: The Master said, "Lush pines and tall bamboos. A student asked, "What is the essential meaning of this? The Master said, "It is not enough for me alone to view;

I leave it for you, my guest, to behold. A scholar read the Master’s verses on the Pure Land and asked, "When the Buddha preached this sutra, the Buddhas of the six directions manifested their broad and long tongues to bear witness. Now, what is so different about the verses spoken by our Master?"
Zheng asked, "Master, even a layman’s tongue is not short. He asked again, "What is inconceivable merit? The Master replied, "A person in the street ahead calls for his dog;
a person in the alley behind scolds his cat. He asked once more, "How old is the Master this year? The Master replied, "I have reached the age of one hundred and twenty."
The Master said, "Speaking of years, I have not seen a single bit of meat. Why have you become so withered and emaciated?
A monk asked, "In every place one enters the Dharma-realm, and in every thought one perceives Vairocana. What is Vairocana? The Master said, "One need not defecate on clean ground.
[The Master] cited Zhaozhou Zen Master’s question to Touzi: "When a person who has died the great death comes back to life, what then? Touzi said, "Not."
"Permit me to travel by night so that I may arrive at dawn. The Master composed a verse, saying: "The thirty-six constituents are all reduced to ashes, Leaving behind only a pair of withered eyes.

Placed upon the nine-fold thoroughfare after the deep night, They create light where there was no light. [He then] raised the public case of the World-Honored One holding up the flower and composed a verse, saying:
"The wondrous accord between teacher and disciple is like a mustard seed entering a needle's eye; Like the ocean and the mountain, there is nowhere [it does not reach]."

Investigating: Having once cast my eyes into the flash of a flint-stone spark, I have finally come to know that the Buddhas and Patriarchs do not transmit a mind. He raises the title of the scripture with the character "丱" (guǎ).
The verse says: Before black and white are distinguished, one has already fallen into partiality; how can one endure such deliberation and the labor of exhaustive study?
The sages and worthies of India and this land—whose nostrils reach toward heaven—are all pierced through. He showed the verse to the Preceptor, saying: "Carrying a hoe everywhere, he sells his skill;
three or two coppers are enough for his livelihood. He clears the fields of others, yet his own field..."
The wasteland is cleared away. To the monks: The subtle mysteries within the Dharma are a physician’s eye; the profound mechanism above is the dust upon the realm.
At the side of the black lacquer bucket, the hoop has snapped; in the land of Great Peace, one is a person of freedom. Sitting quietly in the cold crags, this illness is difficult to cure.
How could a man of spirit ever be willing to deceive himself? A single step turned takes one no further than this; only then does one believe that within the dust, the Dharma-realm is vast.

The Master once gave this instruction in his room: "Before the Buddha appeared in the world and before the Patriarch came from the West, there were originally no such names as 'Buddha-dharma' or 'worldly dharma.
How do you express that single phrase which stands far beyond the ghost-cave of the Black Mountains? He also said: "Since the Buddha..."
He emerged from the world. Since the Patriarch came from the West, the Buddha-dharma and worldly dharmas have been established in mutual relation, yet they do not violate the gate of transformation.

"Bring forth a phrase of the Way," he said. He further remarked: "The Buddha arises within the gate of opposition between ordinary people and sages; worldly dharmas and Buddha-dharmas are merely names forcibly established.
Set them all aside to one side; try to bring forth a phrase that is the fundamental portion of a monk. He also said: "In ordinary times..."
His exchanges in speech and dialogue were exceedingly plain and yet profoundly inconceivable.
When someone asked him, "What is this Buddha-nature that you inherently possess? he would instead turn his eyes upward and remain speechless.

He also said, "Since you have become a son of the Buddha and aspire to the stage of Buddhahood, why is it that you find the single word 'Buddha' most unpleasant to hear? In his later years, the Master retired from public life.
In the willow lanes of the capital city, he manifested parinirvāṇa on the sixteenth day of the first month of the *xin-si* year of the Wanli era.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa outside the Xiaoxi Gate. He reached a worldly age of seventy and a monastic seniority (*saṃgha-vassa*) of forty-eight.
One day at dawn, Master Baoying of Longshu Hermitage on Mount Wutai, a successor of Chan Master Dachu Hong, attained realization upon beholding the morning star. He composed a verse, saying:
"The sun rises from the eastern mountain; The moon sinks behind the western ridge. Yesterday and today have never been two different things."

Master Chufeng resided on Bimoya Cliff at Mount Wutai for over ten years. He lived on wild fruits and drank from mountain streams; others could not endure such hardship, yet the Master remained as serene as ever. One day, hearing the sound of a firecracker, he attained great enlightenment. He composed a verse, saying: The body is like a withered tree, The mind is like cold ashes. When the wind blows through the withered tree, It stirs up the cold ashes.

Suddenly, the firecracker explodes— A flash of light fills the world. The old woman’s staff is broken, And the demon’s cave is overturned. The mountain peaks are all leveled, And the rivers flow back to their source. The Great Way is revealed, And the True Path is clear. I have seen the Buddha, And I have heard the Dharma. My doubts are now resolved, And my heart is at ease. I bow to the Buddhas of the three times, And pay homage to the Patriarchs of the ten directions. I vow that all sentient beings Shall together attain liberation.
The eyes protrude from a withered log; its majestic divine light illuminates the four continents. Appearing wherever it touches, people do not realize it;
how many times has spring passed and autumn returned?
A monk asked Master Yudang, "What is the Way? The Master said, "Look under your feet. The monk asked, "How should one practice it?
The Master said, "Go straight ahead.
[He was] the Dharma heir of Chan Master Wuzu Kung.
Chan Master Wuhuan Guzhan Xingchong of Chexi, Suzhou, was the son of the Zhang family of Xiushui.
Initially appearing as a layman, he met Wunü and subsequently attained a realization. He soon left the household life to follow Wunü and received the tonsure. One day, Wunü asked the Master:
"Jingshan’s verse on the Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials says: 'To utter a single phrase that penetrates to the very bone and marrow—the Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials.'"
"Severing and shielding. Among these two phrases, Master Zhongshan wished to take one as his guiding principle. "Which one do you think would be better? the Master asked.
Zhaozhou said, "Which one did you ask about just now, Reverend? Zhongshan glared at him and scolded, "How can you be so dull-witted?
The Master replied, "It is precisely because you have penetrated me to the very marrow, Reverend. Zhongshan said, "Not so. It is for the sake of you alone."

[The Master] said, "I have already attained it. [Wu] Qu asked, "What will you do about the great assembly? The Master said, "If I were to take it up, I would not refuse, but I would betray the former sages and lose my successors.
Wu Qu said, "So it is, so it is. The Master went to Mount Jing to build a thatched hut and compiled the *Recorded Sayings* of Wu Qu.
One day, he returned to pay his respects. Wu Qu asked, "What have you been doing lately? The Master said, "I have bought a piece of land."
Tian received the original deed and wrote a request for the Master’s signature. He immediately presented the compiled copy.
Quan hurriedly took it and unfolded it to look at it, saying, "This is mine; what about yours? The Master said, "Master, you must not encroach on another's path or snatch away their market.
Quan then threw the compiled copy down, and the Master immediately stepped out. After a short while, he presented a verse. Quan said, "This is..."
"Did you do anything? The Master said, "I am merely blowing on the air of rice and gruel. If you say there was something done, you would be failing the Master by no small measure.
Qiu nodded his head. Later, after taking up residence, he addressed the assembly: "The Great Way has no front or back; the ultimate principle transcends words and explanations."
Transcending the Three Vehicles and loftily surpassing the Ten Stages, where the ten thousand dharmas cannot reach, there is a singular brilliance.

Before the differentiation of sentient beings and Buddhas, the spiritual source alone shines. Not falling into seeing or hearing, not following sound or form—there is not a single hair’s breadth of anything here.
Throughout the entire world, the extraordinary matter is fully revealed. Even if one were to attain realization at the tip of a staff or take responsibility under a shout, it would still be...

This is merely a provisional accommodation. Even if, at present, one were to further forget both light and objects and attain a state of mental equanimity, this ultimate state would still not be the definitive point.
Therefore it is said: "The path that points upward has not been transmitted by the thousand sages; students weary their bodies like monkeys grasping at reflections.
When one arrives here, there is no practice and no understanding, no illumination and no function, no principle and no phenomena. It is like a long sword leaning against the sky—凛 (lǐn).
His divine majesty is chilling; like an iron ox, his mechanism cannot be ensnared. Today, before those with clear eyes, I dare not conceal or cover it;
I shall open it wide, revealing the eight characters. Holding up his whisk, he said: "Do you all understand?
Shining through antiquity and soaring through the present, it is just this: a single idle body within the great chiliocosm. He addressed the assembly: "At the summit of the solitary peak..."

Taking long strides across the great chiliocosm, one encounters few true companions at the crossroads of the ten directions. Paying no homage to Vimalakīrti, nor showing reverence to Dharma Master Fu.
After a long silence: "Lifting my head to gaze beyond the heavens—who is such a person? Addressing the assembly: "The three realms are mind-only;

the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only. He plants his staff firmly and says: "Last night, the seasonal rain dripped upon the empty steps; a single expanse of green moss has been moistened throughout."
[He] drenched [the assembly with water]. He addressed the assembly: "The substance of the Great Way is vast; the long sky leaves no trace. Pressing down the clouds, another message is communicated.
Born together and dying together, like the wind blowing and the grass bowing. Now tell me: is it better to hold fast for the sake of others, or is it better to let go for the sake of others?"
Heaven and earth joined together are an earthen cake; the sun and moon, the two orbs, are a celestial ball. To the assembly:
"Clearly manifest upon the tips of a hundred blades of grass; clearly manifest is the meaning of the Patriarchs. This makes old Master Pang laugh to death, yet even now he remains fast asleep.

When Luzu saw someone, he would simply turn his back to the wall, unable to exchange words of greeting. Beimoshan rushed toward him and raised his pitchfork; he was utterly devoid of courtesy. Nan Shan...
A turtle’s nose is not as good as a dead eel; the tweezers at West Monastery are just like blunt saws. But tell me, how does Mahākāruṇika save beings?
The Universal Monarch has never yet cast away his three inches. Before the world, one hears first the sound of axes and hatchets. *Ascending the hall for the Buddha-Bathing ceremony:*
"You displayed your ugliness within the Jeta Grove; you revealed your form again before the hall of the Ancient Buddha.
Were it not for the power of the Sunlight Samādhi, how could your body have been washed clean? "Great assembly, Śākyamuni the Old Man has taken birth today.
I wonder, at this moment, has he yet touched the ground? A monk stepped forward and said, "He has already touched the ground. The Master said, "Have you seen him?"
"Who says this? The monk was speechless. The Master said, "A ladle divining an empty sound. A monk asked, "When the principle of pure emptiness ultimately has no body, what then?
The Master said, "A seeker of the Way should be thus. The monk asked, "Is there anything further beyond this? The Master said, "The heron is hidden in the snow;
one sees it only when it flies. The parrot is concealed in the willows; one knows it only when it speaks. [Question: "Harmony... (The Master did not speak.)
“Yet after a hundred years, where will one go? The Master said, “Beneath a thousand pine trees, at the tips of a hundred blades of grass.
While the Master was tending a fire, a monk asked, “What is the self-nature, the original, true Buddha? The Master said, “Bring me a bundle of firewood.
When the monk carried the wood on his shoulder back to him, he asked again. The Master said, “This slave does not even know good from bad,” and struck him.
The monk asked, "What is the Most Supreme Vehicle? The Master said, "A rattan vine piercing through; bamboo strips binding. The monk asked, "What is the underlying meaning?

The Master said, "Thirty years from now. Another monk came to pay his respects. The Master asked, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "Mount Lu. The Master said, "An ancient said, 'Do not seek the place of descent on Mount Lu;
the elephant king’s nostrils needlessly reach toward the heavens. What is the descent point of Mount Lu?"

[The Master] said, "I ask that you, Preceptor, show me respect. The Master then bowed his head and withdrew. He then presented a verse on the recitation of the Buddha’s name: To bring forth the mind to recite the Buddha’s name, follow the path of principle;

He sat in the dharma seat and preached the Dharma. He further received imperial favor and was appointed to serve as the abbot of Bao’en Temple in Jinling.

The Master declined the position on the grounds of his advanced age. In the spring of the following year, he took up his staff and returned to Tongxuan. On the third day of the seventh month, he manifested slight illness.

On the fifth day, he wrote a letter by hand to the Dharma-protecting official Qi, the Imperial Censor. On the sixth day, a monk arrived from the capital and asked: "When you shout, do you take it as a shout? When you strike with a staff, do you take it as a staff?"
[The Master said: "Understand! Entering hell is like being shot by an arrow. Ultimately, how do you understand this? The Master then struck him. The monk bowed.
The Master said, "A thousand phrases and ten thousand words all stem from self-realization. If you do not realize yourself, you will never cease receiving blows.
At dawn on the seventh day, he inspected the craftsmen as usual. At noon, he returned to his quarters and told his attendant monk that he was very weary; he then went to bed.
After a short while, he finally rose from his seat. Before he had even finished settling into the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), he passed away peacefully.
His secular age was seventy-seven, and his years as a monk were forty-six. His entire body was escorted back to Tiantong and interred in a stupa on the right ridge of Huazhi Monastery.
Chan Master Tianyin Yuanxiu of Qingshan in Changzhou was the son of the Min family of Jingxi. Having lost his father at a young age, he supported his mother by selling vegetables.

Whenever he heard of the noble conduct of sages and worthies, he was able to put it into practice immediately. His grandfather lived in a *caṇḍāla* quarter out of a sense of righteousness and yielding.
The Master felt pity for him and was not pleased; he constantly held the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.

When he reached the age of twenty, he listened to lectures on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, which states that all sentient beings, due to their ignorance of the eternally abiding true mind—the essence of pure nature and luminosity—employ various deluded thoughts.
Because these perceptions are not true, there is cyclic existence. Trembling with realization that there is the great matter of birth and death, he went to seek out Master Hanyou at Longchi.
At twenty-four, he received ordination and investigated the original face prior to the birth of one's parents.

For a long time he had not entered [the state of realization]. One day, as Huanchu was exiting the kiln, his fellow practitioner remarked, "I have heard that Bodhisattvas appear at the four great sacred mountains with vast and magnificent spiritual powers.
Huanchu said, "They are no less abundant right here. The Master stepped forward and asked, "What are the spiritual powers right here?
Huanchu replied, "Bring the bricks quickly! Upon these words, the Master attained realization; from that moment on, his practice became increasingly refined.

Cai was idly perusing the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* when he reached the passage where the Buddha said to Ānanda, "This is not your mind. Suddenly, he lost his original point of reference. He then traveled north to Huihuan.
Master [Cai] closed himself in retreat at Longchi, where he studied the public cases (*gong'an*) of the ancients. Furthermore, he could not let go of the Yunmen koan regarding the fan.
He investigated it with great effort for two years until, upon hearing a donkey bray, he attained great enlightenment, saying: "Suddenly I hear the donkey cry."
Startled, the person present burst into laughter. Ten thousand distinctions and a thousand differences—neither sound nor form, yet a clamor.

He unlocked the barrier for his fellow practitioner, Master Míyún, who then proceeded to the capital to pay his respects to Huàn at Pùzhào Temple. Huàn said, "It has been three years since we last met; let us each present what we have realized.

Next he moved to Faji, and later resided at Ba’en. Ascending the hall, he said: "Chan is not a matter of intellectual understanding; the Way transcends all merit and achievement.

If you wish to dwell here, you must completely cast off everything you have learned in the past;
you must investigate your own fundamental nature with total purity and attain a clear understanding before you may succeed. If you do not act in this way, you will merely waste your efforts in vain.
