A Zen practitioner asked the Master, "Whom have you studied under that you now dwell on this mountain? The Master replied, "I have never yet traveled as a pilgrim (*xingjiao*). The practitioner said, "Is it not..."
"Can one judge the whole world by a single corner? The Master approved of these words.

He subsequently traveled to Hangzhou to visit the Great Master Lianchi, and later journeyed north to pay his respects to the elders Wuyan, Daguan, and Ruifeng, all of whom regarded him as extraordinary. Upon returning to his staff, he resided at Shouchang.
Ascending the hall, he held up the incense and addressed the assembly, saying: "Do you understand? This is that which the Buddhas of the three periods have never exhausted."
All at once they were cast toward the Sahā world; even Śākyamuni Buddha could not exhaust them, nor have the successive patriarchs of India and China exhausted them.
Today, this mountain monk takes them up with a casual hand to deliberate with the assembly:
Are these not the separate transmission outside the teachings and the profound purport within the scriptures? They encompass heaven and earth and follow the waves.
Is it not the surging waves? Is it not the cutting off of all currents and the raising up for examination? Is it not the manifestation of great function, a probing pole and shadow-grass?
Is it not the brandishing of the Vajra Jewel Sword in the open sun? To speak according to reality, it is inexhaustible throughout kalpas;
yet, those who possess the eye can discern and distinguish: white as white, black as black, rather than lumping everything together as a single mass.
Only then can one determine right from wrong within the monastic community and verify the orthodoxy or heterodoxy of practitioners.

Thereafter, whether responding to the holy or the mundane, one will naturally not be deceived by those who feign enlightenment; every action and gesture will accord with circumstances without missing its mark.
Yet this Way has long been fragmented and obscured. Among the assembly, those of great wisdom should be prepared to sacrifice their very lives and exert all their strength to rectify it.
Support them. Make awakening your goal. To benefit both self and others, one lifetime will not suffice; you must prepare for another.
Only by exhausting three lifetimes will you naturally attain it. As the ancients said: "If one does not enter the great ocean of birth and death, it is difficult to obtain the priceless jewel."
This is still for those of dull faculties. A clever man knows its wondrousness upon hearing it once. Even so, without the spring breeze, the flowers will not bloom;
yet let us not say that once the flowers have bloomed, they are blown away by the wind. [He] ascended the hall and said: "The Buddhas constantly preach the Dharma;
there is no need for deliberation or conjecture. What Dharma is this? 'The heavens are dark blue and the earth is yellow; the universe is vast and ancient.'"
Whether one penetrates the lineage or masters the teachings, it matters only that you directly take responsibility. What is it you must take responsibility for?
Clouds rise and bring rain; dew gathers and turns to frost. A dragon does not dwell in stagnant water; a fierce tiger does not walk by the roadside.
If you can pass through these pivotal points, why need you wish to go to the Western Land? Without asking about former Buddhas or later patriarchs, the nostrils are all alike in their release.

Light. How does one emit light? Its transformation covers the grasses and trees, its grace extends to the ten thousand regions. Śākyamuni was unwilling to reveal it; Bodhidharma concealed it for nine years.
Mount Emei does not begrudge his verbal karma; with a single stroke, he proclaims it for the sake of the assembly.
But tell me, how does he proclaim it? He brandishes his ruler once and says: "Do not speak of others' shortcomings, nor rely on your own strengths. [He ascends the hall.]

When the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month arrives, monasteries provide congee. For what reason? It is nothing other than to conform to worldly custom. Within the school of the patch-robed monks, it is not necessary to act in this way.
Have you not heard that "The Buddhas of the three periods do not know 'there is,' yet the cat and the white ox do know 'there is'?
If that were so, the Buddhas of the three periods would already be standing in the wind's shadow; how much more so the Buddha Kāśyapa! Now tell me: [what is it?]
"What is so superior about the *lilu* (wildcat) and the white ox compared to the Buddhas? The Head Seat replied, "It is because gold is smelted in the great furnace and jade emerges from Lan-tian.
The Master said, "Even though this is so, the Jewel Monastery cannot help but drive out both the wildcat and the white ox together through the triple gate. Why?
To uphold the fundamental principles and establish the regulations, to revitalize the monastic community, and to bring peace to the seas and clarity to the rivers—this is the true mandate."
"Go! All you fine fellows are gathered back into the treasure city; the conjured city is toppled so that no one remains.
The Head Seat said, "When you say, 'The conjured city is toppled so that no one remains,' this may be acceptable from your own perspective, Master, but it is not so for me."
The Master said, "And what about you? Zuo said, "I idly carry a cloth bag with nothing to do; I laugh at waiting for someone on the street. The Master said, "That too is just an idle lute string.
He then descended from his seat. Ascending the hall, he said: "In the vast sky there is no path, yet Zen practitioners walk therein.
When white waves overflow the heavens, the wise can seize them. Even if one passes through the ten-thousand-fathom profound gate, one still falls on 'that side.'"
Emerging from a well a thousand feet deep, one ultimately remains on this shore. Disregarding a hidden store of pure gold, why linger over a mended bag or a broken bowl?
Walking upon level ground, the heart is startled; treading on a precipice, the spirit is bold. Within the scope of one's own true nature, the eye of wisdom discerns all.
"What about one who does not involve themselves in these causes and conditions? What, then, is their coming and going? The Head Seat replied, "Flipping and turning—how truly strange!
Truly surpassing the three thousand who are not yet taken in. The Master said, "Be careful. [He then ascended the hall for the Buddha's Birthday of Guanyin.]
The fivefold true incense has already been prepared; clouds of radiance arise, pervading the three thousandfold world-system.

Universally perfuming the realm of True Suchness throughout the three periods of time, it is used to pray for the present Emperor’s ten-thousand-fold myriad years. Furthermore, we hope that the ministers and officials of the court, along with the military and civilians of the entire nation, may together rejoice under the sky of Yao.
Great Being Avalokiteśvara, you have come with joy! I, [Name], have a question to ask. Great Being, in truth...
"Is this today's birthday? It is simply like the sky having no cover and the earth having no bottom—from where do all the sentient and insentient beings of the world arise?
If you can speak it, then you are one with the Great Being, seventy-three and eighty-four; if you cannot speak it, you shall not escape being struck with the staff.
After a long silence, he said, "I have already told you before. When it comes to benevolence, do not yield; think deeply!"
The Master said, "I record this for the sake of the King of the Correct Dharma (Zhengfaming Wang). For now, let him receive thirty blows. He ascended the hall, struck his fly-whisk once, and said:
"Matters within the School of the Patriarchs are difficult to express in words; the precincts of the Great Way allow no room for deliberation.

To casually manifest a single pivot is like the blade of the Tai’a sword leaving its scabbard—those who encounter it die before a moment has passed. It is like a poison-smeared drum: when struck, those who hear it [perish]."
Once this is lost, one cannot turn back even in the blink of an eye. It is said that on a wondrous peak with its towering precipices, wild beasts find no place to hide;

beneath the crystalline radiance of the jewel-trees, numinous birds find no branch on which to perch. In its application, it single-mindedly pursues the golden-haired lion back to his wild cave, and directly tracks the iron-browed beast into the deep mountains.

Sweeping away the comets that threaten the world, brushing aside the dregs of worldly defilement; lifting up those who have fallen into pits and ravines, and revealing those streams of beings who are lost in delusion or trapped within their stagnant shells—such was his merit.

He caused the Dharma-realm, the world-realm, and the space-realm to be perceived as a single body, and enabled the paths of Buddhas, humans, and hell-beings to merge into a single harmony of all phenomena. Nevertheless, even though it was thus, it was still not yet [the ultimate].
Regarding the matter of transcending: tell me, how do you speak that single phrase beyond all categories and limits?

*Ei!* When the true command is not yet exercised, the head is cut off first; when the great function is unleashed, even sages and worthies are moved to sorrow. I have stood for a long time; take care.

Among his disciples, he revitalized the three monasteries of Baofeng and Shouchang, and separately established more than twenty hermitages and cloisters. He did not rely on outside support nor did he seek patronage.
The Master Huazhu once said, "In all things, preserve this Way; in every flavor, trust in prior karma. In his later years, he became even more diligent;
until the age of seventy, he still mingled with laborers, never ceasing his work of plowing and digging. His chamber was desolate, containing nothing but his implements for practice.

King Yi looked toward the Master’s virtue and morality, praising him deeply. He often sighed, "The time since the Sage has passed so long; it is fortunate that this old man remains. Ten thousand... [times].
On the seventh day of the twelfth month of the *ding-si* year, the Master returned from the fields and said to the assembly, "From this point forward, this old monk shall no longer lay stones.
The assembly was all astonished. On the eve of the New Year, he ascended the hall and said: "This year, there is only this moment remaining."
"I ask you all: do you know it or not? That matter has never yet been personally struck. You must apply yourselves with constant and meticulous effort.
He spoke again, saying, "This is the final instruction I entrust to you. The assembly should cherish it with utmost care.
On the thirteenth day of the new year, he manifested slight illness and consequently ceased eating. He said, "I am not ill; I shall soon depart. Ten.

On the fourth day, he wrote a letter by hand bidding farewell to his old friends. On the morning of the seventeenth, he rose early, gathered the assembly, and took up his brush to write in large characters:
"Today, I have clearly pointed out [the way]. Having cast down his brush, he sat upright and passed away. During the cremation, the flames were five colors;
his cranial bone and various teeth remained unburnt. A stupa was erected in the abbot’s quarters. His secular age was seventy-one, and his monastic seniority was forty-four.
The thirty-sixth generation descendant of Dajian,

Chan Master Zhanyuan Yuancheng of Xianxing Monastery at Yunmen in Xiangsheng Prefecture— a successor of Chan Master Da’ue Nian— was the son of the Xia family of that same prefecture; his mother was surnamed Gu.
In a dream, a monk entered his room and he became pregnant. After his parents passed away, he fell into extreme poverty and served as a postal guard.

Having mistakenly submitted official documents, he feared disgrace and fled to seek refuge with Yinfeng. Yinfeng asked him, "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name? After three days and nights, he suddenly attained realization.

At the age of twenty, he went to Tianhuangshan to follow Miaofeng, where he shaved his head and received the precepts. There, he happened to hear Zen practitioners discussing the teachings of the Great Master Fu.
The Master silently comprehended the verse on the body; he was then able to memorize the scriptures and understand all their principles.
He subsequently went to Yunqi to receive full ordination, and upon returning, he secluded himself in the Baolin hermitage.

Recalling the dialogue between Qianfeng regarding "raising one" and "not raising two," he attained a sudden and great enlightenment, composing a verse that said: "Raising one, raising two—these are but external signs; Within this very place, there is fundamentally neither right nor wrong."
The melody of the "Snow Song" is sublime; few can comprehend it. Only Shaoyang was granted permission to harmonize with it in perfect accord.

How could these two elders ever have moved their tongues? Yet throughout the various quarters, people vainly knit their brows. To deliberate upon this is like a hawk flying to Silla; to mark the boat in search of a sword is fundamentally delusion.
Returning once more to Yunqi, Yunqi raised the story of Gaofeng’s "clay ox at the bottom of the sea. The Master then pushed forward a monk standing nearby and said, "The assembly!"
[This is] the certification. On another day, when a monk returned from the fire-bathing ceremony, Xiqi asked, "Where has the deceased monk gone after his transition?
The Master said, "Thank you for your concern, Preceptor. Xiqi then withdrew. Chan Master Cizhou Nian came from Beijing and stayed at Fengtou. The Master went to visit him to seek certification;
they subsequently established the ritual of teacher and disciple (the dialogue is contained in the chapter on Cizhou). The *Wanli* year, Jia...
In the year of the Tiger, he opened the Fayunmen Guangxiao Monastery. Subsequently, he moved to the Xiangsheng Monastery at Dongta on Mount Jing.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The fan of Yunmen leaps and bounds; today I pick it up for you to laugh at. Why does the pillar conceive and give birth to a son who cries out so loudly?
Tell me, Great Assembly, what sound is this? Is there anyone here who understands the message? If there is no one..."
"I know. I, the mountain monk, shall speak on his behalf. He made a "wa-wa" sound and said, "If you all can laugh, then nothing has ever been lacking.
But if you ask further how it is, it will remain unresolved until the year of the donkey. "Is there anyone among you who would like to pose a question? If so, come forward.
This was merely intended to "beat the grass to startle the snake. As soon as a monk stepped out, the Master said:
Truly, this is a field of karma. [The Master] took up his staff and descended from the seat. He ascended the hall and said: "The cold wind blows fiercely in the midst of true winter;
leaves fall from the gardens, revealing their fundamental nature. When the profuse branches have withered away, what remains is the true reality—why need one so earnestly inquire of the master?
The laws of nature follow a cycle: once withered, there must surely be flourishing. Although at present one may be impoverished to the very bone, come next year..."
"Old Laughing Spring Wind. Ascending the hall, as soon as the Master took his seat, he suddenly heard a cock crow and said:
"Aha! The Venerable Red-Headed One has already turned the fundamental Dharma-wheel of the primary truth for all of you.
What further news do you seek? If you do not understand, I shall raise it once more. Striking the whisk, he said: "This is sound; does it exist?"
The ears hear everything; one is certainly not deaf. Raising his whisk, he said: "This is form; those with eyes see it;
one is certainly not blind. There is not even a hair’s breadth of deception here. It is said: "Calling for Little Jade repeatedly was originally no matter at all;

it was simply that the husband wished to recognize the sound. Ascending the hall, he said: "This old fellow does not know even the first stroke of a character, yet he forcibly steps forward before others to speak."
While preaching the Dharma, he mistakenly read "Zeng Shen" as "Lu San. The entire assembly in the hall burst into laughter. There is a wondrousness within this laugh;

if you can awaken to its underlying meaning, it will pierce through that very first vital point. After a long silence, he said: "To move one's countenance and manifest the ancient path is not to fall into the trap of silent stillness.
In the year Yimao, while residing at Mount Jing, he ascended the hall for a formal discourse and said: "The incense has already been offered."
I do not dare to extol the Buddha-dharma. Why? You all possess a single mass of radiance that has been unobscured since antiquity;
one must not urinate upon level ground. Nevertheless, having been invited by you, my fellow brothers, I cannot remain silent.
I shall briefly raise the title as a mere echo. But tell me, what is this title? Is it not evident today?
Is this for the opening of the summer retreat? Generally, in all quarters, the fifteenth day of the fourth month is established as the fixed rule for the commencement of the retreat.

Here at the new Jing Mountain, however, the eleventh day of the fifth month is taken as the standard. Although the dates differ—early or late—the essential point is to take the realization of the ultimate meaning as the standard.
It is like rowing a boat: though one departs early and another departs late, they arrive at the same shore. Great Assembly!
Do you wish to know the news of reaching the other shore? Have you not seen it said in the Sūtra: "In a single thought-moment, one universally contemplates immeasurable kalpas;
neither going nor coming, nor even abiding. Thus understanding the affairs of the three periods of time, one transcends all expedient means and achieves the Ten Powers.
If you can realize this point, take Great Perfect Enlightenment as your monastery, and let your body and mind dwell in peace within the Wisdom of Equality.
The lands as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions are, in their entirety, a single site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
It was never bound throughout immeasurable kalpas of the past, nor has it ever been released throughout immeasurable kalpas of the future. Birth and death are within it; nirvana is also within it.

Even down to such distinctions as right and wrong, gain and loss, the heterodox and the orthodox, the sage and the ordinary person, liberation and non-liberation, saṃsāra and non-saṃsāra—all are contained within this.
Within it, is there still any place for you to apply your mind? Is there still any room for your calculating deliberations?
"Ha! Suppose suddenly someone from among the assembly were to come forward and say: 'New Elder, today you have been invited to expound the Dharma of our school.

Why do you instead cite sutras and treatises to spread such tangled complications? What kind of mental state is this? At such a point, I, this mountain monk, would have no words with which to respond;
I could only briefly borrow the tracks of the ancients to try to stop his mouth. For instance, as for the former..."
Jingshan held up a bamboo stick and said: "This cannot be called a bamboo stick, yet it cannot not be called a bamboo stick.
To call it a bamboo stick is to offend; not to call it a bamboo stick is to turn one's back on it.
I, this mountain monk, cannot help but imitate him. He then held up a whisk and said: "This cannot be called a whisk, yet it cannot not be called a whisk."
A whisk: to call it a whisk is to encounter it; not to call it a whisk is to turn one’s back on it.
One may neither speak nor remain silent; one may neither shift the pivot nor settle upon words. Between these lies a single phrase that belongs to this mountain monk.
"There is one phrase that belongs to all of you; there is one phrase that belongs to this mountain monk which is precisely what belongs to all of you;
and there is one phrase that belongs to all of you which is precisely what belongs to this mountain monk. Herein there is both host and guest, and both illumination and function.
Is there anyone among the assembly who can distinguish these? A monk brushed his sleeves and left. The Master said, "Just now..."
Arising from this very source, it now collapses of its own accord. He then descended from his seat for a small discourse (*xiao can*): "The mist and rain steal away the mountain colors;
The stream wind carries the sound of the water here. Originally, every dharma is thus; Do not let the conscious mind force an arrangement."
If you interpret this within the context of sensory objects, I grant you one eye; if you interpret it within the context of the Buddha-dharma, I shall break your head.
Why? Because there is no such blade in the treasury of our King. [The Master] addressed the assembly: "Heaven attains the One and becomes clear;
Earth attains the One and becomes tranquil; the Sovereign attains the One and the world is at peace. Yet, these are of no use within the sphere of the patch-robed monk. Why?
It is also said: "The myriad dharmas return to the One; to what place does the One return? Initially, the Master resided at Jiaxi Temple in Beijing.

One day, while strolling with Grand Master Da, Dharma Master Yuechuan, Tao Shikuí, and the two Imperial Historians Huang Shengxuan to view the moon, Shengxuan lay down and asked about the karmic conditions of Mazu’s moon-viewing. The Master said, "You sleep, I stand."
"I may not preach the Dharma for you. Be careful; rise quickly and apologize. Yuechuan said, "The Secretariat Scholar has missed his chance.
Grand Master Da said, "My own words do not equal those of this old man.

When the Master arrived in Hangzhou, several learned masters, including Wen Gu and Hui Wen, as well as various patrons of the Dharma, each prepared a letter of invitation for him. In Hui Wen’s letter, he wrote: "Today..."
"The assembly wishes to have a formal meeting with the Preceptor. If the Preceptor comes, he will already have fallen into the realm of emotional consciousness;

if the Preceptor does not come, it would still be a lack of compassion. Having read this, the Master tore up the note and said, "This hired hand has come before this old monk only to meet his own defeat.
As soon as the Master arrived, he ascended the hall and stood facing south. Huìwén said, "Preceptor..."
"Do not try to show off your skill at the gate of the axe-handle. The Master then gave him a slap and said, "Speak quickly!
Speak quickly! Wénmù’s face turned red and he remained speechless. The Master said, "You dead man! Wénmù immediately led his assembly to prostrate themselves.

Later, while the Master, Chan Master Wúniàn, and the official Táo Shíkùi were sitting around a brazier, Táo said, "Chan Master Wúniàn is here; I beg you for a phrase that represents your true attainment."

He brought this up for illustration. The Master said, "Facing the fire, my back is still cold. Su Yunpu, the Provincial Commissioner, asked, "The embroidered mandarin ducks are displayed for you to behold;
the golden needle is not passed on to others. What is the golden needle?
The Master said, "This mountain monk traveled once through the capital and did not encounter a single person. As Su was about to offer a reply, the Master said, "An ancient Buddha has passed by."
"It has been a long time since he left. The Master went to visit Chan Master Wunian and asked, "The ancients said it is like a single flake of snow flying onto a red-hot furnace.
Tell me, did those ancients possess the eye that penetrates the barrier or not? Wunian replied, "I do not see what 'ancient' there is.
The Master suddenly pointed behind him and said, "What about the one right there? Wunian then simply ceased speaking. The Master’s life was one of liberation.

[Omitted for brevity. Briefly stated: Whomever he encountered, regardless of noble or humble status, he treated with a single flavor of his true nature. Throughout his five years presiding over the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), there was no activity for the benefit and salvation of sentient beings that he did not undertake.
In the twelfth month of the sixth year of the Tianqi era, he delivered words of entrustment at Xianxing Temple.
On the fourth day, he ascended the hall at Tianhua. His disciple Mingzhi informed him that he was going to Jiuhua. The Master said: "You go; I, the old monk, shall now rise."

Cheng again conversed with the assembly until the second watch of the night, when he passed away while lying on his right side. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa on the northern slope of Bowu Mountain.
He was sixty-six years of age and thirty-eight years in the monastic order.
Chan Master Xinyue Huixi of Shaoshi on Mount Song was a successor of Chan Master Daoshao of Shaoshi. He was a native of the Liu clan from Mancheng in Baoding.

Having left the household life at Pujisi, he happened to read the *Transmission of the Lamp*. Upon reaching the passage where a monk asked Xuansha, "What is the seamless stupa? Xuansha replied, "This..."

While sewing a robe, he suddenly attained a realization of its magnitude. He went to see Wuyan, and after a long time, he achieved thorough penetration. Wuyan bestowed upon him a verse, saying: "The Esoteric Dharma has no dharma to bestow;
If it is to be transmitted, how can it be transmitted? In the place where there is neither transmission nor bestowal, Brightness and darkness are wondrously shared by all."
Later, there was no word of his passing. Master [Xuanjue] succeeded him as abbot.
Chan Master Wuyi Yuanlai of Boshan in Guangxin Prefecture was a Dharma heir of Chan Master Jing of Shouchang. He was born into the Sha clan of Shucheng; at birth, he was clothed in white.
He was named Bao. He strictly abstained from meat and alcohol. At the age of sixteen, he traveled to Jinling to listen to lectures, whereupon he ceased his studies of literary texts.
He went to Mount Wutai to follow Master Tong of Jing’an and undergo ordination. Initially, he visited Shouchang at E’feng but did not find resonance there;
he then departed and again paid a visit to Baofang. Shouchang asked him: "Ants know how to scurry toward the place of stench; flies tend to fly toward the side of the foul odor."
"This concerns the side of the ruler and the side of the minister. The Master said, "It concerns the side of the minister. Chang scolded him, saying, "There are many who will laugh at you!
The Master said, "What was previously discussed was all correct. Why is it not so here? Chang said, "This one is not;
therefore, all those others are not. The Master then became indignant. Upon seeing that the statue of the temple guardian (gārala) had fallen to the ground, he [took action].
[The Master] returned to his province. He lived separately in the Zongmeng Hall for two years. One day, while using the toilet, he saw a man climbing a tree; he attained great enlightenment.
He hurried to see Chang, who said, "With what kind of eyes did that old woman burn down the hermitage? The Master replied, "It adds luster to the gold.
Chang then raised the public case of Chan Master Xuanze: "When the dragon roars, mist rises; when the tiger howls, the wind arises. The Master...
He stood and presented this verse: "Killing and bringing to life, each vies for mastery; each possesses its own marvel. How could the dim-fleshed eyes perceive them?

Though it emits light, it does not follow the whims of the age; As before, the spring breeze chases the sound of hooves. Chang nodded in approval. While residing at Boshan, he ascended the hall and said:
"The Buddhas appear in the world for the sake of the single great cause and condition. It cannot be fully captured even upon many scrolls of fine silk. Boshan...
The appearance in the world is also for the sake of this one great cause and condition. A single strand of white silk passes straight through the head;
Old Yan once entrusted this to me, and how many among gods and men have been deceived by its heat!
Today, Boshan takes it up with a casual hand and presents it clearly, so that everyone’s nostrils may reach toward heaven and every person’s heels may touch the ground—like a precious red jewel.
A mirror reflects the myriad phenomena without omission; it is like a jade lock and golden key that opens a thousand gates with total penetration.
Brothers, this matter is not attained through meritorious deeds, nor through cultivation and realization, nor through conceptual thought, nor through study, nor through meditative concentration.
There are some who refine their own body and mind until they become like withered wood.
Cold ashes remain for a hundred years in stillness; in the end, they are but a single dead person. This has no connection whatsoever to the matter of one's own fundamental nature.

Therefore, Xuansha said: "Even if you attain a state like the moon’s reflection in a clear pool or the sound of a bell in a silent night—unimpaired by every strike and undispersed by the ripples of the waves—it is still merely a matter on the shore of birth and death. This is the sphere of action for those who practice the Way.
It is like fire melting ice; once an arrow has left the bowstring, it has no power to return. Brothers, you must take your standard from the light;

do not steal the light in the darkness. Having caught the spring colors of the nine avenues on the streets of willows and flowers, and having brought the autumn radiance of the eight directions from the banks of the lotuses, let your application be without deficiency and your movement with the Dharma be free and easy. Brothers!
Furthermore, tell me: what is the sphere of practice for Boshan? After a long silence, he said: "I have a pair of hands that are poor and bare;
I do not disdain to bow to those who are ordinary. A monk asked: "What is the meaning of 'a silver bowl filled with snow' and 'the bright moon hiding among the herons'?
The Master said: "Bare bones and emaciated mountains encircled by purple mist; a stream choked off, a small brook where green moss grows long. [The monk] asked again as before.
"What is 'merit'? The Master said, "Three people share the same spring. "What is 'shared merit'? The Master said, "A strongman carries a drum-stick.
"What is 'merit upon merit'? The Master said, "A monkey climbs a dew-pillar. "It is not permitted to strike or sing both together;
please show me the wondrous harmony of the central point. The Master said, "High and low clouds wind around the tree. "I thank the Master for his answer."
[The Master] said, "The words have passed. The Master continued, "From afar and near, birds carry blossoms. He ascended the hall and said: "Today, Boshan does not speak of the existence of dharmas;
he does not speak of the non-existence of dharmas; he does not speak of both existence and non-existence; nor does he speak of neither existence nor non-existence.

Transcending the four propositions and severing the hundred negations, the stone man nods his head and the green mountains knit their brows. Deep winter has earned the warmth of spring; it breaks [the ice]."
Mist parting, he enters the emerald heights through the clouds. Ascending the hall, he asked: "What is the Buddha? The most spiritual being in the worlds of the ten directions. "What is the Dharma?
The ancient road stretches far, its moss and lichen slippery. Still taking the Buddha and the Dharma to inquire into their source:
"Clouds disperse across the vast sky, cranes cry out to heaven; not a speck of dust remains, as pure as if washed clean. Three monkeys tossing coins at night. To all you brothers:
Zhong: "Matters within the ancestral school are by no means trivial. Not a single word or phrase can be explained away even by the commentaries of the entire Tripitaka.

The patriarchs of successive generations possessed profound mechanisms and vast wisdom; their hidden stirrings and secret movements could topple Mount Sumeru. They struck their staffs and strode across with bold defiance."
Painting colors in the void; casting the great trichiliocosm beyond the four quarters. Tell me, where can one reach out and grasp it?
Therefore it is said: "He does not stay when caught in a net; he does not turn his head when called. The ancient sages made no arrangements, and until now there has been no fixed location.
Great Master Xuansha’s such compassionate and earnest heart was intended only for you all to know this.
Only when you reach the point of falling [into realization] will you truly attain it. Brothers, in the deep, dark blue expanse, the woodcutter does not need to borrow a path to return home;
when the fabric is woven densely, the shuttle-woman sets aside her golden needle to weave by night. Incense fades within the brocade curtains, and dew moistens the lotus blossoms.
A pure whistling arises from the inner chambers, and subtle words are breathed upon shared pillows. When feelings are rich and intentions are harmonized—let me ask you, brothers: what is this?

"Do you understand yet, or not? After a long silence, he said, "A distinct episode of elegance; I do not compete with people over its length or brevity. A monk asked, "What is 'falling into sound and form'?
The Master said, "The bridge is broken, the wild waters divide. The monk asked, "What is 'falling into categories'?
The Master said, "A solitary boat is raised upon the vast plain. The monk asked, "What is 'falling into nobility'? The Master—
He said: "Tearing asunder several layers of the pure world, riding a jade elephant backward to pursue the qilin.
When the Master first resided at Boshan, he subsequently moved to Dongyan, Dayang, and Gushan in Min, and then to Tianjie in Jinling.
He returned once more to Boshan and passed away in the autumn of the third year of the Chongzhen era. The Head Seat asked, "How is the Master’s health? The Master replied, "It is quite sufficient."
He had enjoyed but a brief existence. Zuo asked, "Is there anyone who is not ill? The Master said, "Why do you act as if it were a great heat?
Zuo said, "I come and go with freedom; please speak a single phrase. The Master wrote for him the four characters "Li-li-fen-ming" (Clearly Distinct).
He then set down his brush, sat in meditation, and passed away. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at this very mountain. He was fifty-six years old.
Chan Master Jianling Yuanying of Dongyuan was the son of the Feng family of Jianyang. His father was Tianzai and his mother was Wu. He was born in the Dingchou year of the Wanli era.
In his youth, he followed Yixin at Huxiao Rock to receive instruction. Later, he studied under Wuming.

One day, while casually reading the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, he reached the passage where Vimalakīrti asks, "Why is this room empty and devoid of attendants? to which Vimalakīrti replies, "The lands of all Buddhas..."

The earth, too, was entirely empty. Suddenly and expansively, he attained realization and entered [the Way]. He composed a verse, saying: "Once consciousness is shattered, it is not worth half a coin;
Pity those who have groped for it for so many years. All lineages of the school are but deceivers of the heart; What need is there to speak of a separate transmission from the West?"
He entered the master’s quarters to present his work to Ming. Ming said, "Zhaozhou exposed the old woman; tell me, where was she exposed?
The Master replied with a stern voice, "Old monk, do not act so strangely. Ming expressed his appreciation for this. Later, when he opened a branch at Yizhi Hermitage, he ascended the hall and said:
"The Buddha-dharma is fundamentally not many; the Southern Dipper pierces the Northern River. All of it comes down to these twenty-one characters. He then descended.

Having exhausted the influence of ghosts, spirits, and māras, he subsequently retired to live in seclusion at Wuyi. He passed away at the age of fifty-four, with thirty-six years of monastic seniority.
Chan Master Shouchang Qi’an Yuanmi of Jianchang Prefecture was the son of the Wang family of Nanchang. He studied under Wuming.
E-feng showed him the matter of the countenance prior to the birth of one's parents. One day, while pushing a millstone, he accidentally struck it with his hand and attained realization.
He composed a verse containing the lines: "The original face need not be sought; a single point of spiritual clarity spans past and present.
Later, upon hearing the cry of a frog, he attained thorough certification. One day, he said to Wu-ming, "My faculties are inferior; by good fortune..."
Having encountered the Upādhyāya, I have been able to escape the sea of suffering; yet I still fear that my past habitual tendencies will be difficult to eliminate.
Yesterday, before the Dharma-protecting deities, I made this vow: "In this life, my merit is meager and my wisdom is short; I dare not recklessly create obstacles.

May I remain in the stage of a student for the rest of my life, never part from virtuous spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) in every birth, and may I be fully endowed with merit and wisdom to repay the kindness of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. This is my aspiration.
This was his aspiration. Wuming said, "To bring about benefit and salvation, none but those with two feet can do so. You have deeply understood the source and its course.
Chan Master Yongjue Yuanxian of Gushan in Fuzhou was a native of Jianyang; his clan name was Cai. At the age of twenty, he was enrolled as a scholar in the local prefecture.

Xiang was reading in a mountain hermitage when he heard a monk reciting the sutras. Upon reaching the passage, "At that time, I manifested for him a body of pure radiance," he attained a state of great joy.
Later, he saw Shouchang present his own understanding; Shouchang urged him to contemplate the koan of the "dry dung pellet.
At the age of forty, Xiang abandoned his home and family; Shouchang performed the tonsure for him. One day, as Shouchang was returning from the fields, the Master went out to meet him and asked:
"What is the body of pure radiance? Chang shook out his robes and stood there. The Master said, "Is this it, or is there anything more?
Chang brushed away his robe and departed. The Master followed him into the hall;

before he could open his mouth, Chang took up his staff and struck him three times, saying, "Henceforth, do not be so casual. The following year, Chang passed away. The Master returned to Min by boat. Subsequently—
At Yanzhin, he heard a monk reciting the sighs and coughs of the Buddhas, and as they all snapped their fingers together, he suddenly saw through the point of Shouchang’s application.
He composed a verse, which says: The golden rooster pecks through the azure lapis lazuli; Ten thousand cessations and a thousand restings are known only to oneself.
Reclining peacefully on a single sail under a clear sky, On the mountain ahead, the rain-birds no longer cry. Ascending the hall, [he said]: "This year, May has passed its fifth day again."
The Dharma-bell rings and the Dharma-drum beats. What need is there for "how" or "what"? To bring forth the present by citing the past, he spreads both hands and says:
"In the hall of the Buddha-Dharma, the two hands interlace; the lamp-stand and the lantern dance together. O worthy ones, can you take this up?
He picks up his staff and strikes it once, saying: "When the weather is clear and dry, one refuses to walk; one waits until the rain drenches one's head. Then he sets it down.
Zuò. *Xùdēng Cúnggǎo*, Scroll Eleven;
*Xùdēng Cúnggǎo*, Scroll Twelve.
Compiled by the monk Sizu of Eastern Wu, Tongwen;
edited by the Layman of Lize, Shipei of Huating; the succession of Dharma heirs remains undetermined.
Chan Master Fojue of Qingzhou (of the Yunmen lineage) composed a verse on Master Yaoshan’s Lion: "A single color surpasses all pointing out;
within a world of white silver, he groans and sighs. Transcendently, he knocks it down and then raises it up again—how can this compare to the spring breeze, ever new under the sun?"

When National Teacher Yuantongshan (a successor of the Yunmen lineage under Fojue) traveled from Jiangyou to Yanjing and stayed at Dasheng Temple, he engaged in a night conversation with Fojue and Haitang.
At that time, the Master was only twelve years old and stood in attendance to their right.
Yunju said, "This mountain monk has come from the south, yet I have never once struck upon a single person who understands the Buddha-dharma with the tip of my staff.
The Master joined his palms and stepped forward, saying, "It is simply that your staff, Reverend, is too short.
Yunju was greatly startled and said, "I pray you, take this man to continue my Linji lineage. The Master replied, "How could there be two—Yunmen and Linji? Yunju praised him.
The Emperor rewarded him unstintingly. When Emperor Jin Sejong visited the Shrine of the Auspicious Image at Sengan-sa, he asked the Master, "Is it proper to pay homage, or is it improper?
The Master replied, "To pay homage is to show mutual respect and honor; not to pay homage is for each to claim their own supremacy. The Emperor was greatly pleased.

Later, while residing at Yansheng, he addressed the assembly, citing Dongshan: "At the end of summer and the beginning of autumn, brothers, whether you go east or west, you must head toward a place ten thousand miles away where there is not a single inch of grass.
He continued, "But as for that 'ten thousand miles without an inch of grass'—how does one go there?
Shishuang said, "Stepping out the door is already grass. Dayang said, "Even if you do not step out the door..."
"It is also a place where the grass grows rank. The Master said, "Tell me now: how would you express it beneath your own feet?
If you say, 'Ten thousand miles, not an inch of grass,' I will grant that you have seen Dongshan.
If you say, 'Stepping out the door is already grass,' I will grant that you have seen Shishuang. If you say, 'Not stepping out the door is also a place where the grass grows rank'—"
"I permit you to see Dayang; if you cannot say anything at all, I permit you to see Yansheng. Why?
Because 'only a fine breeze comes upon the mat, and no idle talk falls among men. He addressed the assembly, citing the story of Master Yunmen regarding the "Avalokiteśvara glutinous rice cake.
The Master said, "The old man of Shaoyang may indeed be said to have sung with ever-higher notes, yet those who join in the harmony grow ever fewer. Like...
Now, turning back toward the tip of the whisk at Yansheng, I enter the Fangwang Samādhi. Entering meditative concentration in the east, I arise in the west;
even entering concentration in a male body, I arise in a female body. Do you understand? The wild landscape is no longer interrupted by mountains.
The moonlight flows directly into the water.

Regarding the Chan Master Xuanwu Yu of Qingshou Monastery in Yanjing (a successor of the Yunmen lineage to Yuan Tong), King Jin Hyeonjong dispatched an imperial messenger carrying a sheet of paper upon which the two characters "Heart-Buddha" (心佛) were written.
The King asked the Master, "What kind of characters are these? The Master replied, "They are not the Heart."

"It is not the Buddha. This pleased the Emperor. On the following day, he bestowed upon him a long-short verse (ci'ou-tz'u) which said: "If one can only achieve purity, what need is there to inquire about the causes and conditions of the myriad dharmas?

In daily life, act without effort; throughout the twelve periods of the day, harbor no further doubt. One must always remain autonomous; recognize that from the beginning there has been no obstruction.
The Buddhas and their minds are one and the same; if the mind relies upon the Buddha, even that is but dust. The Master replied: "There is none."
To treat non-action as something to be cultivated is still bondage; illumination and function are simultaneous—lightning flashing and stars streaming would already be too slow.
To say "neither mind nor Buddha" and yet call it "neither mind" is still a thing. When both person and environment are empty, the myriad phenomena are reflected within a single mirror.
The lay practitioner Zhao Wenru of Huangshan (a successor in the Yunmen lineage to Yuantong) once composed a verse that says: "Delusive thoughts are originally and fundamentally true;
To try to remove them is to raise yet another layer of dust. In speech and thought, movement and stillness—who provides the power? If you look closely, there are not two people."
When Master Ding of Gaoyou State (a successor of Xuanwu in the Yunmen lineage) first visited Xuanwu, the master raised the following case in his room:
A monk asked Xuansha, "What is the pure Dharma-body? Xuansha replied, "It is dripping with pus. At this, the Master attained realization.
Later, when a monk asked, "What does the golden fish that has passed through the net eat? the Master replied, "Dry dung."
Chan Master Yun’an Qing of Jingshan, Hangzhou, was a native of Jianyang. When a monk asked Yangqi, "What is the Buddha?
Yangqi replied, "A three-legged donkey prancing on its hooves. The monk asked, "Is it not this very thing?
Yangqi said, "The Elder of Hunan. He composed a verse on this: Yangqi’s one donkey, Its eyes flashing like lightning, Tramples all people underfoot.
To speak of "three legs" is already too much.
Chan Master Juchuanhai of Zhulin composed a verse on wind bells that says: Copper lips and iron tongues, so sharp and new;

Hung from the corner of the tower, they have not counted the passing springs. The hundreds of thousands of *samādhi* dharmas beyond words— Through the wind, they are spoken to those who truly understand.
Chan Master Xuming Jiaoheng of Daqingshou Temple in Yanjing was the son of the Wang family of Rencheng in Jizhou.
Previously, a monk named Fuan from Ciji Temple in Bianjing had been living in mountain seclusion for many years; one day, he passed away while leaning against a tree in Mangshan Village.
That evening, his mother dreamed that this monk came to seek lodging. Upon waking, she gave birth to the Master. He left home at the age of seven and [at ten]...
Fifth, while traveling abroad, he heard that the Dharma assembly of Master Bao at Puzhao Monastery in Zhengzhou was flourishing, so he went there to pay his respects.

He visited and inquired day and night, yet he did not attain any realization. Later, on another occasion when he was traveling to Suizhou, he suddenly recalled the incident of striking the wooden board while riding on horseback;
at that moment, all conditioned phenomena ceased to arise. As they were about to reach Hetou Pass, his companion warned him, "Brother, this river..."
"It is a ford. The Master dismounted from his horse; grief and joy welled up within him until he shed tears. Upon returning, he told Bao about this.
Bao said, "This stiffened corpse seems as though it wishes to move. He then showed him the kōan of the Sun-Face Buddha and Moon-Face Buddha.

Later, upon hearing the sound of the wooden board, he attained a sudden, direct realization. He presented a verse, saying: "Sun-face, Moon-face— Stars stream, lightning flashes. If you hesitate even further,"
An arrow struck him in the face. "Alas! Bao said, "From this day forward, I can no longer deceive you.
Later, he resided at Puzhao Monastery in Jizhou, and subsequently moved to Qingshou Monastery by imperial decree from Emperor Chang of the Zhenzong reign.

On the tenth day of the seventh month in the autumn of the Ji-mao year of the Xingding era, he took up his brush and wrote a verse. Its final line read: "Eh! One, two, three, four, five, six, seven. He sat upright and passed away.
Chan Master Jianshan Lai of Zhenzhou was asked by a monk, "Where is the stupa of Iron Ox Worthy? The Master pointed his finger at him.
Suddenly, [the monk] attained awakening and presented this verse: "Iron Ox, Iron Ox! Do not seek anything else.
When someone asks me, I simply hold up my finger."
Chan Master Yuantong of Tongxuan Hermitage on Yuxi once composed the *Hundred Questions* to inspire his disciples. The first question asked:
"Why is the bottomless boatman's vessel without leakage and solid? He raised his whisk and said, "I have finished preaching Chan for you;
how do you understand this? He then picked up his staff and said, "Is there anyone who can descend [into the water] from the tip of this staff?"
He uttered a turning phrase. Then he drew a circle and said, "The Buddhas of the three periods and the six generations of patriarchs are all contained within this.
How do you understand this? He then pointed a finger toward the empty space and said, "Tell me, what does this single point clarify?
He then held up one finger and said, "The Venerable Guizong released [his realization] right here."
The Great Radiance turns the Great Dharma Wheel. Do you people see it yet? He said again: "A broken-legged cauldron for one’s livelihood;
a pierced-heart bowl for one’s daily life. Sitting peacefully within the Tongxuan Hermitage, he pays no heed to the affairs before the mountain, which are as numerous as hemp seeds.
Now tell me, who is it that sits so peacefully?
The Great Master Yuanfan Huihong of the Tiele Monastery on Mount Wutai was reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Upon reaching the passage, "When one person gives rise to true awakening and returns to the source, the empty space of the ten directions all vanishes," he suddenly attained great enlightenment.

He then traveled to Hesuo to see Chan Master Wen and presented his realization to him. Wen certified his attainment. At the time of his death, he spoke this verse: "Sixty years of springtime, plus eight more years."
When the floating clouds have vanished, the blue sky is revealed. At the moment of departure, he kicked over Mount Sumeru. Later that night, the moon was perfectly full atop the mountain.
He changed his robes and passed away while seated.
Chan Master Huikong Yuanmo of Jiangshan in Jianning Prefecture was the son of the Su family of Gutian. [Year] Dade Gengzi.
While in meditative absorption, he traveled to Mount Jiangshan, the site of Chan Master Xuanjiang’s practice hall.
An old man came forward to greet him, saying, "I have guarded this mountain for five hundred years. Having finished speaking, he transformed into a black dragon and departed.

Upon awakening, [the Master] said, "I shall return to this mountain," and subsequently went there to establish a hermitage. One day, he told the assembly, "In the past, in the presence of the Buddha, my name was Hui..."

The Bodhisattva Kūṭadanta has now completed his work of transformation and is about to enter parinirvāṇa. For this reason, he preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths to the assembly and further spoke in verse:
"For over forty years I have dwelt amidst the secular dust; Now, at last, I reveal the Honored One within. A night wind arose from the east upon the crag;
It blew the blossoms open, filling the trees with spring. An iron boat has neither rudder nor sail; Yet it is steered into..."
Within the nature-sea of the golden lotus, the final pivot is now revealed. White clouds have never been separate from the vast sky;

mountains, rivers, and the great earth are sought but leave no trace. When empty space is struck through, the ultimate reality is seen. Even if an iron wheel were to spin upon the crown of one’s head.

"The original nature is perfectly luminous and never lost. He spoke again: "In the Western Heaven, the third patriarch, the Venerable Śāṇakavāsin, concealed himself at Mount Gajaśaila and manifested the Dragon’s Vigorous Stride Samādhi.
There he preached the Dharma to subdue the various non-Buddhists, and subsequently transformed into fire and self-immolated.
Now, before this Elephant Trunk Rock, I shall likewise do so. Having finished speaking, clouds and mist rose up on all sides, and thunder...
A heavy rain fell. He transformed himself into fire and immolated himself. His stupa is located to the west of the hermitage.
Chan Master Fuxian Daowu of Puzhao Temple in Zhengzhou was the son of the Guan clan from Lintao and Lanzhou.
While staying overnight at Wanzidian Inn, he heard the neighing of a horse and attained sudden, great enlightenment. Upon returning, he told his mother: "I have picked up something on the road."
“One thing. His mother asked, “What thing? The Master said, “That which has not been seen through since beginningless time. His mother struck him with her palm and said, “What joy is there in that?

He then took leave of his mother to travel to various regions for study. His mother asked, “Where will you go? The Master replied, “Water flowing must reach the sea; a crane emerges from atop the white clouds.
He then went to visit Chan Master Baizhang Haiyun, under whom he received the seal of certification. The second year of the Taiding era...
In the fourth year [of the Tianbao era], Zhuzhu Puzhao appeared. Wearing a white shirt and riding a yellow calf, he wandered through Luoyang while blowing a short flute.
He once said: "If you call me an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), I have previously come from the rank of the sages. If you call me a sage, I am now going back to the rank of the ordinary.
If you say I am neither ordinary nor sage, I have instead found a separate place of practice atop the crown of Vairocana."—Tài.
In the fifth year of the Heping era, he entered nirvana.
In the fifth year of the Jiayou era, Chan Master Pujue Chunpeng of Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou received an imperial decree returning the territory of Jiu Li Song to the Jiqing Monastery.
He ascended the hall and said: "A single plot of vacant land before the mountain; from vast kalpas past, it has had no boundaries."
Having arrived, this morning he has returned once more. He sits firmly cutting off both the head and the tail;
east is so, west is so—there is nothing that is not so, whether traversing north or south. Ultimately, how does one repay his kindness?
Ten *li* of lotus blossoms, nine *li* of pine trees—a single incense stick before the Hall of Direct Pointing.
Chan Master Chang of Xuedou in Mingzhou was a senior disciple of Hengshan. He was not well-versed in literary texts but specialized exclusively in the practice of *dhyāna*.

His peers called him "Chang-Daruma" (Chang the Dharma). The gāthās and verses he composed were characterized by the perfect integration of principle and phenomena, with rhythms that were harmonious and flowing.
His verse on the Iron Ox says: Rolled out from within the furnace of a hundred refinements, Its horns and features are majestic, its body utterly free of dust.
Striking him was of no avail; one could not move him. This time, he truly did not enter the womb. A verse by Haimen says:
"The karmic winds blow up waves like mountains; How many fishermen find it difficult to set foot [therein]? Only by risking life and casting away the body can one force one's way in;

Then one knows that the jade door has never been locked. A verse on the bitter bamboo shoots says: "The purple robes are stripped away until they are white as silver; In the cauldron of a hundred boils..."
Obtaining a body through transmigration—those who have experienced such bitter suffering do not believe this; yet when one casually chews upon it, the flavor is entirely real.
Xichan’s verse says: "Beyond the hundred-foot pole, cease asking for the way; At the solitary peak and highest summit, nourish a leisurely body.
Though the dilapidated hut has no covering, It is difficult to explain one's private affairs to others."
Lady Ding of Haotou in Huangyan, Taizhou, whose name was Juezhen and whose style name was Zhuxin, initially experienced a realization while tending the fields at Weiyu Mountain.
She subsequently left her family home to build a dwelling for herself, and further studied under Guyu of Yongquan.
Jianquan said, "Why are you, a daughter of a good family, running hither and thither? An said, "I have come specifically to pay my respects to the Master.
Jianquan said, "There is no room for you here. An then clapped his hands once and said, "That which you have used for thirty years has been caught out today!
Jianquan then desisted. An then went to Yanshan to visit Wujie at Chunyu Hermitage; as soon as he entered—
Anan asked, "The spring rain is like rich manure; travelers loathe its mud. Baizhang said, "Not so, not so.
As Anan was about to offer further words, he was shouted out by Baizhang. Later in life, Anan established a reception hall beside Mingyin Temple in the district.
One monk, carrying his pack and hat, went straight into his quarters. Anan asked, "What kind of monk are you? The monk replied, "A traveling monk (xingjue seng). Anan suddenly—
Pointing to his feet, he said, "I do not know why my straw sandals have been torn. The monk remained silent.
Huian then took his pack and hat and threw them out, saying, "There is no place here for you to set foot. One day, Chan Master Mingyin Kui came to visit him.
Huian asked, "I have heard it said that you, Elder, fathered a son last night—is this true? Mingyin replied, "Tell me, is it a boy or a girl?"
The nun An said: "A rooster runs off with a lamp-bowl; a turtle bites a fishing rod.
Mingzhou Yuyuan Mian was the cousin of the attendant Kongshe. In his youth he possessed great resolve, but unfortunately died young.
He once composed a verse for a fellow practitioner monk traveling to Mount Tai and Mount Yan, which began: "The bird’s nest blew its cloth-hair; the attendant..."

One who understands this immediately awakens and departs. Although it does not involve verbal explanations, it has already become a public proclamation: "The clouds atop Mount Tiantai; the trees within Mount Yandang.
From here on, you must deliberate well; do not touch upon the taboo that stands head-on. The verse for the end of life says: Birth is fundamentally not birth;
death likewise is not death. Bimā holds up his staff; Juiti points upward with his finger.
The barber Zhang, whose name was De, was a native of Xiashui in Ningbo. For generations his family had served as attendants at the Great Compassion Hall (Daci Gongtang).

While listening to the Dharma with the assembly, he attained a realization. One day, during a heavy snowfall, a novice monk rolled snow into the shape of a Buddha image; the entire assembly then composed verses in praise of it.
Birth also follows; he then recited a verse: "A single flower is held aloft, bringing forth a Tathāgata; Six petals unfold in a circle, their smiling faces revealed.
If one recognizes that the skull is originally water, One does not enter the womb within Māyā’s palace."
The Head Seat Lingjiang Hao of Yongfu relied on Gulin while residing as the First Seat at Yongfu in Raoyang.
During the summer retreat, he held the whisk. A monk asked, "What is it like when taking a step forward? The Seat said, "Bumping into walls and crashing into barriers.

The monk asked, "What is it like when taking a step back? The Seat said, "Falling into pits and dropping into ravines. The monk asked, "What is it like when neither advancing nor retreating? The Seat said:
The "Man Who Dies Standing on Ground" (the master was a successor of Baoning Mao).
The late Senior Seat Sushou’s life-long kōan was profoundly hidden; few recognized it.

During the Tianli era, a monk obtained three of his hand-written verses on "Expressing My Feelings While Dwelling in the Mountains" and went to Zituo to request that Master Zhuyuan provide a commentary.
Zhu Yuan said: "People everywhere regret that he did not appear in this world and did not preach the Dharma.

Now, having read these three verses, it is like the sound of a great golden bell or a large bronze gong; once struck, all other sounds are silenced. Can one say he did not preach the Dharma? The verses say:

'Having finished reading the *Lamp Transmission*, my hair has already turned white. In the pursuit of merit and deeds, how many lakṣas have we still vied for? Rising from my midday nap, the dust [of the world]... "
The table is full; half the eaves are bathed in the slanting sun as flowers fall upon the courtyard. This pointed-roof cottage is not built low; above it are tall forests, and below it lies a pond.
Through the long night, a startling wind sweeps across the yellow leaves, like when the rain comes beneath a thicket of *páng* grass.
The light of this floating world is naturally short; I have inscribed these verses merely to respond to the passing years. Today I stand with my back turned beneath the tall pines.
In the western wind, several crows are scattered about.
At Luohan Temple on Yanshan, the Head Seat Zen Master Zheng was blind in his eyes, yet his realization of the Way was clear and bright.
Every morning, he personally swept the grounds. Someone asked him, "Have you swept this patch of ground clean? The Master held up his broom and showed it to him. Furthermore—
A question was asked: "In the realm of true purity, there has never been a single speck of dust; what is there to sweep? The Master then held up a broom to demonstrate.
He once composed a verse on Mount Jiuniu, which says: "For four or five years they have lived in herds, Coming with spring and departing with autumn, sated by wind and smoke.
The clear stream has water, yet they have never drunk from it; The green fields are unplowed, yet they sleep forevermore. Each and every one of them—look at their heels!"
All touch the ground; every head and every nostril reaches toward heaven. Usually they dwell atop a thousand peaks;

when people from all over the world arrive, how can one lead them? Yuan’an Huì, the Librarian of Jingci Monastery, was a native of Lin’ān. He studied under Huījī at Jingci and resided in the Móngtáng Hall. Because...
There is a verse regarding the practice in the Nirvana Hall which says: "The single path to Nirvana has been completely overturned; The effort required at every turn is not difficult to see.
While washing one's face, one suddenly touches the nose; A mountain can be well hidden within the eye of a needle. Huiji praised it highly.
The Abbot of Kuai-an on Mount Tianmu in Hangzhou was a native of Suzhou. By nature he was quick-witted and proficient in both Buddhist and secular classics.
He was a close friend of Pingshi Di and lived in seclusion among the mountain crags and valleys, avoiding contact with the world.

Only the descendants of the Hong family from the foot of the mountain would come and go to provide him with offerings. One night, a woman of the Hong family dreamed that the Abbot arrived at her house riding in a palanquin.

Upon awakening, he gave birth to a son. The following morning, he climbed the mountain to await him; indeed, the child had already transformed and departed. Consequently, he named the boy Yingkui (應魁) and styled him Shiyuan (士元).
In his youth, he studied the classics and was enrolled in the local school. He married and fathered children. At the age of thirty, one day he suddenly attained a profound realization.
He then abandoned his household and tied up thatched grass at the summit of the Eastern Peak to dwell there, practicing the Way with diligent effort day and night. One day, [the sky became] empty...
When Master Shì was fleeing from bandits, he passed by his hermitage at Mount Jing.
Observing his dignified and elegant demeanor and his composed responses, Shì questioned him regarding his background; thus he learned that he was the reincarnation of Yishan.
He then said to him, "In your previous life, you were an inseparable friend with Elder Píngshí. That elder is now nearly ninety years old, yet his hearing and sight remain keen."
Ming: "Why do you not send word? Have you seen how one dream and two awakenings are as one in both dreaming and waking?
The Master joyfully took up his brush and composed a verse to send him, saying: "I send these words to Old Tiantong Pingshi: A single thought is neither now nor then.
If you wish to hear the midnight bell of Hanshan, The Wujiang River remains as ever, merging with the azure sky."

Chan Master Juezhao Hui of Shouchang in Wenzhou once spent the summer retreat at Jingci Monastery. On the wall of the eastern latrine quarters hung a watercolor image of the Great Being (Avalokiteśvara). The Master prostrated before it morning and evening, praying with great earnestness. One day, he suddenly saw the water from the pure flask gush forth from the wall; his entire body was filled with joy and clarity. From that time on, his wisdom-mirror grew ever more luminous. He once composed a verse, which says: The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the Buddha. The Buddha is not the Buddha, for the Buddha is the wall. If one can see the wall as the Buddha, Then the Buddha is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the Dharma. The Dharma is not the Dharma, for the Dharma is the wall. If one can see the wall as the Dharma, Then the Dharma is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the self. The self is not the self, for the self is the wall. If one can see the wall as the self, Then the self is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is emptiness. Emptiness is not emptiness, for emptiness is the wall. If one can see the wall as emptiness, Then emptiness is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the mind. The mind is not the mind, for the mind is the wall. If one can see the wall as the mind, Then the mind is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the Way. The Way is not the Way, for the Way is the wall. If one can see the wall as the Way, Then the Way is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the realm. The realm is not the realm, for the realm is the wall. If one can see the wall as the realm, Then the realm is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the source. The source is not the source, for the source is the wall. If one can see the wall as the source, Then the source is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the gate. The gate is not the gate, for the gate is the wall. If one can see the wall as the gate, Then the gate is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the root. The root is not the root, for the root is the wall. If one can see the wall as the root, Then the root is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the foundation. The foundation is not the foundation, for the foundation is the wall. If one can see the wall as the foundation, Then the foundation is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the beginning. The beginning is not the beginning, for the beginning is the wall. If one can see the wall as the beginning, Then the beginning is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the end. The end is not the end, for the end is the wall. If one can see the wall as the end, Then the end is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the middle. The middle is not the middle, for the middle is the wall. If one can see the wall as the middle, Then the middle is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the whole. The whole is not the whole, for the whole is the wall. If one can see the wall as the whole, Then the whole is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the part. The part is not the part, for the part is the wall. If one can see the wall as the part, Then the part is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the one. The one is not the one, for the one is the wall. If one can see the wall as the one, Then the one is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the many. The many is not the many, for the many is the wall. If one can see the wall as the many, Then the many is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the absolute. The absolute is not the absolute, for the absolute is the wall. If one can see the wall as the absolute, Then the absolute is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the relative. The relative is not the relative, for the relative is the wall. If one can see the wall as the relative, Then the relative is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the phenomenon. The phenomenon is not the phenomenon, for the phenomenon is the wall. If one can see the wall as the phenomenon, Then the phenomenon is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the noumenon. The noumenon is not the noumenon, for the noumenon is the wall. If one can see the wall as the noumenon, Then the noumenon is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the teacher. The teacher is not the teacher, for the teacher is the wall. If one can see the wall as the teacher, Then the teacher is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the disciple. The disciple is not the disciple, for the disciple is the wall. If one can see the wall as the disciple, Then the disciple is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the master. The master is not the master, for the master is the wall. If one can see the wall as the master, Then the master is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the servant. The servant is not the servant, for the servant is the wall. If one can see the wall as the servant, Then the servant is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the vessel. The vessel is not the vessel, for the vessel is the wall. If one can see the wall as the vessel, Then the vessel is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the content. The content is not the content, for the content is the wall. If one can see the wall as the content, Then the content is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the container. The container is not the container, for the container is the wall. If one can see the wall as the container, Then the container is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the contained. The contained is not the contained, for the contained is the wall. If one can see the wall as the contained, Then the contained is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the light. The light is not the light, for the light is the wall. If one can see the wall as the light, Then the light is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the darkness. The darkness is not the darkness, for the darkness is the wall. If one can see the wall as the darkness, Then the darkness is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the bright. The bright is not the bright, for the bright is the wall. If one can see the wall as the bright, Then the bright is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the dark. The dark is not the dark, for the dark is the wall. If one can see the wall as the dark, Then the dark is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the empty. The full is not the full, for the full is the wall. If one can see the wall as the full, Then the full is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the formless. The formless is not the formless, for the formless is the wall. If one can see the wall as the formless, Then the formless is truly the wall. The wall is not a wall, for the wall is the formed. The formed is not the formed, for the formed is the wall. If one can see the wall as the formed, Then the formed is truly the wall.
"Before one has reached the ground of perfection—square or round—how many times have I leaned upon the railing in solitary grief? Today is the third day, tomorrow the fourth;
snow and frost easily settle upon the heads of men. Hearing this, those with resolve will surely be stirred to action;
for such is the power of sincere devotion to move others.

Chan Master Seng’an Si of Lingyun in Wenzhou was by nature upright and resolute. A native of Ninghai in Taizhou, he was the eldest of four brothers who simultaneously resolved to leave the household life.
He distributed his ancestral inheritance entirely among his relatives and traveled extensively, visiting various masters throughout the land.

Later, he emerged into the world at Lingyun, subsequently moving to Lingyan. On the occasion of the summer retreat, he ascended the hall and spoke on the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* (The Great Perfect Enlightenment).
"Cow horns and horse horns serve as my monastery’s melon basket, gourd basket, and vegetable basket.

[The Master] ascends the hall and brings up the story of Zhaozhou’s "The dog has no Buddha-nature," offering this verse: "The dog has no Buddha-nature; The dog has Buddha-nature. The monkey frets, clutching its head."
When the dog ran, it shook its mouth. In his later years, the Master retired to the front mountain of Lingyun.
In the year Jia-shen of the Zhi Zheng era, Kongshi went with several monks to pay him a visit. At that time, the Master was over ninety years old;

with thick eyebrows and white hair, he stood tall and upright as he stepped out, trailing his sandals. As he walked, he asked, "Where have you come from? Kongshi replied, "From Jiangxin. The Master said, "Deep."
It was several hundred *zhang* [in height]. The man said, "Do not deceive an old monk. The Master said, "Sit for a moment and drink some tea.
As he looked closely at the wall, he saw an inscribed poem denouncing monks; its style was quite similar to that of Hanshan. The verse read:

"The Five Pestilences do not strike his head, yet he has shaved it bald; A yellow cloth covers his body, and thus he is a monk. He understands neither the Buddha-dharma nor the worldly dharma; He eats like a pig..."
The dog was extremely capable; after a brief moment, it took its leave from the empty room, not daring to again encounter its sharp edge.
The layman Huang Min, courtesy name Jinjing, was a native of Yiwu in Wuzhou.

At the beginning of the Tianli era, an imperial decree summoned all monks and literati skilled in calligraphy to assemble at Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou to gild the characters for the Great Canon of the Venerable Scriptures. The layman also [participated].

He anticipated this. Whenever he ate, he insisted on being in the company of the assembly of monks; if special preparations were made for him alone, he was displeased, even to the point of reviling them and departing without eating.
Once, he inscribed a poem on a hanging cliff depicting an ink orchid, which read: "The spring breeze blows equally upon all, yet the slender stalks sway differently."
What can one do when entrusting one’s body to such a lofty height? It is merely following others in creating inverted perceptions.

One must see the moment of letting go at the precipice. Furthermore, he inscribed a eulogy for the portrait of Dongpo: "The Fifth Patriarch Chan Master was a man beyond this world; long ago in Saṃsāra, he severed the causes of birth.
Who would take a hand that sketches empty space to seek his body outside the body from years past? He also inscribed [a eulogy] for the portrait of Huangzhou (Shanggu).

He said: "It would have made the old Huìtáng of that year laugh to death; meeting him, he simply said, 'The fragrance of the osmanthus. When one opens this portrait, his features remain exactly as they were;
how could there ever be any difference in the length of his nostrils? This scholar was renowned in his generation for his literary works and flourished as a preeminent Confucian master of his era.
Because his realization had reached the subtlest depths, he unconsciously accorded with the Sage’s intent. How much more so when he lived among our own kind?"
To be willing to distinguish oneself in this way is indeed commendable.
The verse sent by the Chief Seat Xuan-an of Yuwang Monastery in Mingzhou to the Hermitage Master Wo-yun says: "In the garden of yellow gold, horses gallop in competition;
For a mere inch, many raise their swords in suspicion. The moon shines upon a thousand trees of plum blossoms like snow; One reclines amidst the clouds."
Upon returning from a dream while resting his head on a pillow, the Head Seat Huàn’ān of Mingzhou Tiántóng composed this verse for paying respects at the ancestral pagoda of Yìng’ān:

"A slumbering tiger, its stripes glimpsed through a tube; he took Zhōngfēng as his mountain of refuge. Had he not obtained that single broken sand-bowl, his descendants would have had nothing to beg for."
It would indeed be difficult to remain alive.
The West Hall Abbot Yong of Muzhong at Tiantong in Mingzhou composed a verse on silkworms that says: "When the mulberry trees are exhausted and the field cleared, only then does the heart find rest;

The diligent work of weaving the silk is gathered into a single cocoon. Only when one can enter the burning furnace and the boiling cauldron Is one truly able to benefit others with but a single thread."
Tou Fulong of Yixing, *Upāsaka* [Name Omitted], composed a verse on hearing the rain while sitting in meditation: "Drops dripping from the eaves are perfectly clear;
