On the twenty-eighth day of the twelfth month. He once praised himself, saying: "Nine out of ten strokes do not resemble the likeness; they vex the painter to death. Perhaps this one is close enough."
Quan kept it to offer as a ritual gift. If one says it was the Way, then it remains two things; if one says it was not two things, [he would give] thirty blows.
At the time of his death, he informed the assembly half a month in advance, saying, "I am about to depart for another place. No one could fathom this.
When the appointed day arrived, he manifested a slight illness and passed away while sitting upright, facing west.
Zibo Daguan Zhenke Dashi was the son of Shen of Jigu. By nature, he was bold and fierce;
as a youth, he did not dally in play and took no pleasure in seeing women. At the age of seventeen, he shaved his head and traveled to study under various masters.

Upon hearing the recitation of Zhang Zhuo’s verse—“To sever delusive thoughts is to increase one’s illness; to turn toward True Suchness is likewise a deviation”—he harbored great doubt. One day, during a meal...
Suddenly, he attained great enlightenment and said, "Had I been under the seat of Linji or Deshan, a single slap would have awakened me; why use such talk of 'how' and 'what'?
He traveled north to the capital to study under Bianrong. In the autumn of the Gui Mao year of the Wanli era, the so-called "Seditious Book" (yaoshu) incident suddenly broke out.
The Master met with misfortune. Previously, Emperor Shenzong had personally transcribed the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra; by chance, a drop of perspiration fell and soaked the paper.

Suspecting it should be placed in a new case, he sent a close attendant to consult the Master. The Master presented this verse in response: "A single drop of Imperial sweat is a bridge and raft for ten thousand generations."
The Infinite Dharma-Treasury emitted light from this [place], whereupon the Emperor was greatly delighted and paid close attention to him. Upon reading the memorial, he felt profound pity for him;
yet, as one within the Dharma could not escape it, the decree reached him. The imperial edict merely ordered a thorough investigation.

During the interrogation, the Master remained composed in spirit and countenance, maintaining his principles with great rectitude. With his aged and infirm body, he underwent every form of flogging and torture until—
He did not yield even unto death. On the fifth day of the twelfth month, he was cast into prison. When the judicial authorities sentenced him to death, the Master spoke a verse, saying:
"A single laugh has long had its own cause; Who would have known that the Great Mass of Earth could not tolerate a speck of dust? From this moment on, I shall gather up my mortal feet;
The flower upon the iron stake will bloom without waiting for spring. He spoke further, saying: "If worldly laws are such as this, what is the use of remaining here for long? Thereupon—
After finishing his bath, he instructed his attendant, saying, "I am going now. Please convey my thanks to all the Dharma protectors in Jiangnan.
He then spoke this verse: "When affairs arise, one finally beholds the heroic bone; Master Da and Mr. Wu—how could this not be a karmic affinity? I shall return westward, while you go north;
Our conversations over many lifetimes will be even more clear and resonant. Having finished speaking, he sat upright and passed away. (His writings include the *Zibai ji*.)
Chan Master Wunian Shendao of Huangbo in Ruizhou was the son of the Xiong family of Macheng in Huangzhou.
Once, while traveling to Mount Dang, an elderly monk said to him, "A single grain of rice from the ten directions is as heavy as Mount Sumeru;

if you do not realize the Way, you shall return wearing fur and horns. The Master was struck with awe. He further heard a monk cite a question asked of Daixiu: "How is it?"... [The Master] was startled.

"This is the meaning of coming from the West. Xiu replied, "Yellow gourd, eggplant. The Master was greatly perplexed; he subsequently traveled to Mount Wutai and Mount Funiu, visiting and questioning various spiritual teachers everywhere.
One night, hearing the sounds of laughter and weeping mingling together, he attained realization.

On another day, he accidentally struck his head with the lid of a cupboard, and sweat poured down his entire body. Clapping his hands, he laughed and said, "The whole earth is this very state of non-thought—what is there to doubt?"
One day, while at Longhu with the layman Zhuo Wujie, we went to Sima Mountain. A lecturer happened to arrive there, and the layman asked him: "The nature is fundamentally pure;
how did the mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise? After the lecturer had finished his exposition according to the text, the layman continued: [the rest of the dialogue follows].
The layman turned and said to the Master, "Try to say something. As the Master was about to open his mouth, the layman gave him a push on the knee and said, "What about this?
The Master suddenly attained great enlightenment. He spoke a verse: "For over forty years I did not cease my efforts; I sought and sought until the traces vanished.
Now, having sought to the point of no reliance, I finally regret the efforts I wrongly applied before. [He] stayed.
Later, a monk asked, "Does the Way have fruit, or does it have no fruit? The Master said, "To say it has fruit or to say it has no fruit—both are equally slander.

The monk asked, "How then can one attain it? The Master said, "Seeking nothing, one attains it. The monk asked, "What is the essence of the Way? The Master said, "My mouth is full; I cannot speak of it.
The monk asked, "What is it like when the four elements disperse? The Master raised his fist and said, "This!"
"It does not belong to the four great elements. [The student] asked, "The ancients said, 'Expel the throat, lips, and mouth, and bring forth a single phrase.
How would you speak this one phrase? The Master said, "I do not expel my throat, lips, and mouth; you, for your part, try and speak a phrase."
The monk had no reply. The Master said, "Your mouth has been stuffed shut by sounds. He asked, "Is it true that seeing one's nature is to become a Buddha?
The Master said, "Yes. [The monk] asked, "Since nature is formless, how can it be seen? The Master said, "Nature is indeed possessed of form; it is simply that you do not see it.
[The monk] said, "I beg the Master to point it out so that I may see it. The Master said, "I say that you do not see it. He asked, "If..."
"How does one transcend birth and death? The Master called to the assembly; the monks responded. The Master said, "Come forth from here.
A monk asked, "I do not understand the words spoken by the Master. The Master said, "If you were to understand them, what would that avail?

He further wrote in a letter to a friend: "Sitting motionless in the mountains, I hear no news of the world. To study the Way, one must seize the sharp intensity of the initial resolve. Thus he spoke.
One must seek a clear understanding; only then, when encountering circumstances and conditions in daily life, can one achieve liberation.
Otherwise, as days and months pass, one will gradually forget one's diligent practice and remain mired in worldly sentiments.

Nowadays, those who study the Way merely seek verbal cleverness and intellectual sharpness, forgetting their own original nature (the *mūla-prakṛti*). They wait until illness strikes their very person before they realize it is time to act.
In times of turmoil and confusion, not even a single word is of any use. Furthermore, do not resent yourself for failing to apply your mind or for errors in your resolve;
instead, you might say that even the ancient sages and Buddhas were no different. This is to slander the True Dharma Wheel of the Tathāgata.
You have not yet awakened from your dream—do not misinterpret this! A single word or half-sentence from the ancient sages is like a hair-cutting sword or tempered steel.

Rice nailed down; soup of wooden splinters; a drum smeared with lethal poison. There is no place for you to listen, no place for you to take a bite, no place for you to apply your intent, and no place for you to draw near.
Meeting on a narrow path, you blink and miss it. Reaching this point, emotions wither and thoughts cease;
reflection is exhausted and the spirit is spent. Cold and heat are both forgotten, sleep and food are abandoned. It is beyond all grasp.

In that moment, he suddenly attained a profound awakening. The mind that had been running after external objects was instantly stilled. He experienced a joy and clarity that surpassed anything in his life.
No longer did he pursue sounds or forms; all intellectual knowledge and views completely vanished. Distinctions between right and wrong left no trace.

Having reached this state, all cleverness, understanding, and the duality of subject and object—along with supernormal powers—were surrendered like casting them away into the hands of others. Day and night he remained as if dull-witted or mute, with a heart that was empty within its own belly.

The people of the world cannot recognize it; ghosts and spirits cannot see it. Where would Old Yan have eyes to look? This is precisely true mastery. To believe without practicing increases one's deluded self-view;
to speak as if enlightened, yet remain confused when confronted with objects, is futile. To practice asceticism without belief merely increases the merit of ignorance.
When awakening and practice are both complete, madness vanishes and idle talk ceases. In the narrow alley, with a single bamboo bowl and a ladle of water, there is [true contentment].
Regarding the attainment and loss [of realization]: Chan Master Fāngtàn Yífēng of Bǎimǎ Temple in Kuízhōu was the son of the Luó family of Dázhōu.

He attended upon Wúshān Hóngzǔ (Yún'ān) Wángshī of Jīnfó Mountain and was instructed to contemplate: "What is the pivot that ghosts and spirits cannot perceive? After three years, he attained a profound realization.

He left the gorges to visit various spiritual teachers at length. He then built a thatched hut by the Double Stream (Shuangxi). One day while cooking his midday meal, he heard a sound from within the steamer; suddenly, he attained great enlightenment.
He composed a verse containing the lines, "The white clouds and blue peaks all nod their heads together. He frequently resided in mountain hermitages throughout Zhejiang.
In his youth, Master Yin of Qingping Zhenji in Hangzhou once relied upon him.
One day, the Master raised the koan of Qingfeng’s “A young boy comes seeking fire” and interrogated him, saying: "Qingfeng spoke thus, and Fayan also spoke thus;
why is it that one attained enlightenment while the other did not? Yin replied: "Initially, because he sought to settle his mind through conscious cognition, he did not attain enlightenment."

Later, he directly took up the task and was thus able to achieve great enlightenment. The Master suddenly raised his fist, struck the desk once, and said in a stern voice, "If that is so, have you now attained great enlightenment?
Yinyuan hesitated; the Master then scolded him severely and drove him out. Yinyuan was left with sweat pouring down his back.
From this point on, he applied himself to his studies with indignant resolve. In the *Renchen* year of the Wanli era, the Master returned to Baima. A monk...

A questioner asked, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey? The Master replied, "Fire burns at both ends; there is smoke at only one. The Master constantly held a small hand-drum (*tiao*) in his hand;
on one side of the drum was written the character "Chū" (矗), and on the other side, the character "Bēn" (犇). Whenever he responded to an occasion, he would frequently raise and shake it.
He entered nirvana and was interred at Longshen Mountain.
Chan Master Yang’an Xin of Ehu in Guangxinfu was the son of the Zhu family from Shangrao in the prefecture.

Once, while visiting relatives, he encountered a practitioner discussing the meaning of the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*). At these words, the Master thoroughly realized the great principle that all things and the self are equal.
He went to Taitong in Luoyang to shave his head, then returned south to Jiaoshan to observe the winter retreat. There, he heard the sound of a boat being pushed through the river.
Having attained realization, he composed a verse, saying: "The night is still and the river is vast; the sound of the boat being pushed back and forth—know not where it goes."
The burden was light on one side. He went to visit Huashan, where he heard the master’s “one piece of livelihood not included in the six” koan and harbored doubts.
After seven days of intense exertion, his body and mind were suddenly liberated. He then returned to his hometown and resided at Lingshan.

He once painted a great circle on the wall and said: "In writing the interior, do not let it become black; in writing the exterior, do not let it be damaged by white. If someone [should enter] toward this circle...
"Those who can provide a commentary on the inner circle and the outer periphery may be permitted to study the Way without doubt; otherwise, it is all merely a matter of regret.
Later, he moved to Ehu, where for ten years he did not establish a formal seat. When Yuanwu came to visit, they reached mutual accord through the "Mu" (No) koan of Zhaozhou.
Yuanwu requested to occupy the position, and [the Master] presented him with a verse, saying: "Ten years at Ehu, the position remained vacant; one day, by karmic conditions..."
Why establish [this] at such a young age? Two eyebrows and eight strands of hair—know that Buddhas and Patriarchs allow no passage before them.

Furthermore, he once placed it within the "Room of the Gateless Lock" to test those who would come after. He wrote a verse: "The lock left behind from ancient times, Rely on your wisdom-key to open it.
If you lack the method to open the lock, Even if we meet, there is no need to enter. The final day of the second month, the Dingmao year of the Wanli era.
He ascended the hall to preach the Dharma, prepared a vegetarian feast to bid farewell, and further presented this verse:
Within eighty-odd years of illusory dreams, An iron ox has plowed through the great void. As I depart, I entrust you with this one phrase: At midnight, the golden sun glows with crimson light.
He passed away while sitting upright.
The Great Master Hanshan Deqing of Caoxi in Shaoyou was the son of the Cai family of Quanpiao. In his youth, he studied the Confucian classics.
At the age of twelve, he paid homage to Master Lin at Ba’en Temple and took him as his teacher. At nineteen, he shaved his head and received the full precepts, becoming a friend to Miaofeng.
While casually reading the *Zhao Lun*, I came upon the passage concerning the Brahmin who returned home with white hair after leaving the household life.
A neighbor saw him and said, "Is that still the same man from before? The Brahmin replied, "I am the same man as before, yet I am not the man of before.
Suddenly, I had an awakening and said: "Only today do I know that my nostrils point downward. Miaofeng asked, "What have you attained? The Master replied, "Last night, two lumps of clay..."
The ox fought and entered the water; to this day, there has been no further news. Feng laughed and said, "I am glad you have the capital for living on the mountain.
He then went to the capital city of Yan to visit Master Xiaoyan. Xiaoyan asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From the South.
Xiaoyan asked, "Do you remember the path by which you came? The Master replied, "Once passed, it is finished. Xiaoyan said, "You have indeed arrived at the place of division."
Ming bowed to the Master. Later, he was falsely accused by a Daoist priest (huángguān) for privately founding a temple and was sentenced to military exile in Leizhou.
Upon arriving in Shaoyang, he paid homage to the Patriarch, offering this verse: "The single drop from Caoxi is the source of the numinous spring;

It flows into the vast ocean, its waves lapping against the heavens. How many fish and dragons vie to undergo transformation? Yet the single stream at the source remains cool and clear. Eleven years passed.

In the year of the Rabbit (1279), he retired to Caoxi. It was not until nine years later that he resumed his monastic robes and returned to Mount Kuanglu, where he built a hermitage on Wuru Peak with the intention of living out his final years in seclusion.
After several years, he was again requested to return to Caoxi. Not long after, he suddenly addressed the assembly, saying:

"My karmic conditions no longer accord with the times; where shall my transformation be entrusted? My mission for this one period is complete; I am about to depart. He then sought a bath, changed his robes, and sat upright.
He passed away while seated. His age was seventy-eight; his years since ordination were fifty-nine. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa on Tianzi Ridge.
The Master once visited Deshan and, before paying homage at the ancestral stupa, composed this verse: "Leisurely stretching out the alms-bowl in front of the hall, the lion playfully tames its cubs."
When meeting face-to-face, it is difficult to turn back; when lowering the head in silence, one has not yet clarified the final phrase, which instead causes doubt to persist to this day.
I ask: regarding the events of three years past, how was it that you came to know them so early? Living in the Mountains: Throughout my life, my traces have wandered east and west;
now in my old age, how could I choose where to perch among the trees? Though my backbone may be as hard as iron, alas, my leg bones are as soft as mud.
Leisurely gazing from a precipitous ravine as clouds arise; sitting facing a solitary peak, listening to the birds' cries. There is no need to further grasp at phrases beyond words;
the sounds and forms before one's eyes are the total presentation.
